explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a ten percent probability of endometrial cancer overall and is investigated in every case, with transvaginal ultrasound as the first line test because endometrial thickness performs well as a triage measure. A thickness at or below 4 mm in a woman not taking hormone therapy has a high negative predictive value and permits conservative management of a single episode, with atrophy the usual explanation. That reassurance does not extend to recurrent or persistent bleeding, for two reasons: the non endometrioid carcinomas, which account for a minority of cases but a disproportionate share of deaths, arise on atrophic endometrium without thickening it, and focal lesions can be missed by both ultrasound and blind biopsy. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy therefore becomes the investigation of choice once bleeding recurs, and women on tamoxifen are assessed hysteroscopically from the outset because the drug produces subendothelial changes that make thickness measurement unreliable.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a ten percent risk of endometrial cancer
A thickness of 4 mm or less permits conservative management of one episode only
Recurrent bleeding requires hysteroscopy regardless of thickness
Serous and clear cell cancers arise on atrophic, non thickened endometrium
Blind sampling misses focal lesions and often yields insufficient tissue when thin
explanation.pearls: Endometrial fluid within the cavity of a postmenopausal woman with bleeding should never be measured as part of the endometrial thickness, and its presence alongside bleeding is itself an indication for hysteroscopic assessment rather than a reassuring finding.

subtopic_detail: Woman with well controlled generalised seizures on an established anticonvulsant attending to plan a first pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28 year old woman who tells you she and her partner want to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that have been fully controlled for four years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having had breakthrough seizures on two previous agents.

She drives to work, has not had a seizure since starting this medication, and is terrified of losing her licence. She takes no other medication and no supplements.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, neurological examination unremarkable, no tremor, no gum hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to a neurologist to plan a change of agent before she conceives
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the anticonvulsants, with major congenital malformation in around ten percent and a substantial dose dependent reduction in childhood cognitive outcome, and both risks operate in the first trimester before most pregnancies are recognised. Any change must be planned and supervised by a neurologist before conception, with cross titration to an agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam and confirmation of continued seizure control, because an abrupt switch risks status epilepticus. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue the current agent at the lowest effective dose and add high dose folic acid
options.rationale: High dose folic acid is recommended for all women on anticonvulsants planning pregnancy and will form part of her care. Folate supplementation does not offset the malformation and neurodevelopmental risks specific to valproate, so continuing the drug on that basis is a common and serious misconception. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the anticonvulsant now given four years of seizure freedom and review in a month
options.rationale: Withdrawal after a prolonged seizure free period is sometimes considered, but only by a neurologist after assessment of seizure type, electroencephalogram and relapse risk, and never abruptly. Unplanned withdrawal risks a seizure, with the consequences of loss of licence, injury and, if she conceives, maternal and fetal hypoxia. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Advise her to conceive on the current agent and change it as soon as she is pregnant
options.rationale: Switching after a positive pregnancy test is too late, because neural tube closure is complete by about 28 days after conception and the highest risk exposure has already occurred. It also introduces a change of anticonvulsant at a time when seizure control matters most. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Reduce the current agent to half the dose now and start folic acid one month before conception
options.rationale: Teratogenic risk with valproate is dose dependent, so reducing the dose does lower it, and that approach is used when no alternative controls the seizures. Halving the dose without specialist supervision risks breakthrough seizures, and the residual risk at any valproate dose remains higher than with the alternative agents. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Around half of pregnancies in Australia are unplanned, so anticonvulsant choice in a woman of reproductive age is made with pregnancy in mind from the outset rather than at the point of conception. Valproate is the outlier among anticonvulsants, with major congenital malformations including neural tube, cardiac, facial and limb defects in roughly one in ten exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental impairment in a substantially larger proportion, both effects rising with dose. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the most reassuring data and are the usual alternatives, although lamotrigine levels fall markedly during pregnancy because of increased glucuronidation and require monitoring with dose adjustment. Once pregnant, women continue high dose folic acid, are managed jointly by obstetric and neurology services, and receive counselling that uncontrolled generalised seizures carry real risks to mother and fetus including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, so stopping treatment is not a safe alternative.
key_points: Valproate carries the highest malformation and neurodevelopmental risk of the anticonvulsants
Both risks are dose dependent and operate in the first trimester
Any change of agent is planned before conception and supervised by a neurologist
High dose folic acid is recommended but does not offset valproate specific risk
Uncontrolled generalised seizures carry their own maternal and fetal risks
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine concentrations can fall by more than half during pregnancy because oestrogen induces its glucuronidation, so levels are monitored through pregnancy and the dose is reduced again promptly after birth to avoid postpartum toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Older woman with urgency and nocturia unimproved by bladder training who is already taking a cholinesterase inhibitor for memory problems
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 78 year old woman with eighteen months of a sudden desperate need to pass urine, eight times by day and three times overnight, with occasional leakage on the way to the toilet. She has completed three months of supervised bladder training and fluid modification with a continence nurse and her diary shows no improvement.

She has no leakage with coughing or lifting. She takes donepezil for mild cognitive impairment, amlodipine, and atorvastatin, and lives alone with support from a daughter who has noticed she is more forgetful in the past year.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Vulval and vaginal epithelium pale and thin, no prolapse beyond the hymen, no pelvic mass, cough stress test negative with a comfortably full bladder, post void residual 35 mL on bladder scan, gait steady with a timed up and go of 11 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine culture no growth, estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), bladder diary confirms urgency with small volume voids and no nocturnal polyuria

lead_in: Which treatment would you add?

options.text: Oxybutynin taken regularly with the dose titrated to symptom response
options.rationale: Oxybutynin is effective for urgency but is the most lipophilic of the antimuscarinics and crosses the blood brain barrier readily, and it directly opposes the cholinergic enhancement her donepezil is intended to provide. Anticholinergic exposure in older adults is associated with confusion, falls and accelerated cognitive decline. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Mirabegron taken regularly with blood pressure monitored after starting
options.rationale: A beta 3 adrenoceptor agonist relaxes the detrusor during filling without any antimuscarinic action, so it avoids both the cognitive risk of anticholinergic burden in an older woman with cognitive impairment and the pharmacological opposition to her cholinesterase inhibitor. It can raise blood pressure, so this is checked after initiation and the drug avoided in severe uncontrolled hypertension. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Desmopressin taken at night with sodium checked in the first week of treatment
options.rationale: Desmopressin is used for nocturnal polyuria, meaning a disproportionate share of the daily urine volume produced overnight, which her bladder diary specifically excludes. It carries a significant risk of hyponatraemia in older adults and is generally avoided above the age of 65. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection at a urogynaecology clinic
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is an effective third line treatment for refractory overactive bladder and would be considered later in her pathway. It requires the ability to perform clean intermittent self catheterisation should retention follow, which is a substantial demand on a woman living alone with cognitive impairment, and oral treatment has not yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Refer for a midurethral sling procedure after urodynamic assessment of her bladder
options.rationale: Continence surgery of this kind treats stress incontinence caused by urethral hypermobility, which is excluded here by the absence of leakage on coughing or lifting and a negative cough stress test. Operating for urgency symptoms does not help and may worsen them. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom complex of urgency with frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology, and it is distinguished from stress incontinence by the history and the cough stress test. First line management is conservative, combining bladder training, fluid and caffeine modification, weight loss and pelvic floor work, and a bladder diary is essential both to characterise the pattern and to exclude nocturnal polyuria. When drug treatment is added, the choice in older adults is dominated by anticholinergic burden, which is cumulatively associated with confusion, falls, constipation and an increased incidence of dementia, and is pharmacologically self defeating in anyone taking a cholinesterase inhibitor. Beta 3 agonists provide comparable efficacy without that burden, with hypertension the main consideration, and refractory symptoms proceed to intradetrusor botulinum toxin, posterior tibial nerve stimulation or sacral neuromodulation.
key_points: A bladder diary distinguishes overactive bladder from nocturnal polyuria
Conservative measures precede any drug treatment
Anticholinergic burden in older adults causes confusion, falls and cognitive decline
Antimuscarinics directly oppose cholinesterase inhibitors
Beta 3 agonists avoid that burden but can raise blood pressure
explanation.pearls: Adding an antimuscarinic to a cholinesterase inhibitor is a recognised prescribing cascade in which each drug blunts the other, and the combination is associated with faster functional decline than either agent alone.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Overactive bladder

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic anterior vaginal wall descent to the hymen in an 82 year old declined for anaesthesia because of severe respiratory disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing an 82 year old woman who describes a dragging feeling and a bulge she can feel at the entrance to the vagina by the end of each day. It is worse after she has been gardening and eases when she lies down.

She has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen and was assessed by the anaesthetic clinic last month as unsuitable for a general or regional anaesthetic. She has completed three months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist without improvement. She is sexually inactive, has had no bleeding, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago. Examination shows anterior wall descent reaching the hymen on straining with well oestrogenised tissue.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descending to the level of the hymen on Valsalva, cervix descending to 2 cm above the hymen, no posterior compartment defect, vaginal epithelium moist and rugated with no ulceration, no adnexal mass, post void residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit a ring pessary in the clinic and review her in the clinic within six weeks
options.rationale: A mechanical support inserted in the outpatient setting relieves the symptoms of descent without an anaesthetic, which is the decisive consideration when she has already been declared unfit for theatre, and a supported first review checks for erosion and retention. Conservative therapy has already been given an adequate trial. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair on the next elective list
options.rationale: Reconstructive surgery is the definitive option for descent that fails conservative management, and it is exactly what the anaesthetic assessment has excluded for this woman. Offering it ignores the risk that ended the surgical pathway last month. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Prescribe a further six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training now
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training is first line for mild descent and for symptoms without a visible bulge, but a documented three month supervised program without benefit has already tested that option. Repeating a failed intervention delays symptom relief without changing the anatomy. (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse)
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves tissue quality and is often used alongside a pessary, but her epithelium is already moist and rugated so there is no atrophy to reverse. It does not support a descended anterior wall by itself. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

options.text: Refer for colpocleisis under local infiltration on the next available theatre list
options.rationale: Obliterative surgery is a genuine option for an older woman who is not sexually active and is a poor candidate for reconstruction, so the near pair question is whether any theatre procedure should precede a clinic fitted device. It still requires an anaesthetic and is considered only after a pessary trial fails. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ descent is present in about half of parous women on examination but only a minority have symptoms, and the symptom that correlates best with the anatomy is the sensation of a bulge. Management runs from lifestyle measures and supervised pelvic floor training for mild symptoms, through vaginal pessaries, to reconstructive or obliterative surgery. A pessary is not merely a holding measure for those awaiting theatre, since a substantial proportion of women continue with one indefinitely by preference, and it is the option of choice for anyone who is unfit for anaesthesia, still planning a pregnancy, or simply declines surgery. Ongoing review is part of the treatment because a neglected device erodes into the vaginal wall.
key_points: The sensation of a bulge is the symptom that tracks the anatomy
Supervised pelvic floor training is first line for mild symptomatic descent
A pessary is definitive therapy in its own right, not only a bridge to surgery
Anaesthetic unfitness moves a pessary ahead of all surgical options
Regular review prevents vaginal erosion and unrecognised retention
explanation.pearls: A woman fitted with a ring pessary should be reviewed within six weeks and then every six months, and topical vaginal oestrogen is usually added because it reduces the rate of erosion in atrophic tissue that is in continuous contact with silicone.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Pelvic organ prolapse

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged unscheduled bleeding five months after insertion of a progestogen implant in a woman who wants to keep the device
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who had a contraceptive implant placed in her upper arm five months ago. She has bled on more days than not since, with episodes lasting eight to ten days, and she has had enough of it but says she does not want to go back to remembering a daily tablet.

She has no pain, no postcoital bleeding and no discharge, and she is in a new relationship since the implant was inserted. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and a self collected swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is negative. Speculum and bimanual examination are normal and the implant is palpable in the correct plane.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Implant palpable subdermally in the medial upper left arm, cervix healthy with no contact bleeding, uterus anteverted and normal size, adnexae non-tender with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, self collected vaginal swab negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-155), ferritin 38 micrograms per litre (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bleeding?

options.text: Remove the implant today and arrange insertion of a hormonal intrauterine device
options.rationale: Switching to an intrauterine system is a reasonable eventual step if medical treatment fails, but removing the device at the first review discards a highly effective method before any treatment has been tried. She has also asked to keep long acting contraception rather than change it now. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Reassure her that the pattern will settle and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Bleeding patterns established by three months predict the pattern for the remaining life of the device, so waiting a further three months is unlikely to change anything. Unscheduled bleeding is the commonest reason for early removal, and untreated it usually ends the method. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Offer a three month course of a combined oral contraceptive alongside the implant
options.rationale: Once pregnancy, infection and a cervical cause have been excluded, a three month course of combined oestrogen and progestogen taken alongside the device is the best supported treatment for troublesome unscheduled bleeding and settles it in most women while the implant stays in place. It directly meets her wish to keep long acting cover. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid to be taken continuously for the next three months
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic treatment reduces the volume of heavy scheduled menstrual loss, and the near pair here is that her problem is the frequency and duration of bleeding rather than the volume. It is also not used continuously for months at a time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and an endometrial biopsy before any other treatment
options.rationale: Structural assessment and sampling belong to women over 45, those with risk factors for endometrial pathology, or those whose bleeding persists after treatment. In a 24 year old with a normal examination and negative swabs the yield is effectively nil. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

explanation.summary: About one in five women using a progestogen implant has frequent or prolonged unscheduled bleeding, and it is by far the commonest reason the device is removed early. The assessment is short and specific: exclude pregnancy, test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, check that cervical screening is up to date, and examine the cervix, because a new relationship or a cervical lesion changes the answer entirely. When that work up is clear, the bleeding reflects a thin unstable endometrium under continuous progestogen rather than any pathology. A three month course of combined hormonal treatment is the best supported medical option, with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory as an alternative, and women should be told before insertion that the pattern is unpredictable so that it is not a surprise.
key_points: Unscheduled bleeding is the leading reason for early implant removal
Exclude pregnancy, chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and a cervical cause first
The pattern at three months predicts the pattern for the device's life
A three month combined hormonal course is the best supported treatment
Structural imaging is reserved for older women or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Counselling before insertion that about one in five women will bleed unpredictably and one in five will have no bleeding at all substantially reduces early removal rates, because most discontinuation is driven by surprise rather than by the volume of blood lost.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old requesting the three monthly progestogen injection whose mother has raised concerns about bone strength
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16 year old who has come in with her mother asking for the contraceptive injection because her friend uses it and she does not want anything she has to think about. She has regular periods, no medical problems and takes no medication.

Her mother has read that the injection weakens bones and wants to know whether her daughter should have a bone density scan first. She eats normally, plays netball twice a week and has never had a fracture. She is competent to consent and has discussed the decision with you alone as well as with her mother present. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, no features of an eating disorder, secondary sexual characteristics fully developed, general examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice and management?

options.text: Decline the injection because of her age and offer the combined pill as an alternative
options.rationale: Adolescence is not a contraindication to this method in Australian practice, and refusing the method she will actually use in favour of a daily tablet predictably raises her risk of an unintended pregnancy. The combined pill remains a reasonable option if she chooses it, not a substitute for her decision. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Arrange a dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan before the first injection is given
options.rationale: Bone densitometry is not recommended before or during use of this method because the reference ranges are not validated in adolescents and the result would not change management in a healthy young woman. It medicalises a reversible effect and delays contraception. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give the injection now and plan to stop the method after two years of continuous use
options.rationale: A fixed two year ceiling was once advised but current Australian guidance is to review the choice periodically rather than to impose a stopping date, since density recovers after discontinuation. A scheduled stop can leave a young woman without effective cover for no measured benefit. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Give the injection now, with advice on calcium, vitamin D and weight bearing exercise
options.rationale: Age alone does not restrict this method, and the small reversible fall in bone mineral density recovers after the injections stop, so the balance in an adolescent at risk of an unintended pregnancy favours giving it with bone healthy advice. Efficacy and her preference for a method she does not have to remember both support proceeding. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Give the injection now and add a daily oestrogen tablet to protect her bone density
options.rationale: Adding oestrogen for bone protection alone is not supported and exposes her to thrombotic risk for no proven gain. The near pair is that combined hormonal treatment is used for bleeding problems on progestogen only methods, which is a different indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

explanation.summary: The three monthly injectable progestogen suppresses ovulation and produces a modest fall in bone mineral density that is greatest in the first two years of use, is largest in adolescents who are still accruing peak bone mass, and reverses after the method is stopped. No study has shown an increase in fracture risk attributable to the method, so Australian guidance does not restrict it by age and does not impose a maximum duration. The practical response to a family's concern is accurate information plus attention to the things that genuinely build bone, namely adequate calcium and vitamin D, weight bearing exercise and avoidance of smoking. Return of fertility is delayed by a median of several months after the last injection, which is a more common practical issue than bone density.
key_points: Bone density falls modestly and recovers after the method is stopped
No increase in fracture risk has been demonstrated for this method
Age under 18 is not a contraindication in Australian practice
Densitometry before or during use is not recommended
Return of fertility is delayed by a median of several months
explanation.pearls: Fertility returns a median of nine months after the last injection, so a woman who may want to conceive within a year should be steered towards a method with immediate reversibility such as an implant or an intrauterine device.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Painful glazed erosions at the vestibule with a lacy white border and oral changes in a woman failing topical steroid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman with eighteen months of vulval soreness and burning that makes intercourse impossible. She describes rawness rather than itch and says the skin feels like it is peeling.

Her general practitioner has treated her for thrush three times and then prescribed a potent topical corticosteroid ointment for eight weeks, which helped a little but never cleared it. She has also had sore gums for the past year and her dentist has commented on white streaks inside her cheeks. She has hypothyroidism on thyroxine. Examination shows glazed red erosions at the vestibule with a fine white lacy margin, loss of the labia minora, and narrowing of the introitus.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions around the vestibule with a reticulate white border, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing admitting one finger with discomfort, no thickened white plaques over the perianal skin, buccal mucosa with bilateral white lacy striae, vaginal walls erythematous with a serous discharge
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab negative for candida and bacterial vaginosis, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take a vulval biopsy from the centre of an erosion and stop all topical treatment
options.rationale: A biopsy through the floor of an erosion yields only ulcer slough without the epidermal changes the pathologist needs. Stopping treatment while waiting also allows further scarring of an introitus that is already narrowed. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus

options.text: Prescribe a further course of oral fluconazole and repeat the vaginal swab afterwards
options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis causes itch with curdy discharge and responds to antifungals, and she has already failed three courses with a negative swab. Continuing to treat an excluded infection is the pattern that delays this diagnosis by years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Genitourinary changes after menopause cause dryness and dyspareunia with pale thin tissue, not erosions with a lacy border, and they do not affect the mouth. Oestrogen is a useful adjunct but it will not heal an inflammatory dermatosis. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

options.text: Refer for examination under anaesthesia with surgical division of the narrowed introitus
options.rationale: Surgery to a vulva with active erosive inflammation reliably provokes further scarring and new lesions at the incision, and it is reserved for stable disease that has been medically controlled. The near pair is that adhesiolysis can be appropriate once the dermatosis is quiescent. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Take a vulval biopsy from the edge of an erosion and continue ultrapotent steroid
options.rationale: Erosive disease with a reticulate white border, oral involvement and architectural loss needs histological confirmation because it differs from the commoner white sclerotic condition in treatment, in vaginal involvement and in the need for dilator use. Sampling the edge rather than the base of an erosion gives interpretable tissue while treatment continues. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Chronic vulval symptoms are frequently treated as candidiasis for years before the underlying dermatosis is recognised, and the clue is the absence of itch with a burning raw quality and failure of repeated antifungal courses. Erosive disease of the vulva and vagina is distinguished from the sclerotic white condition by glazed erosions with a lacy reticulate margin, by involvement of the vagina producing a discharge and adhesions, and by mucosal disease elsewhere, especially in the mouth. Histology is worth obtaining because the two conditions differ in management and because both carry a risk of squamous carcinoma at the site. Treatment combines ultrapotent topical corticosteroid to the vulva, intravaginal corticosteroid where the vagina is involved, dilators to preserve the introitus, and specialist input for refractory disease.
key_points: Burning and rawness rather than itch suggests erosive disease
A reticulate white margin and oral striae point away from the sclerotic form
Vaginal involvement with adhesions occurs in the erosive form only
Biopsy the edge of an erosion, never the base
Both vulval dermatoses carry a long term risk of squamous carcinoma
explanation.pearls: The combination of erosive vulval, vaginal and gingival disease defines the vulvovaginal gingival syndrome, and these women need intravaginal corticosteroid plus regular dilator use because vaginal adhesions can obliterate the upper vagina within months of uncontrolled inflammation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval lichen planus

subtopic_detail: Monthly lower abdominal pain for six months with no menarche and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus in a fully developed adolescent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 14 year old girl referred by her general practitioner with six months of lower abdominal pain that comes for three or four days each month and then goes completely. She has never had a period.

Her breasts developed at 11 and she has full pubic and axillary hair. She has grown 9 cm in the last two years. Over the last fortnight she has also been going to the toilet more often and feeling that she cannot empty her bladder properly. Abdominal examination finds a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus. Inspection of the introitus shows a tense bluish membrane that bulges when she strains.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass palpable to 4 cm below the umbilicus, tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus on Valsalva with no visible vaginal opening, normal external genitalia otherwise, no inguinal masses
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, post void bladder scan 180 mL, pelvic ultrasound showing a distended vagina filled with echogenic fluid and a normal uterus and both ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Arrange needle aspiration of the collection in the clinic under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: Aspiration decompresses the collection temporarily but leaves the obstruction in place so it refills, and puncturing the membrane introduces organisms into retained blood, risking pyocolpos. Definitive drainage requires an adequate opening. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive continuously to suppress further bleeding now
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression stops further accumulation and is used as a holding measure when surgery must be delayed, but it does nothing for the litre of blood already trapped or for the urinary retention it is causing. The near pair is that suppression treats the inflow while surgery treats the obstruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: Arrange surgical incision and drainage of the obstructed outflow tract in theatre
options.rationale: Cyclical pain with normal secondary sexual development, a distended vagina on imaging and a bulging membrane identifies an obstructed outflow tract, and the treatment is a formal incision of the membrane under anaesthesia with drainage of the retained blood. Doing it in theatre allows adequate excision and prevents restenosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Arrange a karyotype and measure gonadotrophins before any procedure is undertaken
options.rationale: Chromosomal and hormonal testing is the pathway for absent menstruation without cyclical pain, where the question is whether a uterus and functioning ovaries exist. Her ultrasound has already shown a normal uterus and ovaries and her pain is cyclical. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any decision on treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when the ultrasound suggests a more complex obstruction such as a transverse septum or a duplicated system, since the surgical approach differs. A thin bulging membrane visible at the introitus with a normal uterus does not need it. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

explanation.summary: An adolescent with normal secondary sexual development, no menstruation and cyclical pain has an obstructed outflow tract until proven otherwise, and the diagnosis is usually made on inspection of the introitus that is too often omitted. Retained menstrual blood distends the vagina and later the uterus and tubes, and the mass can compress the bladder neck to cause urinary frequency or frank retention, or the rectum to cause constipation. Ultrasound confirms a fluid filled vagina with a normal uterus and ovaries, which separates this from absent uterine development or gonadal dysgenesis where there is no cyclical pain. Definitive treatment is surgical incision of the obstructing membrane with drainage, and long term outcomes including fertility are good, although retrograde spill during the years of obstruction gives a higher rate of endometriosis.
key_points: Cyclical pain with absent menstruation signals obstruction, not ovarian failure
Normal breast and pubic hair development indicates functioning ovaries
Urinary frequency or retention reflects mass effect on the bladder neck
Inspection of the introitus makes the diagnosis in most cases
Karyotype and gonadotrophins belong to amenorrhoea without cyclical pain
explanation.pearls: Retained menstrual blood in an obstructed tract refluxes through the tubes, so these girls carry a substantially higher lifetime rate of endometriosis and should be told that persisting pelvic pain after surgery deserves assessment rather than reassurance.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: Milky discharge from both breasts with six months of absent periods and a mildly raised prolactin in a woman recently started on an antiemetic
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who has noticed a milky fluid coming from both nipples when she showers, and who has not had a period for six months. She has never been pregnant.

She has had nausea from gastroparesis for the last eight months and her gastroenterologist started her on domperidone seven months ago, which she takes three times a day. She has no headache and no change in her vision, and she has not gained weight or become constipated. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. Her serum prolactin taken this morning after a rushed walk from the car park is 1180 milliunits per litre.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features, no goitre, no striae or proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1180 milliunits per litre (less than 500), urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), follicle stimulating hormone 4.1 international units per litre, luteinising hormone 3.6 international units per litre, oestradiol 180 picomoles per litre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast this week
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated once pregnancy, medication, hypothyroidism and renal impairment have been excluded, or immediately if there is headache, visual field loss or a markedly higher level. Imaging now will find incidental lesions in a proportion of normal people and confuse a drug effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cabergoline twice weekly and review her prolactin level again in eight weeks
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist treats a prolactin secreting adenoma, which has not been demonstrated, and giving it alongside a dopamine antagonist sets the two drugs against each other while worsening her gastroparesis. Treatment precedes diagnosis here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive to restore her periods and review in three months
options.rationale: Restoring a withdrawal bleed masks the marker that is being used to monitor the underlying problem and treats neither the discharge nor its cause. Oestrogen replacement has a place once a cause is established and hypogonadism is expected to persist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Discuss stopping the antiemetic with her gastroenterologist and repeat the prolactin
options.rationale: A dopamine antagonist started one month before the symptoms began is a sufficient explanation for a prolactin at this level, and drug induced elevation is confirmed by the fall after the agent is withdrawn or substituted. Consulting the prescriber keeps her gastric symptoms managed while the test is repeated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange a macroprolactin assay and consider the result sufficient if it is positive
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that explains a raised laboratory value in a woman with no symptoms, and the near pair is that it is the right test for an incidental elevation rather than for a woman with discharge and absent periods. Her symptoms indicate biologically active hormone. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing

explanation.summary: Raised prolactin suppresses gonadotrophin pulsatility, which is why the clinical picture combines milky discharge with absent or infrequent periods and sometimes reduced libido or bone loss. The work up runs pregnancy, medication review, thyroid function and renal function before any imaging, because drugs are the commonest cause outside pregnancy and lactation, with dopamine antagonists, antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, verapamil and oestrogens the usual culprits. Levels also rise transiently with stress, venepuncture, exercise and nipple stimulation, so a modest elevation is repeated on a rested sample before it is acted on. Very high levels of several thousand milliunits per litre, or any level with headache or visual field loss, bypass this sequence and go straight to pituitary imaging.
key_points: Exclude pregnancy, drugs, hypothyroidism and renal failure before imaging
Dopamine antagonists are the commonest drug cause of elevation
Stress, exercise and nipple stimulation raise the level transiently
Headache or visual field loss mandates immediate pituitary imaging
Suppressed gonadotrophins explain the absent periods and low oestradiol
explanation.pearls: A prolactin above about 5000 milliunits per litre nearly always indicates a prolactin secreting adenoma rather than a drug effect, whereas antipsychotics and antiemetics usually produce levels between 1000 and 3000, so the number itself steers whether imaging can wait for a drug washout.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Prolactin testing

subtopic_detail: Leakage only on coughing and running eight months after a second vaginal birth with a normal bladder diary and no urgency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33 year old woman eight months after the vaginal birth of her second child. She leaks a small amount of urine when she coughs, sneezes or runs after her toddler, and has stopped going to her exercise class because of it.

She never leaks on the way to the toilet and does not get a sudden overwhelming need to go. She empties her bladder five times a day and does not wake at night for it. Her bladder diary shows a normal fluid intake of 1.8 litres and voided volumes between 250 and 400 mL. She has completed her family and is not breastfeeding. Examination shows a well healed perineum and she can hold a voluntary pelvic floor contraction for three seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well healed second degree perineal repair, no vaginal wall descent on Valsalva, voluntary pelvic floor contraction palpable but weak and held for 3 seconds, leakage of a small volume of urine observed on cough with a comfortably full bladder, post void residual volume 25 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine negative on culture, urine dipstick negative for blood nitrites and glucose

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for a supervised pelvic floor muscle training program of at least three months
options.rationale: Leakage confined to effort with no urgency and a normal diary defines the effort related pattern, and supervised training with a continence physiotherapist cures or substantially improves the majority and is recommended before any drug or operation. Supervision matters because unsupervised leaflets produce markedly poorer results. (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia: Urinary incontinence in women)
source_refs: Continence Foundation of Australia: Urinary incontinence in women

options.text: Refer to a urogynaecologist for a midurethral sling on the next available elective list
options.rationale: Surgery is considered only after an adequate supervised conservative program has failed, and in Australia sling procedures now carry a formal informed consent and audit pathway. Offering it first skips the treatment that would resolve most cases without a permanent implant. (Source: RANZCOG: Midurethral slings)

options.text: Start an antimuscarinic and arrange a bladder training program with fluid advice
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy and bladder retraining treat urgency with frequency and urgency leakage, and the near pair is that both patterns leak urine but only one is preceded by an overwhelming need to void. She never leaks on the way to the toilet. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology)

options.text: Arrange urodynamic studies before committing her to any particular treatment pathway
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear symptoms, previous continence surgery, voiding difficulty or a discordant history, since it does not improve outcomes in straightforward effort related leakage. Her diary, examination and cough test are all concordant. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen and review her symptoms again in three months
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen helps leakage associated with urogenital atrophy after menopause, which produces pale thin tissue and often urgency as well. She is 33 with well oestrogenised tissue and no atrophy to treat. (Source: Australian Menopause Society: Vaginal oestrogen)

explanation.summary: Urinary leakage affects about one in three Australian women at some point and the first task is to separate effort related leakage from urgency leakage, because the treatments diverge completely. Effort related leakage happens instantaneously with a rise in abdominal pressure, involves small volumes, and is not preceded by a warning sensation, while urgency leakage follows a sudden compelling need and often involves larger volumes and night waking. A bladder diary over three days, a urine culture to exclude infection, a post void residual and a cough test with a comfortably full bladder answer most questions without specialised testing. Supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months is first line for effort related leakage, with continence pessaries or surgery considered after that, and duloxetine occupying a small niche for women who decline both.
key_points: Leakage without a preceding urge indicates an effort related mechanism
A three day bladder diary and a post void residual guide most decisions
Supervised training outperforms written instructions given alone
Urodynamics is for discordant, mixed or previously operated cases
Surgery follows an adequate conservative trial, not the other way around
explanation.pearls: A minimum of three months of supervised training with at least eight contractions three times daily is the benchmark before declaring conservative therapy to have failed, and a woman who cannot produce a palpable voluntary contraction at all should be taught with biofeedback rather than sent away with a handout.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Urinary incontinence in women

subtopic_detail: Three second trimester losses at 16 to 19 weeks with painless cervical dilatation twice and a normal antiphospholipid and karyotype screen
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman in the recurrent loss clinic. She has had three pregnancies, lost at 16, 18 and 19 weeks, and on two of those occasions the membranes were found bulging through an open cervix when she presented with pressure but no contractions and no bleeding.

She has never had a term birth. She has had no cervical surgery and no procedures on the uterus. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies were negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin are normal, and parental karyotypes are normal. A transvaginal ultrasound today reports a heart shaped uterine cavity with a broad midline indentation and a smooth flat external fundal contour.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, cervix closed and 3 cm long on speculum with no scarring, uterus anteverted and normal size, adnexae non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent, parental karyotypes normal, transvaginal ultrasound showing a midline cavity indentation of 12 mm with an external fundal contour that is flat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic resection of the midline tissue on the next available theatre list
options.rationale: Resection is the treatment once a septum is confirmed, but operating on a fused double horned uterus on the basis of the cavity shape alone risks entering the myometrium and perforating. The external contour is what separates the two and it has not yet been measured properly. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange three dimensional ultrasound to define the cavity and fundal contour precisely
options.rationale: A deep midline indentation with a flat external contour suggests a residual septum rather than a fused double horned uterus, and the two are managed completely differently, so the contour must be measured before anyone operates. Coronal three dimensional imaging gives that measurement without an anaesthetic and is the recommended first line test. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange elective cervical cerclage at 12 weeks in her next pregnancy without imaging
options.rationale: A history based suture is a genuine option for painless mid trimester dilatation, and it may still be offered later, but committing to it while an untreated structural cause is on the scan attributes the losses to the cervix alone. The near pair is that both conditions produce painless second trimester loss and they can coexist. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency)

options.text: Start low dose aspirin with prophylactic low molecular weight heparin in the next pregnancy
options.rationale: Combined aspirin and heparin is the treatment for antiphospholipid syndrome, which requires a persistently positive antibody on two occasions twelve weeks apart. Both sets of her antibodies were negative, so this treats a disease she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Start vaginal progesterone from 16 weeks in the next pregnancy and monitor her cervix
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix measured in the current pregnancy, which is a surveillance based decision made after 16 weeks. It is not a substitute for defining a uterine anomaly before she conceives. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is investigated for antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid and glucose control, parental chromosomes and uterine structure, and in a woman with mid trimester losses the uterine cavity carries more weight than it does with early losses. The critical structural distinction is between a septate uterus, where a fibrous midline partition sits inside a single fused muscular body with a normal external contour, and a bicornuate uterus, where the external fundus is indented because the two horns never fused. Only the first is amenable to hysteroscopic resection, which improves live birth rates, whereas resecting the midline of a bicornuate uterus risks perforation and does not help. Three dimensional ultrasound in the coronal plane has largely replaced laparoscopy with hysteroscopy as the way to measure the external contour and the depth of the indentation.
key_points: Mid trimester painless loss raises both cervical and structural causes
The external fundal contour separates a septate from a bicornuate uterus
Only a septum is treated by hysteroscopic resection
Three dimensional coronal imaging replaces laparoscopy for the contour
Antiphospholipid treatment requires persistently positive antibodies
explanation.pearls: An external fundal indentation deeper than 10 mm below the interostial line indicates a bicornuate uterus rather than a septum, and that single measurement decides whether hysteroscopic resection is safe or contraindicated.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Recurrent pregnancy loss

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old with no menstruation, full breast development, sparse pubic hair and a short blind ending vagina with bilateral groin swellings
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16 year old who has never menstruated. Her breasts developed at 12 and she has grown to 176 cm, taller than both parents.

She has almost no pubic or axillary hair, which she says has never bothered her. She has never had cyclical abdominal pain of any kind. She has a firm mobile swelling in each groin that her mother assumed were hernias. On examination the external genitalia are female and the vagina is 4 cm long and ends blindly. A pelvic ultrasound performed this morning reports no uterus and no ovaries, with soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Height 176 cm, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, normal female external genitalia, vagina 4 cm long ending blindly with no cervix visible, firm mobile 3 cm swelling in each inguinal canal, no acne or clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with no uterus and no ovaries identified and soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals, testosterone 18 nanomoles per litre (female range 0.5-2.6), luteinising hormone 14 international units per litre, follicle stimulating hormone 5 international units per litre, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and both inguinal canals with contrast
options.rationale: Imaging maps the gonads and any rudimentary structures, and it will be needed when planning gonadectomy, but it cannot say which chromosomes are present. Ultrasound has already shown the essential anatomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

options.text: Measurement of serum anti Mullerian hormone with inhibin B on a morning sample
options.rationale: These markers reflect gonadal tissue activity and are elevated in this condition, which is supportive rather than diagnostic, since the same pattern occurs in other disorders of sex development. They do not identify the chromosomal complement. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development

options.text: Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample sent to a cytogenetics laboratory
options.rationale: Full breast development with absent pubic hair, a male range testosterone and an absent uterus indicate a 46 XY individual whose tissues cannot respond to androgen, with breast growth driven by aromatised oestrogen. The karyotype distinguishes this from absent uterine development in a 46 XX individual, which is the other cause of a blind vagina at this age. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation)

options.text: Measurement of serum 17 hydroxyprogesterone with a short synacthen stimulation test
options.rationale: Adrenal enzyme testing is for virilisation of a 46 XX individual, which presents with excess rather than absent sexual hair and with ambiguous genitalia in infancy. Her pattern is the opposite, with absent hair and unvirilised external genitalia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of the structures found in both inguinal canals
options.rationale: Histology of the gonads is obtained at the time of planned removal rather than as the diagnostic step, and an operation before the chromosomes are known risks removing tissue that is the source of her oestrogen. The near pair is that biopsy and karyotype both identify the gonadal type but only one is a blood test. (Source: RANZCOG: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology)

explanation.summary: Absent menstruation with a blind ending vagina and no uterus on imaging has two principal explanations in adolescence, and the sexual hair pattern separates them at the bedside. A 46 XX individual with absent uterine and upper vaginal development has normal pubic and axillary hair, functioning ovaries, normal female testosterone and often associated renal or skeletal anomalies. A 46 XY individual whose androgen receptor does not function has sparse or absent sexual hair, a male range testosterone, gonads that may sit in the inguinal canals, and taller than average stature. Management in the second case includes disclosure handled by an experienced multidisciplinary team, oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy, vaginal dilators where the vagina is short, and a discussion of gonadal tumour risk that guides the timing of removal.
key_points: Absent pubic hair with full breast development suggests androgen insensitivity
A male range testosterone in a phenotypic female is the decisive laboratory clue
Karyotype separates the two main causes of a blind vagina with no uterus
Gonads in the inguinal canal in this setting are testes, not ovaries
Normal pubic hair with an absent uterus points to Mullerian agenesis instead
explanation.pearls: The malignant potential of intra-abdominal gonads in complete androgen insensitivity is low before puberty but rises with age, so current practice defers gonadectomy until after spontaneous pubertal breast development is complete rather than removing them in childhood.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Disorders of sex development

subtopic_detail: Four months of bloating and early satiety in a postmenopausal woman with a solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and ascites
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman who has felt bloated for four months and now fills up after a few mouthfuls. She has lost 4 kg without trying and has been to the toilet more often to pass urine.

She went through menopause at 51 and has had no vaginal bleeding. She was treated for irritable bowel symptoms for the last three months without improvement. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at 58 and a maternal aunt had breast cancer at 44. Abdominal examination finds shifting dullness and a firm mass arising from the pelvis. The ultrasound she had yesterday describes a 9 cm solid mass with papillary projections and internal blood flow, with free fluid in the abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching 5 cm above the symphysis, no hepatomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no vaginal bleeding on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound showing a 9 cm solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and internal vascularity plus moderate ascites, CA125 640 units per millilitre (less than 35), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), albumin 33 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to a gynaecological oncology centre for staging and multidisciplinary care
options.rationale: A postmenopausal woman with a solid vascular adnexal mass, ascites and a markedly raised marker has a high risk of malignancy, and survival is better when primary surgery is performed by a subspecialist within a multidisciplinary service. That referral is made on the clinical and imaging picture rather than after further local tests. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic removal of the adnexal mass
options.rationale: Laparoscopic removal of a suspicious mass outside a specialist centre risks rupture and upstaging, and it leaves the woman without the full staging procedure she is likely to need. The near pair is that the same operation in a specialist unit forms part of a planned cytoreduction. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer to the interventional suite for diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis this week
options.rationale: Drainage relieves symptomatic distension and cytology can support the diagnosis, but neither changes the destination and a paracentesis performed first can delay the specialist referral. Symptom relief is arranged by the receiving unit as part of the plan. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy and gastroscopy to exclude a gastrointestinal primary tumour first
options.rationale: A gastrointestinal primary with ovarian deposits is worth considering when the masses are bilateral with a normal marker or when bowel symptoms dominate, and endoscopy is then arranged by the treating team. Making it the first step delays definitive referral by weeks. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer for genetic counselling and germline testing before any surgical decision is taken
options.rationale: Her family history does warrant germline testing and it is now offered to all women with this diagnosis, but it is arranged alongside treatment rather than before it. Waiting for a genetics appointment before referral costs time that affects outcome. (Source: eviQ: Ovarian cancer genetic testing)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer is diagnosed late in three quarters of Australian women because the early symptoms of bloating, early satiety, abdominal pain and urinary frequency are common and non-specific, and they are frequently attributed to irritable bowel syndrome. New onset of these symptoms in a woman over 50, particularly if persistent for more than a few weeks, should prompt pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound and a CA125. Features that raise concern on imaging are solid components, papillary projections, internal vascularity, bilaterality and ascites. Referral to a gynaecological oncology service confers a measurable survival benefit through complete staging and optimal cytoreduction, and germline testing is now offered to every woman with high grade serous disease because it guides both her treatment and her relatives' risk.
key_points: Bloating and early satiety in a woman over 50 warrant pelvic imaging
Irritable bowel syndrome rarely presents for the first time after 50
Solid components, papillary projections and ascites raise malignancy risk
Subspecialist surgery improves survival and completeness of staging
Germline testing is offered to all women with high grade serous disease
explanation.pearls: A new diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome made after the age of 50 should be treated as a diagnostic red flag rather than a label, because it is the single commonest misattribution recorded in the months before an ovarian cancer diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with fever at 24 weeks where the appendix is not visualised on ultrasound and the white cell count sits in the physiological pregnancy range
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy with 18 hours of abdominal pain. It began around her navel and has settled into the right side of her abdomen above the level of her navel, and she has vomited twice and cannot face food.

She has no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms and no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid. Fetal movements are normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She is tender in the right abdomen with voluntary guarding but no rebound. Her urine dipstick shows a trace of leucocytes and no nitrites, and a midstream specimen has been sent. The ultrasound performed an hour ago could not visualise the appendix and reports normal kidneys and normal ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in the right abdomen approximately 4 cm above the umbilicus with voluntary guarding and no rebound or rigidity, uterus soft and non-tender with fundal height consistent with dates, no renal angle tenderness, cervical os closed on speculum with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (pregnancy range 6.0-16.0), neutrophils 13.1 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick with trace leucocytes and no nitrites, transabdominal ultrasound not visualising the appendix with normal kidneys and normal ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast medium
options.rationale: Computed tomography is accurate but delivers ionising radiation to the fetus and is reserved for situations where magnetic resonance is unavailable or the mother is too unstable to tolerate it. The near pair is that both cross sectional studies answer the question and only one avoids radiation. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat transabdominal ultrasound in twelve hours with serial abdominal examination
options.rationale: Serial assessment suits equivocal pain with normal inflammatory markers and no fever, whereas she has a temperature of 38.1 with a C reactive protein of 68 and rising pain. Perforation risk climbs steeply after 24 hours and fetal loss follows perforation in a substantial minority. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with observation and reassessment by the surgical team later
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone are used for a walled off inflammatory mass on imaging, which has not been demonstrated, and starting them without a diagnosis blunts the signs that would otherwise force a decision. The diagnostic question has to be settled first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen performed without gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: When ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix in a pregnant woman with a convincing clinical picture, magnetic resonance imaging is the recommended next study because it images the right iliac fossa reliably without ionising radiation and reduces the negative appendicectomy rate. Gadolinium is avoided because it crosses the placenta. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy on the emergency list without any further imaging beforehand
options.rationale: Proceeding straight to theatre is correct when the picture is unequivocal with peritonism, and she has voluntary guarding without rebound or rigidity alongside an unconfirmed diagnosis. Negative appendicectomy in pregnancy carries a measurable rate of fetal loss and preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Imaging in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Appendicitis is the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy, affecting roughly one in a thousand pregnancies, and it is harder to recognise because the enlarging uterus displaces the appendix upward and laterally, nausea and vomiting are expected in pregnancy, and the white cell count rises physiologically to as high as 16 x10 to the ninth per litre. Ultrasound is the first imaging study because it is safe and available, but the appendix is not visualised in a large proportion of pregnant women, particularly in the second and third trimesters. Magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium has become the recommended second line study in Australian practice, with high sensitivity and specificity and no ionising radiation, and it substantially reduces the number of normal appendices removed. Delay is the real danger, since perforation rates rise sharply after 24 hours of symptoms and fetal loss follows perforation far more often than it follows an uncomplicated operation.
key_points: The appendix migrates upward and laterally as the uterus enlarges
A white cell count up to 16 x10^9/L can be physiological in pregnancy
Ultrasound frequently fails to visualise the appendix after the first trimester
Magnetic resonance without gadolinium is the recommended second line study
Perforation rather than surgery is what threatens the pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Gadolinium crosses the placenta and is associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, so magnetic resonance in pregnancy is performed unenhanced, and an unenhanced study is sufficient to diagnose or exclude appendicitis in the great majority of cases.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Appendicitis in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Contraceptive choice for a woman with focal epilepsy on carbamazepine who has already conceived once on a combined pill and does not want pregnancy for five years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman with focal epilepsy that has been seizure free for three years on carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily. She conceived unexpectedly two years ago while taking a combined oral contraceptive every day and had a termination.

She has two children, does not want another pregnancy for at least five years, and is adamant she will not rely on remembering anything daily. She has heavy but regular periods and a haemoglobin of 112 g/L. Her blood pressure is normal, she does not smoke and she has no history of thrombosis. Her neurologist has documented that carbamazepine is the only agent that has controlled her seizures and wants it continued.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, cardiovascular and abdominal examination normal, pelvic examination normal with a mobile anteverted uterus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), ferritin 16 micrograms per litre (30-200), urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive method should you recommend first?

options.text: A subdermal etonogestrel implant inserted at the next available clinic appointment
options.rationale: The implant is long acting and requires no daily action, but the progestogen it releases is cleared systemically and enzyme inducing drugs lower the circulating level enough to risk failure. The near pair is that both are progestogen devices yet only the intrauterine one escapes hepatic induction. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive containing 50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol daily
options.rationale: Increasing the oestrogen dose to compensate for induction is not reliable, is unlicensed for this purpose and she has already conceived on a combined pill. It also returns her to the daily regimen she has explicitly rejected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: A progestogen only pill taken continuously with condoms used as a second method
options.rationale: Oral progestogen is also subject to enzyme induction and depends on daily adherence within a narrow window, and adding condoms shifts the burden of effectiveness onto a method with a high typical use failure rate. Neither element matches a five year plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: A three monthly depot medroxyprogesterone injection with a shortened dosing interval
options.rationale: The injection is one of the few systemic progestogen methods that remains effective with enzyme inducing drugs, so the standard interval is retained rather than shortened, but it neither lasts five years nor reduces her menstrual loss. Shortening the interval adds bone exposure for no benefit. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted at the next available appointment
options.rationale: The intrauterine route delivers progestogen locally so hepatic enzyme induction does not reduce its contraceptive effect, and it gives five or more years of cover with no daily action required. It also reduces menstrual loss substantially, which matters with her iron deficiency. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Enzyme inducing antiepileptic drugs including carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, topiramate at higher doses and oxcarbazepine accelerate hepatic metabolism of systemically absorbed steroid hormones, reducing the effectiveness of the combined pill, the progestogen only pill, the implant and emergency levonorgestrel. The methods that are unaffected are the copper intrauterine device, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, whose action is predominantly local, and the depot injection, which achieves levels high enough to remain reliable at the usual interval. The interaction also runs the other way for some combinations, since oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels and risks seizures. Choosing well matters disproportionately here because unplanned pregnancy on a teratogenic antiepileptic carries a substantial risk of major malformation, and preconception folate and drug review should be discussed at the same visit.
key_points: Enzyme inducers reduce the efficacy of the pill, the mini pill and the implant
Both intrauterine devices and the depot injection remain effective
Raising the oestrogen dose is not a reliable workaround
Oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels
The intrauterine system also treats heavy menstrual loss
explanation.pearls: A woman on an enzyme inducing antiepileptic who needs emergency contraception should be offered a copper intrauterine device, and if she declines, the oral levonorgestrel dose is doubled to 3 mg, because the standard 1.5 mg dose is substantially less effective under induction.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

subtopic_detail: A seven centimetre multiloculated adnexal collection still febrile after forty eight hours of intravenous antibiotics for pelvic infection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman admitted two days ago with lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and cervical motion tenderness. She has been on intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin and metronidazole since admission.

Her pain has not settled, she continues to spike temperatures and she looks tired but is not confused. Her abdomen is tender in both iliac fossae with voluntary guarding but no rebound and no board like rigidity. A serum pregnancy test taken on admission was negative. A repeat transvaginal ultrasound today reports a 7 cm multiloculated collection incorporating the left tube and ovary, with no free fluid elsewhere in the abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in both iliac fossae with voluntary guarding, no rebound tenderness and no rigidity, bowel sounds present, cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 214 mg/L rising from 168 on admission (less than 5), serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, transvaginal ultrasound reports a 7 cm multiloculated left tubo-ovarian collection with no free intraperitoneal fluid, blood cultures no growth to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Change to oral doxycycline and metronidazole and plan discharge tomorrow
options.rationale: Stepping down to oral therapy is appropriate once there has been a clear clinical response, which has not occurred here with rising inflammatory markers and continuing fever. Discharging an undrained collection risks rupture and generalised peritonitis. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Continue the current antibiotics and reassess after a further seven days
options.rationale: Failure to respond by 48 to 72 hours is the recognised trigger for intervention rather than for a longer trial of the same therapy. Antibiotics penetrate an established abscess cavity poorly regardless of how long they are continued. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic inflammatory disease)

options.text: Proceed to total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
