options.rationale: Radical surgery is reserved for a ruptured abscess with peritonitis or for disease that persists after drainage, and it removes fertility in a young woman without first trying a conservative option. The absence of rebound tenderness, rigidity and free fluid argues against rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic inflammatory disease)

options.text: Arrange image guided drainage of the collection and continue antibiotics
options.rationale: An abscess larger than about 7 cm, or any collection that has not responded by 48 to 72 hours of appropriate intravenous therapy, needs drainage, and image guided transvaginal or percutaneous drainage achieves this while preserving the tube and ovary. Antibiotics continue alongside because drainage alone does not treat the surrounding pelvic infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic inflammatory disease)

options.text: Add intravenous vancomycin and reassess after a further seventy two hours
options.rationale: Broadening cover towards resistant Gram positive organisms does not address the physical barrier of an undrained cavity, and the usual organisms here are polymicrobial anaerobes and enteric flora already covered by the current regimen. Adding a further agent substitutes drug escalation for source control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Tubo-ovarian abscess is the most serious complication of ascending pelvic infection and behaves as a surgical collection rather than as a soft tissue infection, so the principle of source control applies. Most women are managed initially with broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gonococci, chlamydia and anaerobes, and about two thirds respond, with response judged at 48 to 72 hours on fever, pain and inflammatory markers. Failure to respond in that window, or an abscess above about 7 cm at the outset, predicts antibiotic failure and is the trigger for drainage, which is now usually image guided rather than open. Rupture presents with peritonism and haemodynamic instability and is a surgical emergency, so the absence of rebound tenderness and free fluid is what permits the less invasive route here.
key_points: Response to antibiotics is assessed at 48 to 72 hours, not later
Abscesses above about 7 cm respond poorly to antibiotics alone
Image guided drainage preserves the tube and ovary where possible
Antibiotics continue after drainage to treat the surrounding infection
Peritonism with free fluid suggests rupture and mandates surgery
explanation.pearls: A tubo-ovarian abscess in a woman with an intrauterine device does not require removal of the device before treatment is started, but if there is no clinical improvement within 48 to 72 hours the device should be removed at the same time as drainage is arranged.

subtopic_detail: Heavy painful periods with a globally enlarged tender uterus and junctional zone thickening on magnetic resonance imaging at forty one
stem:
You are the gynaecologist seeing a 41 year old woman with four years of progressively heavier and more painful periods. She describes flooding through a pad in an hour on her worst days and cramping that starts several days before bleeding begins and continues throughout.

Her two children were born by normal vaginal delivery and she does not wish to conceive again. On examination the uterus is bulky, globular and tender, estimated at a 10 week size, with no adnexal masses. An endometrial biopsy taken last month showed proliferative endometrium with no hyperplasia and no atypia. Magnetic resonance imaging reports a diffusely thickened junctional zone of 15 mm with no discrete myometrial lesion and a normal endometrial thickness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bulky globular tender uterus of approximately 10 week size, mobile with no adnexal masses, cervix appears normal with a recent negative cervical screening test
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, endometrial biopsy shows proliferative endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia, magnetic resonance imaging reports a diffusely thickened junctional zone of 15 mm with no discrete myometrial lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system and review in six months
options.rationale: Local progestogen delivery thins the endometrium and acts directly on the affected myometrium, which reduces both the bleeding and the dysmenorrhoea that characterise this condition, and it is the recommended first line treatment for a woman who has completed her family but wishes to avoid surgery. It also treats the iron deficiency driver by reducing blood loss rather than only replacing iron. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start combined oral contraception continuously and review her in six months
options.rationale: Continuous combined hormonal contraception is a reasonable option and does help the pain, but it controls heavy bleeding less effectively than local progestogen and becomes harder to justify as cardiovascular risk factors accumulate with age. It is the alternative when an intrauterine device is declined or cannot be placed. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the lesion and review postoperatively
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic resection treats a discrete intracavity lesion such as a submucosal fibroid or a polyp, and the imaging here reports diffuse myometrial change with no discrete lesion to resect. The near pair here is that the same operation would be first line had the imaging shown a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist alone and review in six months
options.rationale: Agonist therapy produces a hypo-oestrogenic state that shrinks the uterus but causes bone loss and vasomotor symptoms, so it is used for a limited period before surgery rather than as ongoing treatment, and then with add back therapy. Using it alone for six months is not an appropriate first line strategy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and review in the interventional clinic
options.rationale: Embolisation is an option for symptomatic disease that has failed medical therapy, and its results in diffuse myometrial disease are less durable than in fibroids. Offering an invasive procedure before any medical treatment has been tried inverts the usual order. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adenomyosis)

explanation.summary: A globular tender uterus with heavy painful periods and a thickened junctional zone on magnetic resonance imaging describes adenomyosis, in which endometrial glands and stroma lie within the myometrium and the surrounding muscle hypertrophies. The condition overlaps clinically with fibroids, and the distinction matters because a discrete fibroid may be resectable or embolisable while diffuse disease is not. A junctional zone thickness above 12 mm is the usual imaging threshold, and transvaginal ultrasound showing a globular uterus, myometrial cysts and asymmetric wall thickening is often sufficient without magnetic resonance imaging. Because symptoms are oestrogen dependent, they remit at menopause, so the goal in a woman in her forties is effective symptom control for the remaining reproductive years rather than definitive surgery in every case.
key_points: A junctional zone above 12 mm supports adenomyosis rather than fibroids
Diffuse myometrial disease has no discrete lesion available for resection
Local progestogen treats both the bleeding and the dysmenorrhoea
Iron deficiency should be corrected alongside treating the cause
Symptoms are oestrogen dependent and remit after menopause
explanation.pearls: Expulsion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system is more frequent in an adenomyotic or fibroid enlarged uterus than in a normal one, so arrange a string check at six weeks and warn the woman that a return of heavy bleeding may mean the device has been expelled rather than that it has failed.

subtopic_detail: Burning pain reproduced by cotton bud touch at the vestibule with normal vulval skin and negative swabs in a twenty six year old
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman with eighteen months of burning discomfort at the entrance to the vagina that occurs only when something touches it, including tampons and intercourse. She has no pain at rest and no itch, and she has used several courses of antifungal cream and pessaries bought over the counter without benefit.

She has been on the same combined oral contraceptive pill for three years and has regular withdrawal bleeds. On examination the vulval skin is of normal colour and architecture with no loss of the labia minora, no fissuring and no white plaques. A cotton bud applied lightly to the vestibule reproduces her pain sharply at the six o'clock position, while the same pressure on the labia majora and the perineum is painless. Her pelvic floor muscles feel tight and tender on gentle digital examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no loss of labia minora and no scarring, no white plaques or fissures, well oestrogenised moist vestibular mucosa, cotton bud test positive at the vestibule and negative on the labia majora, hypertonic tender levator ani on digital examination
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab shows normal flora with no candida on microscopy or culture, nucleic acid amplification testing negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, vaginal pH 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe a course of topical clobetasol and review her in eight weeks
options.rationale: A potent topical corticosteroid treats an inflammatory vulval dermatosis, which would show altered skin colour, texture or architecture, and none of that is present. Prolonged use on normal vestibular skin risks atrophy without addressing the pain. (Source: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole weekly for six months and review after that
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is for culture confirmed recurrent candidiasis, and both microscopy and culture are negative here after she has already failed empirical antifungals. Repeating a treatment that has not worked reinforces the belief that this is an infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for vestibulectomy and review her in the surgical outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Surgical excision of the vestibule is reserved for well localised disease that has failed a full course of conservative treatment, and operating on a woman with an untreated hypertonic pelvic floor commonly leaves the pain unchanged. It is a last resort rather than an opening move. (Source: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia

options.text: Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy and start a topical local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Pain provoked only by touch at the vestibule with normal skin and negative swabs is localised provoked vulvodynia, and the pelvic floor hypertonicity found on examination is both a consequence and a perpetuating cause, so physiotherapy is central to first line care. Topical local anaesthetic applied before provoking activity reduces the pain and allows the desensitisation work to proceed. (Source: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly and review her in eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is useful where the vestibule is atrophic, which is typically seen after menopause or occasionally with low dose combined contraception, and the mucosa here is described as well oestrogenised. The near pair here is that vestibular atrophy can produce an identical cotton bud test, which is why the appearance of the mucosa is examined before treating. (Source: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain lasting at least three months without a clinically identifiable cause, and it is subdivided by whether the pain is provoked or spontaneous and by whether it is localised or generalised. The commonest pattern in younger women is localised provoked pain at the vestibule, in which the skin looks entirely normal and the diagnosis rests on the cotton bud test together with negative infective and dermatological findings. Many women have had repeated empirical antifungal treatment before the diagnosis is made, and that history of failed treatment is itself a useful clue. Management is multimodal, combining education, removal of irritants, pelvic floor physiotherapy, topical agents and, where central sensitisation is prominent, a neuromodulating agent such as amitriptyline, with psychological and sexual therapy for the impact on relationships.
key_points: Normal vulval architecture excludes lichen sclerosus and lichen planus
The cotton bud test localises the pain and is the key bedside examination
Pelvic floor hypertonicity is both a consequence and a perpetuating cause
Repeated failed antifungal courses point away from candidiasis
Surgery is considered only after conservative treatment has failed
explanation.pearls: Amitriptyline started at 10 mg at night and titrated slowly is the usual oral agent when topical treatment and physiotherapy are insufficient, and women should be told to expect six to eight weeks before judging the response rather than stopping after a fortnight.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Vulvovaginal Disease: Vulvodynia

subtopic_detail: Frothy discharge with motile flagellates on wet mount at ten weeks gestation with a vaginal pH of 5.5
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman at ten weeks in her first pregnancy who reports three weeks of a heavy, frothy, yellow-green discharge with soreness and an offensive smell. She has recently moved to your town from a remote area of the Northern Territory.

She has used a clotrimazole pessary without improvement. On speculum examination there is a copious frothy discharge and the cervix has a punctate red appearance. The vaginal pH is 5.5. Wet mount microscopy shows motile flagellated organisms and no hyphae or spores, and nucleic acid amplification testing is negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. She has one regular sexual partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Copious frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, punctate erythema of the ectocervix, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus consistent with dates, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.5, wet mount microscopy shows motile flagellated organisms with no hyphae or spores, nucleic acid amplification testing negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, syphilis and blood borne virus serology negative, urine culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose with treatment of her partner
options.rationale: Fluconazole treats candidiasis, which is excluded by the absence of hyphae and spores and by a pH above 4.5, and oral azole exposure in the first trimester is best avoided. She has already failed a topical azole for the same presumed diagnosis. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Oral metronidazole 2 g as a single dose with treatment of her partner
options.rationale: Motile flagellates on wet mount with a raised pH and a punctate cervix identify trichomoniasis, which is treated with oral nitroimidazole therapy, and partner treatment is required because it is sexually transmitted and reinfection is otherwise the rule. Metronidazole is not teratogenic and Australian guidance is to treat in pregnancy rather than defer, because the infection is itself associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Defer treatment until the second trimester and treat her partner now
options.rationale: Deferring was older advice based on theoretical first trimester concerns that subsequent data have not supported, and it leaves an infection associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes untreated for months. Treating only the partner also guarantees reinfection once she resumes intercourse. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Topical clotrimazole for six nights with treatment of her regular partner
options.rationale: Topical azole treatment has already failed and has no activity against a protozoal infection. The near pair here is that a thick white discharge with a normal pH and hyphae on microscopy would be the picture for which this is correct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg with treatment of her regular partner
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone targets gonococcal infection, which has been excluded by negative nucleic acid amplification testing, and it has no activity against protozoa. Empirical cover for an organism already excluded adds no benefit. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is uncommon in urban Australian practice but remains highly prevalent in some remote communities, so geography is a genuine part of the pre test probability. The classic findings of frothy yellow-green discharge, a raised vaginal pH and a punctate cervix are individually insensitive, and nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive than microscopy, so a negative wet mount does not exclude the diagnosis where suspicion is high. In pregnancy the infection is associated with preterm birth, premature rupture of the membranes and low birth weight, and Australian guidance is to treat when it is found rather than to defer to the second trimester. Because it is sexually transmitted, partner treatment, testing for co-existing infections and a test of reinfection at three months are part of the plan.
key_points: A vaginal pH above 4.5 argues against candidiasis as the cause
Nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive than wet mount microscopy
Treatment in pregnancy is recommended rather than deferred
Partner treatment is required or reinfection follows
Test for co-existing sexually transmitted infections at the same visit
explanation.pearls: Retest for reinfection at three months rather than performing a test of cure at two weeks, because treatment failure is uncommon while reinfection from an untreated partner is the usual reason for recurrence.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: Type three female genital cutting identified at the booking visit in a primigravida at fourteen weeks who wants a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a booking visit for a 26 year old primigravida at 14 weeks who arrived in Australia four years ago. She tells you through a professional interpreter that she was cut as a child, that passing urine takes a long time and that she has recurrent urinary infections.

She says she would like to give birth vaginally and asks what will happen. On examination the labia are fused with a narrowed posterior opening admitting one fingertip, the clitoris and labia minora are not identifiable, and the urethral meatus cannot be visualised. There is no scar tenderness and no keloid. Her pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated and the dating ultrasound is consistent with her dates.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fused labia with a narrowed vaginal opening admitting one fingertip, clitoris and labia minora not identifiable, urethral meatus not visualised, no keloid or scar tenderness, uterine size consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound consistent with menstrual dates, booking bloods within normal limits, midstream urine culture grows Escherichia coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her genital tract?

options.text: Plan deinfibulation during established labour in the first stage
options.rationale: Deinfibulation can be performed in labour if the woman presents undiagnosed, but planning it that way forfeits the chance for unhurried consent, adequate analgesia and healing before birth. It also leaves her urinary symptoms untreated for the rest of the pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at thirty nine weeks gestation
options.rationale: Previous genital cutting is not by itself an indication for caesarean section, and performing one leaves the obstruction and the urinary symptoms in place for future pregnancies. The woman has clearly expressed a preference for vaginal birth, which deinfibulation makes achievable. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Offer deinfibulation in the second trimester after counselling
options.rationale: Antenatal deinfibulation, usually offered around 20 weeks, allows the procedure to be discussed with an interpreter and consented properly, performed under regional or local anaesthesia, and healed well before labour, and it relieves the urinary and menstrual symptoms caused by the obstruction. Planned antenatal repair also avoids an emergency incision at a point when the woman cannot participate in the decision. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Defer discussion of delivery options until the third trimester
options.rationale: Deferring removes the window in which antenatal deinfibulation is best performed and leaves the woman without information she needs to plan her birth. Early discussion with an interpreter is a core part of booking care in this situation. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Plan reinfibulation after the birth if she requests it at delivery
options.rationale: Reinfibulation is unlawful throughout Australia and cannot be offered or performed regardless of a request, and this should be explained sensitively at the antenatal visit rather than at delivery. Repair after birth restores anatomy without recreating the occlusion. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

explanation.summary: Female genital mutilation is classified into four types, and the infibulated form with fused labia and a narrowed opening is the one that obstructs urinary flow, menstruation, intercourse and birth. Care begins with a professional interpreter rather than a family member, and with an explicit statement that the woman is not at fault and will not be judged, because fear of a hostile reaction is a major barrier to disclosure. Antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester is the preferred approach where the opening is inadequate, because it allows proper consent, a planned anaesthetic and healing before labour, and it treats the urinary symptoms at the same time. Performing or arranging the procedure on a child, and reinfibulation at any age, are criminal offences in every Australian jurisdiction, and clinicians have child protection obligations where a daughter may be at risk.
key_points: A professional interpreter rather than a family member is used for the discussion
Previous cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean section
Antenatal deinfibulation around 20 weeks allows consent, anaesthesia and healing
Urinary obstruction and recurrent infection are treated by the same procedure
Reinfibulation is unlawful in Australia and cannot be offered
explanation.pearls: The deinfibulation incision is made anteriorly along the midline raphe up to the point where the urethral meatus becomes visible, since cutting further risks injury to the urethra and cutting less leaves the obstruction unrelieved.

sources.label: Department of Health Australia: Female genital mutilation information for health professionals
BMJ Best Practice: Female genital mutilation

subtopic_detail: Failure of lactation with fatigue and dizziness six weeks after a postpartum haemorrhage requiring six units of red cells
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 32 year old woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. Her delivery was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 3200 mL requiring six units of red cells and a period of hypotension before she was stabilised.

She says her milk never came in properly and she stopped trying to breastfeed at two weeks. She feels exhausted, cold and light headed when she stands up quickly, and she has not had a period. She scores 4 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and says her mood is fine but her body is not. Her lying blood pressure is 102/64 mmHg falling to 84/52 mmHg on standing, and her ferritin has normalised since the transfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg lying and 84/52 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale with dry skin, no goitre, breasts soft and non engorged, no axillary hair regrowth since delivery, uterus involuted, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30 to 200), sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone alone and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Where the pituitary is the site of damage, thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal or low despite a low free thyroxine, so measuring it alone produces a falsely reassuring result. Thyroid stimulating hormone is only a reliable screen when the pituitary is known to be intact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Fatigue after birth is often attributed to depression, but her Edinburgh score is low, she reports her mood as intact, and postural hypotension with hyponatraemia is not explained by a mood disorder. Treating empirically here would delay a diagnosis with a risk of adrenal crisis. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Measure ferritin and start oral iron, then review her in four weeks
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is the obvious candidate after a large haemorrhage, but her ferritin has already normalised after transfusion, which removes it as the explanation. The near pair here is that identical fatigue with a low ferritin would make iron replacement the right answer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure early morning cortisol, free thyroxine and prolactin together
options.rationale: Failure of lactation, amenorrhoea, loss of axillary hair, postural hypotension and hyponatraemia after a haemorrhage with hypotension point to anterior pituitary infarction, so the axes must be tested together rather than one at a time. A low or inappropriately normal prolactin alongside a low free thyroxine and a low early morning cortisol establishes the pattern of central rather than end organ failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before any bloods
options.rationale: Imaging is useful once hypopituitarism is biochemically established, particularly to exclude an alternative lesion, but it does not tell you which axes are failing or how urgently replacement is needed. Biochemistry precedes imaging in this sequence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypopituitarism)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is infarction of the anterior pituitary caused by hypotension at or after delivery, and the gland is vulnerable because it enlarges in pregnancy while its portal blood supply is a low pressure system. The classic first clue is failure of lactation, because prolactin secreting cells are affected early, followed by amenorrhoea, loss of axillary and pubic hair, cold intolerance and fatigue. Presentation is often delayed by months or years because the deficiencies are partial and easily attributed to the ordinary exhaustion of new parenthood, so a deliberate link back to the haemorrhage is what makes the diagnosis. The posterior pituitary is usually spared, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon, and the danger of missing the diagnosis is an adrenal crisis precipitated by an intercurrent illness.
key_points: Failure of lactation after a haemorrhage with hypotension is the sentinel symptom
Thyroid stimulating hormone is unreliable when the pituitary is the site of damage
Hyponatraemia with postural hypotension suggests cortisol deficiency
All anterior pituitary axes are assessed together rather than sequentially
Imaging follows rather than precedes the biochemical diagnosis
explanation.pearls: When both cortisol and thyroxine deficiency are confirmed, hydrocortisone must be started before thyroxine, because thyroid hormone raises cortisol clearance and replacing thyroxine first can precipitate an adrenal crisis within days.

sources.label: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

subtopic_detail: Severe limb and back pain at twenty six weeks in a woman with haemoglobin SS disease whose oxygen saturation and chest examination are normal
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit to see a 29 year old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy who has haemoglobin SS disease. She describes severe pain in both thighs and her lower back that began yesterday and is now worse than the pain she usually manages at home with paracetamol.

She has had no fever, no cough and no shortness of breath. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her oxygen saturation is 98 per cent breathing room air. Her haemoglobin today is 79 g/L, which her notes record as her usual baseline, and her reticulocyte count is appropriately raised. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140 beats per minute with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain, chest clear on auscultation with equal air entry, no focal neurological deficit, no calf swelling or tenderness, uterus soft and non tender with no contractions palpable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 79 g/L at her recorded baseline (115 to 155), reticulocytes appropriately raised, white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 8 mg/L (less than 5), chest radiograph not yet performed, cardiotocograph normal with baseline 140 beats per minute and normal variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her pain?

options.text: Admit for intravenous morphine with hydration and thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: A painful crisis in pregnancy requires prompt, adequate opioid analgesia, with the aim of giving the first dose within 30 minutes, alongside fluids, warmth and oxygen if saturations fall, and low molecular weight heparin because pregnancy and the crisis are additive thrombotic risks. Morphine is the preferred strong opioid in this setting and is titrated to effect rather than withheld out of concern about the fetus. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy

options.text: Admit for intramuscular pethidine with hydration and thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: Pethidine is specifically avoided in this condition because its metabolite norpethidine accumulates and lowers the seizure threshold, and repeated intramuscular injections are poorly tolerated during a prolonged crisis. Other strong opioids provide equivalent analgesia without that hazard. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy

options.text: Admit for oral paracetamol alone with hydration and thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: Simple analgesia has already failed at home and is inadequate for a severe crisis, and undertreatment of pain is a well documented failure in the care of this condition. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are also restricted after 32 weeks, which further narrows the non opioid options later in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy

options.text: Admit for urgent exchange transfusion with hydration and thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke, multi organ failure or a crisis unresponsive to full supportive care, none of which applies to a woman with clear lungs, normal saturations and a haemoglobin at her own baseline. Transfusing reflexively exposes her to alloimmunisation that complicates later care. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy

options.text: Discharge on oral oxycodone with hydration advice and thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: A severe crisis in pregnancy warrants admission for monitoring, because acute chest syndrome can develop over the following 24 to 72 hours and fetal surveillance is required. Discharge also removes the observation that would detect that deterioration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sickle cell disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Sickle cell disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy increases both the frequency of painful crises and the risk of pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and venous thromboembolism in women with sickle cell disease, so care is shared between obstetrics and haematology from booking. A painful crisis is a clinical diagnosis with no confirmatory test, and the single most common failure in its management is inadequate and delayed analgesia, often driven by misplaced concern about opioid use. Acute chest syndrome is the complication that turns a painful crisis into a life threatening illness, and it typically appears one to three days into an admission, which is why a woman with clear lungs on arrival still needs inpatient observation. Exchange transfusion has a defined set of indications and is not a treatment for uncomplicated pain.
key_points: Adequate opioid analgesia should be given within 30 minutes of assessment
Pethidine is avoided because norpethidine lowers the seizure threshold
A haemoglobin at the woman's own baseline argues against an aplastic or sequestration crisis
Acute chest syndrome typically develops 24 to 72 hours into an admission
Low molecular weight heparin is given because the risks are additive
explanation.pearls: Any woman with sickle cell disease admitted with a painful crisis who develops a new oxygen requirement, fever or chest signs should have an urgent chest radiograph and be discussed for exchange transfusion, because acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in this group and deteriorates over hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of sickle cell disease in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Sickle cell disease in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: An anti-Kell antibody titre of 1 in 16 at twenty weeks with a partner heterozygous for the Kell antigen
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her antibody screen at booking detected anti-Kell, and the repeat titre today is 1 in 16.

She received two units of red cells after a retained placenta in her first pregnancy, and that baby was well with no jaundice. Her blood group is O RhD positive, so anti-D is not relevant to her care. Genotyping shows her partner is heterozygous for the Kell antigen, and cell free fetal DNA testing reports the fetus as Kell antigen positive. The anatomy ultrasound today is structurally normal with no ascites, no skin oedema and a normal amniotic fluid volume.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, fetal movements reported as normal, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Maternal blood group O RhD positive, antibody screen positive for anti-Kell with a titre of 1 in 16, paternal genotype heterozygous for the Kell antigen, cell free fetal DNA reports the fetus as Kell antigen positive, anatomy ultrasound structurally normal with no ascites or skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for fetal surveillance?

options.text: Repeat the antibody titre monthly and intervene when it reaches 1 in 32
options.rationale: Titres correlate poorly with the severity of fetal anaemia for this antibody, because the mechanism is suppression of erythroid precursors rather than haemolysis of circulating cells, so a modest titre can accompany severe anaemia. Referral thresholds for this antibody are accordingly lower than for anti-D and titre alone does not guide timing. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Arrange serial amniocentesis for amniotic fluid bilirubin from 24 weeks
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid bilirubin measurement assumes anaemia is produced by haemolysis, which generates the bilirubin being measured, and it therefore underestimates severity when the mechanism is marrow suppression. It has in any case been superseded by non invasive Doppler assessment, which avoids the procedure related risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Give anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 and 34 weeks and continue routine care
options.rationale: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation to the RhD antigen only, and this woman is RhD positive with an antibody to a different red cell antigen entirely. There is no immunoglobulin preparation that prevents or treats sensitisation to this antigen. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Plan delivery at 37 weeks with no additional antenatal surveillance
options.rationale: Severe fetal anaemia and hydrops can develop well before term, so a delivery plan without surveillance leaves a treatable condition undetected in the interim. Intrauterine transfusion in the second and third trimesters is what prevents that outcome. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn

options.text: Refer for serial middle cerebral artery Doppler velocity surveillance
options.rationale: With an antigen positive fetus confirmed, surveillance is by serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity in a fetal medicine unit, since a value above 1.5 multiples of the median predicts moderate to severe anaemia and triggers fetal blood sampling with intrauterine transfusion. This non invasive measure is particularly important for this antibody because the titre is an unreliable guide to severity. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

explanation.summary: Red cell alloimmunisation is no longer dominated by anti-D since routine prophylaxis, so antibodies such as anti-Kell, anti-c and anti-E now account for much of the serious disease seen in practice. Anti-Kell is distinctive because the antigen is expressed on erythroid progenitors, so the antibody suppresses red cell production in the fetal marrow in addition to causing haemolysis, and the result is anaemia with comparatively little bilirubin production. That mechanism explains two practical consequences: maternal titres and amniotic fluid bilirubin both underestimate severity, and referral thresholds for this antibody are set lower than for anti-D. Management therefore rests on establishing the fetal antigen status, by cell free fetal DNA where available or by paternal genotyping, and then on serial middle cerebral artery Doppler in a unit able to perform intrauterine transfusion.
key_points: The antigen is expressed on erythroid precursors, so marrow suppression occurs
Titres correlate poorly with severity for this antibody
Amniotic fluid bilirubin underestimates anaemia when haemolysis is not the mechanism
A heterozygous partner means the fetal antigen status must be determined
Peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median triggers intervention
explanation.pearls: Because anti-Kell suppresses erythropoiesis rather than simply destroying circulating cells, an affected fetus can be severely anaemic with a maternal titre as low as 1 in 8, which is why that titre rather than the 1 in 32 used for anti-D is the usual referral threshold.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Guidelines on the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin
BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn

subtopic_detail: Immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative parvovirus serology at sixteen weeks in a childcare worker exposed to slapped cheek rash
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 30 year old childcare worker at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. Three weeks ago several children in her room developed a bright red rash on both cheeks, and a fortnight ago she had two days of aching joints in her hands and a mild fever that she put down to a virus.

She feels well now and reports normal fetal movements for her gestation. She asks whether the outbreak at work could harm the baby. Her serology taken this week reports immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative for parvovirus B19, with rubella immunoglobulin G immune and cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking. An ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling currently, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative, rubella immunoglobulin G immune, cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking bloods, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound shows a structurally normal fetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and continue routine antenatal care without extra surveillance
options.rationale: Recent maternal infection at this gestation carries a real risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops over the following weeks, and a single normal scan at the time of diagnosis does not exclude it developing later. The risk window is the reason surveillance is time limited rather than absent. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy because of the risk of fetal abnormality
options.rationale: This virus does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome, and the fetal risk is a treatable anaemia rather than structural damage, with the great majority of pregnancies proceeding normally. Offering termination misrepresents the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange weekly ultrasound for fetal anaemia and hydrops for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, performed weekly for 8 to 12 weeks after maternal infection, detects developing anaemia at a stage when intrauterine transfusion can be given and hydrops reversed. Surveillance is time limited because the risk is concentrated in that interval and falls away afterwards. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother and continue routine care
options.rationale: There is no evidence that maternal immunoglobulin prevents fetal infection or anaemia with this virus, and it would replace the surveillance that actually changes outcome. The effective intervention is transfusion of the fetus once anaemia is detected. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid testing and then reassess
options.rationale: Confirming that the fetus is infected does not alter management, because treatment is triggered by anaemia rather than by infection, and amniocentesis carries a procedure related loss rate and a risk of worsening transplacental passage. The near pair here is cytomegalovirus, where amniocentesis does change counselling and is appropriate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum in children and a self limiting arthropathy in adults, and around half of pregnant women are already immune, so establishing susceptibility with paired immunoglobulin M and G is the first step after an exposure. The virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the fetal consequence is aplastic anaemia that can progress to high output cardiac failure and hydrops, with the risk highest when infection occurs before 20 weeks and concentrated in the 8 to 12 weeks following maternal infection. Unlike cytomegalovirus and rubella, it does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome or late neurodevelopmental sequelae in survivors, which substantially changes the tone of counselling. The intervention that alters outcome is intrauterine transfusion for detected anaemia, and spontaneous resolution of mild hydrops also occurs, so surveillance rather than intervention is the initial response.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M positive with immunoglobulin G negative indicates very recent infection
Fetal risk is anaemia and hydrops rather than structural malformation
Risk is concentrated in the 8 to 12 weeks after maternal infection
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity detects anaemia non invasively
Intrauterine transfusion can reverse hydrops and is the effective intervention
explanation.pearls: Fetal hydrops from this infection can resolve spontaneously as the fetal marrow recovers, so a fetus with early hydrops and a peak systolic velocity below 1.5 multiples of the median is watched closely rather than transfused immediately.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

subtopic_detail: Fever with diarrhoea and backache at thirty weeks after eating soft cheese and pre prepared salad with a negative urine dipstick
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 33 year old woman at 30 weeks who has had two days of fever, muscle aches, headache and loose stools. She has no urinary frequency, no dysuria and no loin tenderness, and she has no cough or sore throat.

She tells you she has been careful with food but ate a soft cheese platter and a pre prepared supermarket salad at a family gathering five days ago. She looks flushed and unwell. Her uterus is soft and non tender with no contractions, and the cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 165 beats per minute with reduced variability that has not been present on previous traces. Her urine dipstick is negative for nitrites, leucocytes and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 165 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Flushed and unwell, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft with a non tender uterus, no renal angle tenderness, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick negative for nitrites leucocytes and protein, cardiotocograph baseline 165 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and start oral azithromycin pending the results
options.rationale: A macrolide is not reliable therapy for the organism suggested by this food history and illness pattern, and oral therapy is inadequate for a febrile bacteraemic pregnant woman with fetal compromise on the trace. Intravenous therapy is required while cultures are processed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin empirically
options.rationale: A febrile flu like illness with diarrhoea after eating high risk foods in the third trimester, with an unexplained fetal tachycardia, should be treated as listeriosis until blood cultures exclude it, and high dose intravenous penicillin or amoxicillin is the effective regimen. Empirical treatment is started before confirmation because delay is associated with fetal loss, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start oral cefalexin pending the culture result
options.rationale: Cephalosporins have no useful activity against this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to the entire class, so a reflex choice of cephalosporin for a febrile pregnant woman would leave the infection untreated. A negative urine dipstick also argues against the urinary source cefalexin would be chosen for. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take a stool culture and withhold antibiotics pending the stool result
options.rationale: Stool culture is insensitive for this organism and the diagnosis is made on blood culture, so waiting for stool results both delays and misdirects the investigation. Withholding antibiotics in a bacteraemic pregnant woman with fetal tachycardia is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous ceftriaxone empirically today
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is a reasonable empirical choice for many infections in pregnancy but shares the class wide gap in activity against this organism. The near pair here is that ceftriaxone plus a penicillin would cover both possibilities, whereas ceftriaxone alone leaves the very diagnosis the food history suggests untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Listeriosis is rare but disproportionately affects pregnant women, in whom cell mediated immunity is relatively suppressed, and the maternal illness is often mild and non specific with fever, myalgia, headache and diarrhoea rather than a dramatic sepsis picture. The clue is usually the food history, since the organism grows at refrigeration temperatures and is associated with soft cheeses, pre prepared salads, deli meats, pate and smoked seafood, all of which are covered by Australian food safety advice in pregnancy. Diagnosis is by blood culture, because stool culture is insensitive and serology is not useful, and the laboratory should be told that listeriosis is suspected. The critical prescribing point is that the organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, so the standard empirical cephalosporin chosen for a febrile pregnant woman will miss it, and high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is required.
key_points: Maternal illness is often mild and non specific despite serious fetal risk
The food history is frequently the only pointer to the diagnosis
Diagnosis is by blood culture, since stool culture is insensitive
The organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins
Unexplained fetal tachycardia may be the first sign of fetal infection
explanation.pearls: Australian food safety advice in pregnancy targets this organism specifically because it multiplies at refrigerator temperatures, which is why chilled ready to eat foods such as pre prepared salads, soft cheeses and cold deli meats are the recognised vehicles rather than food left unrefrigerated.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: Hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea with an early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone of 9 nmol/L in a twenty three year old
stem:
You are the gynaecologist seeing a 23 year old woman with coarse dark hair on her upper lip, chin and lower abdomen that she has been waxing since she was 15, and periods that come every six to ten weeks. She is not currently seeking pregnancy and takes no regular medication.

Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and there is no acanthosis nigricans, no abdominal striae and no proximal muscle weakness. Her voice is unchanged, her clitoris is of normal size and the hair growth has been slowly progressive since adolescence rather than appearing over months. An early follicular blood test taken at 8 in the morning shows a 17 hydroxyprogesterone of 9 nmol/L, with a mildly raised total testosterone and a normal prolactin.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 14 with terminal hair on the upper lip, chin, lower abdomen and thighs, no acanthosis nigricans, no striae, no proximal myopathy, normal clitoral size, no temporal balding
data_table.Investigations: Early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone 9 nmol/L taken at 0800 (less than 6), total testosterone mildly elevated, sex hormone binding globulin within normal limits, prolactin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate mildly elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill and review her in six months
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is appropriate treatment for hirsutism and cycle control once the cause is established, but starting it now suppresses the androgens and makes the diagnostic test uninterpretable for months. The diagnosis matters because it changes genetic counselling and fertility advice. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Start metformin and refer for lifestyle support, then review in six months
options.rationale: Metformin and lifestyle measures address insulin resistance, which is not suggested by a body mass index of 22 with no acanthosis nigricans, and they do not treat an adrenal enzyme defect. Assuming polycystic ovary syndrome without excluding its mimics is the anti pattern here. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and then reassess
options.rationale: Polycystic ovarian morphology is common in young women and is frequently present in this condition as well, so the scan cannot distinguish between them. Ultrasound is also not required for the diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome when oligomenorrhoea and hyperandrogenism are both present. (Source: International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Arrange an adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulation test before treatment
options.rationale: A basal early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone above about 6 nmol/L cannot distinguish a partial 21 hydroxylase deficiency from polycystic ovary syndrome, and the stimulated value is what separates them, with a marked rise after synthetic adrenocorticotrophic hormone confirming the enzyme defect. Confirming it matters because it changes reproductive counselling, since a partner who is a carrier creates a risk of a severely affected child. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Measure a twenty four hour urinary free cortisol and then reassess her
options.rationale: Cortisol excess is excluded clinically by the absence of striae, proximal myopathy, central obesity and hypertension, so screening for it has a very low pre test probability. The near pair here is that rapidly progressive virilisation with those physical signs would make cortisol and androgen secreting tumours the priority instead. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the conditions that must be excluded before it is made are non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and, where features suggest it, an androgen secreting tumour or cortisol excess. Non-classical 21 hydroxylase deficiency is the mimic that most often escapes detection, since it presents in adolescence or early adulthood with hirsutism, acne and irregular cycles that are clinically indistinguishable from the syndrome, and polycystic ovarian morphology is frequently present as well. An early follicular morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone is the screening test, and values above roughly 6 nmol/L require an adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulation test, while values above about 30 nmol/L are diagnostic without stimulation. Rapid onset over months with virilisation, meaning voice change, clitoromegaly and temporal balding, shifts the priority to imaging for an androgen secreting tumour.
key_points: Polycystic ovary syndrome requires exclusion of its endocrine mimics
The screening test is 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the early follicular phase before 8 am
Stimulation testing separates a partial enzyme defect from the syndrome
Polycystic ovarian morphology does not distinguish between the two
Rapid virilisation suggests a tumour rather than either diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Diagnosing non-classical 21 hydroxylase deficiency changes preconception care rather than day to day treatment, because a woman with the condition whose partner carries a severe mutation has a risk of a child with the salt wasting classical form, so partner genotyping is offered before she conceives.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism
International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

subtopic_detail: Screening for gestational diabetes at twenty six weeks two years after sleeve gastrectomy in a woman with post prandial dizziness
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 34 year old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had a sleeve gastrectomy two years ago and her weight has been stable for the past year at a body mass index of 29 kg per square metre.

She tells you that if she eats anything sweet on an empty stomach she feels hot, shaky and light headed about twenty minutes later, and then washed out an hour or so after that. She takes the multivitamin, iron and vitamin B12 supplements prescribed by the bariatric service. Her booking glycated haemoglobin was 5.2 per cent, her fetal growth is on the 45th centile and her amniotic fluid volume is normal. She has been booked for a glucose tolerance test tomorrow morning and asks whether she should attend.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg per square metre, symphysis fundal height 26 cm consistent with dates, well healed laparoscopic port sites
data_table.Investigations: Booking glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.5), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200), vitamin B12 within normal limits, growth ultrasound at the 45th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to screening her for gestational diabetes?

options.text: Arrange one week of fasting and post prandial capillary glucose monitoring
options.rationale: After sleeve gastrectomy the rapid delivery of a glucose load to the small bowel produces an exaggerated early peak followed by reactive hypoglycaemia, so the test both provokes distressing symptoms and yields values that cannot be interpreted against thresholds derived from an intact stomach. A week of home capillary glucose profiles measures her actual glycaemic exposure across normal meals and is the recommended alternative in this group. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Proceed with the standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks
options.rationale: The standard load is exactly what provokes dumping and reactive hypoglycaemia after this operation, and the resulting curve is uninterpretable because the diagnostic thresholds assume normal gastric emptying. Her description of symptoms after sweet food on an empty stomach predicts that response. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Measure glycated haemoglobin alone and repeat the measurement at 32 weeks
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin is lowered in pregnancy by increased red cell turnover and is further distorted by the iron deficiency common after bariatric surgery, so it is insensitive for gestational hyperglycaemia. It is useful at booking to detect pre existing diabetes rather than to screen in the third trimester. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Measure a random plasma glucose alone and repeat the test at 32 weeks
options.rationale: A single unstandardised value has poor sensitivity and cannot characterise the fasting and post prandial pattern that determines whether treatment is needed. It would miss the woman whose fasting values are normal but whose post prandial excursions are not. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Gestational diabetes)

options.text: Omit screening because bariatric surgery removes the risk of diabetes
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery reduces but does not abolish the risk, and these women remain more likely than the general obstetric population to develop hyperglycaemia in pregnancy. The near pair here is that the operation changes how she is screened, not whether she is screened. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy after bariatric surgery is increasingly common and brings a distinct set of considerations, including micronutrient deficiency, a smaller for gestational age tendency, and an altered response to a glucose load. After a sleeve gastrectomy or a bypass, gastric emptying is accelerated, so a 75 g drink produces an early exaggerated glucose peak, a brisk insulin response and then symptomatic hypoglycaemia at two hours, a pattern that is both unpleasant and impossible to score against standard diagnostic thresholds. Australian practice in this group is to substitute a week of capillary glucose monitoring, using the same fasting and post prandial targets that would be applied to treat gestational diabetes. Nutritional surveillance runs alongside, since iron, vitamin B12, folate and fat soluble vitamin deficiencies are common and affect both the woman and the fetus.
key_points: Accelerated gastric emptying makes the standard glucose load uninterpretable
Dumping with reactive hypoglycaemia is provoked by the test itself
Capillary glucose profiles over a week are the recommended substitute
Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in pregnancy and after bariatric surgery
The operation changes how screening is done rather than whether it is done
explanation.pearls: Women who have had a bypass rather than a sleeve are additionally at risk of internal herniation as the uterus enlarges, so any pregnant woman with previous bariatric surgery and persistent or severe abdominal pain needs surgical assessment rather than reassurance that it is a pregnancy symptom.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Toxoplasma seroconversion detected at eleven weeks on repeat serology with low avidity immunoglobulin G
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 29 year old woman at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had serology taken privately before conception that was negative for toxoplasma immunoglobulin G, and a repeat panel taken last week because of a two week illness with tender neck glands and fatigue.

She keeps two cats and has been emptying the litter tray herself, and she gardens without gloves. The repeat serology is immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, and the reference laboratory reports this as consistent with infection acquired within the last three months. She feels well now. Ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with a crown rump length consistent with dates.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Small mobile non tender posterior cervical lymph nodes, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Preconception toxoplasma immunoglobulin G negative, current toxoplasma immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound reports a structurally normal fetus with crown rump length consistent with dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start oral azithromycin and arrange monthly ultrasound until delivery
options.rationale: Azithromycin has some activity against the organism but is not the agent used to reduce vertical transmission, and monthly imaging is less intensive than the surveillance an infected pregnancy requires. Choosing an unproven agent forfeits the benefit of the established one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid immediately now
options.rationale: This combination is used when fetal infection has been confirmed, and pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist that is avoided in the first trimester because of teratogenicity. Giving it before the fetal status is known exposes the fetus to the drug without evidence that it is infected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the risk of congenital infection
options.rationale: Transmission risk at 11 weeks is low, around 5 to 10 per cent, and most infected pregnancies proceed to a normal outcome, particularly with treatment. Offering termination before the fetal status is even established misrepresents the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure and continue routine care since maternal infection is benign
options.rationale: Maternal illness is indeed mild or silent, but that says nothing about the fetal consequences, which include chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification and hydrocephalus when transmission occurs early. The near pair here is that seroconversion before conception genuinely does not require action, whereas seroconversion during pregnancy does. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Start spiramycin and arrange amniocentesis for nucleic acid testing
options.rationale: Spiramycin concentrates in the placenta and is started immediately to reduce transmission across it, without crossing to treat the fetus, while amniocentesis for nucleic acid amplification testing from 18 weeks and at least four weeks after seroconversion establishes whether transmission has occurred. That result determines whether she continues spiramycin or switches to the regimen that treats established fetal infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Australia does not screen routinely for toxoplasma in pregnancy, so the diagnosis is usually made after a clinically suspicious illness or an incidental test, and interpreting the serology is the first difficulty because immunoglobulin M persists for months to years after infection. Avidity testing resolves this, since low avidity immunoglobulin G indicates recent infection while high avidity effectively excludes infection within the preceding three to four months, and a documented preconception negative result makes the timing unambiguous as it does here. The risk of transmission rises through pregnancy while the severity of fetal disease falls, so early infection is uncommon but damaging and late infection is common but usually mild or subclinical. Management follows a two branch algorithm, with spiramycin given to reduce transmission while the fetal status is determined, then either continued or replaced by pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid if fetal infection is confirmed.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M persists long after infection and cannot date it alone
Low avidity immunoglobulin G indicates infection within the last three to four months
Transmission risk rises with gestation while severity of fetal disease falls
Spiramycin reduces transmission but does not cross to treat the fetus
Amniocentesis result determines which treatment branch is followed
explanation.pearls: Amniocentesis for toxoplasma nucleic acid testing should be delayed until at least 18 weeks and at least four weeks after the estimated time of maternal infection, because sampling earlier produces false negatives before the organism has crossed the placenta in detectable amounts.

subtopic_detail: Bleeding after intercourse in a woman whose most recent primary screening test for human papillomavirus was negative, with a fleshy growth visible at the cervical os
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who has had spotting after intercourse on most occasions for the past four months, and occasionally a small amount of brown loss between periods. Her cycles are otherwise regular and not heavy.

She has had two vaginal births, uses condoms for contraception and has never smoked. Her cervical screening test 14 months ago was reported as human papillomavirus not detected. On speculum examination there is a smooth fleshy pedunculated lesion about 12 mm across protruding from the external os, and touching it with a swab reproduces a small amount of bleeding. The cervix is otherwise smooth, the vaginal walls look healthy and there is no abnormal discharge. Bimanual examination shows a normal sized mobile non-tender uterus with no adnexal mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 12 mm lesion protruding from the external cervical os that bleeds on contact, remainder of the cervix smooth with no friability, healthy vaginal walls, uterus normal size mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test 14 months ago reported human papillomavirus not detected, urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Repeat the primary human papillomavirus screening test today
options.rationale: A repeat screening test in under five years does not address a visible cervical lesion, and a negative result would be falsely reassuring because screening is not designed to assess a mass that can be seen. Symptomatic visible lesions are investigated on their own merits regardless of screening status. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review her again in three months
options.rationale: An antifibrinolytic treats heavy menstrual bleeding from a normal uterine cavity and does nothing for contact bleeding from a discrete cervical lesion. Delaying assessment by three months leaves a visible lesion unexamined histologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics and gynaecology)

options.text: Remove the lesion and send it for histological examination
options.rationale: A symptomatic pedunculated cervical lesion is removed so that the postcoital bleeding is treated and the tissue can be examined, because although the great majority are benign polyps a small proportion harbour malignancy that no amount of screening will detect. Removal of a small pedunculated polyp can be performed in the clinic by avulsion with polyp forceps, with hysteroscopic removal reserved for a broad based lesion or one arising from the canal. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities

options.text: Take endocervical swabs and treat for pelvic inflammatory disease
options.rationale: Chlamydial cervicitis causes a friable inflamed cervix with discharge rather than a discrete pedunculated mass, and there is no discharge, pelvic tenderness or cervical excitation here. Swabs remain reasonable opportunistic practice but antibiotics do not treat the lesion causing her bleeding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling first
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual and postmenopausal bleeding where the cavity is the suspected source, and it is not the priority when a bleeding lesion is directly visible on the cervix. Imaging is added if bleeding persists after the visible lesion has been removed. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

explanation.summary: Postcoital bleeding always requires the cervix to be seen, because the differential runs from benign polyps and ectropion through chlamydial cervicitis to invasive cervical cancer. Australia's primary human papillomavirus screening program has high sensitivity for the precursors of squamous cancer, but it is a screening test for asymptomatic women and a negative result does not exclude a symptomatic lesion, partly because some adenocarcinomas and rarer histological types are less reliably detected. This is why the national guidance separates the screening pathway from the investigation of symptoms: any woman with persistent unexplained postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding requires examination and, where a lesion is seen, histology, irrespective of her screening history. Cervical polyps are the commonest visible cause and removal is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: A negative screening test never excludes a symptomatic visible cervical lesion
Postcoital bleeding mandates direct visualisation of the cervix
Removal of a symptomatic polyp is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Small pedunculated polyps can be avulsed in clinic; broad based lesions need hysteroscopy
Persistent bleeding after polypectomy prompts endometrial assessment
explanation.pearls: Around 1 in 200 to 1 in 1000 clinically typical cervical polyps contains malignancy or premalignancy on histology, which is the entire reason the specimen goes to the laboratory rather than the bin after an otherwise routine clinic avulsion.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the management of screen-detected abnormalities
RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal uterine bleeding

subtopic_detail: Antenatal serology at twelve weeks showing no protective antibody against rubella in a woman with no record of childhood immunisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing the results of the first antenatal visit for a 27 year old woman at 12 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She arrived in Australia as a teenager and has no immunisation records from her country of birth.

She is well, has no rash and reports no recent contact with anyone unwell. Her booking bloods show rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, and her varicella IgG is protective. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are all negative, her blood group is O positive with no atypical antibodies, and her full blood count is within normal limits. She asks what should be done about the rubella result.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, varicella IgG protective, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative, human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, blood group O positive with antibody screen negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rubella status?

options.text: Reassure her, as the absent IgM excludes any risk to this pregnancy
options.rationale: A negative IgM shows she has no current infection but says nothing about her susceptibility, which is precisely what the low IgG demonstrates and what leaves her at risk for the remainder of this pregnancy and in future ones. Conflating absence of current infection with immunity is the reasoning error here. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.text: Give measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at her next antenatal visit
options.rationale: This is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy, so administering it antenatally is the specific error being tested even though the woman genuinely needs the vaccine. The indication is correct and only the timing is wrong. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy

options.text: Give rubella immunoglobulin now and repeat her serology in four weeks
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has a limited and contested role after a significant exposure in a non-immune pregnant woman and has no place in the absence of any exposure. It does not produce lasting protection and is not a substitute for vaccination. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination in pregnancy)
