You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care to a 29 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. For six weeks she has had pain across the front of her pelvis and over both buttocks that is worst when she turns in bed, climbs stairs or stands on one leg to dress.

She works as a primary school teacher and is now walking with a waddling gait and taking paracetamol most days. Fetal movements are normal and there have been no contractions, no vaginal loss and no urinary symptoms. Her blood pressure and urinalysis at each visit have been unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tenderness on direct palpation over the pubic symphysis and over both sacroiliac joints, pain reproduced on the active straight leg raise and on the posterior pelvic pain provocation test, full painless range of movement at both hips, no lumbar spine tenderness, normal power and reflexes in both legs with intact perineal sensation, uterus soft and non tender with fundal height consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein, nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Advise rest from work with avoidance of all weight bearing activity until delivery, and certify her as unfit for duties
options.rationale: Prolonged rest and complete avoidance of loading worsen deconditioning and pain and are explicitly not recommended, and graded activity within pain limits is the goal instead. Workplace modification may well be needed but is tailored rather than delivered as blanket rest. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints, and review her once it has been reported
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for features suggesting another pathology, such as radicular pain with neurological deficit, saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction, fever or a history of malignancy, none of which are present. Pelvic girdle pain is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by provocation testing. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Refer her to a pelvic health physiotherapist for an individualised exercise program and a pelvic support belt
options.rationale: Pregnancy related pelvic girdle pain responds best to physiotherapy that combines education, activity modification, stabilising exercise and a pelvic support belt, and this has the strongest evidence of any intervention for the condition. Simple analgesia with paracetamol continues alongside, but the referral is the step that changes her function. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug at the lowest effective dose for her pelvic pain
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are avoided in the second half of pregnancy because of the risk of constriction of the ductus arteriosus and of oligohydramnios through reduced fetal renal perfusion. Paracetamol remains the analgesic of choice with physiotherapy as the mainstay. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Book an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks on the grounds that vaginal birth will aggravate her pelvic symptoms
options.rationale: Caesarean section does not improve pelvic girdle pain outcomes and adds surgical morbidity to a woman who already has reduced mobility, so the condition alone is not an indication. Birth planning instead focuses on positioning, avoiding extremes of hip abduction and documenting her comfortable range. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy related pelvic girdle pain affects around one in five pregnancies and arises from altered load transfer through the pelvic ring under the influence of increasing mass, changed posture and ligamentous laxity. It is diagnosed clinically by pain located between the iliac crest and the gluteal fold, with or without symphyseal pain, reproduced by provocation tests such as the posterior pelvic pain provocation test and the active straight leg raise, and it is distinguished from lumbar radicular pain by the absence of dermatomal sensory loss, weakness or reflex change. Management is conservative and multimodal, centring on physiotherapy delivered by a clinician experienced in pelvic health, activity modification, a pelvic support belt and paracetamol, with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs avoided after the first half of pregnancy. Most women improve substantially within three months of birth, and persistent severe symptoms warrant ongoing physiotherapy rather than imaging. Red flags that redirect the assessment include fever, neurological deficit, bladder or bowel dysfunction and pain that is unrelieved by rest.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, using pain location plus provocation tests, and imaging is not required.
Physiotherapy with education, stabilising exercise and a support belt is the first line intervention.
Complete rest is counterproductive; graded activity within pain limits is recommended.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are avoided after about twenty weeks because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios.
Neurological deficit, fever or bladder dysfunction move the assessment away from pelvic girdle pain.
explanation.pearls: The active straight leg raise doubles as a treatment guide: if the leg lifts more easily when the examiner compresses the pelvis, a pelvic support belt worn low over the greater trochanters is likely to relieve symptoms.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: Interventions for preventing and treating pelvic and back pain in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain with shallow attachment on day nine postpartum where feeding has not yet been formally assessed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman nine days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. She describes a stabbing pain each time the baby attaches that eases part way through the feed, and she has started to dread feeds.

Her sister told her the baby has a tongue tie and that it needs cutting. The baby feeds for about fifty minutes each time, ten times a day, and regained birthweight yesterday. There is no breast lump, redness or fever.

data_table.Examination: Both nipples with a wedge shaped compression line and a shallow superficial fissure at the base of the left nipple, no cracks or exudate, breasts soft after feeds with no erythema or focal tenderness, infant with a thin membrane from the floor of the mouth to just behind the tongue tip, tongue elevates to the mid mouth when crying and extends to the lower lip margin, infant alert with moist mucous membranes and normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Infant weight 3420 g today with birthweight 3390 g, eight wet nappies and four yellow stools in the last 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer the baby for immediate frenotomy on the basis of the visible membrane and her description of painful attachment
options.rationale: Division is considered only when a restrictive tongue tie is demonstrated to be impairing feeding after a structured feeding assessment, because a visible frenulum is present in many babies who feed without difficulty. Cutting first means a proportion of women keep the pain and lose the chance to fix the attachment. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

options.text: Arrange a structured feeding assessment with a lactation consultant to observe positioning, attachment and milk transfer
options.rationale: Nipple pain with a wedge shaped compression line is the signature of shallow attachment, which is the commonest cause of nipple trauma and is correctable, and an observed feed is the only way to assess positioning, attachment, suck and transfer together. The assessment also determines whether any tongue restriction is functionally significant before irreversible intervention is considered. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

options.text: Prescribe topical miconazole gel for the infant and an antifungal cream for both nipples after each feed for two weeks
options.rationale: Candidal nipple infection causes burning pain that persists after the feed and is often accompanied by oral plaques or a persistent nappy rash, whereas pain that occurs on attachment and eases during the feed is mechanical. Treating for thrush here would delay the correction of attachment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Advise expressing and giving all feeds by bottle for two weeks so that the nipple fissure has a chance to heal fully
options.rationale: Two weeks of exclusive expressing at this stage risks supply and often ends direct breastfeeding altogether, and it leaves the attachment problem uncorrected for when feeds resume. Short term expressing has a place only when trauma is so severe that feeding cannot continue while attachment is being corrected. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain)

options.text: Commence oral domperidone to increase her supply and recommend she offer formula top ups after each breastfeed
options.rationale: Her baby has regained birthweight with eight wet nappies a day, so supply is adequate and there is no indication for a galactagogue or for supplementation. Domperidone also carries a dose related risk of QT prolongation and is used only for demonstrated low supply after feeding technique has been optimised. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Nipple pain is the commonest reason women stop breastfeeding in the first fortnight, and the great majority of cases are caused by shallow attachment rather than by infection or tongue tie. The history that points to a mechanical cause is pain at the moment of attachment that eases as the feed progresses, and the examination finding is a compressed, wedge shaped or blanched nipple after the feed with fissuring at the base. Candidal infection by contrast causes burning that persists or worsens after feeds, while bacterial infection produces a weeping fissure with surrounding erythema. Ankyloglossia is common, present in up to ten per cent of infants, but only a minority of visible ties restrict function, so Australian guidance requires a structured feeding assessment demonstrating impaired function before frenotomy is offered. Early skilled support preserves breastfeeding: most women whose attachment is corrected report a substantial reduction in pain within days without any procedure on the baby.
key_points: Pain at attachment that eases during the feed, with a wedge shaped compression line, indicates shallow attachment.
Burning pain persisting after feeds with oral plaques suggests candida, a different problem with a different treatment.
A visible frenulum is common and does not itself indicate frenotomy; functional restriction must be demonstrated.
A structured feeding assessment observing positioning, attachment and transfer is the pivotal investigation.
Adequate weight gain and wet nappies exclude low supply and remove any indication for galactagogues or top ups.
explanation.pearls: Assess the tongue functionally rather than by appearance: an infant who can elevate the tongue to the mid mouth with the jaw open and extend it past the lower gum has adequate mobility, and pain in that setting is almost always attachment related.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Australasian College of Physicians: Position statement on ankyloglossia

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine device visible below the gestational sac on ultrasound at seven weeks in a continuing pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in an early pregnancy assessment clinic seeing a 33 year old woman with a positive pregnancy test who has a copper intrauterine device in place, inserted two years ago. She has two children and wishes to continue this pregnancy.

She has had light spotting for two days but no pain, fever or discharge. She could not feel her threads when she checked last month and did not seek review at the time.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, speculum examination showing a closed cervix with threads visible at the external os and a small amount of old blood in the vagina, uterus consistent with dates on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine gestational sac with a fetal pole and cardiac activity at 7 weeks 1 day, the intrauterine device lying in the lower uterine cavity below the gestational sac, no adnexal mass, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give a prophylactic course of oral doxycycline and defer any decision about the device until the second trimester scan
options.rationale: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy after the first trimester because of effects on developing teeth and bone, and prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce the obstetric risks of a retained device. Deferring past the first trimester also forfeits the window in which removal is easiest and most beneficial. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Leave the device in place and arrange serial ultrasound surveillance for chorioamnionitis through the second trimester
options.rationale: Retention is associated with roughly double the rate of second trimester loss, preterm birth and intrauterine infection, and ultrasound surveillance cannot prevent those outcomes. Leaving the device is the fallback when the threads are not visible and removal would require instrumentation of the uterus. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic retrieval of the device under general anaesthesia on the next available elective operating list
options.rationale: Hysteroscopy in an ongoing pregnancy distends the cavity with fluid and carries a far higher risk of membrane rupture and pregnancy loss than simple traction on visible threads. It is not used for device retrieval in a continuing pregnancy. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Remove the device now by gentle traction on the visible threads, having counselled her about the small risk of miscarriage
options.rationale: When the threads are visible and the device lies below the gestational sac, early removal roughly halves the rates of miscarriage, preterm birth and chorioamnionitis compared with leaving it in situ, so removal is recommended despite a small immediate procedural risk. The conversation covers that a proportion of women miscarry around the time of removal even though the overall risk is lower with removal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

options.text: Refer her for uterine artery Doppler assessment at twelve weeks and manage the pregnancy as high risk without intervention
options.rationale: Uterine artery Doppler is used to stratify risk of pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction and says nothing about the risks created by a retained intrauterine device. Labelling the pregnancy high risk without acting on the modifiable factor leaves the actual hazard untouched. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with an intrauterine device in situ is uncommon but carries substantially increased risks of miscarriage, second trimester loss, chorioamnionitis and preterm birth if the device remains through the pregnancy. The first step in any woman with a positive test and a device in place is to establish the location of the pregnancy, because the proportion of pregnancies that are ectopic is higher in device users even though the absolute risk of ectopic pregnancy is lower than in women using no contraception. Once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed and the woman wishes to continue, removal is recommended when the threads are visible, ideally in the first trimester, and this reduces adverse outcomes by roughly half compared with retention. If the threads are not visible, blind instrumentation is avoided and the device is left in place with counselling about the elevated risks and the need to seek review for fever, pain or bleeding. The device is documented in the notes so that it is sought at delivery and after the placenta is examined.
key_points: Confirm the location of the pregnancy first, since device users who conceive have a higher proportion of ectopic pregnancies.
With visible threads and a continuing intrauterine pregnancy, early removal halves the risks of loss, preterm birth and infection.
If the threads are not visible, the device is left in place rather than blindly instrumented.
Hysteroscopic retrieval is not used in a continuing pregnancy because of the risk of membrane rupture.
Document the retained device so that it is looked for at birth and with the placenta.
explanation.pearls: The single practical determinant of management is whether the threads are visible at the external os: visible threads mean gentle traction in clinic, and absent threads mean counselling and retention, with no role for blind hooks or hysteroscopy in a wanted ongoing pregnancy.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Intrauterine contraception

subtopic_detail: A tense tender vulval swelling with fluctuance at the posterior introitus in a woman with a second episode in two years
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 28 year old woman with three days of increasing pain at the entrance to the vagina on the right, now so severe that she cannot sit or walk comfortably.

She had a similar swelling on the same side two years ago that was drained with a scalpel incision in this department and recurred within four months. She is otherwise well, uses condoms for contraception and had a negative sexual health screen six months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant swelling of 4 cm at the right posterior introitus displacing the labium laterally, overlying skin erythematous and thinned at one point, marked tenderness on palpation, no surrounding induration extending onto the thigh or perineum, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, cervix healthy on speculum examination with no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, self collected vaginal swab for nucleic acid testing sent for chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange excision of the entire gland under general anaesthesia and send the specimen for histological examination
options.rationale: Gland excision carries risks of significant bleeding from the underlying vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia, and it is reserved for repeated recurrence after lesser procedures or when malignancy is suspected. Malignancy is considered particularly in women over forty with a solid or irregular mass. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Incise and drain the abscess under local anaesthesia and pack the cavity with ribbon gauze for removal in 48 hours
options.rationale: Simple incision with packing relieves pain but the tract closes over as it heals, which is why recurrence approaches one in three and why this woman is back with a second episode on the same side. It remains acceptable where a catheter is unavailable. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for seven days and arrange outpatient review at the end of the course
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not resolve a tense fluctuant collection, which needs drainage, and they are added only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, pregnancy or immunosuppression. Relying on them here prolongs severe pain and risks spontaneous rupture with an unstructured tract. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange marsupialisation of the gland on the next elective theatre list and manage her pain with oral analgesia meanwhile
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is an effective definitive option but requires theatre and usually regional or general anaesthesia, and making her wait with a tense abscess is not acceptable. It is generally reserved for recurrence after catheter drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Incise the abscess under local anaesthesia and insert a balloon tipped catheter to be left in place for four weeks
options.rationale: Insertion of a balloon tipped catheter after incision creates a permanent epithelialised drainage tract and reduces recurrence to roughly five to fifteen per cent, compared with about a third after simple incision and drainage, which is the pattern she has already experienced. The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia and the catheter remains for four to six weeks while the tract epithelialises. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

explanation.summary: A Bartholin abscess forms when the duct of the greater vestibular gland obstructs and the retained secretion becomes infected, typically with mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than with a sexually transmissible organism, although testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is still offered. The key management principle is that drainage must create a tract that stays open, because a cavity that simply collapses and heals recurs in around a third of women. Insertion of a balloon tipped catheter through a small incision, left in place for four to six weeks, allows the tract to epithelialise and reduces recurrence substantially while being performed under local anaesthesia in the emergency department or clinic. Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression rather than routinely. In women over forty, and in any woman with a solid, fixed or irregular mass, biopsy or excision is considered because carcinoma of the gland, though rare, presents in this way.
key_points: Drainage that leaves a patent epithelialised tract is what prevents recurrence, not the drainage itself.
Balloon catheter insertion reduces recurrence to roughly five to fifteen per cent compared with about a third after simple incision.
Antibiotics are adjunctive and indicated for cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression.
Marsupialisation and gland excision are reserved for recurrence after catheter drainage.
A solid or irregular vulval mass, particularly over the age of forty, prompts biopsy for carcinoma.
explanation.pearls: Place the incision on the mucosal surface just outside the hymenal ring rather than on the skin of the labium, because a tract that opens into the vestibule drains along the gland's natural course and a skin incision tends to produce a scarred, poorly draining channel.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses
BMJ Best Practice: Bartholin cyst and abscess

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with vomiting at twenty six weeks where ultrasound of the appendix is non diagnostic
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked by the surgical team to review a 30 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation who has had 18 hours of central abdominal pain that has moved to the right side, with nausea and two vomits and no appetite.

She has had no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms and no vaginal loss, and she reports normal fetal movements. She has had no previous abdominal surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 152 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness with guarding in the right flank at the level of the umbilicus, pain worse when she lies on her left side, uterus soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, no renal angle tenderness, cardiotocograph with normal baseline variability and no decelerations, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (5.5 to 15.0 in pregnancy) with neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine with no organisms and no pyuria, lipase within normal limits, transabdominal ultrasound reporting the appendix as not visualised with no free fluid and a normal right kidney

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen without gadolinium contrast, to be reported urgently by the radiologist
options.rationale: When ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix in pregnancy, magnetic resonance imaging is the next investigation because it has high sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis, involves no ionising radiation and reliably identifies alternative diagnoses. Gadolinium is omitted as it crosses the placenta and is avoided unless the benefit is compelling. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids and observation with serial examination and repeat inflammatory markers in 12 hours
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable when the clinical probability is low, but she has migratory pain, localised guarding, fever and a neutrophilia, and perforation risk rises sharply with each hour of delay in pregnancy. Fetal loss after perforated appendicitis is several times that of uncomplicated appendicitis, so the diagnostic pathway is accelerated rather than paused. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics and plan non operative management with a repeat ultrasound scan in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotic only management of appendicitis has a high failure rate and is not the standard approach in pregnancy, where perforation threatens the pregnancy as well as the woman. Repeating a scan that has already failed to see the appendix is unlikely to change the picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast and abdominal shielding applied
options.rationale: Computed tomography is accurate and is used when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or the woman is too unstable to lie still for it, but it delivers fetal radiation exposure that is avoidable when a comparable test exists. Shielding does not meaningfully reduce the internal scatter dose to the uterus. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Give intramuscular betamethasone and arrange transfer to a tertiary centre before any further imaging is undertaken
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is given when preterm birth is anticipated within seven days, and she has no uterine activity or cervical change, so it does not take precedence over establishing the diagnosis. If surgery is required, steroid cover and transfer can be arranged in parallel rather than instead of imaging. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Appendicitis is the commonest non obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy and is harder to diagnose because the appendix is displaced upward and laterally by the growing uterus, nausea and leucocytosis are physiological, and abdominal guarding is blunted by a lax anterior wall. Ultrasound is the appropriate first imaging test, being safe and often diagnostic, but the appendix is frequently not visualised beyond the first trimester. Magnetic resonance imaging is then the investigation of choice, with sensitivity and specificity above ninety per cent, no ionising radiation and the additional benefit of identifying alternative causes such as ovarian torsion, degenerating fibroid, pyelonephritis and biliary disease. Delay is the main driver of harm: perforation raises fetal loss rates several fold and increases preterm birth, so the diagnostic pathway is compressed rather than extended. Laparoscopic appendicectomy is safe in experienced hands through all trimesters, and management is multidisciplinary with obstetric input on fetal monitoring, thromboprophylaxis and corticosteroid cover if preterm birth becomes likely.
key_points: The appendix shifts upward and laterally with advancing gestation, so pain localises above and lateral to the usual point.
Leucocytosis is physiological in pregnancy, which reduces the value of the white cell count in isolation.
Ultrasound is the first imaging test, and non visualisation of the appendix is common after the first trimester.
Magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium is the next test and also identifies alternative diagnoses.
Perforation substantially increases fetal loss and preterm birth, so diagnostic delay is the principal hazard.
explanation.pearls: A neutrophil count above about 80 per cent of the total white cell count is far more discriminating than the absolute white cell count in pregnancy, because the physiological leucocytosis of pregnancy does not usually produce that degree of left shift.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids

subtopic_detail: Continuous urinary leakage beginning three days after a prolonged obstructed labour with a stillbirth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional hospital seeing a 24 year old woman who arrived in Australia two years ago. She gave birth three weeks ago overseas while visiting family, after three days in labour in a village with no operating theatre, and her baby was stillborn.

Since the fourth day after the birth she has leaked urine continuously, day and night, and now wears folded cloth. She is dry between episodes of nothing, describes no urge before leakage, and has developed a rash on the inner thighs. She has no fever and her lochia stopped a week ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Ammoniacal odour with continuous clear fluid pooling in the vagina on speculum examination, an area of loss of tissue of about 1 cm in the anterior vaginal wall just below the bladder neck with surrounding induration, excoriated erythematous skin over both inner thighs, uterus involuted and non tender, no abdominal distension or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 74 micromol/L (45 to 90), midstream urine with mixed growth and pyuria, dye test with methylene blue instilled into the bladder showing blue staining of the vaginal swab

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer her for immediate surgical repair of the defect on the next available gynaecology operating list this week
options.rationale: Operating into inflamed, oedematous and partly necrotic tissue in the first weeks after an obstructed labour fistula gives a high rate of breakdown, and repair is conventionally deferred until the tissues are healthy, generally around three months after the injury. Continuous drainage in the meantime is what maximises the chance of spontaneous closure and of a successful later repair. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for continuous bladder drainage and refer her to a urogynaecology service
options.rationale: Continuous bladder drainage keeps the bladder empty so that the fistulous tract has the best chance of closing spontaneously, which occurs in a meaningful proportion of small fresh fistulas, and it immediately stops the skin damage and the social consequences of constant leakage. Specialist referral then plans nutritional support, skin care and definitive repair when the tissues have healed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Commence anticholinergic therapy for detrusor overactivity and arrange formal urodynamic studies in the coming weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat urgency incontinence, in which leakage follows an urge and the woman is dry between episodes, whereas she leaks continuously without urge and blue dye has already passed into the vagina. Urodynamics has no role once a fistula is demonstrated. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Prescribe oral trimethoprim for seven days and review her once the urinary tract infection has been fully treated
options.rationale: Pyuria and mixed growth are expected when urine pools in the vagina and the perineum is constantly wet, so treating the culture result does not address the cause and delays definitive care. Antibiotics are given for symptomatic infection alongside drainage rather than in place of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer her for pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist and review her progress in three months
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training is the first line treatment for stress incontinence, where leakage accompanies coughing or exertion and the pelvic floor is intact, and it cannot close an epithelialised communication between bladder and vagina. Offering it here would leave her leaking for another three months. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

explanation.summary: Obstetric vesicovaginal fistula is caused by pressure necrosis of the bladder base and anterior vaginal wall trapped between the fetal head and the pubic symphysis during prolonged obstructed labour, and it is rare where caesarean section is accessible but remains a major cause of morbidity worldwide. The presentation is continuous painless leakage of urine beginning a few days after the birth, usually after a labour that ended in stillbirth, and the associated injuries may include foot drop from lumbosacral plexus compression, vaginal stenosis and secondary amenorrhoea. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a dye test in which methylene blue instilled into the bladder stains a vaginal swab, and by imaging or examination under anaesthesia to define the site and size and to exclude a ureteric fistula, in which the dye test is negative. Early management is continuous catheter drainage, which allows some small fresh fistulas to close spontaneously, together with skin barrier care, nutrition and treatment of infection. Definitive repair is undertaken by an experienced surgeon once inflammation has settled, and women need psychological and social support because the condition frequently brings isolation and stigma.
key_points: Continuous painless leakage starting days after a prolonged obstructed labour is the hallmark presentation.
A positive dye test localises the leak to the bladder; a negative test with ongoing leakage suggests a ureteric fistula.
Continuous catheter drainage is the immediate treatment and allows some fresh fistulas to close without surgery.
Repair is deferred until the tissues are healthy, conventionally around three months after injury.
Associated injuries include foot drop, vaginal stenosis and amenorrhoea, and psychosocial support is integral.
explanation.pearls: If the dye test is negative but leakage continues, the next step is a three swab test with intravenous indigo carmine or contrast imaging, because a ureterovaginal fistula leaks urine that never enters the bladder and will therefore never stain blue.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

subtopic_detail: Planning intrapartum care at booking for a woman with type three female genital cutting in her first pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a booking visit for a 26 year old woman at 13 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy, who came to Australia as a child. Through a professional interpreter she says she was cut as a girl in her country of birth and that passing urine takes several minutes.

She has intercourse with difficulty and has never had a cervical screening test. She asks what will happen when the baby is born and says her mother expects her to be closed again afterwards.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fused labial tissue forming a horizontal bridge across the introitus with a posterior opening of approximately 8 mm, clitoral tissue not visible, no vulval ulceration or discharge, no inclusion cyst palpable, abdominal examination consistent with 13 weeks gestation
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods unremarkable with haemoglobin 118 g/L (110 to 140), dating ultrasound consistent with 13 weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her care?

options.text: Book an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the safest mode of birth and counsel her accordingly at this visit
options.rationale: Female genital cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean section, and recommending surgery to avoid addressing the infibulation exposes her to operative risk and to the same problem in future pregnancies. Mode of birth is decided on the usual obstetric grounds after deinfibulation has been arranged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Plan deinfibulation in the first stage of labour under epidural analgesia, with no antenatal genital procedure offered
options.rationale: Deinfibulation during labour is an acceptable fallback when a woman declines the antenatal procedure or presents late, but it is performed under time pressure by whoever is on duty and removes the opportunity for unhurried consent and healing. Offering only this option narrows her choices without clinical justification. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Offer antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester and document that reinfibulation will not be performed after the birth
options.rationale: Antenatal deinfibulation, usually offered around the second trimester, allows vaginal examination, catheterisation and birth without an emergency procedure and gives the woman time to recover and to adjust before labour. Reinfibulation is unlawful throughout Australia and this is explained clearly and non judgementally to the woman at the same consultation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Make a mandatory report to the state child protection service about the procedure she underwent as a child overseas
options.rationale: Reporting obligations attach to a child currently at risk, so the trigger would be a daughter or another girl in the family who might be cut, not the historical cutting of an adult patient. Reporting an adult woman for her own childhood experience breaches her confidence and deters women from seeking maternity care. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Defer any genital examination or discussion until 36 weeks so that she can settle into antenatal care with her midwife
options.rationale: Delaying the conversation to 36 weeks leaves no time for an antenatal procedure, for urological assessment of her voiding difficulty, or for interpreter supported discussion of her preferences. Early identification is the step that opens every subsequent option. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

explanation.summary: Female genital cutting is classified by the World Health Organization into four types, of which type three, infibulation, involves narrowing of the vaginal opening by creating a covering seal and is the type that causes obstructed voiding, dyspareunia, recurrent infection and difficulty with intrapartum examination and birth. Australian maternity care identifies affected women early, ideally at booking, using a professional interpreter rather than a family member, and offers deinfibulation antenatally, usually in the second trimester, so that the procedure is unhurried and healed before labour. Intrapartum deinfibulation remains available for women who decline or who present late. Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions and this is explained respectfully rather than punitively, acknowledging family expectations while being clear about the legal position. Child protection obligations relate to girls currently at risk, so the relevant question is whether any daughter or other child in the family may be taken overseas for cutting, and the woman herself is a patient rather than a subject of reporting.
key_points: Type three cutting narrows the introitus and causes voiding difficulty, dyspareunia and intrapartum obstruction.
Antenatal deinfibulation, usually in the second trimester, is offered so the procedure is planned rather than emergent.
Cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean section.
Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful in Australia and is discussed openly and without judgement.
Mandatory reporting concerns girls at current risk, not the adult woman's own history.
explanation.pearls: A professional interpreter who is not a family member is a clinical requirement rather than a courtesy in these consultations, because disclosure of cutting, of its type, and of family pressure for reinfibulation is unlikely when a relative is interpreting.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting
World Health Organization: Care of girls and women living with female genital mutilation

subtopic_detail: Inability to void 14 hours after an instrumental birth with a palpable bladder and a large residual volume
stem:
You are the obstetric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a 32 year old woman who gave birth 14 hours ago by forceps with an epidural in place and a second degree perineal tear repaired in theatre.

She has not passed urine since the birth. She feels a constant dull ache low in her abdomen and says she cannot tell when she needs to go. The midwife has tried a warm shower and privacy without success.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Uterus firm and central at the level of the umbilicus and displaced to the right, bladder palpable midway to the umbilicus, perineal repair intact with moderate oedema, lochia moderate without clots, lower limb power and sensation fully recovered from the epidural
data_table.Investigations: Bladder scan showing a residual volume of 780 mL, urine dipstick from earlier catheter specimen negative for nitrites and leucocytes, haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange urgent renal tract ultrasound and urology review before deciding whether the bladder needs to be drained
options.rationale: Imaging of the upper tracts is considered if retention persists despite adequate drainage or if renal function deteriorates, not before the bladder has been emptied. Delaying drainage while awaiting a scan prolongs the overdistension that causes lasting detrusor injury. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention

options.text: Perform a single in and out catheterisation now and rescan her bladder if she has not voided in the next 6 hours
options.rationale: A single intermittent catheterisation is appropriate for smaller volumes of around 500 mL or less where the bladder has not been grossly overdistended, but leaving a bladder that has already held nearly 800 mL to fill again risks repeated overdistension. The larger the volume and the longer the duration, the stronger the case for continuous drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention

options.text: Prescribe oral bethanechol to stimulate detrusor contraction and reassess her ability to void after the first two doses
options.rationale: Cholinergic agents have not been shown to resolve postpartum retention and carry cholinergic adverse effects, so they are not part of Australian practice for this problem. The mechanism here is a stretched, temporarily hypocontractile detrusor plus perineal pain and oedema, which drainage and analgesia address. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for presumed infection and encourage oral fluids with a repeat bladder scan in 4 hours
options.rationale: She has no fever and a bland dipstick, so there is no infection to treat, and increasing fluid intake without drainage further distends an already overfilled bladder. Antibiotics are given later only if symptomatic infection develops during catheter use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter for free drainage over 24 to 48 hours and then perform a formal trial of void
options.rationale: Overt postpartum retention with a volume of this size is treated by continuous drainage for at least 24 to 48 hours, which allows the overstretched detrusor to recover and prevents the permanent damage caused by repeated overdistension. A documented trial of void with post void residual measurement then confirms recovery before the catheter is removed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention

explanation.summary: Postpartum urinary retention is common and underdiagnosed, and it is classified as overt when the woman cannot void within about six hours of birth or catheter removal, and covert when she voids but retains a post void residual above about 150 mL. Risk factors include regional analgesia, instrumental birth, prolonged second stage, perineal trauma and a first birth, and the mechanism combines reduced bladder sensation, detrusor hypocontractility and pain with perineal oedema. The danger is overdistension injury: a bladder repeatedly stretched beyond about 700 to 1000 mL can sustain lasting detrusor damage with chronic voiding dysfunction. Management is prompt drainage, continuous rather than intermittent when volumes are large or duration is long, alongside adequate analgesia, mobilisation and review of constipation. A documented trial of void with post void residual measurement confirms recovery, and persisting retention after two failed trials warrants urogynaecology or urology referral and consideration of clean intermittent self catheterisation.
key_points: Overt retention is failure to void within about six hours of birth or of catheter removal.
Epidural analgesia, instrumental birth, prolonged second stage and perineal trauma are the main risk factors.
Volumes approaching or exceeding about 700 mL indicate continuous drainage rather than a single catheterisation.
Overdistension can cause permanent detrusor damage, so drainage takes priority over investigation.
Recovery is confirmed by a documented trial of void with post void residual measurement.
explanation.pearls: Measure a post void residual before discharge in any woman who had an epidural or an instrumental birth, because covert retention with a residual above 150 mL is common, causes no symptoms at the time and is the group that presents weeks later with incomplete emptying and recurrent infection.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Postpartum urinary retention

subtopic_detail: An asymptomatic simple ovarian cyst of eight centimetres found at the dating scan in the first trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman at 12 weeks gestation whose dating ultrasound reported an ovarian cyst. She has no pain and had no symptoms before the scan, and the pregnancy was conceived spontaneously.

She has heard that the cyst could twist and asks whether it should be taken out before it causes trouble. She has no personal or family history of ovarian or breast cancer.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with no palpable mass, uterus not palpable abdominally, no ascites, no supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine pregnancy at 12 weeks 2 days, a right ovarian cyst of 8.2 cm that is unilocular and anechoic with thin smooth walls, no solid components, no papillary projections and no internal vascularity on colour Doppler, left ovary normal, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic cystectomy in the second trimester to eliminate the risk of torsion later in the pregnancy
options.rationale: Elective surgery in pregnancy carries risks of miscarriage, preterm birth and anaesthetic complications, and most simple cysts of this appearance resolve or remain asymptomatic, so intervention is reserved for symptoms, torsion, rupture or features suspicious for malignancy. When surgery is genuinely needed the second trimester is indeed the preferred window. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy

options.text: Measure serum cancer antigen 125 now and refer her to gynaecological oncology if the level is above the standard cut off
options.rationale: Cancer antigen 125 rises physiologically in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester and around delivery, so it performs poorly as a discriminator and generates unnecessary alarm and referral. Risk assessment in pregnancy rests on ultrasound morphology rather than on serum markers. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis without contrast to characterise the cyst before deciding on management
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is helpful when ultrasound is indeterminate or when a complex or solid lesion needs further characterisation, whereas a unilocular anechoic cyst with thin walls and no vascularity is already fully characterised as simple. Adding imaging here delays reassurance without changing management. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy

options.text: Plan conservative management with a repeat ultrasound in the second trimester and advice about symptoms of torsion
options.rationale: A simple unilocular anechoic cyst with no solid or vascular components carries a very low risk of malignancy and a majority of such cysts resolve or remain stable during pregnancy, so surveillance with a repeat scan is appropriate. Safety netting about sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting matters because torsion is the complication that would change the plan. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst in the clinic and send the aspirated fluid for cytological examination
options.rationale: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate, cytology of cyst fluid is unreliable for excluding malignancy, and spillage of the contents of an unexpectedly malignant cyst worsens the prognosis. It is not part of the management of an adnexal cyst in pregnancy. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Adnexal masses are found in a small percentage of pregnancies, usually incidentally at the dating or morphology scan, and the great majority are benign functional cysts, corpus luteum cysts or mature teratomas. Ultrasound morphology drives management: a unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid areas, no papillary projections and no internal Doppler flow is classified as simple and carries a very low risk of malignancy at any size, whereas solid components, thick septations, papillary projections, ascites and internal vascularity raise concern. Serum tumour markers including cancer antigen 125 and alpha fetoprotein are altered by pregnancy itself and are unreliable for risk assessment. Conservative management with interval ultrasound is appropriate for simple cysts, while surgery is indicated for suspicious morphology, for acute complications such as torsion or rupture, and sometimes for very large masses obstructing the birth canal, and elective surgery is best timed to the second trimester when organogenesis is complete and the uterus is not yet obstructing access. Torsion risk is highest in masses between about six and ten centimetres and in the first trimester and early puerperium.
key_points: Ultrasound morphology, not size alone and not tumour markers, determines the risk of malignancy in pregnancy.
Cancer antigen 125 rises physiologically in pregnancy and should not be used as a screening discriminator.
Simple unilocular anechoic cysts are managed expectantly with interval scanning.
Surgery, when needed, is timed to the second trimester unless there is an acute complication.
Torsion is most likely in masses of about six to ten centimetres, and warrants explicit safety netting.
explanation.pearls: Corpus luteum cysts are the commonest adnexal finding in the first trimester and usually regress by around sixteen weeks as placental progesterone production takes over, which is why the interval scan is timed for the second trimester rather than repeated at a few weeks.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy
Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer clinical practice guidance

subtopic_detail: Escalating perineal pain with a tense unilateral vulval swelling four hours after a vaginal birth and a falling haemoglobin
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite four hours after a 26 year old woman gave birth to her first baby with a vacuum extraction and a mediolateral episiotomy that was repaired in the birth suite.

She is asking for more pain relief despite paracetamol, an anti inflammatory suppository and 10 mg of oral oxycodone, and says the pain feels like sitting on a hot rock. Her vaginal loss has been light since the birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense purple swelling of 8 cm involving the right labium majus and extending towards the ischiorectal fossa, exquisitely tender with taut shiny overlying skin, episiotomy repair intact with no active bleeding at the suture line, uterus firm and central at the umbilicus, light lochia on the pad, no vaginal wall bulge above the introitus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (115 to 165) compared with 121 g/L at admission, platelets 198 x10^9/L (150 to 400), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2), fibrinogen 4.6 g/L (2.0 to 4.5 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Apply an ice pack with firm perineal pressure, give intravenous morphine, and reassess her swelling in two hours
options.rationale: Conservative measures suit a small stable haematoma of less than about five centimetres in a haemodynamically normal woman, and they cannot control an expanding collection that has already dropped the haemoglobin by nearly 40 g/L. Watching for two hours here allows further concealed loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Give a 500 microgram dose of intramuscular ergometrine and commence an oxytocin infusion to improve uterine tone
options.rationale: Uterotonics treat bleeding from an atonic uterus, and her uterus is firm and central with light lochia, so the loss is from a vessel in the perineal tissues rather than from the placental bed. Ergometrine would also raise her blood pressure without addressing the source. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells on the ward and repeat the full blood count in four hours before any procedure
options.rationale: Transfusion supports her circulating volume but does not stop the bleeding, and a haematoma that continues to expand will simply absorb the transfused blood. Resuscitation runs in parallel with definitive surgical control rather than replacing it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter, request an urgent pelvic computed tomography angiogram, and consider embolisation of the vessel
options.rationale: Interventional radiology has an established role in a stable woman with a deep pelvic or supralevator haematoma that is difficult to reach surgically, but transferring an unstable woman with an accessible vulval collection to the radiology suite delays control. Direct surgical exploration is faster and definitive here. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Transfer her to theatre for evacuation of the haematoma with ligation of bleeding vessels, resuscitating as she goes
options.rationale: A large tense haematoma with tachycardia, hypotension and a haemoglobin fall of this magnitude needs surgical evacuation under anaesthesia with identification and ligation of the bleeding vessel, drainage and re-suture, and resuscitation proceeds alongside rather than before transfer. Definitive control is the only intervention that stops ongoing concealed loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Puerperal genital tract haematomas complicate roughly one in a thousand births and are a form of concealed postpartum haemorrhage in which the woman can lose a litre or more into the perineal, paravaginal or retroperitoneal tissues with very little visible loss. The clinical signature is severe perineal or rectal pain out of proportion to the birth trauma, unrelieved by standard analgesia, with tachycardia and a falling haemoglobin, and instrumental birth, episiotomy, first birth and prolonged second stage are the main risk factors. Infralevator haematomas are visible as a tense vulval or paravaginal swelling, while supralevator collections present with pain, unexplained shock or urinary retention and may need imaging to define. Small stable collections can be managed with ice, analgesia and observation, but an expanding haematoma, or one causing haemodynamic compromise, requires evacuation in theatre with ligation of bleeding points, drainage and repair. Antibiotics are usually given because these cavities become infected, and the woman needs debriefing and postnatal review because pain and pelvic floor symptoms can persist.
key_points: Severe perineal pain unresponsive to standard analgesia after birth is the cardinal symptom of a genital tract haematoma.
Blood loss is concealed, so tachycardia and a falling haemoglobin appear before any visible bleeding.
A firm well contracted uterus with light lochia points away from atony and towards a tissue haematoma.
Small stable collections are managed conservatively; expanding or compromising collections go to theatre.
Deep supralevator haematomas may warrant imaging and interventional radiology when the woman is stable.
explanation.pearls: Pain requiring escalating opioid within hours of a repaired episiotomy is a haemorrhage sign rather than an analgesia problem, and the bedside step that catches it is palpating the labia and performing a gentle vaginal examination rather than writing up a further opioid dose.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of postpartum haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation with pulmonary oedema at thirty weeks in a woman with previously undiagnosed rheumatic mitral stenosis
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on call when a 29 year old woman at 30 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy arrives by ambulance unable to lie flat. She grew up overseas and had rheumatic fever as a child, and she has had increasing breathlessness for three weeks that she and her midwife attributed to the pregnancy.

Tonight her heart started racing while she was cooking and she became acutely short of breath. She reports normal fetal movements and has had no contractions or vaginal loss. She is sitting upright, speaking in short phrases, and her oxygen saturation improves with oxygen by mask.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 156 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 102/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 90 per cent on room air improving to 96 per cent on 8 litres per minute by mask, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 160 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Bilateral inspiratory crackles to the mid zones, elevated jugular venous pressure, loud first heart sound with an opening snap and a low pitched diastolic murmur at the apex, no peripheral oedema, uterus soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, cardiotocograph with a baseline of 160 beats per minute, reduced variability and no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing atrial fibrillation at 156 beats per minute with no ST deviation, chest radiograph with upper lobe venous diversion and interstitial oedema, bedside echocardiogram showing a thickened doming mitral valve with a mitral valve area of 1.0 cm2, left atrial enlargement and preserved left ventricular systolic function, troponin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step in her management?

options.text: Give intravenous metoprolol in small increments to slow the ventricular rate, with intravenous furosemide and therapeutic enoxaparin
options.rationale: Rate control with a cardioselective beta blocker, diuresis and anticoagulation is exactly the right medical package for this physiology, and it is the treatment she receives as soon as her rhythm is addressed. It is not the immediate step because she is in pulmonary oedema with hypoxia and fetal compromise from a new arrhythmia, which meets the threshold for restoring sinus rhythm rather than titrating drugs. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous digoxin as a loading dose for rate control and reassess her respiratory status after the loading is complete
options.rationale: Digoxin acts slowly, controls rate poorly during high sympathetic drive, and does not address the loss of atrial contraction that has precipitated this decompensation. It has a secondary role in pregnancy where beta blockade is contraindicated or insufficient. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy

options.text: Proceed to emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia to relieve the cardiovascular burden of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Delivery in an unstable woman with severe mitral stenosis and uncontrolled tachycardia is hazardous, because the autotransfusion that follows uterine contraction and delivery acutely increases preload across a fixed obstruction. The maternal condition is stabilised first, and delivery is planned with cardiac anaesthetic and cardiology input. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy

options.text: Perform synchronised direct current cardioversion under sedation with continuous fetal monitoring and left lateral tilt
options.rationale: New atrial fibrillation causing pulmonary oedema and hypoxia in severe mitral stenosis is haemodynamic instability, and electrical cardioversion is both safe in pregnancy and the fastest way to restore the atrial contribution to filling across a fixed obstruction. Anticoagulation with heparin is started around the procedure and rate control, diuresis and cardiology review follow once sinus rhythm is restored. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy

options.text: Give an intravenous fluid bolus to improve diastolic filling across the stenotic valve and then reassess her oxygen requirement
options.rationale: Adding volume to a woman in pulmonary oedema with a fixed obstruction to left atrial emptying raises left atrial pressure further and worsens the oedema. Preload dependence matters in aortic stenosis and in right ventricular infarction, not in decompensated mitral stenosis with pulmonary congestion. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Rheumatic mitral stenosis is the valve lesion most likely to decompensate in pregnancy because the fixed orifice cannot accommodate the forty per cent rise in cardiac output and the fall in systemic vascular resistance, and the shortened diastolic filling time of tachycardia further reduces flow across the valve. Women frequently present for the first time in the late second or early third trimester with breathlessness, and a valve area at or below about 1.0 cm2 represents severe stenosis with high risk of pulmonary oedema, arrhythmia and fetal growth restriction. Atrial fibrillation is the classic precipitant of acute decompensation because atrial systole contributes a disproportionate share of filling across a stenotic valve. When the arrhythmia causes haemodynamic instability, synchronised cardioversion is performed regardless of gestation, with fetal monitoring and left lateral tilt, and it does not harm the fetus. Ongoing care involves beta blockade for rate control, cautious diuresis, therapeutic anticoagulation because of the very high thromboembolic risk of mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation, and multidisciplinary planning for a vaginal birth with a short passive second stage or an assisted birth, since the greatest haemodynamic strain occurs immediately after delivery.
key_points: Mitral stenosis decompensates in pregnancy because increased output and tachycardia both reduce flow across a fixed orifice.
A mitral valve area of about 1.0 cm2 or less indicates severe stenosis with a high risk of pulmonary oedema and arrhythmia.
Loss of atrial systole in new atrial fibrillation is the classic trigger for acute decompensation.
Synchronised cardioversion is safe at any gestation and is indicated for haemodynamic instability.
Anticoagulation is mandatory in mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation because of the high embolic risk.
explanation.pearls: The most dangerous moment is not the birth itself but the first ten to twenty minutes after delivery, when autotransfusion from the contracting uterus abruptly raises preload across a fixed valve, which is why these women are monitored in a high dependency setting through that period rather than returned to a postnatal ward.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart disease in pregnancy
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Cardiac disease in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Intensely itchy raised lesions arising within the abdominal stretch marks at 36 weeks with the navel spared
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 36 weeks gestation who has developed an intensely itchy rash over the past five days. She describes raised red patches that started in the silvery marks on her lower abdomen and have since spread to her thighs and buttocks.

The itch is worst in the evening and is disturbing her sleep. She has no itching of her palms or soles and no dark urine. She takes no regular medications and has no personal or family history of skin disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Erythematous urticated papules and plaques arising within the abdominal striae with coalescence into plaques on the outer thighs and buttocks, a clear rim of uninvolved skin immediately around the umbilicus, no vesicles or bullae anywhere, no excoriation of the palms or soles, symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, serum bile acids 4 micromol/L (less than 10), full blood count within normal limits, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat the serum bile acids and liver function tests again in one week
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid treats intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, in which the itch is worst on the palms and soles, there is no primary rash, and bile acids are elevated. Normal bile acids with a visible primary eruption rules that diagnosis out here. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks gestation on the grounds that her symptoms are unlikely to settle before then
options.rationale: Early delivery is offered in pregnancy dermatoses only when there is a fetal risk, as with pemphigoid gestationis, and polymorphic eruption carries no such risk. Delivering a woman at 37 weeks for a benign itch exposes the baby to avoidable late preterm morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence and start systemic corticosteroids while awaiting the histology result
options.rationale: Immunofluorescence showing linear C3 along the basement membrane is how pemphigoid gestationis is confirmed, and that condition begins around the umbilicus and blisters, which is the exact inverse of this distribution. Biopsy is worth doing when bullae appear or when the periumbilical skin is the focus rather than the spared area. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment with emollients and explain that the rash resolves after the birth
options.rationale: Involvement of the striae with sparing of the periumbilical skin and an absence of blistering identifies polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which is benign, carries no fetal risk and is controlled with topical corticosteroid and emollients until delivery. Symptoms settle within days to weeks after birth and recurrence in later pregnancies is uncommon. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Prescribe a topical antifungal cream for the abdominal and thigh lesions and review her again in the antenatal clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Tinea and candidal intertrigo produce a scaly annular or satellite pattern in skin folds rather than urticated plaques arising within striae. An antifungal would be the correct choice for a well demarcated scaly ring with central clearing under the abdominal apron. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, also known as pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy, is the commonest specific dermatosis of pregnancy and typically appears in the third trimester of a first pregnancy, particularly where there has been rapid abdominal distension from a large baby or a multiple pregnancy.
