Its distribution is the diagnostic feature: lesions arise within the abdominal striae and characteristically spare a rim of skin around the umbilicus, then spread centrifugally to the thighs, buttocks and arms while sparing the face, palms and soles. The main differential is pemphigoid gestationis, an autoimmune blistering disease that begins periumbilically, forms tense bullae, and is associated with small for gestational age babies and preterm birth, so it needs biopsy and systemic treatment. Intrahepatic cholestasis is excluded by the presence of a primary rash and normal bile acids, since cholestatic itch is generalised without a primary eruption. Polymorphic eruption resolves spontaneously after delivery and is managed symptomatically.
key_points: Lesions within the striae with periumbilical sparing define polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.
Pemphigoid gestationis starts around the umbilicus, blisters, and carries fetal risk.
Normal bile acids with a visible primary rash exclude intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Topical corticosteroid and emollients control symptoms until spontaneous resolution after birth.
No fetal surveillance or early delivery is required for polymorphic eruption.
explanation.pearls: Pemphigoid gestationis recurs in around three quarters of subsequent pregnancies and can flare with the combined oral contraceptive pill or at menstruation, so a woman with that diagnosis needs both prepregnancy counselling and a progestogen only or non hormonal contraceptive choice afterwards.

subtopic_detail: Disabling headache on the second postnatal day that is present on sitting up and gone within minutes of lying flat
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked to see a 29 year old woman on the postnatal ward two days after a normal vaginal birth with an epidural. She describes a severe headache across the front and back of her head that begins within a minute of sitting upright and disappears almost completely when she lies down.

She is unable to sit up to feed her baby and has not been out of bed today. The anaesthetic record documents a dural puncture with the epidural needle at insertion. She has no visual disturbance, no weakness and no convulsion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated with no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, cranial nerves intact with full eye movements, no focal limb weakness, reflexes symmetrical, no calf tenderness, epidural insertion site clean with no erythema or discharge
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, platelet count 244 x10^9/L (150 to 400), urine dipstick negative for protein, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue bed rest with regular paracetamol, oral caffeine and encouragement of oral fluids, and review her again in two days
options.rationale: Conservative therapy is a reasonable first response in the first day or for a mild headache, but the evidence that caffeine, fluids and bed rest alter the natural history is poor. Persisting with it in a woman who cannot sit up to feed her baby prolongs disability and delays bonding and mobilisation. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain with venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the cause
options.rationale: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is the dangerous postnatal mimic, but its headache is progressive and non postural and is usually accompanied by focal signs, seizures or papilloedema, none of which are present. Imaging becomes mandatory if the headache loses its postural character or if any neurological sign appears. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Commence an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion and start antihypertensive therapy for probable late onset pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: Postpartum pre-eclampsia does present with headache in the first week, but it comes with hypertension, proteinuria or deranged bloods, and her blood pressure, urine and liver tests are all normal. The strictly postural nature of this headache also does not fit a pre-eclamptic headache. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure and analyse the cerebrospinal fluid for infection
options.rationale: Another dural puncture in a woman who already has a cerebrospinal fluid leak worsens the very problem being treated. Lumbar puncture is reserved for a genuine suspicion of meningitis, which would be signalled by fever, neck stiffness and a non postural headache. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Refer her to the anaesthetic team for an epidural blood patch after explaining the procedure and its likely benefits
options.rationale: A postural headache after a documented dural puncture that prevents a woman caring for her baby is a disabling post dural puncture headache, and an autologous epidural blood patch relieves symptoms in around three quarters of women, usually within an hour. Conservative measures alone leave her bed bound for days to weeks while the dural defect heals. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

explanation.summary: Post dural puncture headache follows loss of cerebrospinal fluid through a dural defect, which lowers intracranial pressure and allows traction on pain sensitive intracranial structures when the woman sits or stands. The defining feature is its postural nature, appearing within minutes of sitting upright and relieved within minutes of lying flat, usually beginning between twelve and seventy two hours after the puncture. Associated features include neck stiffness, tinnitus, hearing change and photophobia, and a sixth nerve palsy is a recognised complication of prolonged traction. The critical clinical discipline is to keep reviewing the postural character, because a headache that becomes constant, or that is accompanied by any focal sign, seizure, fever or papilloedema, demands neuroimaging for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, subdural haematoma or infection. Untreated, the headache usually settles within one to two weeks, but an epidural blood patch shortens that substantially and is offered when symptoms are severe or prolonged.
key_points: A headache that appears on sitting and resolves on lying flat is postural until proven otherwise.
Onset is typically twelve to seventy two hours after the dural puncture.
Loss of the postural character or any focal sign mandates urgent neuroimaging.
Epidural blood patch relieves symptoms in around three quarters of women.
Conservative measures have weak evidence and should not delay definitive treatment in disabling cases.
explanation.pearls: Women who have had a dural puncture during labour carry a raised risk of chronic headache and backache for years afterwards, so document the event clearly in the discharge summary and arrange anaesthetic follow up rather than leaving the woman to attribute ongoing symptoms to motherhood.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache
BMJ Best Practice: Post dural puncture headache

subtopic_detail: Constant localised pain over a known uterine fibroid at 26 weeks with a low grade temperature and a quiet cervix
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 33 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation who presents with two days of constant pain in the right side of her abdomen. The pain does not come and go and she has felt hot and shivery at times.

A fibroid measuring 8 cm was documented on her 20 week ultrasound. She reports normal fetal movements, no vaginal bleeding and no fluid loss. She has passed urine without discomfort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised over a firm mass palpable in the right side of the uterus, uterus otherwise soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, no offensive vaginal discharge, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine microscopy showing no organisms and no white cells, ultrasound showing an 8 cm intramural fibroid with cystic change and reduced internal vascularity, normal liquor volume, cervical length 38 mm, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for myomectomy to remove the fibroid before the pain and inflammatory response worsen further during the pregnancy
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage and pregnancy loss because the fibroid vasculature is greatly expanded, so it is almost never performed. It is considered only for a pedunculated torted fibroid that cannot be managed conservatively. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids and commence nifedipine tocolysis on the basis that this pain represents established preterm labour
options.rationale: Preterm labour causes intermittent tightenings with cervical change, whereas this pain is constant and the cervix is long and closed with a reassuring cervical length. Tocolysis and steroids would be indicated if contractions with cervical shortening developed. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Start intravenous ampicillin with gentamicin and metronidazole for presumed chorioamnionitis and plan delivery if the fever persists
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis produces uterine tenderness that is generalised rather than confined to a mass, with offensive discharge, maternal and fetal tachycardia and usually ruptured membranes, none of which are present. The localisation of the tenderness to the fibroid itself is what separates the two. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Admit her for analgesia with paracetamol and a short opioid course plus hydration, with observation and expected resolution over days
options.rationale: Localised tenderness over a fibroid with a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and ultrasound cystic change and reduced vascularity is red degeneration, which is an ischaemic infarction of the fibroid as it outgrows its blood supply and settles conservatively over several days to two weeks. Analgesia and hydration are the whole of the treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy on the basis that appendicitis cannot be excluded in a pregnant woman with right sided abdominal pain
options.rationale: Appendicitis is the key surgical differential for right sided pain in pregnancy, but it migrates upward with gestation, causes anorexia and guarding, and would not show cystic change within a fibroid on ultrasound. Surgery is justified when imaging and examination point to the appendix rather than to a known fibroid. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fibroids enlarge under the hormonal and haemodynamic influences of pregnancy, and a proportion outgrow their blood supply and undergo red or carneous degeneration, most often in the second trimester and most often in fibroids larger than about 5 cm. The clinical picture is constant, well localised pain with tenderness confined to the fibroid, a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and a modest rise in inflammatory markers, which together mimic infection convincingly enough that women are frequently given unnecessary antibiotics. Ultrasound supports the diagnosis when it shows cystic or heterogeneous change with reduced vascularity within the lesion. The condition is self limiting and resolves over several days to two weeks with analgesia and hydration, though the pain is often severe enough to require short term opioids. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are effective but are used cautiously and briefly before 32 weeks because of effects on the ductus arteriosus and amniotic fluid.
key_points: Red degeneration causes constant pain localised over the fibroid rather than generalised uterine tenderness.
Low grade fever, leucocytosis and a raised C-reactive protein are expected and do not indicate infection.
Ultrasound showing cystic change with reduced vascularity within the fibroid supports the diagnosis.
Treatment is analgesia and hydration, with resolution over several days to two weeks.
Myomectomy in pregnancy risks catastrophic haemorrhage and is almost never indicated.
explanation.pearls: If a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug is used for red degeneration, keep the course under 48 hours and stop it by 32 weeks gestation, because prolonged exposure closes the ductus arteriosus prematurely and reduces fetal urine output enough to cause oligohydramnios.

subtopic_detail: Daily non prescribed oxycodone use disclosed at booking by a woman at 14 weeks who wants to stop straight away
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic booking a 26 year old woman at 14 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. She discloses that she has been taking around 100 mg of non prescribed oxycodone daily for the past two years and that she injects nothing.

She tells you she is determined to be completely off everything before the baby arrives and asks you to help her stop this week. She has no medical comorbidities, her booking bloods including hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are pending, and her first child lives with her and her partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No stigmata of intravenous drug use, no needle marks, chest clear, abdomen soft with a uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirming a single live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with 14 weeks gestation, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend to her?

options.text: Make an immediate child protection notification about the unborn baby and the older child before discussing treatment options with her
options.rationale: Leading with a statutory notification at disclosure is the single most reliable way to drive a pregnant woman out of antenatal care, and substance use alone without evidence of harm is not a threshold for notification in most Australian jurisdictions. Prenatal reporting is discussed openly with the woman and made when there are genuine concerns about the safety of a child. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Admit her for a supervised rapid inpatient detoxification over the coming week while the pregnancy is still in the second trimester
options.rationale: Withdrawal in pregnancy raises catecholamine levels and has been associated with fetal distress and miscarriage or preterm birth, and relapse rates after detoxification alone exceed three quarters. Detoxification is considered only where the woman declines maintenance and can be supported intensively with close fetal monitoring. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Commence oral naltrexone once she has stopped opioids for several days in order to block any further effect from opioid use
options.rationale: Naltrexone requires the woman to be fully withdrawn before it can be started, which imposes precisely the withdrawal that should be avoided, and safety data in pregnancy remain limited. It is an option for a woman already stable and abstinent who chooses it outside pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Support her plan to cease abruptly this week with symptomatic medication only and review her in the antenatal clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation causes the most severe withdrawal of all the options and carries the highest relapse rate, often to a dose she is no longer tolerant to. Symptomatic treatment alone is appropriate only for a woman with a very low level of dependence who has declined all other options. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Refer her urgently to a specialist drug and alcohol service for stabilisation on opioid agonist treatment alongside her antenatal care
options.rationale: Opioid agonist treatment with methadone or buprenorphine is the standard of care in pregnancy because it removes the cycles of intoxication and withdrawal that cause fetal distress, improves antenatal attendance and markedly improves birth outcomes. Australian guidance is explicit that maintenance, not abstinence, is the goal during pregnancy. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

explanation.summary: Opioid dependence in pregnancy is managed with agonist maintenance rather than withdrawal, because the stability it provides protects the fetus from the repeated episodes of withdrawal that accompany illicit use and because it anchors the woman in antenatal care. Both methadone and buprenorphine are acceptable in Australian practice, with buprenorphine associated with a shorter and milder neonatal abstinence syndrome and methadone associated with better retention in treatment for some women. Doses often need to increase through the third trimester as plasma volume and hepatic metabolism rise, and a woman whose dose is held static may report returning withdrawal symptoms late in pregnancy. Breastfeeding is encouraged on either agonist, as the amount transferred in milk is small and helps settle the neonate. Every such pregnancy needs planning for neonatal abstinence syndrome, which affects a majority of exposed babies and typically appears within the first three days for heroin, later for methadone, and requires a minimum observation period in hospital.
key_points: Opioid agonist maintenance, not detoxification, is the standard of care in pregnancy.
Withdrawal in pregnancy is associated with fetal distress and very high relapse rates.
Agonist doses frequently need to rise in the third trimester because of physiological changes.
Breastfeeding is encouraged on both methadone and buprenorphine.
Substance use alone is not a threshold for child protection notification in most jurisdictions.
explanation.pearls: Plan for a minimum of three to five days of neonatal observation after birth, and longer for methadone exposure, because neonatal abstinence syndrome from methadone can first appear beyond 72 hours of age and up to a week after the last maternal dose.

sources.label: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years
BMJ Best Practice: Opioid use disorder

subtopic_detail: Third episode of severe right upper abdominal pain after fatty food at 18 weeks with gallstones and normal liver tests
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman at 18 weeks gestation who has just recovered from her third episode of severe pain under the right ribs. Each episode has come on an hour or two after a fatty meal, built over about half an hour, lasted around four hours and then faded completely.

She vomited during the current episode and is now comfortable and hungry. She has not been jaundiced and her urine and stool colour have been normal throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no tenderness on deep palpation of the right upper quadrant between episodes, Murphy sign negative, no jaundice of the sclerae, uterus palpable at the level of the umbilicus
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits with a bilirubin of 12 micromol/L (less than 20), lipase 32 U/L (less than 60), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), ultrasound showing multiple mobile gallstones with a normal gallbladder wall thickness and a common bile duct of 4 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manage her conservatively with a low fat diet and analgesia, deferring any operation until at least six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: Expectant management in pregnancy is associated with recurrent attacks in more than half of women and a substantial rate of progression to cholecystitis, pancreatitis or admission, each of which carries its own fetal risk. It is a reasonable choice only for a single mild episode very late in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

options.text: Refer her for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy to clear the biliary tree of the stones causing her pain
options.rationale: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography treats stones in the common bile duct, and her bilirubin, liver enzymes and duct calibre are all normal, so there is nothing in the duct to clear. It would be indicated for obstructive jaundice or gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated duct. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

options.text: Refer her for laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this second trimester after discussing the risks of surgery and of continued symptoms
options.rationale: Recurrent symptomatic gallstones in pregnancy are best treated by laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and the second trimester is the optimal window because organogenesis is complete and the uterus is not yet large enough to obscure access. Deferring surgery exposes her to repeated attacks and to the complications that follow them. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid with the aim of dissolving the gallstones and preventing further episodes of her biliary pain
options.rationale: Dissolution therapy works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder, takes many months and is followed by recurrence in most patients once stopped. It has no role in a woman with recurrent symptomatic multiple stones who needs definitive treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to define the biliary anatomy before any decision about her definitive management
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is safe in the second trimester but is used when common bile duct stones are suspected, and normal liver tests with a 4 mm duct make that very unlikely. Ordering it here delays a decision that the ultrasound and the history have already made clear. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Gallstone disease is common in pregnancy because oestrogen increases biliary cholesterol saturation while progesterone reduces gallbladder motility, and symptomatic stones affect around one in a thousand pregnancies. Biliary colic is distinguished from cholecystitis by its complete resolution between episodes, a negative Murphy sign and normal inflammatory markers, and from choledocholithiasis by normal liver enzymes and a non dilated common bile duct. Historical practice was to defer surgery until after delivery, but this is now known to lead to recurrent admissions, and rates of preterm birth and fetal loss are higher in women managed conservatively than in those who undergo laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The second trimester is preferred because the teratogenic window has passed, the risk of miscarriage is lower than in the first trimester, and the uterus has not yet grown enough to compromise laparoscopic access or increase the risk of preterm labour. Standard laparoscopic precautions in pregnancy include left lateral tilt, open or optical entry, and lower insufflation pressures.
key_points: Complete resolution between attacks with a negative Murphy sign and normal markers indicates biliary colic.
Normal liver enzymes with a non dilated common bile duct effectively exclude duct stones.
Conservative management in pregnancy leads to recurrent attacks in over half of women.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the second trimester is the preferred definitive treatment.
Left lateral tilt and lower insufflation pressures are standard modifications in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Gallstone pancreatitis in pregnancy carries a fetal loss rate of around 10 to 20 per cent if the gallbladder is left in place, which is why definitive cholecystectomy should follow an episode of pancreatitis during the same admission or the same trimester rather than being deferred to after birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

subtopic_detail: Absent periods at sixteen with normal breasts, very sparse pubic hair and no uterus seen on pelvic ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16 year old girl referred because she has never had a period. Her mother reports that her breasts developed normally from about the age of eleven.

She is well, plays netball at a competitive level, has never been underweight and reports no headaches or visual symptoms. She has never been sexually active and has had no cyclical abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Height 175 cm, weight 64 kg, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, no clitoromegaly, no acne or facial hair, external genitalia otherwise normal in appearance, no palpable abdominal or inguinal masses, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound reporting no uterus identified with no structures in either adnexa clearly identified as ovaries, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (2 to 10 follicular), prolactin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to define the Mullerian anatomy and search for any obstructed uterine remnant
options.rationale: Imaging will follow, but it cannot distinguish the two conditions that produce an absent uterus with normal breasts, since both Mullerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity look similar on a scan. The karyotype is what separates them and it must come first. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Administer a progestogen challenge and interpret whether a withdrawal bleed occurs before ordering any further hormonal investigations
options.rationale: A progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium is present, and this patient has no uterus at all, so the result is uninterpretable. It is a useful step in secondary amenorrhoea where the uterus is known to be present. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure a serum testosterone level and request a karyotype, and arrange review in a service with adolescent gynaecology experience
options.rationale: Full breast development with markedly sparse sexual hair and an absent uterus points to complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, in which a 46,XY individual cannot respond to androgens so the uterus regresses under anti-Mullerian hormone while oestrogen from aromatised testosterone produces normal breasts. Testosterone in the male range with a 46,XY karyotype confirms the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to induce regular withdrawal bleeding and review her symptoms in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: Prescribing hormones before a diagnosis is made abandons the diagnostic workup in a young woman who needs to understand her own condition and its implications for fertility and gonadal cancer risk. Oestrogen replacement has a role later, once the diagnosis and the gonadal management plan are settled. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Reassure her that constitutional delay is likely given her athletic training and review her again in six months if periods have not started
options.rationale: Constitutional delay and athletic amenorrhoea both involve delayed or arrested breast development from low oestrogen, whereas this young woman has completed breast development, and neither explains an absent uterus. Reassurance here would leave gonads at risk of malignancy undiagnosed. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development and an absent uterus narrows immediately to two conditions, Mullerian agenesis and complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, and the fastest way to separate them is a karyotype with a serum testosterone. In Mullerian agenesis the karyotype is 46,XX, testosterone is in the female range and pubic and axillary hair are normal because the androgen receptor works. In complete androgen insensitivity the karyotype is 46,XY, testosterone is in the male range, and sexual hair is sparse or absent precisely because the receptor does not function, while breasts develop normally from peripheral aromatisation of that testosterone. The uterus is absent because functioning testicular tissue produced anti-Mullerian hormone in utero. Management is multidisciplinary and includes careful disclosure, psychological support, oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy, vaginal dilator therapy where needed, and a decision about the timing of gonadectomy given the malignancy risk in retained intra-abdominal gonads.
key_points: Normal breasts with an absent uterus narrows to Mullerian agenesis or androgen insensitivity.
Sparse pubic and axillary hair points to androgen insensitivity rather than Mullerian agenesis.
Karyotype with serum testosterone is the discriminating investigation.
Breast development in androgen insensitivity comes from aromatisation of testosterone to oestrogen.
Care is multidisciplinary and includes psychological support and a plan for the gonads.
explanation.pearls: Gonadectomy in complete androgen insensitivity is now usually deferred until after puberty has completed spontaneously, because the malignancy risk before adulthood is under 2 per cent and allowing the endogenous gonads to drive puberty gives better bone density than early removal followed by replacement.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Differences of sex development

subtopic_detail: Fever with hypotension and offensive bleeding three days into a first trimester loss with an open cervical os
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 24 year old woman at 10 weeks gestation. She has had heavy vaginal bleeding for three days and over the past twelve hours has developed rigors and severe constant lower abdominal pain.

Her partner says she has become vague and drowsy in the past hour. She describes the bleeding as smelling foul. Two litres of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent have been given and the blood pressure below is her value after that fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, warm peripheries with a capillary refill of 3 seconds, exquisitely tender uterus enlarged to 10 weeks size, speculum showing offensive purulent blood stained discharge with products of conception visible at an open cervical os
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 310 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), haemoglobin 92 g/L (115 to 165), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150 to 400), international normalised ratio 1.4 (0.8 to 1.2), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures, give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and arrange urgent hysterectomy as the definitive treatment
options.rationale: Hysterectomy sacrifices fertility in a 24 year old and is not needed when suction evacuation will remove the infected tissue. It is reserved for clostridial myonecrosis, uterine perforation or failure to improve after adequate evacuation and antibiotics. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy loss)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures, give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and reassess her for evacuation after forty eight hours
options.rationale: Waiting two days for antibiotics to work leaves the infected focus in place while she is already in septic shock with organ dysfunction. A period of antibiotics before evacuation is appropriate only where the woman is stable and the diagnosis of infection is uncertain. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy loss)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures, give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and administer misoprostol to complete the miscarriage
options.rationale: Medical management is slow and unreliable in an infected uterus and leaves the timing of source control to chance in a woman who is shocked. Misoprostol is a good choice for an incomplete miscarriage in a stable afebrile woman who prefers to avoid surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy loss)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures, give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and proceed to urgent surgical evacuation of the uterus
options.rationale: Septic miscarriage is an infected retained pregnancy, and antibiotics cannot sterilise infected tissue that remains in the uterus, so source control by evacuation must follow the first antibiotic dose without waiting. Delay in evacuation is the commonest contributor to progression to multiorgan failure in these women. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy loss)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures, give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and transfer her to a tertiary centre before any procedure
options.rationale: Transferring a woman in septic shock before source control wastes the hours in which she is most salvageable, and evacuation of the uterus is within the competence of any unit performing gynaecological surgery. Transfer is appropriate after evacuation if intensive care support is unavailable locally. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy loss)

explanation.summary: Septic miscarriage occurs when retained products of conception become infected, usually by a polymicrobial flora ascending from the genital tract, and it remains a leading cause of maternal death where unsafe abortion is common. The presentation combines the features of miscarriage with fever, an exquisitely tender uterus, offensive discharge and the systemic markers of sepsis, and coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury signal established organ dysfunction. Australian management follows the sepsis principles of early cultures, broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics within the hour and aggressive resuscitation, but the decisive step that distinguishes it from other sepsis is prompt surgical source control. Suction evacuation is performed as soon as antibiotics are running and the woman has been resuscitated enough to tolerate anaesthesia, rather than waiting for the fever to settle. Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to rhesus negative women, and Clostridium perfringens infection with myonecrosis or haemolysis is the one scenario that forces consideration of hysterectomy.
key_points: Fever with an exquisitely tender uterus and offensive discharge in miscarriage indicates sepsis.
Antibiotics alone cannot sterilise infected retained products, so evacuation is the source control step.
Resuscitate, culture and give antibiotics within the hour, then evacuate without waiting for defervescence.
Thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy and rising creatinine mark established organ dysfunction.
Hysterectomy is reserved for clostridial myonecrosis, perforation or failure after adequate evacuation.
explanation.pearls: Suspect Clostridium perfringens when a septic miscarriage is accompanied by a haemoglobin falling faster than the observed blood loss explains, because the alpha toxin causes massive intravascular haemolysis and that specific combination is the trigger for urgent hysterectomy rather than evacuation alone.

subtopic_detail: Empty uterus on transvaginal scan with a beta human chorionic gonadotrophin that rises by only twelve per cent in 48 hours
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in an early pregnancy assessment service reviewing a 27 year old woman with six weeks of amenorrhoea. She presented two days ago with light vaginal spotting and mild cramping low in her abdomen, which have not changed since.

She has no shoulder tip pain, no dizziness and no syncope. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease or tubal surgery. She lives fifteen minutes from the hospital and has a partner at home with her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no guarding or rebound, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass palpable, closed cervical os with a trace of old blood
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound at presentation showing an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 9 mm, no adnexal mass and no free fluid, serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 1450 IU/L at presentation and 1624 IU/L 48 hours later, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 165), blood group O rhesus positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer intramuscular methotrexate today and follow her beta human chorionic gonadotrophin on day 4 and day 7 after treatment
options.rationale: Methotrexate given for a pregnancy of unknown location may destroy a viable intrauterine pregnancy that is simply too early or too small to see, which is why the location must be established or the pregnancy shown to be non viable first. It is appropriate once an ectopic is confirmed and the woman meets the treatment criteria. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound with a further beta human chorionic gonadotrophin in 48 hours and give written advice to return urgently
options.rationale: A suboptimal rise of twelve per cent in 48 hours is inconsistent with a viable intrauterine pregnancy but does not localise the pregnancy, so continued surveillance with serial hormone measurement and repeat imaging in a stable woman is the correct course. Written safety netting matters because an ectopic can declare itself between visits. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy today to identify and treat the ectopic pregnancy that this suboptimal hormone rise has demonstrated
options.rationale: Laparoscopy in a haemodynamically stable woman with no adnexal mass and no free fluid frequently finds nothing, since an early tubal pregnancy may be too small to see and a failing intrauterine pregnancy would be missed entirely. Surgery is indicated for haemodynamic compromise or a confirmed ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Perform a uterine evacuation and send the tissue for histology to establish whether chorionic villi confirm an intrauterine pregnancy
options.rationale: Evacuating the uterus terminates any intrauterine pregnancy that may still prove viable and is not justified while that possibility remains open. It has a place only once a pregnancy is known to be non viable and the location remains genuinely uncertain after repeated imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that the pregnancy is simply too early to visualise on the scan and arrange routine antenatal booking with her general practitioner
options.rationale: A rise of well under the expected minimum over 48 hours argues against a viable intrauterine pregnancy, so reassurance and discharge to routine care would miss an ectopic. That reassurance would be appropriate for an appropriately doubling hormone level with a level below the discriminatory zone. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: A pregnancy of unknown location is a positive pregnancy test with no pregnancy visible in or outside the uterus on transvaginal ultrasound, and it is a stage of the diagnostic process rather than a diagnosis in itself. Roughly half resolve as failing intrauterine pregnancies, a third prove to be intrauterine pregnancies too early to see, and the remainder are ectopic, so management balances the risk of treating a wanted pregnancy against the risk of missing a tubal rupture. The 48 hour change in beta human chorionic gonadotrophin is the key discriminator: a rise of at least 53 per cent in 48 hours is consistent with a viable intrauterine pregnancy, a fall of more than half suggests a failing pregnancy, and anything in between is abnormal and demands continued surveillance. The discriminatory zone, above which an intrauterine sac should be visible, is around 1500 to 2000 IU/L on transvaginal scanning but is unreliable in multiple pregnancy. Serial measurement with repeat imaging continues until the pregnancy is located or the hormone level falls below 5 IU/L.
key_points: Pregnancy of unknown location means a positive test with nothing seen in or outside the uterus.
A 48 hour rise of at least 53 per cent is consistent with a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
A rise that is suboptimal but not falling is abnormal and requires continued surveillance.
Methotrexate and uterine evacuation both risk destroying a potentially viable pregnancy.
Surveillance continues until the pregnancy is located or the level falls below 5 IU/L.
explanation.pearls: A beta human chorionic gonadotrophin that plateaus, defined as changing by less than 15 per cent in either direction over 48 hours, carries the highest probability of ectopic pregnancy of any pattern and should prompt discussion of laparoscopy even when the woman remains entirely well.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Early pregnancy assessment

subtopic_detail: Gestational sac implanted within the anterior lower segment scar of two previous caesareans with cardiac activity present
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in an early pregnancy clinic reviewing a 32 year old woman at 7 weeks gestation who has had two previous caesarean sections. She attended for a dating scan and has had no bleeding and no pain.

The sonographer has asked you to review the images with her before the woman leaves. She is haemodynamically stable and is keen to know whether the pregnancy can continue.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with two well healed transverse suprapubic scars, no vaginal bleeding on speculum examination, cervix closed and healthy in appearance
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty endometrial cavity and an empty cervical canal with a gestational sac embedded in the anterior lower uterine segment at the site of the previous scar, myometrial thickness of 2 mm between the sac and the bladder, fetal pole with cardiac activity present, prominent peritrophoblastic flow on colour Doppler, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 28400 IU/L, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115 to 165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange suction curettage on the next available list to evacuate the pregnancy and send the tissue obtained for histological examination
options.rationale: Blind suction curettage cannot reach tissue implanted within the scar and tears the thin residual myometrium, which is why it is associated with torrential haemorrhage and emergency hysterectomy in this condition. Curettage is appropriate for an incomplete miscarriage where the tissue lies within the cavity. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean scar pregnancy)

options.text: Manage her expectantly with weekly beta human chorionic gonadotrophin measurement and repeat ultrasound scanning until the pregnancy resolves
options.rationale: Expectant management of a scar pregnancy with cardiac activity carries a high risk of uterine rupture and massive haemorrhage as the trophoblast invades the residual myometrium and bladder. Observation is reserved for a scar pregnancy with no cardiac activity and a falling hormone level in a fully counselled woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean scar pregnancy)

options.text: Refer her to a tertiary unit for ultrasound guided intragestational injection or planned surgical resection of the implantation site
options.rationale: A caesarean scar pregnancy with cardiac activity and only 2 mm of myometrium beneath it needs targeted treatment delivered directly into the sac or a planned resection of the scar with repair, both performed where interventional radiology and blood bank support are available. Treating the implantation site directly is what avoids the uncontrolled bleeding that follows blind instrumentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean scar pregnancy)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate as an outpatient and review her hormone levels on the fourth and seventh days afterwards
options.rationale: Systemic methotrexate alone fails frequently when the hormone level is high and cardiac activity is present, and the delay while it fails is when rupture occurs. Systemic methotrexate has a role as an adjunct to local treatment or where the hormone level is low and there is no cardiac activity. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean scar pregnancy)

options.text: Counsel her that hysterectomy is the safest definitive option and arrange the procedure once she has had time to consider her family plans
options.rationale: Hysterectomy removes future fertility and is not the first line treatment when uterus conserving options exist and the woman is stable. It is the correct operation for uncontrolled haemorrhage or where conservative treatment has failed in a woman who has completed her family. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean scar pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Caesarean scar pregnancy occurs when the blastocyst implants within the fibrous defect of a previous hysterotomy scar, and its incidence is rising in step with caesarean rates worldwide. Two types are described: one grows towards the uterine cavity and may progress, while the other grows deeply into the scar towards the bladder and behaves like a placenta accreta spectrum disorder, rupturing early. Diagnosis rests on an empty cavity and empty cervical canal with the sac in the anterior lower segment, thin or absent myometrium between the sac and the bladder, and prominent trophoblastic Doppler flow. The condition is dangerous precisely because it is so often mistaken for a normal early pregnancy, a cervical pregnancy or an incomplete miscarriage, and blind instrumentation of the uterus in that mistaken belief causes catastrophic haemorrhage. Continuation of the pregnancy carries a high risk of placenta accreta spectrum, hysterectomy and severe maternal morbidity, so women who choose to continue need explicit counselling and tertiary care.
key_points: An empty cavity and cervical canal with a sac in the anterior lower segment defines a scar pregnancy.
Myometrial thinning between the sac and bladder predicts early rupture and severe bleeding.
Blind suction curettage is associated with torrential haemorrhage and emergency hysterectomy.
Ultrasound guided local injection or planned scar resection are the uterus conserving options.
Continuing the pregnancy carries a high risk of placenta accreta spectrum later in gestation.
explanation.pearls: Measure the residual myometrial thickness explicitly in every scar pregnancy report, because a value under 3 mm predicts both failure of systemic methotrexate and the need for interventional radiology standby, and it is the single number that determines where the woman should be treated.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Early pregnancy assessment

subtopic_detail: Rapidly enlarging solid adnexal mass in a nineteen year old with a raised lactate dehydrogenase and normal alpha fetoprotein
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 19 year old woman referred by her general practitioner with three weeks of increasing abdominal swelling and a dragging discomfort in her lower abdomen. She has noticed her jeans no longer do up.

Her periods have been regular and she has never been pregnant. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She asks directly whether she will still be able to have children.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Firm non tender mass arising from the pelvis and palpable to the level of the umbilicus, no ascites clinically detectable, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no signs of virilisation
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showing a 12 cm solid right adnexal mass with no ascites, no omental deposits, no peritoneal nodularity and no enlarged retroperitoneal nodes, lactate dehydrogenase 820 U/L (120 to 250), alpha fetoprotein 3 micrograms/L (less than 10), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin less than 2 IU/L, CA125 62 U/mL (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an image guided core biopsy of the mass to obtain a tissue diagnosis before committing her to any form of definitive treatment
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected ovarian malignancy risks rupturing the capsule and seeding the peritoneum, which upstages the disease and worsens prognosis. Biopsy is reserved for advanced disease where neoadjuvant chemotherapy is planned and surgery is not the first step. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer her to a gynaecological oncology unit for fertility sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with comprehensive surgical staging
options.rationale: A solid adnexal mass in a young woman with a raised lactate dehydrogenase and disease apparently confined to one ovary is a malignant germ cell tumour, most likely a dysgerminoma, and removing the affected adnexa with staging preserves the uterus and the other ovary. These tumours are exquisitely chemosensitive, so fertility sparing surgery does not compromise survival. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to shell out the lesion and preserve as much normal ovarian tissue on that side as possible
options.rationale: Cystectomy of a solid malignant mass inevitably breaches the capsule and leaves tumour behind in the residual ovary. It is the right operation for a benign appearing cyst such as a dermoid or endometrioma in a young woman. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Refer her for bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with total hysterectomy and omentectomy as the standard staging operation for ovarian cancer
options.rationale: Radical surgery is the standard for epithelial ovarian cancer in older women but needlessly destroys fertility in a teenager with a germ cell tumour confined to one ovary. It becomes appropriate if both ovaries are involved or the uterus is directly invaded. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Commence neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy and plan an interval debulking operation once the mass has responded to treatment
options.rationale: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is used when disease is too extensive to resect completely at the outset, and this mass appears confined to one adnexa with no ascites or peritoneal disease. Primary surgery here provides both treatment and the staging information that determines whether chemotherapy is needed at all. (Source: eviQ: Ovarian germ cell tumours)

explanation.summary: Malignant ovarian germ cell tumours are rare overall but account for the majority of ovarian malignancies in women under twenty, and they characteristically grow rapidly over weeks rather than months. The tumour marker pattern is diagnostically useful: dysgerminoma raises lactate dehydrogenase and sometimes beta human chorionic gonadotrophin, yolk sac tumour raises alpha fetoprotein, and choriocarcinoma raises beta human chorionic gonadotrophin markedly, while a modestly raised CA125 is non specific and common with any large pelvic mass. Because these tumours are usually unilateral, confined at presentation and highly sensitive to platinum based chemotherapy, fertility sparing surgery with removal of the affected adnexa and full staging is standard even for advanced disease, and it does not compromise survival. Torsion and capsule rupture are important acute complications of a rapidly enlarging mass. Long term survival exceeds ninety per cent for early stage disease, and most women who undergo fertility sparing treatment retain normal menstrual and reproductive function.
key_points: A rapidly growing solid adnexal mass in a woman under twenty suggests a germ cell tumour.
Raised lactate dehydrogenase with normal alpha fetoprotein points towards dysgerminoma.
Percutaneous biopsy risks peritoneal seeding and upstaging and should be avoided.
Fertility sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with staging is standard even in advanced disease.
These tumours are highly chemosensitive with long term survival above ninety per cent in early disease.
explanation.pearls: Dysgerminoma is the only ovarian germ cell tumour with a meaningful rate of bilateral involvement, at around 10 to 15 per cent, so the contralateral ovary should be inspected carefully at surgery and any suspicious area biopsied even when preoperative imaging looked normal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Ovarian germ cell tumours

subtopic_detail: Rapidly deteriorating fever and abdominal pain on the fourth postnatal day in a mother whose toddler has a sore throat
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the postnatal ward to see a 31 year old woman on the fourth day after a normal vaginal birth. Over the past six hours she has developed rigors and constant severe lower abdominal pain that she describes as far worse than her afterpains were.

Her three year old at home has been off school with a sore throat this week. Her perineum has a second degree tear repaired at delivery. She is distressed and says she feels like she is dying.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diffuse severe lower abdominal tenderness with guarding, bulky exquisitely tender uterus, heavy offensive lochia, perineal repair intact with surrounding erythema but no crepitus or skin necrosis, capillary refill 4 seconds, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with a neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), C-reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 5.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (45 to 90), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150 to 400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures and arrange urgent pelvic ultrasound to look for retained products before any antibiotic is administered
options.rationale: Imaging is important in puerperal sepsis to identify retained products or an abscess needing drainage, but it follows the first antibiotic dose rather than preceding it. Source control decisions are made in parallel with, not instead of, immediate antimicrobial therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal sepsis)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures and commence oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for presumed endometritis with review in the morning
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are absorbed unreliably in a shocked woman and the delay is measured against an organism that can kill within hours. Oral therapy is appropriate for mild afebrile endometritis in a woman who is systemically well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures and commence intravenous cefazolin alone, escalating the antibiotic cover if she has not improved by morning
options.rationale: Cefazolin covers streptococci but lacks the antitoxin effect of a protein synthesis inhibitor, which is the specific reason clindamycin is added in suspected invasive streptococcal disease. Single agent narrow cover is reasonable for surgical prophylaxis, not for toxin mediated septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures and await the results before starting antibiotics so that the organism and its sensitivities are known
options.rationale: Every hour of delay in antibiotics in septic shock increases mortality measurably, and cultures are taken alongside rather than before treatment. Waiting for sensitivities is only ever reasonable in a stable patient with a chronic infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood and genital tract cultures and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin with clindamycin alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Fulminant puerperal sepsis with a household contact who has pharyngitis points to invasive group A streptococcal infection, for which high dose penicillin is bactericidal and clindamycin is added because it suppresses exotoxin production and works independently of bacterial growth phase. The falling white cell count with thrombocytopenia marks severe sepsis rather than a reassuring result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Invasive group A streptococcal infection is one of the leading direct causes of maternal death in high income countries and characteristically strikes in the first week after birth, often in a woman whose young child has pharyngitis or impetigo. Its hallmark is the speed and severity of the illness relative to the modest local findings, with pain out of proportion, rapid progression to shock and a white cell count that falls rather than rises because neutrophils are consumed and marginated. Because the organism produces superantigen exotoxins, a protein synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin is added to high dose penicillin, since penicillin alone acts on the cell wall and is less effective against a dense stationary phase inoculum. Beyond antibiotics and resuscitation, management includes urgent assessment for a source requiring drainage or debridement, early intensive care involvement, and consideration of intravenous immunoglobulin in streptococcal toxic shock. Household contacts may require screening and the case is notifiable in most Australian jurisdictions.
key_points: Invasive group A streptococcal sepsis peaks in the first week after birth and progresses within hours.
A household contact with sore throat or skin infection is an important epidemiological clue.
Neutropenia with thrombocytopenia in a septic woman indicates severity, not a reassuring result.
Clindamycin is added to penicillin to suppress exotoxin production in toxin mediated disease.
Antibiotics precede imaging, and source control decisions are made in parallel.
explanation.pearls: Pain disproportionate to the clinical findings is the single most useful early warning of invasive group A streptococcal disease, and in the puerperium it should trigger antibiotics within the hour rather than a period of observation, since the interval from first symptom to septic shock can be under twelve hours.

subtopic_detail: Death of one twin at 28 weeks in a shared placenta pregnancy where the survivor appears well on the scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional hospital reviewing a 29 year old woman at 28 weeks gestation in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. She attended today because she felt reduced movements and the sonographer has found no cardiac activity in the first twin.

The second twin is alive and active with a normal amniotic fluid volume and normal umbilical artery Doppler studies. She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain and no contractions, and her growth scans through the pregnancy have been concordant. Her tertiary referral centre is ninety minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, no vaginal bleeding, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirming no cardiac activity in twin one and a normally grown active twin two with an estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile, deepest vertical pocket 4.2 cm, umbilical artery Doppler with normal end diastolic flow, middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 1.2 multiples of the median, full blood count and coagulation profile within normal limits, cardiotocograph of twin two normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange emergency caesarean section now to deliver the surviving twin before any further harm can come to it from the intrauterine death
options.rationale: The haemodynamic event that injures a surviving monochorionic twin occurs at the moment of the co twin's death through acute exsanguination into the low resistance dead circulation, so delivery afterwards cannot prevent an injury that has already happened or not happened. Immediate delivery adds severe prematurity to whatever injury has occurred. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Transfer her to the tertiary fetal medicine service for middle cerebral artery Doppler surveillance, corticosteroids and continued expectant care
options.rationale: Because the injurious event has already passed, the correct course is to give corticosteroids, transfer to a unit with fetal medicine and neonatal intensive care, and continue the pregnancy with Doppler surveillance for fetal anaemia and later neuroimaging of the survivor. Prolonging gestation improves the outcome for a survivor who is currently well. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Induce labour over the next twenty four hours to reduce the maternal risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation from the retained dead twin
options.rationale: Maternal consumptive coagulopathy from a retained dead fetus is rare, takes weeks to develop and is easily monitored with serial coagulation studies, so it does not justify delivering a 28 week survivor. Delivery for coagulopathy would follow demonstrable and progressive derangement of the maternal clotting profile. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Perform intrauterine transfusion to the surviving twin today to correct the acute anaemia caused by transfusion into the dead twin circulation
options.rationale: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 1.2 multiples of the median is normal and does not indicate anaemia, so transfusing would impose the risks of an invasive procedure without an indication. Transfusion is considered when that velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Continue outpatient care locally with weekly cardiotocography and reassure her that the surviving twin is unaffected on today's assessment
options.rationale: Cardiotocography does not detect fetal anaemia or the cerebral injury that is the main concern for the survivor, and a regional unit without fetal medicine cannot provide the Doppler surveillance and neuroimaging required. Outpatient cardiotocography alone would be adequate only for an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Single intrauterine fetal death in a monochorionic pregnancy is fundamentally different from the same event in a dichorionic pregnancy because the twins share a placental circulation through vascular anastomoses. When one twin dies, its vascular bed becomes a low resistance sink and the survivor acutely exsanguinates into it, producing hypotension, anaemia and cerebral hypoperfusion within minutes to hours. This is why the surviving twin carries roughly a 15 per cent risk of neurological handicap and a 25 to 30 per cent risk of abnormal cerebral imaging, and crucially why immediate delivery does not prevent that injury: the damage is done before the death is ever detected. Management therefore aims at optimising the pregnancy rather than ending it, with corticosteroids, transfer to a unit with fetal medicine expertise, middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect anaemia, and fetal magnetic resonance imaging of the survivor's brain some weeks later to inform counselling. Delivery is usually planned for around 34 to 37 weeks unless surveillance deteriorates.
key_points: Shared placental anastomoses mean the survivor exsanguinates into the dead twin at the moment of death.
Immediate delivery cannot reverse an injury that has already occurred and adds prematurity.
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median indicates fetal anaemia.
Fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging weeks later informs counselling about neurological outcome.
Maternal coagulopathy from a retained dead fetus is rare and monitored rather than pre-empted.
explanation.pearls: Delay fetal magnetic resonance imaging of the surviving twin's brain until at least three to four weeks after the co twin's death, because ischaemic injury such as periventricular leukomalacia and porencephaly needs that long to become visible and an early scan is falsely reassuring.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Anti D decision for light bleeding at eleven weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in the early pregnancy assessment service seeing a twenty nine year old woman in her second pregnancy who noticed light fresh bleeding on wiping this morning. It has already stopped and she has had no pain.

Her blood group is O negative with no atypical antibodies on her booking sample, and her first child was born vaginally at term two years ago. A transvaginal ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with eleven weeks and a normal fetal heart rate. The cervix is closed on speculum examination with no active bleeding seen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and not tender, closed cervical os with no blood in the vault, uterus consistent with dates, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), ultrasound shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy at eleven weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Withhold anti D immunoglobulin now and give routine prophylaxis in the third trimester, with a further dose after the birth if the baby is rhesus positive
options.rationale: Sensitising events before twelve weeks with a viable ongoing pregnancy and no instrumentation do not warrant immunoglobulin, because fetomaternal haemorrhage of a volume capable of sensitising is very unlikely at this gestation. Routine antenatal and postnatal prophylaxis continues unchanged. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Give anti D immunoglobulin today and repeat the dose in the third trimester, with a further dose after the birth if the baby is rhesus positive
options.rationale: Treating every episode of light bleeding before twelve weeks in a continuing pregnancy exposes women to a blood product without evidence of benefit. Immunoglobulin before twelve weeks is reserved for ectopic pregnancy, termination, molar pregnancy and miscarriage managed with instrumentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Perform a Kleihauer test today and give anti D immunoglobulin only if fetal cells are detected in the maternal circulation on that sample
options.rationale: Quantification of fetomaternal haemorrhage is used after twenty weeks to determine whether additional doses are needed, and it is not sensitive enough to guide first trimester decisions. It would add cost and delay without changing this management. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti D guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti D guidelines

options.text: Arrange non invasive fetal rhesus genotyping on maternal plasma now and give anti D immunoglobulin today only if the fetus is predicted to be positive
options.rationale: Cell free fetal genotyping is not part of routine publicly funded antenatal care in Australia and is not accurate this early in pregnancy. The decision here is settled by gestation and the nature of the event. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti D immunoglobulin during this pregnancy entirely and give a single dose after the birth if the baby proves to be rhesus positive
options.rationale: Omitting routine antenatal prophylaxis raises the sensitisation rate several fold, because silent fetomaternal haemorrhage in the third trimester is common. Australian practice gives antenatal doses to all non sensitised rhesus negative women. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti D guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti D guidelines

explanation.summary: Rhesus D negative women who are not already sensitised receive immunoglobulin at twenty eight and thirty four weeks and again after the birth of a rhesus positive baby, and additional doses after defined sensitising events. Before twelve weeks the fetoplacental blood volume is so small that threatened miscarriage with a continuing viable pregnancy does not require a dose, and Australian guidance restricts first trimester use to ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, and miscarriage that is managed surgically or with instrumentation. After twelve weeks all sensitising events are covered, including bleeding, abdominal trauma, external cephalic version and invasive procedures. A Kleihauer or flow cytometric estimate of fetomaternal haemorrhage is used from twenty weeks onwards to decide whether more than the standard dose is required. Immunoglobulin is most effective within seventy two hours of the event but still offers partial protection out to about ten days.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage before twelve weeks with a viable pregnancy does not require immunoglobulin.
Ectopic, molar, termination and instrumented miscarriage do require it at any gestation.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at twenty eight and thirty four weeks.
Quantification of fetomaternal haemorrhage guides extra dosing only from twenty weeks.
Give within seventy two hours of a sensitising event where possible.
explanation.pearls: Check that the antibody screen result predates the most recent immunoglobulin dose before calling a woman sensitised, because passively acquired anti D persists for weeks and is regularly misread as immune anti D, leading to unnecessary referral for fetal surveillance.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin
National Blood Authority: Anti D guidelines

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus grown from a routine urine culture at sixteen weeks gestation
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a thirty two year old woman in her first pregnancy. She feels entirely well and mentions no urinary symptoms.

Her routine midstream urine culture taken at booking has grown a heavy pure growth of Streptococcus agalactiae, sensitive to penicillin. She has no drug allergies. She asks whether this means anything for the birth, having read that a swab is usually taken later in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, no vaginal discharge reported
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine culture with heavy pure growth of Streptococcus agalactiae sensitive to penicillin, no white cells reported on microscopy, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the bacteriuria with oral antibiotics now and give intrapartum prophylaxis only if the vaginal and rectal swab taken later proves to be positive
options.rationale: A negative swab in late pregnancy does not overturn documented bacteriuria, because colonisation fluctuates and the urinary isolate marks a heavy burden. This approach leaves a high risk labour uncovered. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Leave the bacteriuria untreated because she has no symptoms, and arrange the routine vaginal and rectal swab at thirty six weeks as for any other woman
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated whatever the organism, because up to a third of untreated women develop pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk rises. This organism carries the additional neonatal implication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat now with oral antibiotics and repeat the urine culture monthly, giving intrapartum prophylaxis only if the organism is grown again later in pregnancy
options.rationale: A test of cure is reasonable but recurrence is not the criterion for prophylaxis, which is triggered by the single documented episode at any point in the pregnancy. Monthly cultures add burden without changing the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Give a course of oral antibiotics now and prescribe daily suppressive antibiotics for the remainder of the pregnancy to eradicate genital tract colonisation
options.rationale: Antenatal eradication of genital colonisation does not work, since the organism recolonises from the bowel within weeks, and prolonged exposure selects resistance and disrupts the maternal and infant microbiome. Protection of the baby is achieved by antibiotics given in labour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat the bacteriuria with oral antibiotics now and plan intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in labour irrespective of any later vaginal swab result
options.rationale: Bacteriuria with this organism indicates heavy genital tract colonisation and independently raises the risk of early onset neonatal disease and of preterm birth, so it earns prophylaxis in labour regardless of later swabs. Treating the bacteriuria itself reduces the risk of pyelonephritis. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Group B streptococcus is carried in the bowel and genital tract of around one in five pregnant women and is the leading cause of early onset neonatal sepsis in Australia. Australian units use either a universal screening approach with a combined low vaginal and rectal swab at around thirty five to thirty seven weeks, or a risk factor based approach, but under both strategies certain findings mandate intrapartum antibiotics on their own. These are bacteriuria with the organism at any point in the current pregnancy and a previous infant with invasive disease, because both indicate a heavy maternal burden and a markedly increased neonatal risk. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is also treated at the time it is found, since untreated bacteriuria in pregnancy leads to pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Intrapartum prophylaxis is intravenous benzylpenicillin given as early in labour as possible, with cefazolin or, for severe allergy, clindamycin guided by susceptibility testing.
key_points: Bacteriuria with this organism at any stage of pregnancy mandates intrapartum prophylaxis.
A later negative vaginal and rectal swab does not cancel that indication.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is always treated when found.
A previous infant with invasive disease is the other absolute indication.
Antenatal eradication of colonisation is ineffective because recolonisation occurs from the bowel.
explanation.pearls: Intravenous benzylpenicillin needs at least four hours before birth to achieve adequate fetal tissue levels, so the drug is charted at the first assessment in labour rather than waiting for established labour or for membranes to rupture.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Group B streptococcal infection

subtopic_detail: Discrepancy of nine days between certain menstrual dates and first trimester crown rump length
stem:
