You are the doctor reviewing a twenty six year old woman at her first antenatal visit. She is certain of her last menstrual period, which was nine weeks and five days ago, and she keeps a period tracking application showing regular twenty eight day cycles.

A dating ultrasound performed yesterday reports a single live intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length of 23 mm, giving a gestational age of eight weeks and four days. The sonographer noted good visualisation and an optimal midsagittal view. She asks which due date you will be using for the rest of the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no palpable uterus, no abnormality on general examination
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a single live intrauterine pregnancy, crown rump length 23 mm corresponding to eight weeks and four days, yolk sac present, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her estimated date of birth?

options.text: Keep the menstrual date for the remainder of the pregnancy, since her cycles are regular and she is certain of the date of her last menstrual period
options.rationale: Menstrual dating assumes ovulation on day fourteen, which is wrong in a substantial minority of regular cycles, and it performs worse than early biometry even when recall is confident. Holding to it here shifts the timing of every later decision. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age

options.text: Take the midpoint between the menstrual and ultrasound estimates as a compromise, and record that single date in her pregnancy record and hand held notes
options.rationale: Averaging two estimates of unequal accuracy degrades the better one and has no basis in any dating protocol. A single explicit rule is what keeps dating consistent between services. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks and set the estimated date of birth from growth over that interval rather than from the single measurement taken yesterday
options.rationale: Interval growth is used to assess wellbeing rather than to assign dates, and a later scan is less accurate for dating because biological variation in size widens with gestation. Redating on a second scan would also risk masking early growth restriction. (Source: ASUM: Statement on normal ultrasonic fetal measurements)
source_refs: ASUM: Statement on normal ultrasonic fetal measurements

options.text: Use the menstrual date now and revise it at the eighteen to twenty week morphology scan if the biometry there suggests a different gestational age
options.rationale: Second trimester biometry has a margin of error of about seven to ten days and should not override a good first trimester measurement. Deferring the decision leaves the pregnancy provisionally misdated through the screening window. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age

options.text: Use the ultrasound measurement to set the estimated date of birth for the remainder of the pregnancy, since the discrepancy exceeds the accepted margin
options.rationale: A first trimester crown rump length measured in an optimal plane is the most accurate estimate of gestational age available, and a discrepancy beyond about five to seven days means the menstrual date is redated. Certainty about the period does not exclude late ovulation or early implantation bleeding mistaken for a period. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age

explanation.summary: Accurate dating underpins aneuploidy screening interpretation, growth assessment, the timing of induction for post dates pregnancy and the definition of prematurity, so it is settled once and then left alone. Crown rump length measured between about seven and thirteen weeks in a good midsagittal plane dates a pregnancy to within about five days, which is better than menstrual dating even with confident recall, because ovulation day varies. Australian practice redates when the ultrasound estimate differs from the menstrual estimate by more than about five to seven days in the first trimester. Beyond thirteen weeks, head circumference and femur length are used, with wider tolerance of about seven to ten days in the second trimester, and after twenty two weeks biometry becomes too imprecise to redate. Once the estimated date of birth is assigned it is not changed by later scans, since apparent discrepancy then reflects growth rather than gestation.
key_points: First trimester crown rump length is the most accurate dating measurement.
Redate when the discrepancy exceeds about five to seven days in the first trimester.
Confident menstrual recall does not correct for variable ovulation timing.
Second trimester biometry carries a wider margin and is a weaker basis for redating.
Dates are assigned once and are not revised on later scans.
explanation.pearls: A crown rump length above eighty four millimetres falls outside the validated dating range, so beyond that point head circumference is used instead, and measuring a flexed or hyperextended fetus in a non midsagittal plane is the commonest technical cause of a spuriously discrepant date.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of gestational age
ASUM: Statement on normal ultrasonic fetal measurements
BMJ Best Practice: Routine antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Four episodes of bacterial vaginosis in twelve months each recurring after menstruation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a thirty four year old woman who has had four episodes of malodorous thin grey discharge in the past year. Each has responded to oral metronidazole and each has returned within a week or two of her period.

She is in a stable relationship with a male partner, uses condoms inconsistently and has no dyspareunia or pelvic pain. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal. She has stopped using vaginal douches after previous advice and asks what can be done to stop the cycle of recurrence.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Homogeneous thin grey vaginal discharge coating the walls, no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness, vulval skin normal with no erythema or fissuring
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH above 4.5, microscopy shows clue cells with scanty lactobacilli, nucleic acid testing negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas, candida not isolated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment and advise a daily oral lactobacillus probiotic preparation taken indefinitely to restore the vaginal flora
options.rationale: Evidence for oral probiotics preventing recurrence remains weak and inconsistent, so they are at best an adjunct to suppression rather than a substitute. Relying on them alone leaves most women recurring. (Source: RACGP: Recurrent bacterial vaginosis)

options.text: Treat each recurrence with an oral antibiotic course as it happens and take swabs before each course to confirm the diagnosis microscopically each time
options.rationale: Repeated treatment of episodes as they arise is exactly the pattern that has failed her over the past year, and it leaves the recurrence rate untouched. Confirming the diagnosis is sensible but does not constitute a management plan. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Treat with an intravaginal antifungal preparation and a topical corticosteroid, and review her when the current symptoms have settled completely
options.rationale: Antifungal and steroid treatment addresses candidiasis and vulval dermatoses, neither of which fits a raised pH with clue cells and absent lactobacilli. Misdirected topical treatment prolongs symptoms and delays the correct plan. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment followed by twice weekly intravaginal metronidazole gel as suppressive therapy for several months
options.rationale: Suppressive intravaginal therapy after an induction course is the approach with the best evidence for reducing recurrence, which otherwise affects more than half of women within six months. The vaginal route limits systemic exposure over the months of treatment. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis

options.text: Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment and prescribe a simultaneous course for her male partner to prevent reintroduction of the organisms
options.rationale: Treating male partners has not reduced recurrence in the trials that tested it and this is not a sexually transmitted infection in the conventional sense. Partner treatment adds antibiotic exposure without benefit. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis reflects loss of lactobacillus dominance and overgrowth of anaerobic organisms, diagnosed by thin homogeneous discharge, a vaginal pH above four point five, clue cells on microscopy and a positive amine test. Recurrence is the rule rather than the exception, with more than half of women affected within six months of treatment, and menstruation is a common trigger because blood raises vaginal pH. For recurrent disease Australian guidance recommends an induction course followed by suppressive intravaginal metronidazole gel given twice weekly for around four to six months, which substantially reduces recurrence while treatment continues. Modifiable contributors worth addressing include douching, and consistent condom use is associated with fewer recurrences. Treatment of male partners has not been shown to help, although trials of partner treatment continue, and asymptomatic women outside pregnancy do not require treatment.
key_points: Diagnosis rests on pH above four point five with clue cells and scanty lactobacilli.
More than half of treated women recur within six months.
Suppressive intravaginal gel twice weekly after induction is the recommended approach for recurrence.
Routine male partner treatment does not reduce recurrence.
Douching should be stopped and consistent condom use encouraged.
explanation.pearls: Warn about a disulfiram like reaction with alcohol during oral metronidazole and for a day afterwards, and note that this condition in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated even though screening of asymptomatic women is not recommended.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Bacterial vaginosis

subtopic_detail: Imminent birth at twenty eight weeks with corticosteroids already given twelve hours earlier
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary unit caring for a thirty one year old woman at twenty eight weeks in her second pregnancy. She was admitted yesterday with regular painful contractions and has progressed despite nifedipine.

She received the first dose of betamethasone twelve hours ago and the second is due this evening. The cervix is now eight centimetres dilated with the vertex at the ischial spines, and the neonatal team has been called. Her low vaginal and rectal swab last week was negative for group B streptococcus, the cardiotocograph is reassuring and she has no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Contracting three in ten minutes, cervix eight centimetres dilated and fully effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting at the spines, uterus not tender between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph with normal baseline and variability and no decelerations, group B streptococcus swab negative last week, white cell count 10.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What additional treatment should be given now?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion until the birth
options.rationale: Magnesium given to women in whom birth before thirty weeks is imminent reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in the surviving child, with a number needed to treat of about sixty three. Benefit is present even when only the loading dose is completed before the birth. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin as prophylaxis against early onset neonatal sepsis, continued at regular intervals until the baby has been born
options.rationale: A negative swab taken within the preceding five weeks and the absence of other risk factors means routine prophylaxis is not indicated here. Preterm labour alone triggers prophylaxis only when the colonisation status is unknown. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: A further course of antenatal corticosteroids given as two additional doses, so that the fetus receives the maximum possible benefit before birth
options.rationale: A repeat course is considered only when the first was given at least seven days earlier and birth again becomes imminent, and extra doses within the same course have no benefit. The second dose of the current course is given on schedule if the pregnancy continues. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: An additional tocolytic agent such as intravenous salbutamol or an oxytocin receptor antagonist, to delay the birth until the corticosteroid course is complete
options.rationale: Tocolysis at eight centimetres with a presenting part at the spines does not work and delays transfer of care to the neonatal team. It also exposes the woman to cardiovascular effects for no fetal gain. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with a macrolide to cover subclinical infection, since infection frequently underlies preterm labour at this gestation with intact membranes
options.rationale: Antibiotics for preterm labour with intact membranes do not prolong pregnancy or improve neonatal outcome and were associated with harm on long term follow up in the largest trial. They are given when membranes have ruptured. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of imminent very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, and Australian and New Zealand guidance recommends it when birth is expected within twenty four hours before thirty weeks of gestation. A loading dose is given intravenously over about twenty to thirty minutes and followed by a maintenance infusion until the birth or for up to twenty four hours, and treatment is worthwhile even when only the loading dose can be completed. Monitoring covers respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output, with the infusion stopped for reduced reflexes or respiratory depression, and calcium gluconate is kept available. Antenatal corticosteroids operate on a separate indication and schedule, with the second dose given at the planned interval rather than accelerated. Tocolysis has no role once labour is advanced, since its only real purpose is to buy time for steroids and for transfer to a unit with neonatal intensive care.
key_points: Magnesium sulfate before thirty weeks reduces cerebral palsy in survivors.
Give it when birth is expected within about twenty four hours.
Partial treatment with the loading dose alone still confers benefit.
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output during the infusion.
Tocolysis is futile once labour is advanced and the presenting part has descended.
explanation.pearls: Magnesium is given here for the baby's brain rather than for seizure prophylaxis, so the regimen and the monitoring differ from eclampsia prevention, and the drug is written as magnesium sulfate in Australian prescribing even though other spellings persist internationally.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Clinical Practice Guideline
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Twin pregnancy at twelve weeks with a single placental mass and a T sign at the membrane insertion
stem:
You are the doctor reviewing a twenty seven year old woman in her first pregnancy after her dating ultrasound. She conceived spontaneously and has had mild nausea only.

The report describes a twin pregnancy at twelve weeks with two live fetuses, a single placental mass and a thin dividing membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle without an intervening wedge of tissue. Both fetuses measure within three days of each other and the nuchal translucency measurements are within normal limits. She asks how her care will differ from that of a friend expecting twins who is being scanned every four weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, uterus palpable at the level of the symphysis pubis, no abnormality on general examination
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows two live fetuses, one placental mass, a thin dividing membrane with a T shaped insertion, concordant crown rump lengths and normal nuchal translucency measurements

lead_in: What surveillance plan should be arranged for this pregnancy?

options.text: Defer the decision about surveillance until the morphology scan, when fetal sex can be determined and used to establish whether the placenta is truly shared
options.rationale: Discordant sex proves separate placentas but concordant sex proves nothing, so the test is useless in exactly the situation where the question arises. Chorionicity is most reliably assigned in the first trimester and should not be revisited later. (Source: ASUM: Guidelines for the performance of first trimester ultrasound)
source_refs: ASUM: Guidelines for the performance of first trimester ultrasound

options.text: Fortnightly ultrasound from sixteen weeks to assess liquor volumes and bladder filling in each sac, with growth assessment added at the usual intervals
options.rationale: A shared placenta carries the risk of twin to twin transfusion, which develops rapidly and is detected by discordant deep vertical pockets before either fetus is compromised. Fortnightly scanning from sixteen weeks is the interval that allows referral for laser therapy in time. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Four weekly ultrasound from twenty four weeks to assess growth and liquor volumes, with umbilical artery Doppler studies added if growth becomes discordant
options.rationale: This is the schedule for twins with separate placentas, whose main risk is growth restriction rather than acute transfusion imbalance. Applied here it would miss the window in which twin to twin transfusion is treatable. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Routine care with the standard morphology scan at twenty weeks and a growth scan in the third trimester, with additional scans arranged if symptoms develop
options.rationale: Twin pregnancy of any type requires more surveillance than singleton care, and symptoms such as rapid abdominal distension appear only once the process is advanced. This plan would leave the highest risk period unmonitored. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Amniocentesis of both sacs to confirm zygosity, followed by four weekly ultrasound surveillance and a plan for birth by caesarean section at term
options.rationale: Chorionicity rather than zygosity determines risk and has already been established on this scan, so an invasive test adds a miscarriage risk for no gain. Mode of birth is decided much later and is not dictated by placentation alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Chorionicity is the single most important determinant of risk in a twin pregnancy and is best assigned in the first trimester, when the T sign of a shared placenta and the lambda or twin peak sign of separate placentas are clearest. Twins sharing a placenta have vascular anastomoses between the circulations and are at risk of twin to twin transfusion syndrome, selective growth restriction and twin anaemia polycythaemia sequence, in addition to the higher background risks of all multiple pregnancies. Australian guidance therefore recommends ultrasound every two weeks from sixteen weeks in these pregnancies, examining deep vertical pockets of liquor, bladder filling and Doppler studies, since transfusion imbalance can develop within a fortnight. Twins with separate placentas are usually scanned about every four weeks from the second trimester, with growth restriction the principal concern. Planned birth is also earlier when the placenta is shared, typically in the mid to late thirties of gestational weeks depending on findings.
key_points: Determine chorionicity in the first trimester using the T sign or the lambda sign.
A shared placenta means fortnightly ultrasound from sixteen weeks.
Twin to twin transfusion is detected through discordant liquor volumes before symptoms appear.
Separate placentas usually mean four weekly surveillance focused on growth.
Same sex fetuses do not establish that the placenta is shared.
explanation.pearls: Sudden maternal abdominal distension and breathlessness in the second trimester of a twin pregnancy with a shared placenta signals acute polyhydramnios from transfusion imbalance and warrants same day referral to a fetal therapy unit, because laser ablation outcomes fall sharply once the recipient develops cardiac compromise.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
ASUM: Guidelines for the performance of first trimester ultrasound

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine device in place with a continuing intrauterine pregnancy at seven weeks and threads visible
stem:
You are the doctor in a community sexual health service seeing a thirty year old woman who has had a positive home pregnancy test. She has a copper intrauterine device that was inserted three years ago.

She wishes to continue the pregnancy. An ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine pregnancy at seven weeks with a fetal heart beat, and the device is seen within the lower uterine cavity below the gestation sac. On speculum examination the threads are visible at the external os. She is well with no bleeding or pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Speculum examination shows device threads visible at the external os, cervix closed with no bleeding, uterus consistent with dates, no adnexal masses or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a single live intrauterine pregnancy at seven weeks with the intrauterine device lying below the gestation sac, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the device in place for the pregnancy, arrange serial ultrasound surveillance and remove it at the time of the birth or at the postnatal visit
options.rationale: Retention roughly doubles the risk of miscarriage and substantially increases second trimester loss, preterm birth and chorioamnionitis. Surveillance detects these complications rather than preventing them. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Leave the device in place until the second trimester and then remove it under ultrasound guidance once the placenta has completed its development
options.rationale: Removal becomes progressively harder and riskier as the pregnancy enlarges and the threads retract into the uterus, so waiting forfeits the safest opportunity. There is no advantage in deferring past the first trimester. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic removal of the device under general anaesthesia in the second trimester, with prophylactic antibiotics given at the time of the procedure
options.rationale: Instrumentation of the gravid uterus under anaesthesia is unnecessary when the threads are visible and simple traction will succeed. It would introduce anaesthetic and procedural risk for no benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Advise that the pregnancy is not viable with a device in the uterus and refer her to discuss options for termination of the pregnancy in a specialist clinic
options.rationale: Pregnancies that continue after device failure can proceed normally once the device is removed, and there is no indication for termination. Framing viability incorrectly would be a serious counselling error. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Remove the device now by gentle traction on the threads, having confirmed the position of the pregnancy, and arrange routine antenatal follow up
options.rationale: Removal when the threads are visible in early pregnancy lowers the risks of miscarriage, preterm birth and intrauterine infection compared with leaving the device in place. The small immediate risk of pregnancy loss at removal is outweighed by those later risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine contraception)

explanation.summary: Intrauterine contraception fails rarely, but when a pregnancy does occur the first step is to establish its location, because the proportion of pregnancies that are ectopic is higher than in the general population even though the absolute risk remains low. Once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed and the woman wishes to continue, the device is removed if the threads are visible, since retention is associated with roughly double the miscarriage rate along with increased second trimester loss, preterm birth, chorioamnionitis and antepartum haemorrhage. Removal itself carries a small immediate risk of pregnancy loss, which is quoted to the woman, but the balance favours removal in the first trimester. When the threads are not visible the device is left in place, ultrasound documents its position, and the woman is counselled about infection symptoms and monitored through the pregnancy. Copper and hormonal devices are managed the same way in this situation.
key_points: Confirm the location of the pregnancy first, since ectopic proportion is raised.
Remove the device in the first trimester when the threads are visible.
Retention doubles the miscarriage risk and raises preterm birth and infection risk.
Removal carries a small immediate risk of loss, which is discussed beforehand.
When threads are not visible the device is left in situ with counselling and surveillance.
explanation.pearls: A woman who conceives with a device in place and reports fever or offensive discharge at any gestation needs urgent assessment for septic miscarriage, which is the complication that makes retention dangerous and which can progress to maternal sepsis within hours.

sources.label: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: Intrauterine contraception

subtopic_detail: Spontaneous labour at thirty seven weeks after a previous classical uterine incision
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a thirty four year old woman in her second pregnancy who has arrived contracting strongly every four minutes at thirty seven weeks.

Her first baby was born at twenty seven weeks by caesarean section for severe early onset pre eclampsia, and the operation report from that admission records a vertical incision in the upper uterine segment. She had hoped for a vaginal birth this time and had not yet had her planned discussion about mode of birth. She is coping well with the contractions and the cardiotocograph is normal. The cervix is four centimetres dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Contracting three in ten minutes lasting fifty seconds, cervix four centimetres dilated and eighty per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting at minus two station, abdomen not tender between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph with normal baseline and variability and no decelerations, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), group and hold sample sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Allow labour to continue with continuous cardiotocography and intravenous access, proceeding to caesarean only if the trace becomes abnormal or progress stalls
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring is the standard safeguard for a transverse lower segment scar, where rupture is rare and often heralded by fetal heart rate changes. With an upper segment scar, rupture can occur through the fundus without warning and before any trace abnormality. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Offer epidural analgesia and review her progress in two hours, planning a caesarean section only if she has not reached full dilatation by that point
options.rationale: This defers an unavoidable operation while the uterus continues to contract against a scar that should not be laboured on, and epidural analgesia can mask the pain of a rupture. Every additional hour of labour adds risk without any prospect of safe vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Give a tocolytic to abolish the contractions and arrange an elective caesarean section on the next available list after a full antenatal discussion
options.rationale: Tocolysis in established labour at four centimetres rarely succeeds and delays definitive management while the risk of rupture persists. The discussion she missed can be held while theatre is prepared. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Arrange ultrasound measurement of the lower uterine segment thickness and use the result to decide between labour and immediate caesarean section
options.rationale: Segment thickness measurement is a research tool with no validated threshold for clinical decisions, and it assesses the lower segment while this scar lies in the fundus. It would delay the operation for information that cannot change it. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Proceed to caesarean section now, informing the anaesthetic and theatre teams and counselling her about the reason while preparations are made
options.rationale: A vertical incision in the upper segment carries a rupture risk of several per cent in labour, many times that of a transverse lower segment scar, and rupture is often catastrophic and poorly predicted by monitoring. Labour is therefore not offered and birth proceeds before labour advances further. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean is appropriate for most women with a single previous transverse lower segment incision, in whom the rupture risk is under one per cent and is usually signalled by fetal heart rate abnormality. A classical or other upper segment vertical incision is different in kind, with a reported rupture risk of several per cent, a tendency to rupture before labour begins and a presentation that is often sudden fetal collapse or maternal haemodynamic compromise rather than a gradual trace change. Such women are counselled antenatally for a planned caesarean at around thirty six to thirty seven weeks, and one who presents in labour needs the operation without delay. Very preterm caesarean sections, particularly before around twenty eight weeks when the lower segment is poorly formed, are the usual reason a classical incision was used, so the operation record from a previous very preterm birth must always be obtained rather than assumed. Other contraindications to planned vaginal birth include previous uterine rupture, previous transmural myomectomy and the usual obstetric indications for caesarean.
key_points: A classical or upper segment vertical scar contraindicates labour.
Rupture of such a scar may occur without warning and without preceding trace changes.
Previous very preterm caesarean is the usual reason a classical incision was used.
Always obtain the operation report rather than relying on the number of previous caesareans.
Planned birth is arranged at around thirty six to thirty seven weeks when the scar is classical.
explanation.pearls: Sudden constant abdominal pain between contractions, loss of the presenting station on vaginal examination and a fetal bradycardia are the classical triad of uterine rupture, and maternal tachycardia with shoulder tip pain from haemoperitoneum can appear before any vaginal bleeding is seen.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section
Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Vaginal birth after caesarean

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive at booking with a viral load above 200000 international units per millilitre
stem:
You are the doctor running the antenatal clinic reviewing a twenty five year old woman at fourteen weeks in her first pregnancy. She was born overseas and has known chronic hepatitis B infection acquired in childhood, and she has never needed treatment.

Her booking bloods confirm hepatitis B surface antigen and e antigen positivity with a viral load of 4 x 10^7 international units per millilitre. Liver enzymes are normal and an ultrasound of the liver shows no cirrhosis. She is not co infected with hepatitis C or human immunodeficiency virus. She asks what can be done to stop the baby catching the infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, liver not enlarged, uterus consistent with dates, body mass index 22 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive, e antigen positive, viral load 4 x 10^7 international units per millilitre, alanine aminotransferase 24 units per litre (5-35), platelets 246 x10^9/L (150-400), hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to reduce transmission?

options.text: Advise against breastfeeding to avoid postnatal transmission, and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of the birth
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is safe once the infant has received immunoprophylaxis and is actively encouraged, provided nipples are not cracked and bleeding. Discouraging it causes harm without reducing transmission. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Start maternal pegylated interferon now to reduce the viral load before the birth, with neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine given within twelve hours
options.rationale: Interferon is contraindicated in pregnancy because of antiproliferative effects on the fetus, and it is not used for this indication. The nucleotide analogue with the best pregnancy safety data is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Start maternal tenofovir in the third trimester and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of birth
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis alone fails in a meaningful proportion of babies born to women with very high viral loads, and third trimester antiviral therapy reduces that residual transmission. The combination of maternal suppression and timely neonatal immunoprophylaxis is what brings transmission close to zero. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Rely on neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine given within twelve hours of birth, and review her viral load again in the third trimester without treatment
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis is essential but leaves a failure rate of around five to ten per cent when the maternal viral load is this high. Measuring the load without acting on it wastes the opportunity to suppress it before birth. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis B in pregnancy)

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at term and ensure the baby receives both immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of the birth
options.rationale: Mode of birth is not an established determinant of vertical transmission for this virus, unlike the situation with unsuppressed human immunodeficiency virus. Operative birth would add maternal morbidity without reducing infant risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment)

explanation.summary: All pregnant women in Australia are screened for hepatitis B surface antigen at booking, and infants of positive women receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus the birth dose of vaccine within twelve hours, followed by the routine schedule and serological testing at around nine to twelve months. That combination prevents most vertical transmission, but it fails in roughly five to ten per cent of infants when the maternal viral load is very high, and e antigen positivity is a marker of that risk. Australian guidance therefore adds maternal antiviral therapy from around twenty eight to thirty two weeks when the viral load exceeds two hundred thousand international units per millilitre, using tenofovir disoproxil because it has the largest safety dataset in pregnancy and a high barrier to resistance. Therapy is usually continued for a period after the birth with monitoring of liver enzymes for a postpartum flare. Caesarean section confers no established benefit and breastfeeding is encouraged once the infant has been immunised.
key_points: Universal antenatal screening identifies women whose infants need immunoprophylaxis.
Immunoglobulin plus vaccine within twelve hours of birth is required for every exposed infant.
Maternal antiviral therapy is added when the viral load exceeds two hundred thousand international units per millilitre.
Tenofovir disoproxil is the preferred agent in pregnancy.
Breastfeeding is safe after immunoprophylaxis and caesarean birth does not reduce transmission.
explanation.pearls: Watch for a hepatitis flare in the months after birth, when immune reconstitution can raise transaminases sharply, particularly if antiviral therapy is stopped, so liver enzymes are checked at intervals through the first six postpartum months rather than assuming the risk ends at delivery.

subtopic_detail: Maternal fever with fetal tachycardia two days after membrane rupture at thirty weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a thirty three year old woman admitted two days ago with ruptured membranes at thirty weeks. She completed a course of betamethasone and has been receiving oral antibiotics as part of expectant management.

Overnight she developed lower abdominal discomfort and now feels hot and shivery. The midwife reports that the liquor draining onto the pad has become offensive. She has no contractions. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 178 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations, and the neonatal unit has a cot available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 178 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender on palpation between contractions, offensive liquor draining, cervix long and closed on speculum examination, no calf tenderness, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, cardiotocograph with a baseline of 178 beats per minute and reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics with tocolysis and magnesium sulfate, arranging transfer to a quaternary centre with a higher level neonatal intensive care unit
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in the presence of intrauterine infection because prolonging the pregnancy is the harm, and transfer is unnecessary when a suitable cot is already available on site. Magnesium for neuroprotection is reasonable but must not delay the birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Start intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and expedite the birth, involving the neonatal and anaesthetic teams while resuscitation continues
options.rationale: Intrauterine infection is the one situation in which expectant management after preterm rupture of membranes is abandoned, because the uterus is the source and both mother and fetus deteriorate while it remains in place. Antibiotics alone do not achieve source control. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Change to intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and continue expectant management, reassessing in six hours to see whether the fever has responded
options.rationale: Waiting for a fever to settle while the infected uterus remains undelivered exposes the fetus to worsening inflammation and the mother to septic shock. Fetal inflammatory injury accumulates during precisely this interval. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics and a second course of corticosteroids, deferring the birth for twenty four hours so that the fetus gains the full benefit
options.rationale: A repeat steroid course has no place when infection mandates immediate birth, and delaying for it trades a marginal respiratory benefit for a substantial infective risk. The first course has already been completed. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Perform amniocentesis to sample the liquor for glucose, Gram stain and culture, and decide on the timing of birth once those results are available
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid analysis is used when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain, not when fever, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, maternal tachycardia and fetal tachycardia are all present. The clinical diagnosis is already made and the delay would be dangerous. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Expectant management after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes aims to gain gestational maturity, and it is supported by corticosteroids, latency antibiotics and surveillance for infection. Chorioamnionitis ends that strategy immediately, because the infected uterine contents are the source and both fetal inflammatory response syndrome and maternal sepsis progress while the pregnancy continues. The diagnosis is clinical, supported by maternal fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor and rising inflammatory markers, and no single test is required to confirm it. Management is intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics with prompt birth, by induction where labour can be achieved safely and by caesarean where it cannot, with neonatal and anaesthetic teams involved early. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection may still be given at this gestation provided it does not delay the birth, and a repeat corticosteroid course is not a reason to wait.
key_points: Chorioamnionitis converts expectant management into expedited birth.
The diagnosis is clinical and does not require amniocentesis.
Antibiotics without source control do not stop fetal inflammatory injury.
Tocolysis is contraindicated once intrauterine infection is suspected.
Neuroprotective magnesium may be given provided it does not delay the birth.
explanation.pearls: Fetal tachycardia above one hundred and sixty beats per minute with reduced variability is often the first sign of intrauterine infection and can precede maternal fever, so a rising baseline in a woman managed expectantly after membrane rupture warrants reassessment for infection rather than simple observation.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Positive syphilis serology at booking in a woman reporting anaphylaxis to penicillin
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic reviewing a twenty two year old woman at sixteen weeks in her first pregnancy. Her booking serology is reactive for syphilis with a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1 in 32, and treponemal specific testing is positive.

She has never been treated and a repeat sample confirms the titre. She recalls facial swelling and difficulty breathing after amoxicillin as a teenager and has avoided penicillins since. She has no rash, no oral or genital ulcers and no neurological or ocular symptoms. The sexual health service can see her this week.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no genital or oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, no cranial nerve abnormality, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32 confirmed on a second sample, treponemal specific antibody positive, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Defer treatment until after the birth given the allergy history, and treat the newborn with a full course of parenteral penicillin under paediatric supervision
options.rationale: Untreated maternal infection causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth and congenital disease long before term, so deferral is not an option. Treating the baby afterwards cannot reverse injury that occurred in utero. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Admit her for penicillin desensitisation in a monitored setting and then treat with intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin according to the disease stage
options.rationale: Penicillin is the only agent reliably shown to treat the fetus as well as the mother, so a documented allergy is managed by desensitisation rather than by substitution. The procedure is performed where anaphylaxis can be treated immediately. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with oral doxycycline for the appropriate duration for the stage of infection and repeat the serological titre monthly until the birth
options.rationale: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy because of effects on fetal bone and teeth, and they do not cross the placenta in concentrations that treat congenital infection. Serological follow up cannot make up for inadequate fetal treatment. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with a course of oral azithromycin and arrange serological follow up with monthly titres and detailed ultrasound assessment of the fetus
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in this organism is widespread and treatment failures with fetal infection have been documented, so it is not an acceptable alternative in pregnancy. Ultrasound surveillance detects established fetal disease rather than preventing it. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines: Syphilis)

options.text: Treat her with a course of intravenous ceftriaxone in the day unit and arrange repeat serology at delivery to confirm an adequate response to the treatment
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has activity but the evidence for preventing congenital infection is limited, and cross reactivity is a consideration in genuine penicillin anaphylaxis. It is not the recommended pathway when desensitisation is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Syphilis is rising in Australia, with outbreaks that have produced congenital cases, so all women are screened at booking and many jurisdictions now repeat testing in the third trimester and at birth in higher incidence regions. Benzathine benzylpenicillin is the only treatment proven to prevent congenital infection, because alternatives either fail to cross the placenta adequately or have documented treatment failures, and this makes desensitisation the standard response to a reported penicillin allergy in pregnancy. Desensitisation is performed in a monitored setting with escalating oral or intravenous doses over several hours and is followed immediately by treatment, since tolerance is lost within days of stopping. The number of weekly doses depends on the stage, with a single dose for early infection and three weekly doses for late or unknown duration disease, and missing a dose in pregnancy means restarting the course. A Jarisch Herxheimer reaction after the first dose can cause fever, uterine contractions and fetal heart rate changes, so treatment in the second half of pregnancy is given where fetal monitoring is available.
key_points: Penicillin is the only treatment that reliably treats the fetus.
Reported penicillin allergy in pregnancy is managed by desensitisation, not substitution.
Doxycycline is contraindicated and macrolide resistance makes azithromycin unreliable.
Staging determines whether one dose or three weekly doses are given.
Untreated infection causes stillbirth, hydrops, preterm birth and congenital disease.
explanation.pearls: Warn about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction within hours of the first dose, since fever with uterine contractions and transient fetal heart rate abnormality is common in the second half of pregnancy and is regularly mistaken for chorioamnionitis or preterm labour, prompting unnecessary intervention.

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis duration after emergency caesarean in a woman with a body mass index of 39
stem:
You are the obstetric resident writing the discharge plan for a thirty six year old woman who had an emergency caesarean section at term for failure to progress after a long labour.

Her body mass index at booking was 39 kg/m2 and she is now thirty six hours post operative. She has been slow to mobilise because of pain and has needed a urinary catheter overnight. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism after a hip replacement. She is breastfeeding, has no wound concerns, and has been receiving enoxaparin since the evening after surgery. She asks how long she will need the injections at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wound dry with no erythema, uterus well contracted, calves soft and non tender with no asymmetry, chest clear on auscultation, mobilising slowly with assistance
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), estimated blood loss at operation 700 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Change to oral rivaroxaban for six weeks after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation while breastfeeding
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants enter breast milk and lack safety data in lactation, so they are avoided while breastfeeding. Low molecular weight heparin is not secreted in clinically significant amounts and remains the drug of choice. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop the heparin now given her postoperative blood loss and falling haemoglobin, and rely on graduated compression stockings with early mobilisation
options.rationale: A blood loss of this order with a stable haemoglobin and a dry wound is not a contraindication to prophylactic dosing. Withholding prophylaxis in a high risk woman exchanges a small bleeding concern for a life threatening thrombotic one. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin for six weeks after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: Emergency caesarean after prolonged labour, obesity, immobility and a first degree family history combine to place her in the highest postnatal risk category, for which extended prophylaxis to six weeks is recommended. Risk remains elevated across the whole puerperium rather than only the first week. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin until discharge from hospital, then use graduated compression stockings alone with advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: Stopping at discharge covers only a fraction of the period of raised risk, and most postnatal events occur after the woman has gone home. Stockings alone are inadequate for a woman with several persisting risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Continue low molecular weight heparin for ten days after the birth, with graduated compression stockings and advice on early mobilisation
options.rationale: A shorter course suits women whose only risk factor is the caesarean itself, whereas the accumulation of risk factors here moves her into the extended duration group. The distinction between the two durations is the point being tested. (Source: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the risk is highest in the first week after birth but stays above baseline for about six weeks. Australian units use risk scoring that counts caesarean section, particularly emergency caesarean after labour, obesity, age, parity, immobility, prolonged labour, postpartum haemorrhage, pre eclampsia, infection, a family history in a first degree relative and known thrombophilia. Women with a single moderate risk factor generally receive prophylaxis for about ten days, while those with a combination of factors or a high risk feature receive it for six weeks after the birth. Low molecular weight heparin is the agent of choice because it does not cross into breast milk in clinically significant amounts, whereas direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in lactation. Prophylactic dosing is compatible with wound healing, and dose adjustment for weight is necessary in obesity.
key_points: Postnatal thrombotic risk remains elevated for about six weeks.
Risk factors are counted cumulatively rather than singly.
A single moderate factor usually warrants about ten days of prophylaxis.
Multiple factors or a high risk feature warrant six weeks.
Low molecular weight heparin is compatible with breastfeeding, unlike direct oral anticoagulants.
explanation.pearls: Prophylactic enoxaparin is dosed by weight rather than given as a fixed dose, because a woman over about ninety kilograms receiving the standard forty milligram dose is underdosed, and weight banded prescribing is a recurring gap identified in maternal mortality reviews.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
BMJ Best Practice: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice at six weeks for a mechanical mitral valve maintained on a low daily warfarin dose
stem:
You are the physician in a joint obstetric medicine clinic seeing a thirty one year old woman who has just discovered she is six weeks pregnant. She has a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement performed eight years ago for rheumatic disease and takes warfarin 2.5 mg daily, with an international normalised ratio that has remained in range at every recent check.

She is in sinus rhythm with good ventricular function on her last echocardiogram and has never had a thromboembolic event. She has read online that her tablets cause birth defects and has already missed two doses out of concern. She wants whichever plan gives her the best chance of a healthy baby and of surviving the pregnancy herself.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound with no murmur of regurgitation, jugular venous pressure not raised, chest clear on auscultation, no peripheral oedema, no signs of embolic phenomena
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.8 (target 2.5-3.5), haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), echocardiogram three months ago with normal prosthetic gradients and normal ventricular function

lead_in: What anticoagulation strategy should you recommend?

options.text: Continue warfarin through the first trimester after full counselling, and change to heparin in the weeks before the planned birth
options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose related and is low at daily doses at or below five milligrams, while warfarin gives the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis, which carries high maternal and fetal mortality. Substitution near term avoids an anticoagulated fetus during labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for the whole pregnancy, with anti factor Xa monitoring and dose adjustment at intervals
options.rationale: Heparin avoids embryopathy but carries a clearly higher rate of valve thrombosis, and failures cluster in women whose peak levels look adequate but whose trough levels fall. It is the preferred option when the warfarin dose required is high rather than low. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to prophylactic low molecular weight heparin with low dose aspirin for the first trimester, then return to warfarin for the remainder
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing is far below what a mechanical mitral prosthesis requires and aspirin does not substitute for anticoagulation. This combination would leave her substantially unprotected during the period of change. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Change to unfractionated heparin by continuous intravenous infusion for the first trimester in hospital, then restart warfarin in the second trimester
options.rationale: Continuous infusion achieves protection but commits a well woman to twelve weeks as an inpatient with line related infection and bleeding risks. It is reserved for the peripartum period or for women in whom other options have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Change to a direct oral anticoagulant for the pregnancy because it avoids both the embryopathy risk and the burden of frequent monitoring visits
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves in any patient after trials showed excess thromboembolism and bleeding, and they are not used in pregnancy. This option is unsafe on two independent grounds. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: A mechanical valve in pregnancy sets maternal thrombotic risk against fetal teratogenic risk, and no strategy removes both. Warfarin provides the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes an embryopathy of nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between about six and twelve weeks, together with fetal intracranial haemorrhage later in pregnancy. Crucially the embryopathy risk is dose dependent, falling to around two to three per cent at daily doses of five milligrams or less, which is why international and Australian guidance supports continuing warfarin through the first trimester at low dose after explicit counselling, while recommending substitution of heparin when the required dose is higher. Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta but carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis even with anti factor Xa monitoring, partly because trough levels fall between doses, and mitral prostheses are more thrombogenic than aortic ones. Warfarin is changed to heparin at around thirty six weeks so that the fetus is not anticoagulated during labour, and a woman who presents in labour on warfarin needs caesarean birth to avoid fetal intracranial haemorrhage.
key_points: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and low at five milligrams daily or less.
Valve thrombosis carries high mortality for both mother and fetus.
Low molecular weight heparin avoids embryopathy but has a higher thrombosis rate.
Mitral prostheses are more thrombogenic than aortic prostheses.
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve.
explanation.pearls: If she presents in labour while still taking warfarin, the fetus is anticoagulated even when the maternal international normalised ratio has been reversed, so caesarean birth is chosen to avoid intracranial haemorrhage from the pressures of a vaginal birth, and vitamin K given to the mother does not protect the baby quickly enough.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology: Cardiovascular disease during pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Porcelain white vulval plaques with loss of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a sixty two year old woman who reports two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has tried several over the counter antifungal creams and a barrier ointment without benefit, and has recently found intercourse painful at the entrance.

She went through menopause at fifty one and has used no hormone therapy. She has autoimmune hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine. She has had no abnormal cervical screening results and no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Porcelain white thickened plaques over both labia majora extending to the perineum in a figure of eight pattern, resorption of the labia minora, clitoral hood fused over the clitoris, several linear excoriations, introital narrowing, no discrete nodule or ulcer, vaginal mucosa normal on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogen, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for two weeks then twice weekly as ongoing maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which produces a pale thin vaginal mucosa with dryness rather than thickened white vulval plaques with architectural loss. The normal vaginal mucosa here points away from an oestrogen deficient process. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral fluconazole and advise soap avoidance with regular emollient use
options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis is a reasonable initial thought given the itch, but the swab is negative and repeated antifungal creams have already failed, which is the pattern that should prompt reconsideration. Architectural change of this kind is never caused by candida. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone one per cent ointment twice daily for six weeks and then review the symptomatic response
options.rationale: A mild corticosteroid is insufficient to control this condition and undertreatment allows scarring to progress while giving the impression that steroid has been tried. The vulva tolerates potent preparations well, so potency is not the limiting factor. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and release of the introital narrowing before medical therapy
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for persistent functional problems after the inflammation has been medically controlled, because operating on active disease risks recurrent fusion and koebnerisation at the incision. Medical control comes first in almost every case. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment in a reducing regimen over three months with planned clinical review
options.rationale: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line for lichen sclerosus, typically nightly for a month then tapering to alternate nights and twice weekly, and it both relieves symptoms and slows further architectural loss. Planned review matters because long term maintenance reduces scarring and lowers the risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval dermatosis with a bimodal incidence in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women, and it is strongly associated with other autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid disease. The characteristic appearance is porcelain white atrophic or thickened skin in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus, with progressive architectural change including resorption of the labia minora, burying of the clitoris under a fused hood, and introital narrowing. It is frequently misdiagnosed as thrush for years, and repeated failed antifungal treatment is a common part of the history. Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line and is continued as maintenance rather than stopped once symptoms settle, because ongoing treatment reduces both scarring and malignant transformation. Around four to five per cent of women develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, which is why any persistent nodule, ulcer or thickened area needs biopsy.
key_points: Figure of eight white plaques with loss of labia minora and clitoral burying are the defining findings
Strong association with autoimmune disease, especially thyroid disease, supports the diagnosis
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with maintenance rather than symptomatic use only
Long term steroid maintenance reduces both progressive scarring and malignant transformation
Around four to five per cent develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, so new lesions need biopsy
explanation.pearls: A 30 g tube of ultrapotent corticosteroid ointment should last a woman with vulval lichen sclerosus around twelve weeks on a standard reducing regimen, so a tube finished in three weeks signals overuse and one lasting a year signals undertreatment.

subtopic_detail: Third painful fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus in eighteen months after two previous incision and drainage procedures
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a twenty nine year old woman with three days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina on the left. She cannot sit comfortably and has been walking with a limp.

She has had two similar episodes in the past eighteen months, each treated in the emergency department with incision and drainage under local anaesthetic, and each recurring within a few months. She is otherwise well, is afebrile, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant swelling of 4 cm at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus displacing the introitus medially, overlying skin erythematous and pointing, no induration extending into the perineum, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent, result pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin with metronidazole for seven days and review her in the clinic after the course finishes
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not resolve a tense pointing collection, because the problem is an obstructed duct under pressure rather than surrounding cellulitis. Drainage is the therapeutic step and antibiotics are adjunctive at most. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic and arrange follow up with her general practitioner
options.rationale: Simple incision allows the skin edges to reappose within days so the duct reoccludes, which is precisely why she has presented for a third time. Repeating a procedure with a known high recurrence rate does not address the underlying obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Aspirate the collection with a wide bore needle under local anaesthetic and send the aspirate for bacterial culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration empties the cavity without creating a lasting drainage tract, giving the highest recurrence rate of the available options. It is reasonable only as temporising relief when definitive treatment is genuinely unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Insert a balloon tipped word catheter after incision, leaving it in place for four weeks to form an epithelialised tract
options.rationale: With recurrent disease the objective is a permanent drainage tract rather than a further one off evacuation, and a word catheter left for around four weeks allows the tract to epithelialise so the gland can drain in the long term. It is a local anaesthetic office procedure with recurrence rates far below those of simple incision. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next available elective theatre list and manage the pain with oral analgesia
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for repeated failure of tract forming procedures or when malignancy is suspected, because it carries risks of significant bleeding from the vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia. Waiting for an elective list also leaves an acutely painful collection undrained. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vestibule and drain through short ducts, and obstruction of the duct produces a cyst that may become secondarily infected to form an abscess. Most are polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora, but sexually transmitted infection is tested for because it changes partner management rather than because it dominates the microbiology. The central management principle is that a procedure which simply empties the cavity leaves the obstructed duct intact, so recurrence is high, whereas procedures that create a lasting epithelialised tract, such as word catheter insertion or marsupialisation, have much lower recurrence. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression rather than routinely. In women over forty a new Bartholin mass warrants biopsy or excision because of the small but real possibility of carcinoma.
key_points: Duct obstruction is the underlying problem, so emptying the cavity alone predicts recurrence
Word catheter or marsupialisation creates an epithelialised tract and markedly reduces recurrence
The word catheter stays in place for around four weeks to allow the tract to form
Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression
A new Bartholin mass in a woman over forty requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A Bartholin cyst that is asymptomatic and small in a woman under forty needs no intervention at all, so the decision to operate is driven by symptoms and recurrence rather than by the presence of the cyst itself.

subtopic_detail: Wedge shaped breast redness with rigors persisting after twenty four hours of effective milk removal and cold packs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a thirty one year old woman who is sixteen days postpartum and breastfeeding her first baby. She noticed a tender area in the right breast yesterday morning and has been feeding frequently from that side, applying cold packs afterwards and taking regular ibuprofen and paracetamol as advised by the midwife.

Overnight she developed shaking chills and aching limbs. She has a crack at the base of the right nipple which has been present for a week. The baby is feeding every three hours, has plenty of wet nappies and has regained birth weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, warm firm and tender with no discrete fluctuant mass, fissure at the base of the right nipple with no surrounding satellite lesions, no axillary lymphadenopathy, left breast normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue conservative measures with effective milk removal and analgesia, and review the following day if unchanged
options.rationale: Conservative management is the correct first step and has now been given a fair trial of twenty four hours without improvement, which is the point at which antibiotics are indicated. Rigors and a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius also mark a systemic response rather than simple inflammatory engorgement. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for five to seven days and encourage continued feeding from the affected breast
options.rationale: Mastitis that fails twenty four hours of effective milk removal, or that presents with systemic features and a nipple fissure providing a portal of entry, is treated with an antistaphylococcal antibiotic, and flucloxacillin is the Australian first line agent. Feeding continues from the affected side because milk stasis is what perpetuates the process and the milk is safe for the baby. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin and advise expressing and discarding milk from the right breast until the fever settles
options.rationale: Cefalexin is an acceptable alternative for penicillin allergy, but discarding the milk is wrong on both counts, since the milk is safe and stopping feeds from the affected side worsens stasis. Advice to discard also undermines breastfeeding at a vulnerable point. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent breast ultrasound and surgical review for drainage of a probable underlying collection
options.rationale: Ultrasound is indicated when a discrete fluctuant mass is present or when symptoms fail to settle after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, neither of which applies at this point. Imaging now would delay the treatment that is likely to resolve the problem. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole for ductal candidiasis and advise treating the baby with oral antifungal gel as well
options.rationale: Nipple and ductal candidiasis causes bilateral burning pain radiating through the breast after feeds, without fever, wedge shaped erythema or rigors. Treating for fungal infection here addresses the wrong organism entirely. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis begins as inflammation from milk stasis and ductal narrowing rather than as infection, which is why the first response is effective milk removal, cold packs, anti inflammatory analgesia and support with attachment. Antibiotics are added when symptoms fail to improve after about twenty four hours of those measures, when systemic features such as fever and rigors are present, or when a nipple fissure provides an obvious portal of entry. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism, so flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin is first line in Australia with cefalexin or clindamycin for penicillin allergy. Continued breastfeeding from the affected side is safe and therapeutic, and abrupt weaning during mastitis increases the risk of abscess formation. Failure to settle within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, or a discrete fluctuant mass, prompts ultrasound to look for an abscess requiring aspiration.
key_points: Mastitis starts as inflammation from milk stasis, so effective milk removal is the foundation of treatment
Antibiotics are indicated after 24 hours without improvement, or with systemic features or a nipple fissure
Flucloxacillin is the Australian first line agent, with cefalexin or clindamycin for penicillin allergy
Breastfeeding continues from the affected breast, since abrupt weaning increases abscess risk
Ultrasound is reserved for a fluctuant mass or failure to improve after 48 hours of antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis with erythema and peau d'orange, so any breast inflammation that has not fully resolved after a complete antibiotic course requires imaging regardless of how convincing the lactational story was.

subtopic_detail: Urine loss confined to coughing and netball with no nocturia and a normal post void residual in a woman wanting to avoid surgery
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a forty four year old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes and plays netball on Thursday nights. She has two children delivered vaginally, the second with forceps, and has noticed the problem worsening over three years.

She wears a liner most days and has stopped playing in the second half of games. She does not wake at night to pass urine, does not get a sudden compelling urge and has never leaked on the way to the toilet. She tells you she would prefer to avoid an operation if there is anything else worth trying.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no abdominal mass, demonstrable leak from the urethral meatus on coughing with a full bladder, pelvic floor contraction weak and poorly sustained on digital assessment, no prolapse beyond the hymen on straining, vaginal mucosa well oestrogenised
