data_table.Treatment history: Ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily commenced at 22 weeks, self ceased after 10 days for gastrointestinal side effects

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her anaemia?

options.text: Prescribe an oral iron polymaltose preparation and review the full blood count at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Changing the oral salt can reduce gastrointestinal intolerance and is reasonable earlier in pregnancy, but polymaltose is absorbed more slowly than the ferrous salts and reviewing only at 36 weeks leaves no time to change course. This chooses tolerability at the cost of the timeline. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Iron)

options.text: Investigate for a gastrointestinal source of blood loss with faecal occult blood and coeliac serology
options.rationale: Pregnancy itself explains iron deficiency through an expanded red cell mass and fetal demand, and she has no overt bleeding, no family history and two previous uncomplicated pregnancies. Pursuing a gastrointestinal source now would delay treatment that is needed before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion with ferric carboxymaltose in the day assessment unit
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron has been tried and not tolerated, when absorption is impaired, or when the gestation is too advanced for oral repletion to work in time, and at 30 weeks with a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L all three considerations point the same way. Parenteral iron can be given from the second trimester onwards and raises haemoglobin substantially faster than oral therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate at the same dose taken on alternate days with vitamin C
options.rationale: Alternate day dosing genuinely improves absorption by reducing the hepcidin surge and is a sound strategy earlier in pregnancy, but it still takes months to replete stores and she has ten weeks left. The near pair distinction is time available rather than efficacy of the regimen. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and recheck the full blood count the following day
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, active bleeding or imminent birth with severe anaemia, and it carries alloimmunisation and transfusion reaction risks with no benefit to iron stores. She is stable at rest and has ten weeks in which iron can be replaced properly. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy as maternal red cell mass expands and the fetus accumulates iron, mostly in the third trimester, so deficiency is the commonest medical problem of pregnancy in Australia. Ferritin is the most useful single test, with values below 30 micrograms per litre indicating depleted stores even when the haemoglobin is still normal, although it rises as an acute phase reactant and can mislead during infection. Oral iron remains first line and works well when started early and tolerated, with alternate day dosing improving absorption and reducing side effects. Intravenous iron is reserved for intolerance, malabsorption, non response, or a gestation too advanced for oral repletion, and modern preparations allow total dose replacement in a single sitting. Correcting anaemia before birth matters because it reduces the chance that a postpartum haemorrhage of ordinary size becomes a transfusion event.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre indicates depleted iron stores regardless of the haemoglobin.
Oral iron taken on alternate days is absorbed better than daily dosing because of hepcidin kinetics.
Intravenous iron is appropriate from the second trimester for intolerance, malabsorption or late gestation.
Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or active bleeding, not for a number alone.
Correcting antenatal anaemia lowers the transfusion risk if postpartum haemorrhage occurs.
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority through increased fibroblast growth factor 23 activity, so persistent fatigue or bone pain weeks after an infusion warrants a serum phosphate rather than a repeat iron study.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy
NBA: Patient Blood Management Guidelines, Obstetrics

subtopic_detail: selecting first line management of symptomatic anterior compartment prolapse in a woman who has not completed her family
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a feeling of something coming down at the vaginal entrance, worse by the end of a working day and relieved by lying flat.

She had a forceps birth eighteen months ago with a second degree tear and has a 4-year-old from a previous normal birth. She and her partner would like one more child and are not using contraception. She has no urinary incontinence, empties her bladder and bowel completely, and has no pain with intercourse. On examination with Valsalva in the semi-recumbent position, the anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen with no descent of the cervix or posterior wall. She has palpable voluntary pelvic floor contraction with a Modified Oxford score of 2 out of 5 and holds it for two seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen on Valsalva; cervix and posterior wall show no descent; Modified Oxford score 2 out of 5 with a 2 second hold
data_table.Symptoms: Dragging sensation worse at the end of the day, relieved by lying flat; no urinary or faecal incontinence; no incomplete emptying; no dyspareunia
data_table.Obstetric history: Forceps birth 18 months ago with second degree tear, previous normal birth, planning a further pregnancy

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line management?

options.text: Refer for anterior colporrhaphy with a plan to deliver any future pregnancy by caesarean
options.rationale: Reconstructive surgery before a planned pregnancy is generally avoided because a subsequent pregnancy and birth compromises the repair, and recurrence rates after anterior repair are already substantial. Planning a caesarean to protect the repair commits her to abdominal birth for an operation she may not yet need. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen cream three nights per week and review in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen improves atrophic tissue quality and is a useful adjunct around pessary use or surgery in postmenopausal women, but she is premenopausal with normally oestrogenised tissue. It treats a tissue problem she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Arrange urodynamic studies to characterise bladder function before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Urodynamics is indicated where there is bothersome incontinence, suspected voiding dysfunction, or before surgery for a complex case, and she has neither incontinence nor incomplete emptying. Investigating first would delay a treatment that is safe to start on clinical grounds alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

options.text: Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a pelvic health physiotherapist
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is first line for symptomatic prolapse at or above the hymen and improves both symptoms and stage, and her weak but present voluntary contraction is exactly the substrate that responds to a structured program. It is also the option that does not commit her to anything before a planned further pregnancy, which would undo a surgical repair. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)
source_refs: Cochrane: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Prolapse

options.text: Fit a ring pessary in clinic today and arrange a review appointment in three months
options.rationale: A pessary is a reasonable conservative option and is the usual choice when symptoms are severe, when training has failed, or when surgery is not wanted, but it is second line for mild prolapse with an intact voluntary contraction. The near pair distinction is that a pessary supports the prolapse mechanically whereas training addresses the muscle deficit causing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is graded by the position of the leading edge relative to the hymen, and symptoms correlate poorly with stage until the prolapse reaches or passes that landmark. Vaginal birth, particularly instrumental birth, is the dominant risk factor, alongside increasing parity, obesity, chronic cough and constipation, and prolonged heavy lifting. Management follows a ladder from lifestyle and pelvic floor muscle training, through mechanical support with a pessary, to reconstructive or obliterative surgery. Supervised training delivered by a pelvic health physiotherapist is substantially more effective than a leaflet of instructions, and trials show benefit for both symptoms and objective stage in mild to moderate disease. Surgical repair is deferred where further childbearing is planned, since a subsequent birth commonly undoes it.
key_points: Stage is defined by the leading edge relative to the hymen, with symptoms becoming prominent at or beyond it.
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is first line for mild to moderate symptomatic prolapse.
A pessary is the next step for those who do not improve, or who prefer to avoid or defer surgery.
Reconstructive surgery is generally deferred until childbearing is complete.
Address constipation, chronic cough and heavy lifting as modifiable contributors in every case.
explanation.pearls: Around a third of women cannot perform a correct pelvic floor contraction from verbal instruction alone and instead bear down, which is why a digital assessment confirming a lift rather than a push should precede any home exercise program.

sources.label: Cochrane: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Prolapse

subtopic_detail: responding to an undifferentiated febrile illness in the second trimester where the food history changes the antibiotic choice
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 35-year-old woman at 27 weeks in her second pregnancy who has had two days of fever, muscle aches and a headache, and one episode of loose stools yesterday. She has no urinary symptoms, no cough and no rash.

She tells you she has been careful with food but ate a chicken and soft cheese salad from a delicatessen counter four days ago, and that a colleague who shared it has also been unwell. She has had no sick contacts otherwise and no overseas travel. Her cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 165 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations, and she reports normal fetal movements until this morning. Her urine dipstick is negative for nitrites and leucocytes, her chest is clear on auscultation, and her abdomen is soft with no uterine tenderness and no contractions on the tocograph.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108, blood pressure 106/62, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 165
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender, no rash, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes
data_table.Monitoring: Cardiotocograph baseline 165 with reduced variability, no decelerations, no uterine activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antimicrobial management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous ceftriaxone with a single dose of azithromycin
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is the sensible empirical choice for most community acquired sepsis in pregnancy, which is what makes it the dangerous answer here, because Listeria monocytogenes carries intrinsic resistance to every cephalosporin. Choosing it would leave the one organism the food history points to entirely untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send stool for culture and manage symptomatically with paracetamol and oral fluids
options.rationale: Stool culture has poor yield for this organism and a symptomatic approach ignores a fetal tachycardia with reduced variability, which signals that the fetus is already affected. Invasive disease in pregnancy carries a high rate of fetal loss and preterm birth if antibiotics are delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Listeria in Pregnancy)

options.text: Start oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole and arrange review in the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: This combination does have activity against the organism and is the alternative for a patient with severe penicillin allergy, but oral therapy and outpatient review are inadequate for suspected invasive disease with an abnormal fetal trace. Trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist and is avoided where an alternative exists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir and arrange serology for cytomegalovirus and parvovirus B19
options.rationale: Viral serology is worth sending as part of a broad workup, and these agents do cause fetal infection, but neither produces an acute febrile illness of this tempo with a raised C reactive protein and neutrophilia. Treating a viral cause would delay the antibiotics that the food history and fetal trace demand. (Source: RANZCOG: Listeria in Pregnancy)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin
options.rationale: A febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms after high risk food in a pregnant woman must be treated as invasive listeriosis until blood cultures exclude it, and the organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins. Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin, with gentamicin added for synergy in invasive disease, is the required regimen and blood culture is the only test that reliably makes the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are roughly ten to twenty times more susceptible to invasive listeriosis than the general population because cell mediated immunity is attenuated, and the organism has a particular tropism for the placenta. The maternal illness is often mild and flu like, with fever, myalgia and sometimes diarrhoea, which is why the food history does so much of the diagnostic work: soft and unpasteurised cheeses, pre-prepared salads, cold cured meats, pate, smoked seafood and rockmelon are the classic vehicles. Fetal consequences are severe and out of proportion to the maternal illness, including miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis or meningitis. Blood culture is the diagnostic test, since stool culture is insensitive and serology is not useful. The critical prescribing point is intrinsic cephalosporin resistance, which makes the default empirical choice for sepsis in pregnancy the wrong one.
key_points: Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, including ceftriaxone.
Blood culture is the diagnostic test; stool culture and serology are not reliable.
Maternal illness is often mild while fetal outcomes are severe, so treat on suspicion.
Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is the backbone, with gentamicin added for synergy in invasive disease.
High risk foods include soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads, pate, cold cured meats and smoked seafood.
explanation.pearls: The incubation period for invasive listeriosis can stretch to as long as 70 days, so a food history limited to the past week will miss the exposure and the question needs to be asked across the preceding two months.

subtopic_detail: responding to modest painless bleeding with an abrupt fetal heart rate change immediately after membranes are ruptured
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 30-year-old woman at 39 weeks in her first pregnancy is in spontaneous labour at 5 cm dilated with the fetal head at station minus 1. The midwife performs an artificial rupture of membranes to augment progress.

Clear liquor drains, followed immediately by about 80 mL of fresh dark red blood. Within 90 seconds the fetal heart rate falls from a baseline of 145 to a sustained 70 beats per minute with no recovery between contractions. The mother's pulse is 88 and her blood pressure is 122/74, and she reports no abdominal pain at all. Her uterus is soft between contractions and non tender on palpation. She had a twin pregnancy conceived by in vitro fertilisation that reduced to a singleton at nine weeks, and her 20 week morphology scan noted a low lying placenta that had migrated on a repeat scan at 34 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 70
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender between contractions, cervix 5 cm dilated, vertex at station minus 1, approximately 80 mL fresh dark red blood per vaginam
data_table.Monitoring: Fetal heart rate fell from a baseline of 145 to a sustained 70 within 90 seconds of membrane rupture, no recovery between contractions
data_table.History: In vitro fertilisation conception, twin pregnancy reduced to singleton at 9 weeks, low lying placenta at 20 weeks that had migrated by 34 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Call for immediate caesarean section and transfer to theatre without waiting for investigations
options.rationale: Painless bleeding beginning at the moment of membrane rupture with an immediate sustained fetal bradycardia, in a soft non tender uterus and a haemodynamically normal mother, indicates that the bleeding is fetal rather than maternal and the fetal blood volume is measured in a few hundred millilitres. Survival depends on delivery within minutes, so nothing may be allowed to delay transfer to theatre. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa Praevia)

options.text: Perform an Apt test on the vaginal blood to establish whether it is of fetal origin first
options.rationale: The alkali denaturation test does distinguish fetal from maternal haemoglobin and is the classical teaching point, but performing it consumes minutes that the fetus does not have. The clinical triad has already answered the question the test would answer. (Source: RCOG Green-top 27b: Vasa Praevia)

options.text: Give a subcutaneous terbutaline tocolytic, reposition to left lateral and observe the trace
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation with tocolysis and repositioning is the right response to a bradycardia caused by uterine hyperstimulation or cord compression, where relieving the mechanical cause restores oxygenation. Here the fetus is exsanguinating, so improving placental perfusion does not address the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

options.text: Site two large bore cannulas, cross match four units and commence maternal fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Maternal resuscitation is the correct priority for placental abruption or praevia, where the blood lost is the mother's, but here she is normotensive with a soft uterus and the 80 mL lost is a trivial maternal volume. Preparing maternal blood products treats the wrong circulation. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Perform a fetal scalp blood sample to measure lactate and decide on delivery from the result
options.rationale: Scalp sampling is used to clarify an equivocal trace in a stable fetus, and a sustained bradycardia below 80 beats per minute is an absolute contraindication because it is already a decision to deliver. Taking the sample would also add further blood loss from a fetus that is bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes unprotected fetal vessels running through the membranes across or near the internal os, unsupported by placental tissue or cord, and it arises most often from a velamentous cord insertion or from vessels bridging the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta. Risk factors include in vitro fertilisation conception, a multiple pregnancy including one reduced to a singleton, and a low lying placenta in the second trimester even when it later migrates. When the membranes rupture the vessels tear and the fetus bleeds, and because total fetal blood volume at term is only around 250 to 350 mL, exsanguination occurs within minutes. The clinical signature is painless bleeding at the moment of rupture with an immediate profound fetal heart rate abnormality in a mother whose observations remain entirely normal. Antenatally diagnosed cases are managed with corticosteroids, hospital admission in the third trimester and elective caesarean before labour, which converts a condition with very high perinatal mortality into one with survival above 95 per cent.
key_points: Suspect it when bleeding begins exactly at membrane rupture and the fetal heart rate collapses immediately.
The mother stays haemodynamically normal because the blood being lost is fetal.
A soft non tender uterus argues against abruption, which is the main competing diagnosis.
Risk factors are assisted conception, velamentous or bilobed placenta, and a second trimester low lying placenta.
Antenatal diagnosis with planned caesarean before labour transforms survival.
explanation.pearls: A low lying placenta found at the 20 week scan warrants deliberate assessment of the cord insertion site on the follow up scan, because migration of the placenta does not move a velamentous insertion and this is the one chance to diagnose vasa praevia before labour.

subtopic_detail: sequencing replacement against uterotonic drugs when the fundus cannot be felt after a controlled cord traction delivery of the placenta
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite three minutes after the delivery of the placenta in a 24-year-old woman who has just had her first baby. The midwife had given oxytocin with the anterior shoulder and delivered the placenta by controlled cord traction.

The mother is pale, sweating and complaining of severe lower abdominal pain, and she has vomited once. She has lost approximately 600 mL so far. On abdominal palpation you cannot identify a fundus at all, and there is a distinct dimple where you expect it to be. Inspecting the vulva you see a smooth dark red mass at the introitus with the placenta still adherent to it. She has received no other medication. Her observations are being repeated every two minutes and the anaesthetic registrar is already in the room with two cannulas sited.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 58, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No fundus palpable abdominally with a dimple at the expected site; smooth dark red mass visible at the introitus with the placenta still attached
data_table.Blood loss: Approximately 600 mL since delivery of the placenta
data_table.Drugs given: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly with the anterior shoulder, nothing since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly to contract the uterus and control the bleeding
options.rationale: Any uterotonic given before the uterus is replaced closes the cervical ring around the inverted fundus and makes replacement far harder or impossible, sometimes committing the woman to laparotomy. This is the central anti-pattern of the presentation, because a bleeding postpartum uterus otherwise calls for a uterotonic reflexively. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Attempt immediate manual replacement of the uterus with the placenta left attached
options.rationale: Replacement is attempted at once because the cervical ring tightens with every passing minute, and the placenta is left in place during the manoeuvre since detaching it first opens the placental bed and worsens the bleeding. The fundus is pushed back through the ring along the axis of the vagina using the palm and fingertips, beginning with the part that inverted last. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)
source_refs: WHO: Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth

options.text: Remove the placenta manually first, then attempt replacement of the uterus through the cervix
options.rationale: Separating the placenta before replacement converts a partially controlled situation into torrential haemorrhage from the exposed placental bed, and it makes the fundus no easier to reduce. The near pair distinction is sequence, since the placenta is removed after the uterus is back inside and a uterotonic has been given. (Source: WHO: Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth)
source_refs: WHO: Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and inflate it with warmed sodium chloride
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade treats atonic bleeding from a uterus that is in its normal position, and it cannot be placed into a cavity that is turned inside out. It has a genuine role later if atony persists after successful replacement. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give atropine 600 micrograms intravenously for the bradycardia and reassess the blood pressure
options.rationale: The bradycardia is vagally mediated by traction on the infundibulopelvic ligaments and resolves once the uterus is replaced, so treating the heart rate alone leaves the cause running. The degree of shock here is also out of proportion to the 600 mL lost, which is itself the clue that a neurogenic component is present. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is rare but is one of the few obstetric emergencies in which the reflexive correct action for the usual problem is the wrong one. It is associated with excessive cord traction before placental separation, a fundal placental implantation, a short cord and uterine overdistension, though it also occurs without any identifiable cause. The presentation combines shock that appears disproportionate to the measured blood loss, a vagally mediated bradycardia rather than the expected tachycardia, severe lower abdominal pain, and the absence of a palpable fundus. Management is immediate manual replacement with the placenta still attached, uterotonics withheld until the uterus is back in position, and full resuscitation running in parallel. If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic replacement with warm fluid instilled into the vagina or surgical correction is required, and uterine relaxants such as glyceryl trinitrate or a volatile anaesthetic may be needed to relax the constriction ring.
key_points: Shock out of proportion to measured blood loss, with bradycardia rather than tachycardia, is the signature.
Replace the uterus first; withhold every uterotonic until it is back in position.
Leave the placenta attached during replacement to avoid opening the placental bed.
Give a uterotonic immediately after successful replacement and keep a hand in place until the uterus contracts.
If manual replacement fails, use hydrostatic replacement or proceed to surgical correction.
explanation.pearls: A constriction ring that blocks manual replacement is relaxed with glyceryl trinitrate 50 to 100 micrograms intravenously or sublingual spray, which acts within about a minute and buys the window for a second attempt before theatre is required.

sources.label: WHO: Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth

subtopic_detail: managing abdominal distension with haemoconcentration in the week after oocyte retrieval and embryo transfer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 29-year-old woman who had oocyte retrieval eight days ago followed by a fresh embryo transfer three days later. She describes abdominal swelling, tight clothing, breathlessness lying flat, and nausea, and she has gained 4 kg since the retrieval.

She has polycystic ovary syndrome and 32 oocytes were collected. She passed urine twice yesterday and once so far today. She has no calf pain, no chest pain and no fever. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and is uncomfortable but not peritonitic, and her chest has reduced air entry at both bases. A bedside ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries measuring 11 cm on the right and 10 cm on the left with moderate free fluid in the abdomen, and no adnexal torsion is evident with preserved arterial and venous flow to both ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, blood pressure 102/68, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, uncomfortable but not peritonitic, reduced air entry at both lung bases, calves soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.51 (0.33 to 0.45), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 129 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45 to 90), albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50)
data_table.Imaging: Ovaries 11 cm right and 10 cm left with moderate free intraperitoneal fluid; arterial and venous flow preserved in both ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with oral fluids, simple analgesia and review in the fertility clinic in three days
options.rationale: Outpatient management is appropriate for mild to moderate disease in a woman who is passing urine well and can drink freely, and her oliguria, haematocrit and breathlessness place her outside that group. A three day interval would allow thrombosis or renal failure to develop unobserved. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome)

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone with metronidazole after blood cultures for presumed pelvic sepsis
options.rationale: The white cell count is genuinely raised, which makes infection a reasonable consideration, but leucocytosis is characteristic of this syndrome itself and she is afebrile with no localising signs. Antibiotics alone would leave the haemoconcentration and thrombotic risk untreated. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome)

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis
options.rationale: Severe disease with a haematocrit above 0.45, oliguria, tense ascites and breathlessness requires admission, careful volume expansion to restore intravascular volume, and drainage of ascites which relieves both the respiratory restriction and the abdominal compartment effect on renal perfusion. Thromboprophylaxis is mandatory rather than optional, because haemoconcentration combined with very high oestradiol produces a thrombotic risk that persists for weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome)

options.text: Admit for intravenous furosemide, fluid restriction and daily weights until the ascites settles
options.rationale: The fluid has shifted out of the intravascular compartment rather than being in excess of it, so a diuretic deepens the haemoconcentration and raises the thrombotic risk further. Diuretics have a narrow role only after intravascular volume has been restored and oliguria persists. (Source: RCOG Green-top 5: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent laparoscopy to decompress the ovaries and drain the intraperitoneal fluid
options.rationale: Surgery on hyperstimulated ovaries risks catastrophic bleeding from friable enlarged tissue and is reserved for torsion, rupture with instability, or an ectopic pregnancy. Preserved arterial and venous flow with an abdomen that is not peritonitic argues against all of those. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is an iatrogenic condition driven by vascular endothelial growth factor released from luteinised granulosa cells under the influence of human chorionic gonadotrophin, which increases capillary permeability and moves fluid from the intravascular space into the peritoneal and pleural cavities. Risk is highest in young women, those with polycystic ovary syndrome, high antral follicle counts, high oestradiol levels and large numbers of oocytes retrieved. Early onset disease appears within a week of the trigger injection, while late onset disease at around eight to ten days is driven by human chorionic gonadotrophin from an implanting pregnancy and tends to be more severe and more prolonged. Severity is graded on haematocrit, urine output, ascites, and the presence of renal or respiratory compromise, and the management principles are volume expansion, drainage of tense ascites, thromboprophylaxis and avoidance of diuretics and surgery. Prevention through antagonist protocols, agonist triggers and elective freezing of all embryos has substantially reduced the incidence.
key_points: Fluid shifts out of the intravascular space, so the patient is intravascularly deplete despite gross ascites.
Haematocrit above 0.45 with oliguria marks severe disease requiring admission.
Thromboprophylaxis is mandatory and continues for weeks, since the prothrombotic state outlasts the ascites.
Avoid diuretics until intravascular volume is restored, and avoid surgery unless torsion or rupture is present.
Late onset disease driven by an implanting pregnancy is more severe and longer lasting than early onset disease.
explanation.pearls: Thrombosis in this syndrome characteristically affects the upper body, with internal jugular, subclavian and axillary veins the classical sites, so a woman reporting neck or arm swelling after oocyte retrieval needs upper limb venous imaging rather than a leg Doppler.

subtopic_detail: deciding on immunoglobulin versus antiviral prophylaxis after a household chickenpox contact in a woman with uncertain immunity
stem:
You are the general practice registrar telephoned by a 26-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her 4-year-old nephew stayed overnight at her house two days ago and developed a widespread blistering rash yesterday morning, which their family doctor has diagnosed as chickenpox.

She grew up overseas, has no vaccination records, and cannot recall ever having had chickenpox or shingles herself. She spent the evening reading to him and sharing the same living room for several hours. She feels entirely well today with no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms. You arrange an urgent varicella zoster immunoglobulin G serology which the laboratory telephones back this afternoon as negative. It is now 48 hours since the exposure, and the hospital pharmacy confirms that zoster immunoglobulin is in stock.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash anywhere, chest clear, no mucosal lesions
data_table.Investigations: Varicella zoster virus immunoglobulin G negative on urgent serology
data_table.Exposure details: Several hours of indoor face to face contact 48 hours ago with a child whose vesicular rash appeared the following morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir prophylaxis today and continue it for the next fourteen days
options.rationale: Antivirals are the treatment once a rash appears and are given within 24 hours of its onset, and prophylactic use from day 7 after exposure is an alternative only where immunoglobulin is unavailable. Immunoglobulin is preferred where stock exists, which the pharmacy has confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in Pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange an urgent amniocentesis to test amniotic fluid for varicella zoster virus by polymerase chain reaction
options.rationale: Invasive testing is premature in a woman who has not developed infection and carries a procedure related loss risk for no benefit. It has a limited role only after confirmed maternal infection, and even then detailed ultrasound surveillance is generally preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in Pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that immunity is likely despite the serology and arrange a repeat test in two weeks
options.rationale: Assuming immunity in the face of a negative result and an absent history removes the only opportunity to act within the prophylaxis window, and a repeat test in two weeks would simply document seroconversion after the fact. Recall of childhood chickenpox is unreliable, which is why the serology was sent. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Give zoster immunoglobulin now and advise her to report any rash or respiratory symptom immediately
options.rationale: A seronegative pregnant woman with significant exposure should receive zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and ideally within 96 hours, since it attenuates maternal disease and reduces the risk of severe varicella pneumonia. At 48 hours she is comfortably inside the window, and the advice to report symptoms matters because immunoglobulin attenuates rather than prevents infection. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Give a dose of live attenuated varicella vaccine now and a second dose in four weeks
options.rationale: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, and post exposure vaccination would in any case be too slow to generate protection before the incubation period ends. Vaccination is the right answer for a seronegative woman postpartum, which is the near pair distinction of timing rather than of agent. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy carries two distinct risks: severe maternal disease, particularly varicella pneumonia which is markedly more dangerous in pregnancy and especially in the third trimester, and fetal infection. Congenital varicella syndrome, with limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring, eye and neurological abnormalities, complicates roughly 1 to 2 per cent of maternal infections occurring before 28 weeks and is very rare thereafter. Infection around the time of birth, specifically from about five days before to two days after delivery, produces severe neonatal varicella because the baby receives the virus without protective maternal antibody. Around 90 per cent of Australian adults are seropositive, so the first step for any exposed woman with an uncertain history is urgent serology. A seronegative woman with significant exposure receives zoster immunoglobulin within 96 hours, and a woman who develops a rash receives oral aciclovir or valaciclovir started within 24 hours.
key_points: Send urgent varicella serology for any exposed pregnant woman with no clear history of infection or vaccination.
Zoster immunoglobulin is given to seronegative women within 96 hours of significant exposure.
Immunoglobulin attenuates rather than prevents disease, so ongoing symptom surveillance is still required.
Live attenuated varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and is given postpartum instead.
Congenital varicella syndrome risk is confined largely to infection before 28 weeks and is around 1 to 2 per cent.
explanation.pearls: Delivery occurring between five days before and two days after the onset of a maternal rash is the highest risk window for neonatal varicella, and the neonate requires zoster immunoglobulin at birth regardless of how well the mother appears.

subtopic_detail: separating two third trimester liver disorders when the blood pressure is normal and the glucose is low
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks in her first pregnancy with five days of nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant discomfort, and two days of feeling increasingly confused, which her partner noticed before she did.

She has had no itch, no headache and no visual disturbance. Her blood pressure has been recorded between 106/62 and 118/70 at every antenatal visit including today, and her urine protein to creatinine ratio is 12 mg/mmol (less than 30). She is mildly jaundiced with asterixis on examination, and she is drowsy but rousable and orientated to place. Her uterus is soft and non tender, the cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 155 with reduced variability, and an ultrasound shows a bright liver with normal hepatic and portal venous flow and no biliary dilatation. Her paracetamol level is undetectable and her viral hepatitis serology is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 104, blood pressure 112/66, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 155
data_table.Examination: Mildly jaundiced, asterixis present, drowsy but rousable, uterus soft and non tender, no oedema, no epigastric tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 2.4 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8), international normalised ratio 2.1 (0.9 to 1.3), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.9 to 6.2 in pregnancy), alanine aminotransferase 340 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 78 micromol/L (less than 20), creatinine 148 micromol/L (35 to 70), urate 0.48 mmol/L (0.14 to 0.35), platelets 186 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haptoglobin within normal limits, blood film shows no fragmented red cells
data_table.Other: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (less than 30), paracetamol undetectable, ultrasound shows a bright liver with normal vascular flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start magnesium sulfate and intravenous labetalol and expedite birth for severe pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: This would be the correct pathway for the haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets variant, which is the principal competing diagnosis, but her blood pressure has never been raised, her protein to creatinine ratio is normal, her platelets are normal and there is no haemolysis on film or haptoglobin. Magnesium also accumulates dangerously when the creatinine is rising, so giving it without an indication adds risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and measure serum bile acids, planning birth at 37 weeks
options.rationale: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is the other common third trimester liver disorder, but it presents with itch as the dominant symptom and does not cause hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy or encephalopathy. She has no itch at all, which removes the cardinal feature. (Source: GESA: Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous N-acetylcysteine and continue expectant management with daily liver function tests
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine is used as an adjunct in non paracetamol acute liver failure and is reasonable alongside definitive treatment, but her paracetamol level is undetectable and expectant management allows a deteriorating maternal and fetal state to continue. Continuing the pregnancy is the error, since the placenta is the source of the metabolic insult. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.text: Commence therapeutic plasma exchange and defer birth until the international normalised ratio normalises
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is used for thrombotic microangiopathies and occasionally as salvage after delivery, and the absence of fragmented cells with a normal haptoglobin and platelet count argues against that mechanism. Deferring birth until clotting normalises is self defeating, because the coagulopathy will not correct while the placenta remains in situ. (Source: GESA: Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Correct the glucose and coagulopathy and expedite birth after stabilisation in a tertiary centre
options.rationale: Hypoglycaemia with a coagulopathy out of proportion to the platelet count, encephalopathy and a normal blood pressure points to acute fatty liver of pregnancy, in which the liver fails to synthesise glucose and clotting factors and the only definitive treatment is delivery. Stabilisation with dextrose and blood products comes first because operating on an uncorrected coagulopathy causes catastrophic bleeding, but birth must follow without waiting for the liver to recover. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but rapidly progressive microvesicular steatosis of the third trimester, linked in a proportion of cases to fetal long chain 3-hydroxyacyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency, where accumulated fetal fatty acid metabolites overwhelm the maternal liver. It overlaps clinically with the haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets syndrome, and the two can coexist, but several features separate them: hypoglycaemia, marked coagulopathy with a low fibrinogen in the presence of a normal platelet count, encephalopathy, and frequently a normal blood pressure with no significant proteinuria. The Swansea criteria formalise this pattern using vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia or polyuria, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin and urate, hypoglycaemia, raised transaminases and ammonia, renal impairment, coagulopathy, ascites or a bright liver on imaging, and microvesicular steatosis on biopsy. Management is supportive stabilisation followed by prompt delivery whatever the gestation, with intensive care involvement and anticipation of postpartum haemorrhage. Most women recover liver function over days to weeks, and the infant should be tested for the fatty acid oxidation defect.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia is the single most useful discriminator from the hypertensive liver syndromes.
A raised international normalised ratio with a low fibrinogen and normal platelets suggests synthetic failure rather than consumption.
Normal blood pressure and normal proteinuria do not exclude it and in fact point towards it.
Delivery is the definitive treatment and must not await recovery of liver function.
Screen the infant for long chain 3-hydroxyacyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency after birth.
explanation.pearls: Fibrinogen normally rises to 4 to 6 g/L by the third trimester, so a level of 1.4 g/L represents profound synthetic failure and predicts postpartum haemorrhage, and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate should be given to reach at least 2 g/L before any operative birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic and adjunct choice in atonic postpartum haemorrhage following syntocinon failure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birthing suite for postpartum haemorrhage. A 32 year old G2P1 woman had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4100 gram baby 20 minutes ago following a two hour second stage. She has a history of well controlled asthma and no cardiovascular disease. Her blood pressure runs 108/68 mmHg at booking.

The placenta was delivered intact 12 minutes ago after active management with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units. Since delivery she has passed an estimated 950 mL of fresh blood into the collection drape. On assessment she has pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. The uterus is palpable at the umbilicus and boggy. Two intravenous cannulae are in place and 1 L of Hartmann solution has been running wide open. A second team member has commenced bimanual uterine massage. The perineum shows no active bleeding from tears; there is no clinical suspicion of retained placenta on inspection. Group and hold is done and cross match is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Uterine tone: Palpable at umbilicus, boggy, bimanual massage in progress
data_table.Blood loss: Approximately 950 mL fresh blood in drape 20 min post birth
data_table.Placenta: Delivered intact 12 min ago after IM oxytocin 10 units
data_table.Perineum: No active tear bleeding, no retained tissue on inspection
data_table.History: G2P1, well controlled asthma, booking BP 108/68 mmHg, no cardiovascular disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step for uterine atony?

options.text: Intramuscular misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual single dose alone and continued bimanual uterine massage while awaiting the cross matched blood products from the transfusion service
options.rationale: Misoprostol alone is a low-resource option; IV oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine plus TXA is the preferred multi-agent approach in a well-equipped birthing unit. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram every fifteen minutes to a maximum of eight doses and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g slow bolus over ten minutes with continued uterine massage
options.rationale: Carboprost is third-line uterotonic (after oxytocin and ergometrine); it is contraindicated in asthma given her history. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1 L Hartmann over four hours plus intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram and tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over ten minutes
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH pathway: after initial oxytocin bolus failure give IV oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine (BP normotensive) plus TXA within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g single bolus over ten minutes only and continue bimanual uterine massage with reassessment of tone at fifteen minutes before further pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: TXA alone does not treat uterine atony; oxytocin infusion plus a second uterotonic must be given concurrently. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intrauterine tamponade with a Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL and packing of the vagina below with vaginal gauze while awaiting transfer to theatre for further definitive management
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade follows failure of pharmacological uterotonics; step up pharmacotherapy first before mechanical management. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage is defined as blood loss above 500 mL after vaginal birth or 1000 mL after caesarean, or any loss causing haemodynamic compromise. Uterine atony causes 70 percent of primary PPH. The RANZCOG stepwise pharmacological approach starts with oxytocin: 5 units IV bolus or 10 units IM at delivery, then IV infusion 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours if bleeding continues. Second-line ergometrine 250 microgram IM (contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia, heart disease). Third-line carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes to maximum 2 mg (contraindicated in asthma). Fourth line misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual or rectal. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces death from bleeding (WOMAN trial). Mechanical management (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and surgical measures follow if bleeding persists despite maximal pharmacology.
key_points: Uterotonic order: oxytocin -> ergometrine -> carboprost -> misoprostol.
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma; ergometrine in hypertension.
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: Atonic PPH after oxytocin failure and normal BP without asthma: give oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine 250 microgram IM plus tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old G3P1 woman at 28+4 weeks gestation admitted to the birth suite with regular painful contractions every 3 minutes for the last two hours. She has a history of one previous term normal vaginal birth. Her pregnancy has been low risk with normal morphology scan and midpregnancy blood pressures 110/70 mmHg.

On arrival her pulse rate is 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC, fetal heart rate 148 per minute on cardiotocography with normal variability and no decelerations. Speculum examination reveals clear liquor draining and a partly effaced cervix; digital examination shows cervix 3 cm dilated and 60 percent effaced. Fetal fibronectin is not done given ruptured membranes. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular first dose was given ninety minutes ago and nifedipine 20 mg oral tocolysis has been started. Ultrasound at admission confirms cephalic presentation, estimated fetal weight 1200 grams (25th centile), normal liquor volume and normal Doppler indices.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Speculum and vaginal exam: Clear liquor draining, cervix 3 cm dilated 60 percent effaced
data_table.Cardiotocography: Fetal heart rate 148 /min baseline, normal variability, no decelerations
data_table.Ultrasound: Cephalic, estimated fetal weight 1200 g (25th centile), normal liquor, normal Dopplers
data_table.Given so far: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 90 min ago, nifedipine 20 mg oral commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention for neuroprotection?

options.text: Intravenous betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for two further doses and defer any magnesium sulfate therapy until closer to imminent delivery is confirmed at less than 30 minutes
options.rationale: Betamethasone is IM, and MgSO4 should be commenced when birth is expected within 24 hours below 30 weeks (not deferred to imminent delivery). (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 2 g per hour infusion for 12 hours only irrespective of the timing of birth with cessation at that fixed endpoint
options.rationale: The RANZCOG dose is 1 g/h maintenance (not 2 g/h) and duration is up to 24 hours or until birth; higher dose increases toxicity without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g loading over 20 minutes then 2 g per hour infusion for the total of 24 hours only with continued nifedipine tocolysis co-administration
options.rationale: 6 g loading is the pre-eclampsia dose, not the neuroprotection dose; combining higher MgSO4 with nifedipine risks profound hypotension. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion for 24 hours or until birth whichever is sooner and continue monitoring reflexes
options.rationale: MgSO4 for neuroprotection is indicated for imminent preterm birth below 30 weeks; dose is 4 g loading then 1 g/h until birth or 24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g single loading bolus only over 20 minutes with no ongoing infusion and reassess for further dose at 12 hours after the loading dose
options.rationale: Loading dose alone is insufficient; a maintenance infusion is required until birth or 24 hours for sustained neuroprotection. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the preterm fetus reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in babies born below 30 weeks gestation (NNT approximately 46). RANZCOG recommends offering MgSO4 when preterm birth is anticipated within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks. The neuroprotection dose is 4 g loading over 20 to 30 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion until birth or for 24 hours whichever is sooner. This is a lower maintenance dose than the pre-eclampsia protocol (4 g load then 1-2 g/h). Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote for magnesium toxicity. Nifedipine and MgSO4 can be co-administered but blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored closely for additive hypotension.
key_points: MgSO4 neuroprotection: below 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours.
Dose: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/h until birth or 24 hours.
Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output; calcium gluconate is antidote.
explanation.pearls: Threatened preterm birth below 30 weeks gestation gets magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/h infusion for neuroprotection - lower maintenance dose than the pre-eclampsia protocol.

sources.label: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgical management for a tubal ectopic pregnancy under the RANZCOG bhCG threshold
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30 year old G2P0 woman referred from the emergency department with light vaginal spotting and mild right iliac fossa discomfort for two days at 7 weeks gestation by last menstrual period. She has one previous first trimester miscarriage two years ago and no other medical or surgical history.

On assessment she has pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Speculum shows a closed cervical os and scant blood in the vault. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an empty uterus with a thin decidualised endometrium (endometrial thickness 8 mm), and a 22 mm right adnexal mass separate from the ovary with a yolk sac but no fetal pole and no fetal cardiac activity. There is a trace of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin is 3800 IU/L. Full blood count, liver and renal function, and blood group are normal; she is Rhesus positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Abdominal exam: Soft, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Speculum: Closed cervical os, scant blood in vault
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Empty uterus (endometrium 8 mm), right adnexal mass 22 mm with yolk sac, no fetal pole, no cardiac activity, trace free fluid pouch of Douglas
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 3800 IU/L, FBC/LFT/UEC normal, Rhesus positive
data_table.History: G2P0, previous first-trimester miscarriage, 7 weeks by LMP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscular with follow up serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin at day 4 and day 7 and weekly thereafter until non-pregnant range
options.rationale: RANZCOG criteria met: haemodynamically stable, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, bhCG <5000, no significant pain, no contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right fallopian tube given the haemodynamic stability and clear intact contralateral tube visualised at ultrasound with anticipated future fertility
options.rationale: Surgery is offered but not mandatory here; methotrexate is a valid alternative and preferred when RANZCOG criteria for medical management are met. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly beta human chorionic gonadotropin monitoring only, no methotrexate and no surgery, awaiting spontaneous resolution over the coming weeks in outpatient clinic review
options.rationale: Expectant management is only for bhCG <1500 with declining trend and no cardiac activity on ultrasound; her level of 3800 exceeds this. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the right fallopian tube to preserve tubal patency with intraoperative beta human chorionic gonadotropin measurement post trophoblast removal from the tube
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is offered when the contralateral tube is diseased/absent (preserve fertility); with a normal contralateral tube, salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast risk. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate regimen 50 mg per square metre intramuscular on day 0 and day 4 with baseline liver function tests repeated on day 7 for standard monitoring after therapy
options.rationale: Two-dose regimen is reserved for high bhCG (>5000 with normal criteria otherwise) or fetal cardiac activity; single dose is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: A tubal ectopic pregnancy is confirmed by an empty uterus with an adnexal mass containing a yolk sac or fetal pole and positive serum beta-hCG. RANZCOG offers three management options based on haemodynamic status and specific criteria. Expectant management: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 1500 with declining trend, no fetal cardiac activity. Methotrexate: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 5000, no fetal cardiac activity, mass below 3.5 cm, no significant pain or haemorrhage, no contraindications (hepatic, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding), reliable follow-up. Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with bhCG on days 4 and 7, expect 15 percent decline day 4 to 7. Surgical: haemodynamically unstable, ruptured, contraindications to methotrexate, or above criteria not met. Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is normal.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: stable, bhCG below 5000, no cardiac activity, mass below 3.5 cm.
Single dose 50 mg/m2 IM with day 4 and 7 bhCG monitoring.
Salpingectomy over salpingostomy when the other tube is normal.
explanation.pearls: A stable ectopic with bhCG 3800 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm and no contraindications meets RANZCOG criteria for single-dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of HELLP syndrome without severe hypertension and immediate management priorities
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old G1P0 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation who presents at 03:00 with two days of increasing right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg. Her pregnancy has been otherwise low risk on routine antenatal care; the 20 week morphology scan was normal.

On assessment she has pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degC, fetal heart rate 152 per minute on cardiotocography with reduced variability but no decelerations. She is alert with mild epigastric tenderness on palpation but no rebound. Reflexes are normal. Urinalysis shows protein 2+. Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-140), platelet count 84 x10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 780 U/L (120-250), aspartate aminotransferase 190 U/L (below 35), alanine aminotransferase 168 U/L, bilirubin 32 micromol/L, blood film shows schistocytes, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), urate 0.42 mmol/L, coagulation profile within normal limits. Urine protein creatinine ratio is 128 mg per mmol. Ultrasound shows appropriate growth on the 30th centile and normal Dopplers.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 /min, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC, FHR 152 /min
data_table.Symptoms and signs: Right upper quadrant pain 2 days, nausea, mild epigastric tenderness, reflexes normal, urine protein 2+
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L (105-140), platelets 84 x10^9/L, LDH 780 U/L (120-250), AST 190 U/L, ALT 168 U/L, bilirubin 32 micromol/L, schistocytes on film, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), urate 0.42 mmol/L
data_table.Cardiotocography: FHR 152 baseline, reduced variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg immediate release loading dose and admit for expectant management with twice daily blood pressure and bloods aiming for spontaneous labour after 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: HELLP with worsening bloods is not amenable to expectant management to term; delivery within 24-48 hours after steroid cover is required. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate loading 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion with betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular first dose and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: HELLP with organ dysfunction at 33+2 weeks warrants steroid cover for lung maturation, MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis and expedited delivery within 24-48 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus every 20 minutes and admit for oral nifedipine slow release 30 mg twice daily and continued monitoring with delivery planned only if blood pressure reaches 160/110
options.rationale: Her blood pressure is not in the severe range; HELLP diagnosis itself (not the BP) drives the delivery decision. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia within one hour without steroid cover and platelet transfusion pre operatively targeting platelet count above 100 x10^9 per L
options.rationale: Immediate delivery within an hour without steroid cover misses the neonatal benefit of 24-48 hours of betamethasone; her stability allows time for both steroids and MgSO4. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg twelve hourly for HELLP-specific corticosteroid therapy and admit for expectant management with delivery planned at 37 weeks after platelet recovery
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not improve maternal or perinatal outcomes in HELLP and does not obviate the need to deliver at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) can occur without severe hypertension; the diagnosis is clinical and laboratory. Tennessee criteria: platelets below 100 x10^9/L, AST above 70 U/L, LDH above 600 U/L, or microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated bilirubin). HELLP is a severe manifestation of pre-eclampsia even if BP is not severe range. Management priorities: magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g load then 1 g/h), corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation if 24 to 34+6 weeks (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart), delivery within 24-48 hours regardless of gestation beyond 32-34 weeks. Antihypertensives target BP below 160/110. Dexamethasone does not improve maternal outcomes in HELLP itself but standard antenatal corticosteroid course is given for fetal lung maturation.
key_points: HELLP can occur without severe hypertension; diagnosis is haematologic and hepatic.
Deliver within 24-48 hours regardless of BP; give steroid cover if 24 to 34+6 weeks.
Give MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis; treat only severe range BP with antihypertensives.
explanation.pearls: HELLP with platelets 84 x10^9/L and AST 190 U/L at 33+2 weeks: give betamethasone for lung maturation, MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis, plan delivery within 24-48 hours - do not manage expectantly.

subtopic_detail: Choice of surgical procedure for tubal ectopic pregnancy when the contralateral tube is absent from prior surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in theatre with your consultant to manage a 33 year old G3P0 woman with an unstable tubal ectopic pregnancy. Two years ago she had a right salpingectomy for a ruptured right tubal ectopic. She has been trying to conceive spontaneously for the past six months. She has no other medical history.

She presented tonight with acute left iliac fossa pain and fainting. On arrival she had pulse rate 132 per minute, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degC. She received 1 L Hartmann and 1 unit packed red cells and was transferred immediately to theatre. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin was 4200 IU/L. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a left adnexal mass 30 mm with visible yolk sac in the tube and no fetal cardiac activity, and moderate free fluid throughout the pelvis and paracolic gutters. Diagnostic laparoscopy confirms a left ampullary ectopic in the mid tube with active bleeding from the fimbriated end; the tube itself is intact with viable serosa. The right tube is absent from prior surgery. Uterus and ovaries appear healthy.

data_table.Vital signs on arrival: Pulse rate 132 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degC
data_table.Resuscitation: 1 L Hartmann and 1 unit packed red cells given, transferred to theatre
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Left adnexal mass 30 mm with yolk sac, no fetal cardiac activity, moderate free fluid pelvis and paracolic gutters
data_table.Laparoscopic findings: Left ampullary ectopic mid tube, active bleeding from fimbriated end, tube intact and viable, right tube absent (previous salpingectomy), uterus and ovaries healthy
data_table.Fertility history: Trying to conceive 6 months, prior right salpingectomy 2 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical procedure now?

options.text: Intraoperative methotrexate 50 mg per square metre injection into the tubal mass with tube preservation and post operative serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin monitoring to zero
options.rationale: Local methotrexate has no established role in acute haemodynamically unstable ectopic; definitive surgical removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the left fallopian tube preserving tubal patency to allow future spontaneous conception given that the right tube is absent from the previous salpingectomy
options.rationale: Salpingostomy would preserve a tube already implicated in a recurrent ectopic; recurrent ectopic on this tube is a bigger risk than the fertility gain from preservation. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left fallopian tube with haemostasis and washout given the persistent trophoblast risk and higher recurrent ectopic risk in a diseased contralateral remnant
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy, recurrent ectopic in the only remaining tube dominates; salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic than salpingostomy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy only with drainage of haemoperitoneum and postoperative single dose intramuscular methotrexate for management of the ectopic tissue left in situ within the tube
options.rationale: Leaving an actively bleeding ectopic in situ risks catastrophic haemorrhage; methotrexate is contraindicated post haemoperitoneum with instability. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left tube plus contralateral prophylactic oophorectomy given a history of previous ipsilateral ovarian involvement in prior ectopic surgery
options.rationale: Prophylactic oophorectomy has no place in current ectopic management and would eliminate spontaneous fertility. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Surgical management of tubal ectopic can be salpingectomy or salpingostomy. Salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast rates (0 to 4 percent versus 4 to 15 percent for salpingostomy) and lower recurrent ectopic risk in the operated tube. RANZCOG recommends salpingectomy over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is normal, because subsequent intrauterine pregnancy rates are similar and salpingectomy avoids persistent trophoblast follow-up. When the contralateral tube is diseased or absent, tube preservation via salpingostomy was traditionally recommended to preserve spontaneous fertility; however, when the affected tube is the ONLY remaining tube, recurrent ectopic risk becomes dominant. Contemporary practice weighs recurrent ectopic risk against fertility gain and, when the tube is haemodynamically unstable with significant tubal damage, salpingectomy plus assisted reproduction referral is the safer default.
key_points: Salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast and lower recurrent ectopic on that tube.
Prior contralateral salpingectomy: recurrent ectopic risk in the only tube dominates.
Prefer salpingectomy plus IVF referral over salpingostomy in this inversion.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral salpingectomy flips the classic answer: current tubal ectopic with prior right salpingectomy is treated with left salpingectomy plus IVF referral, not salpingostomy, because recurrent ectopic risk in the only tube dominates.

subtopic_detail: Decision timing for emergency caesarean during VBAC with early features of uterine scar dehiscence
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32 year old G2P1 woman at 40+1 weeks in the birthing suite. She had a lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation two years ago and is undergoing a trial of labour after caesarean this pregnancy. Labour has been progressing normally with cervical dilatation 8 cm at last examination two hours ago on oxytocin augmentation for slow progress in first stage.

Her epidural has been effective for the last four hours. On assessment she has pulse rate 108 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC, fetal heart rate 150 per minute on cardiotocography. She reports the sensation of continuous suprapubic pain breaking through her epidural in the last 20 minutes. The abdominal wall is tender between contractions. The cardiotocography shows normal baseline with reduced variability for 20 minutes and three recent late decelerations lasting up to 90 seconds with slow recovery, and a mildly tense abdomen palpable between contractions. On vaginal examination the presenting part is at spines and the cervix is 8 cm dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Cardiotocography: Baseline FHR 150 /min, reduced variability 20 min, three late decelerations up to 90 sec with slow recovery
data_table.Symptoms: Continuous suprapubic pain breaking through epidural 20 min, abdomen tender between contractions
data_table.Vaginal examination: Cervix 8 cm dilated, presenting part at spines, unchanged from 2 hours ago
data_table.Augmentation: Syntocinon infusion running for slow first stage progress
data_table.History: G2P1, previous LSCS for breech 2 years ago, TOLAC this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform amniotomy if not already done and continue augmentation for 30 minutes given the presenting part at spines and estimated fully dilated within an hour based on current progress
options.rationale: Continued augmentation with a suspected uterine scar dehiscence is contraindicated; progress projections do not override the CTG and clinical signs. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Reduce syntocinon rate by half, position her left lateral and give 500 mL Hartmann bolus and reassess cardiotocography for further 20 minutes before deciding on operative delivery
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation delays diagnosis of impending uterine rupture; the pattern is not amenable to conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Give subcutaneous terbutaline 250 microgram for tocolysis and reposition left lateral with maternal facial oxygen and reassess cardiotocography over further 30 minutes
options.rationale: Tocolysis for suspected uterine rupture postpones definitive delivery and risks catastrophic haemorrhage; immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Stop syntocinon and proceed immediately to emergency caesarean section under the epidural top up for suspected uterine scar dehiscence or rupture with senior obstetric and paediatric attendance
options.rationale: New continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen between contractions, fetal compromise on CTG in a TOLAC on oxytocin is uterine scar dehiscence until proven otherwise. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Fetal scalp lactate sampling to quantify degree of fetal compromise and if lactate below 4.2 mmol per L continue conservative management with intrauterine resuscitation and repeat cardiotocography
options.rationale: Fetal blood sampling is contraindicated with suspected uterine rupture; the diagnosis is clinical not biochemical. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture in trial of labour after caesarean occurs in approximately 0.5 percent (0.7 to 0.9 percent with induction and augmentation). Warning signs include fetal heart rate abnormalities (most common - late decelerations, prolonged decelerations, fetal bradycardia), continuous abdominal pain breaking through epidural, maternal tachycardia, cessation of contractions, loss of station, vaginal bleeding, and haemodynamic instability. Diagnosis is clinical; immediate delivery by caesarean is required. Oxytocin should be stopped and delivery expedited without waiting for further evidence. Fetal scalp lactate sampling, intrauterine resuscitation and tocolysis are contraindicated as they delay definitive management. Maternal outcomes are excellent with prompt delivery; delay above 20 to 30 minutes from onset of warning signs is associated with hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury and fetal death.
key_points: Uterine rupture warning signs: FHR abnormality, continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen.
Rupture risk 0.5 percent TOLAC baseline, higher with oxytocin augmentation.
Diagnosis is clinical; immediate emergency caesarean, no delay for FBS or resuscitation.
explanation.pearls: TOLAC with new continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen between contractions and late decelerations on syntocinon is uterine scar dehiscence: stop syntocinon and proceed immediately to caesarean, no scalp lactate or tocolysis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement
