subtopic_detail: Priorities in management of complete molar pregnancy with clinical and biochemical hyperthyroidism at diagnosis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 29 year old G1P0 woman at 13 weeks by dates who presents with heavy vaginal bleeding for three days, tremor and one episode of vomiting per day for one week. She has no medical history and takes no regular medications. Her mother has Hashimoto thyroiditis.

On assessment she has pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degC. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and warm moist palms. There is no goitre and no proptosis on eye examination. Speculum shows heavy bleeding through a partly open cervix with grape like vesicles in the vault. Uterus is enlarged to 18 weeks size on abdominal palpation. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a "snowstorm" appearance filling the uterine cavity with bilateral theca lutein cysts on the ovaries and no fetal parts. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin is 590000 IU/L. Thyroid function: thyroid stimulating hormone below 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10 to 20), free T3 8 pmol/L (3 to 6). Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 /min, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor outstretched hands, warm moist palms, no goitre, no proptosis, uterus 18 weeks size
data_table.Speculum: Heavy bleeding through partly open cervix, grape-like vesicles in vault
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Snowstorm intrauterine appearance, bilateral theca lutein cysts, no fetal parts
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 590000 IU/L, TSH below 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10-20), free T3 8 pmol/L (3-6), FBC/UEC/LFT within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy under general anaesthesia the same day given the biochemical hyperthyroidism and enlarged uterus at 18 weeks size
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not routine for complete mole; suction evacuation preserves fertility and cures the hyperthyroidism. Hysterectomy is only considered in women over 40 who have completed childbearing. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Oral carbimazole 40 mg daily and defer suction dilatation and evacuation for one week until biochemical euthyroidism is achieved to reduce anaesthetic risk from thyroid storm
options.rationale: The hyperthyroidism resolves with hCG fall after evacuation, so long-course carbimazole is unnecessary and delay risks bleeding progression. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann and misoprostol 400 microgram sublingual for medical evacuation to avoid surgical anaesthetic risk in the context of biochemical hyperthyroidism
options.rationale: Medical evacuation is not recommended for molar pregnancy - suction dilatation and evacuation is preferred to minimise embolisation of trophoblast to lung. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Radioactive iodine 15 mCi single dose and defer any evacuation for four weeks to allow the induced hypothyroidism to develop before considering safe surgical management
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy (including molar); it destroys the thyroid unnecessarily since hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism resolves after evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Oral propranolol 40 mg pre operatively and proceed to suction dilatation and evacuation the same day with anaesthetic and cardiology pre operative review and oxytocin infusion after evacuation is commenced
options.rationale: Molar pregnancy with hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism resolves with molar evacuation; beta blockade controls symptoms preoperatively while definitive treatment is evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

explanation.summary: Complete hydatidiform mole is a gestational trophoblastic disease with grossly elevated beta-hCG that structurally resembles TSH and stimulates the TSH receptor in around 5 percent of cases, causing biochemical or clinical hyperthyroidism. Typical features are vaginal bleeding, uterus large for dates, hyperemesis, early-onset pre-eclampsia, and "snowstorm" ultrasound appearance with theca lutein cysts. Management is suction dilatation and evacuation the same day as diagnosis (medical evacuation is contraindicated due to trophoblast embolisation risk). Preoperative beta blockade with propranolol controls hyperthyroid symptoms; long-course thionamides are unnecessary because thyroid function normalises within days as hCG falls. Anti-D 625 IU IM if Rhesus negative. Post-evacuation weekly beta-hCG to non-pregnant range then monthly for six months. Contraception is essential during follow-up.
key_points: Complete mole causes hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism in around 5 percent of cases.
Suction dilatation and evacuation is first-line treatment; hyperthyroidism resolves with hCG fall.
Preoperative propranolol controls symptoms; long-course carbimazole is unnecessary.
explanation.pearls: Complete molar pregnancy with hyperthyroid features is treated by suction dilatation and evacuation the same day with preoperative propranolol - the hyperthyroidism resolves as hCG falls, so carbimazole and delay are wrong.

subtopic_detail: Uterine inversion diagnosis and immediate management
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite. A G3P2 at 39 weeks gestation has just delivered a healthy 3.9 kg baby vaginally. During active third stage management the midwife applied cord traction with 10 units of oxytocin already given intramuscularly at anterior shoulder delivery. She calls you urgently: the mother has become suddenly light headed, and the midwife feels a large mass in the vagina with no palpable uterine fundus on abdominal examination. Estimated blood loss is 900 mL and increasing at 100 mL every 2 minutes.

Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 74/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air. The placenta is partially separated but still attached to the mass. She has two 16 gauge intravenous cannulas with Hartmann's solution running wide open. Full theatre and anaesthetic teams have been called and are 5 minutes away. Blood is being cross matched.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 74/42, RR 24, SpO2 96% RA
data_table.Vaginal examination: Large firm mass in vagina; fundus absent abdominally
data_table.Blood loss: 900 mL rising at 100 mL every 2 minutes
data_table.Prior actions: 10 units IM oxytocin given at shoulder delivery; cord traction applied

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step now?

options.text: Attempt immediate manual replacement of the inverted uterus with the placenta still attached
options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance calls for immediate manual repositioning (Johnson manoeuvre) without removing an adherent placenta first, since removal worsens haemorrhage; every minute of delay makes reduction harder as the cervical ring contracts (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Remove the placenta manually before any attempt at replacement to reduce weight of the inverted uterus
options.rationale: Manual removal of an attached placenta from an inverted uterus dramatically increases haemorrhage and is contraindicated before replacement (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Give intravenous carboprost 250 micrograms and misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally to control bleeding first
options.rationale: Uterotonics contract the cervical ring around the inversion and make reduction much harder; hold uterotonics until replacement is achieved (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Transfer the patient to theatre now for hysterectomy without any attempt at bedside replacement first
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is a last resort for irreducible inversion; almost all inversions reduce with prompt manual replacement, and hysterectomy without an attempt at replacement is not standard care (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

options.text: Insert an intrauterine Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL to tamponade bleeding while awaiting theatre transfer
options.rationale: A Bakri balloon in an inverted uterus increases the inversion and is inappropriate; balloon tamponade has its role after replacement if atony persists (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage Statement).

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion complicates 1 in 2000 to 1 in 20 000 deliveries and presents with a vaginal mass, absent fundus abdominally, sudden hypotension out of keeping with blood loss (vagal), and shock. The immediate step is manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre): the operator's cupped hand pushes the fundus back through the cervix with the placenta still attached, sustaining pressure for several minutes until the uterus contracts around the hand. Uterotonics are withheld until replacement is achieved because they trap the fundus; once replaced, oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine tone. Under general anaesthesia with terbutaline, magnesium sulfate, or glyceryl trinitrate uterine relaxation is used if bedside reduction fails. Massive transfusion protocol activation is concurrent.
key_points: Manual replacement with placenta still attached is first line
Hold uterotonics until replacement is achieved
Uterine relaxants under anaesthesia if bedside attempts fail
explanation.pearls: The vagal response to inversion (bradycardia and hypotension) may exceed the blood loss and mislead volume assessment; anticipate large fluid and blood requirements at replacement.

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic after failed oxytocin and ergometrine
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a level 3 maternity unit called to a 32 year old primipara 20 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Estimated blood loss is 1400 mL and she is still bleeding briskly per vaginum with a soft boggy uterus. Baseline blood pressure at booking was 118/74 mmHg and antenatal course was unremarkable. She has no known allergies and no personal or family history of asthma.

She has received oxytocin 10 units intramuscular at the birth of the anterior shoulder, an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's solution over 4 hours, and ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular 5 minutes ago. The bladder is empty. The perineum shows a small superficial midline tear that is not bleeding. Vital signs: pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vitals: HR 118; BP 96/58; RR 22; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.9
data_table.Uterotonics given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at birth; oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours; ergometrine 250 microgram IM 5 minutes ago
data_table.Genital tract: Small superficial midline tear, not bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to administer?

options.text: Repeat ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular immediately as a doubled second dose
options.rationale: Ergometrine is capped at a maximum of 500 microgram in 24 hours and its second dose is not the recommended next escalation when uterine tone remains poor; RANZCOG moves to a prostaglandin (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular, may repeat every 15 minutes up to a total of 2 mg
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH pathway steps from oxytocin to ergometrine to carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular for continuing atonic bleeding; carboprost is safe here because there is no history of asthma (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual as the next uterotonic in place of carboprost
options.rationale: Misoprostol is the RANZCOG fallback when parenteral uterotonics are unavailable or contraindicated; carboprost is preferred as second-line when the woman has no asthma contraindication because it acts faster and more reliably than misoprostol (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Initiate a magnesium sulfate loading dose of 4 g intravenous over 20 minutes to relax the uterine vasculature
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is not a PPH uterotonic and would relax the uterus and worsen atony; its role is eclampsia neuroprophylaxis, not haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram/kg intravenous before further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort haemostatic adjunct after failure of uterotonics, mechanical measures, and surgical control, and only when specific coagulation targets have been met; using it now bypasses the standard escalation ladder (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH follows a sequential uterotonic ladder: oxytocin bolus then infusion, ergometrine (if no hypertension), and carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 2 mg as third-line where asthma is not a contraindication. Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous should be given within 3 hours of birth alongside these steps. Misoprostol 800 microgram is the sublingual fallback where parenteral options are unavailable or contraindicated. Recombinant factor VIIa and intrauterine balloon are reserved for continuing haemorrhage after uterotonic failure with correction of coagulopathy.
key_points: Third-line uterotonic in PPH: carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes to 2 mg total
Ergometrine capped at 500 microgram in 24 hours and avoided in hypertension
Give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours of birth alongside uterotonic escalation
explanation.pearls: Carboprost is a bronchoconstrictor; ask about asthma before drawing it up because that single question changes the answer to sublingual misoprostol.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy when diet and metformin fail
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic seeing a 33 year old woman at 30 weeks gestation with dietary-diagnosed gestational diabetes at 26 weeks (fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.9 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT). She has followed the dietitian's plan for 4 weeks and metformin was uptitrated to 2 g daily 2 weeks ago. She has had no hypoglycaemia symptoms and is otherwise well; her weight gain has been within target and fetal growth is on the 45th centile.

Her 2 week home glucose diary shows fasting values consistently between 5.4 and 5.9 mmol/L (target under 5.1) with post-prandial readings on target. Vital signs and urinalysis are unremarkable and blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg.

data_table.Gestation: 30 weeks with GDM diagnosed at 26 weeks
data_table.Current management: Dietary intervention for 4 weeks; metformin 2 g daily for 2 weeks
data_table.Home glucose diary: Fasting 5.4 to 5.9 mmol/L (target <5.1); postprandial on target

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue current therapy and repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Repeat OGTT does not add information once GDM is diagnosed and treated; the fasting values already exceed target and demand pharmacological escalation rather than diagnostic reassessment (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Add rapid-acting insulin lispro before each main meal targeted at post-prandial glucose control
options.rationale: Post-prandial values are within target so mealtime rapid-acting insulin does not address the fasting problem and adds unnecessary hypoglycaemia risk; basal insulin is the intervention that fits the specific pattern (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Add bedtime intermediate-acting isophane insulin titrated to target fasting glucose under 5.1 mmol/L
options.rationale: ADIPS guidance recommends adding basal insulin when fasting glucose remains above target despite metformin and diet in GDM, with bedtime isophane titrated to the fasting target; long-acting analogue insulin is a reasonable alternative but isophane remains the ADIPS default (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Increase the metformin dose to 3 g daily divided across three meals to overcome the residual fasting elevation
options.rationale: Maximum recommended metformin in pregnancy is 2 g daily; further increase does not improve glycaemic outcomes and increases gastrointestinal intolerance without addressing the fasting profile that specifically responds to basal insulin (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Stop metformin and commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg twice daily as the primary sulfonylurea for GDM
options.rationale: Glibenclamide is not recommended in Australian GDM practice because it crosses the placenta and is associated with neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia compared to insulin (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: In gestational diabetes, glycaemic targets are fasting under 5.1 mmol/L and 2 hour post-prandial under 6.7 mmol/L. When lifestyle plus metformin at maximum dose (2 g/day) do not achieve the fasting target, ADIPS recommends adding a basal insulin at bedtime, titrated to the fasting glucose. Rapid-acting mealtime insulin is added later if post-prandial values are also out of range. Sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide are avoided because of placental transfer and neonatal hypoglycaemia. Fetal ultrasound should be repeated at 34 to 36 weeks to guide timing of birth.
key_points: GDM fasting target under 5.1 mmol/L; add basal insulin when metformin fails to reach it
Rapid-acting insulin added mealtime only if post-prandial values exceed 6.7 mmol/L
Sulfonylureas avoided in AU because of placental transfer and neonatal hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: The pattern of glucose failure decides the insulin: fasting hyperglycaemia needs basal, post-prandial needs mealtime; treating the wrong pattern wastes hypoglycaemia budget.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand
RANZCOG C-Obs 7 Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgical management criteria
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 28 year old G2P0 with 6 weeks and 5 days amenorrhoea and 2 days of light per vaginum bleeding without pain. She has one previous first trimester miscarriage and no other medical history. She has an IUD in situ for contraception which is visible on speculum and she is happy to attend for repeat blood tests every 3 to 4 days if needed.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable and non-tender. Vital signs: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Serum beta hCG today is 2400 IU/L, up from 1900 IU/L 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 22 mm right adnexal mass with no yolk sac and no fetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum creatinine, ALT, and full blood count are within normal limits.

data_table.Vitals: HR 78; BP 118/72; RR 14; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7
data_table.Serum bhCG: 2400 IU/L today; 1900 IU/L 48 hours ago (suboptimal rise)
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Empty uterus; right adnexal mass 22 mm; no yolk sac; no fetal cardiac activity; no free fluid
data_table.Laboratory: Creatinine, ALT, and FBC within normal limits
data_table.Social factors: Reliable follow-up available; IUD in situ

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option to offer?

options.text: Uterine evacuation with suction curettage to obtain products for histological diagnosis in the theatre
options.rationale: Diagnostic curettage is not standard in AU practice for ectopic diagnosis, delays treatment, and risks removing a coexisting intrauterine pregnancy; ultrasound and serial bhCG give the diagnosis without curettage (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with serial bhCG on days 4 and 7 in reliable follow-up
options.rationale: This ectopic meets RANZCOG criteria for medical management: stable haemodynamics, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain or free fluid, reliable follow-up, and no medical contraindication to methotrexate; single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with days 4 and 7 bhCG is the standard (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 on days 0 and 4 without checking a follow-up day 7 bhCG level
options.rationale: Single-dose protocol is the default in Australian practice with days 4 and 7 bhCG monitoring; multi-dose regimens are reserved for higher initial bhCG or persistent trophoblast after single dose (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG measurements and clinical review, no pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is limited to a decreasing bhCG under 1500 IU/L with a small mass and no symptoms; this bhCG is rising and above 1500, so medical or surgical management is required (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic salpingectomy without prior consent for medical management as first-line treatment
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated when medical criteria are not met (bhCG 5000 IU/L or above, mass 3.5 cm or above, fetal cardiac activity, haemodynamic instability, severe pain, free fluid, unreliable follow-up); this patient meets medical criteria (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Medical management of tubal ectopic pregnancy with methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscular is acceptable when bhCG is under 5000 IU/L, adnexal mass is under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity is seen, the patient is haemodynamically stable with no significant pain or haemoperitoneum, follow-up is reliable, and there is no contraindication to methotrexate (bloods normal, no breastfeeding, no immunodeficiency). Follow-up bhCG on days 4 and 7 checks for a 15 percent drop; failure triggers a second methotrexate dose or surgery. Expectant management is limited to falling bhCG under 1500 IU/L.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, stable, reliable follow-up
Single dose 50 mg/m2 with days 4 and 7 bhCG in AU practice
Surgery when medical criteria not met or bhCG fails to fall by 15 percent day 4 to 7
explanation.pearls: The bhCG threshold that flips ectopic to surgical management is 5000 IU/L, not 3000; a doubling reference range does not apply once ectopic is diagnosed.

sources.label: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception timing with breastfeeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old G2P2 woman at her 6 week postnatal review. She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term baby every 2 to 3 hours. Her only medical history is migraine without aura for the last 5 years. Her BMI today is 27 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She would like reliable contraception but wants to protect her breastmilk supply and preserve the option of another pregnancy in about 3 years.

She had an uncomplicated vaginal birth without perineal trauma. She is not currently amenorrhoeic as she had a small amount of vaginal bleeding 10 days ago. She is comfortable with an intrauterine device and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Postnatal history: G2P2, 6 weeks postpartum; uncomplicated vaginal birth; exclusive breastfeeding 2 to 3 hourly
data_table.Medical background: Migraine without aura; BMI 27; BP 118/76; no VTE history
data_table.Fertility plan: Desires reliable contraception now; another pregnancy in about 3 years
data_table.Bleeding pattern: Vaginal bleeding 10 days ago; not amenorrhoeic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend?

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks for the next 3 years
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone can delay return to fertility for up to 12 months after cessation, which does not fit a plan to conceive in about 3 years and is less reversible than an IUD or implant (Source: eTG Contraception).

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant with combined oral contraception as backup for the first month
options.rationale: The implant is a reasonable option but combined oral contraception as backup would not be added because combined hormones are avoided in breastfeeding until at least 6 weeks; the recommendation should not include CHC (Source: eTG Contraception).

options.text: Rely on lactational amenorrhoea method alone as her primary contraception for the next 6 months
options.rationale: LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and an infant under 6 months; this patient is not amenorrhoeic which invalidates LAM as her primary method (Source: eTG Contraception).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 microgram ethinylestradiol plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is avoided until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women because of small effects on milk supply and higher VTE risk in the puerperium (Source: eTG Contraception).

options.text: Insertion of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device today with contraception effective immediately
options.rationale: The 52 mg LNG-IUD is a long-acting reversible contraceptive with no impact on breastfeeding, works well in the postpartum period, and provides highly effective contraception aligned with her 3 year plan; insertion at 4 weeks postpartum or later is appropriate (Source: eTG Contraception).

explanation.summary: For a breastfeeding woman at 6 weeks postpartum wanting reliable contraception with rapid reversibility, the LNG-IUD (52 mg) is the highest tier long-acting reversible option and does not affect milk supply. Combined hormonal contraception is deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women because of small milk supply effects and higher puerperal VTE risk. LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and infant under 6 months. Depot medroxyprogesterone has a documented delay in fertility return of up to 12 months, which does not suit a woman planning pregnancy in 3 years.
key_points: LNG-IUD at 4 weeks or later is safe in breastfeeding and gives immediate reliable contraception
Combined hormonal contraception deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women
Depot medroxyprogesterone can delay fertility return by up to 12 months
explanation.pearls: Migraine with aura contraindicates combined hormonal contraception; migraine without aura is a stricter risk to weigh alongside age and vascular risk factors.

subtopic_detail: Tocolysis choice with contraindication to first-line agent
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternity unit assessing a 27 year old G3P1 woman at 30 weeks and 2 days gestation presenting with regular painful uterine tightenings every 4 minutes for 3 hours. She has a history of severe migraine treated with regular propranolol and a normal echocardiogram in her first pregnancy. Antenatal course this pregnancy has been unremarkable and she has had no antepartum haemorrhage.

Vaginal examination is 2 cm dilated and 70 percent effaced with the cephalic vertex at station minus 2. Membranes are intact. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min and moderate variability. Vital signs: pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Fetal fibronectin is positive and a transvaginal cervical length is 18 mm. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular has been given and magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose is running for neuroprotection.

data_table.Gestation and history: G3P1 at 30+2; regular contractions every 4 minutes; propranolol for migraine
data_table.Examination: 2 cm dilated, 70 percent effaced, station -2; membranes intact
data_table.Ultrasound and biomarker: Cervical length 18 mm; fetal fibronectin positive
data_table.Vital signs: HR 88; BP 108/62; RR 18; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.9
data_table.Given so far: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x1; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading for neuroprotection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic to commence?

options.text: Intravenous atosiban 6.75 mg bolus then 300 microgram/min infusion tapered over 48 hours
options.rationale: Atosiban is not available on the PBS in Australia and is not the first-line tocolytic here; nifedipine gives comparable efficacy at lower cost and is preferred (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Intravenous salbutamol infusion titrated to fewer than one contraction in 10 minutes as tocolysis
options.rationale: Salbutamol is contraindicated in a woman on propranolol because the pharmacological antagonism causes unpredictable bronchospasm and cardiovascular effects; salbutamol is no longer preferred for tocolysis in AU because of maternal cardiovascular events (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Oral indometacin 100 mg loading dose then 25 to 50 mg every 6 hours for a total of 48 hours
options.rationale: Indometacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios; at 30+2 the risk is smaller but still concerning and nifedipine is the safer first-line at this gestation (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Continue the magnesium sulfate infusion at a higher rate for both neuroprotection and tocolysis
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate at neuroprotective doses does not provide effective tocolysis; using it for tocolysis has been associated with paediatric mortality signals and is not RANZCOG's tocolytic of choice (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg loading dose then 10 to 20 mg every 6 to 8 hours titrated to contractions
options.rationale: Nifedipine is the RANZCOG first-line tocolytic for women under 34 weeks needing 48 hours of steroid cover; salbutamol is contraindicated because she takes propranolol (beta-blocker interaction risks bronchospasm and haemodynamic instability), and indometacin is avoided at 30 weeks because of ductus arteriosus constriction risk (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

explanation.summary: Tocolysis under 34 weeks buys 48 hours for corticosteroid maturation and inutero transfer, not to prolong pregnancy indefinitely. RANZCOG places nifedipine first because of efficacy, oral route, and safety profile. Beta-agonists such as salbutamol are largely displaced from AU practice because of maternal cardiovascular events, and concurrent propranolol adds a further relative contraindication. Indometacin is avoided beyond 32 weeks and used with caution before; magnesium sulfate is a neuroprotective agent, not a tocolytic, and atosiban is not funded on the PBS.
key_points: Nifedipine first-line tocolytic in AU practice under 34 weeks
Salbutamol contraindicated with concurrent beta-blocker and largely deprecated in AU
Indometacin avoided beyond 32 weeks because of ductus arteriosus constriction
explanation.pearls: Concurrent beta-blocker use flips tocolysis choice away from beta-agonists; check the maternal medication list before drawing up any uterine relaxant.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive selection during severe pre-eclampsia with contraindication to first-line
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation with new onset severe hypertension. She has known moderate asthma with a hospital admission last year and uses a fluticasone-salmeterol preventer daily. She has no other medical history and no known drug allergies. Antenatal care has been shared care through her GP.

Blood pressure on repeat measurements is 172/112 mmHg and 170/108 mmHg 15 minutes apart. She reports a moderate frontal headache but no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain. Reflexes are brisk without clonus. Vital signs: pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Investigations: urinary protein-creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol, platelets 128 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), ALT 62 U/L (under 40), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45 to 90), uric acid 0.42 mmol/L. The cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Symptoms: Frontal headache; no visual disturbance; no epigastric pain
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 128; ALT 62; creatinine 78; uric acid 0.42; urinary PCR 68
data_table.Medication background: Moderate asthma on fluticasone-salmeterol; hospital admission for asthma last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive to give now?

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray 400 microgram every 5 minutes until the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Sublingual GTN is not a SOMANZ first-line antihypertensive for pre-eclampsia; it lacks safety data in pregnancy for this indication and can cause abrupt drops in blood pressure with fetal compromise (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg with a repeat dose in 30 minutes as first-line acute antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Labetalol has beta-blocking activity which is relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma; nifedipine is preferred here even though labetalol is otherwise first-line in SOMANZ (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral methyldopa 500 mg loading dose then 250 to 500 mg three times daily as first-line acute therapy
options.rationale: Methyldopa is an oral maintenance drug for chronic hypertension in pregnancy but is too slow to work for acute severe hypertension where blood pressure must fall within an hour (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg with a repeat dose every 30 minutes as clinically required
options.rationale: SOMANZ preferred first-line antihypertensives for severe hypertension in pregnancy are oral labetalol, oral nifedipine immediate-release, or intravenous hydralazine; oral labetalol is relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma so nifedipine becomes the preferred oral option (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose alone to lower blood pressure and prevent eclampsia
options.rationale: Magnesium is a neuroprotective anticonvulsant, not an antihypertensive; failing to give a specific antihypertensive leaves severe hypertension untreated with stroke risk (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 170 mmHg or above, or diastolic 110 mmHg or above) is a clinical emergency and blood pressure must be controlled within about an hour to lower stroke risk. SOMANZ lists oral labetalol, oral nifedipine immediate-release, and intravenous hydralazine as first-line acute options, with magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis in parallel. In moderate to severe asthma the beta-blocking activity of labetalol makes it relatively contraindicated, so nifedipine (or intravenous hydralazine if oral is impractical) becomes first-line. Methyldopa is oral maintenance therapy, not an acute agent.
key_points: SOMANZ severe hypertension: oral labetalol, oral nifedipine IR, or IV hydralazine as first-line
Labetalol relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma
Methyldopa is maintenance, not acute; magnesium is anticonvulsant, not antihypertensive
explanation.pearls: Comorbid asthma is the most common reason to pick nifedipine over labetalol; the systemic beta-blocking dose in oral labetalol is enough to trigger bronchospasm in an asthmatic.

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia recognition and delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation who has just experienced a sudden painless per vaginum blood loss of about 30 mL immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes at home. She has an in-vitro fertilisation twin pregnancy with a bilobed placenta noted on her 20 week morphology scan and a velamentous cord insertion of the leading twin identified on Doppler ultrasound at 24 weeks.

On arrival she is not in labour. Vital signs: pulse 92/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Twin 1 cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 100/min falling to 80/min with recurrent variable decelerations; twin 2 baseline is 138/min with moderate variability and no decelerations. Speculum examination confirms membranes have ruptured and there is fresh red blood in the vagina without cervical dilatation.

data_table.Gestation and pregnancy: IVF twin pregnancy at 34 weeks; bilobed placenta; velamentous cord insertion of leading twin at 24 weeks
data_table.Presenting event: Sudden painless PV bleed of about 30 mL immediately after SROM
data_table.Twin 1 CTG: Baseline 100/min falling to 80/min with recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Maternal vitals: HR 92; BP 110/68; RR 20; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continuous cardiotocograph monitoring for 4 hours with expectant management if maternal bleeding stops
options.rationale: Expectant management is unsafe once fetal decelerations and painless PV bleeding follow SROM in a woman with a known velamentous cord; fetal exsanguination is minutes not hours (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).

options.text: Insertion of a large-bore intravenous cannula and cross-match 4 maternal red cell units before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: Maternal transfusion cannot rescue fetal exsanguination in vasa praevia; ordering cross-match delays the only intervention that saves the fetus, which is immediate delivery (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section for fetal compromise consistent with ruptured vasa praevia
options.rationale: Painless PV bleeding immediately after SROM in a woman with known velamentous insertion and bilobed placenta and rapid fetal deterioration is ruptured vasa praevia; fetal blood loss is catastrophic within minutes and only category 1 caesarean can save the compromised twin (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer delivery for at least 24 hours for lung maturation
options.rationale: Steroid maturation cannot be waited out in acute vasa praevia with fetal compromise; the diagnosis-to-birth interval determines survival and delay is not an option (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).

options.text: Perform digital vaginal examination to determine cervical dilatation before deciding on mode of delivery
options.rationale: Digital examination through the potentially exposed fetal vessel can worsen haemorrhage; the priority is immediate delivery, not further cervical examination, and prior speculum has already confirmed the bleeding pattern (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os, most often with velamentous cord insertion or bilobed or succenturiate placenta. IVF pregnancies and multiple gestations are additional risk factors. Painless PV bleeding immediately after rupture of membranes with rapid fetal deterioration is vasa praevia until proven otherwise. Fetal blood volume is small (about 250 mL at term) so exsanguination is minutes; category 1 caesarean is the only rescue and antenatal identification of vasa praevia should have prompted elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks before SROM.
key_points: Painless PV bleed immediately after SROM with fetal decelerations is vasa praevia
Category 1 caesarean is the only intervention that rescues the fetus in ruptured vasa praevia
Antenatal Doppler identification of vasa praevia mandates elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
explanation.pearls: Placental abruption bleeds maternal blood and hurts; ruptured vasa praevia bleeds fetal blood and is painless with immediate fetal collapse.

subtopic_detail: Endometrial cancer suspicion in postmenopausal bleeding with atrophic ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 63 year old woman who reports a single episode of light postmenopausal per vaginum bleeding 3 days ago on a background of 12 years of amenorrhoea. She has hypertension controlled on perindopril and takes oral tamoxifen 20 mg daily for the last 18 months following breast cancer surgery. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin.

On examination the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Speculum shows an atrophic-appearing cervix with no visible cause for the bleed. Bimanual examination reveals a small anteverted mobile uterus and no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a homogenous endometrial thickness of 3 mm with no cystic changes and no adnexal abnormality. Cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Presenting complaint: Single episode of light PMB 3 days ago; 12 years amenorrhoea
data_table.Risk factors: BMI 32; T2DM on metformin; tamoxifen 20 mg for 18 months
data_table.Examination: Atrophic cervix; small mobile uterus; no adnexal mass
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Endometrium 3 mm homogenous; no cystic change; no adnexal abnormality
data_table.Screening: Cervical screening up to date and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream for 6 weeks and review if bleeding recurs
options.rationale: Empirical topical oestrogen without excluding malignancy delays diagnosis; RANZCOG requires tissue sampling first regardless of the presumptive diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Reassure the patient and arrange follow-up if there is any further vaginal bleeding
options.rationale: Reassurance without tissue diagnosis is inadequate for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen because the 3 mm threshold does not apply; a single episode still mandates further investigation (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to look for interval endometrial thickening
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound is not appropriate for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen; the risk of missing endometrial carcinoma or hyperplasia is too high to defer tissue sampling (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Order a serum CA-125 and defer further investigation until the result is available
options.rationale: CA-125 is neither sensitive nor specific for endometrial cancer and does not substitute for histology; RANZCOG does not include CA-125 in the PMB pathway (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy despite an endometrial thickness of 3 mm
options.rationale: In women on tamoxifen the endometrial ultrasound thickness threshold is unreliable because tamoxifen produces subendothelial cystic changes that mimic thin atrophic endometrium; RANZCOG mandates hysteroscopy and biopsy for postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen regardless of ultrasound thickness (Source: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. In women not on tamoxifen an endometrial thickness under 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound has a negative predictive value of about 99 percent, so pipelle biopsy is deferred if bleeding does not recur. Tamoxifen changes this rule: subendothelial cystic changes make ultrasound thickness unreliable, so tissue diagnosis by hysteroscopy and biopsy is required regardless of the ultrasound. Obesity and diabetes add background endometrial cancer risk. Deferring investigation for oestrogen cream, serial imaging, or serum markers misses malignancy.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen requires hysteroscopy and biopsy regardless of endometrial thickness
The 4 mm ultrasound threshold is only valid for women not on tamoxifen
Serum CA-125 and topical oestrogen do not substitute for tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen produces subendothelial cysts that read as artefactually thin or thick endometrium; the ultrasound cannot rule out cancer, only histology can.

sources.label: RANZCOG GPS Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding

subtopic_detail: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes with 75 g OGTT
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32 year old primigravida at 27 weeks of pregnancy. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m squared and her mother has type 2 diabetes. She had a raised random glucose of 8.4 mmol/L at booking.

Her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks returns with fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour glucose 8.6 mmol/L (less than 8.5). She has been feeling well with no polyuria or polydipsia. She reports fetal movements are appropriate.

Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Fetal heart rate 148/min. Symphysis fundal height 27 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min; BP 118/76 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 148/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 27 cm; fetal movements appropriate
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.History: Primigravida at 27 weeks; BMI 31; mother has T2DM; booking random glucose 8.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: The result is within normal limits and no further glucose testing is required for the remainder of pregnancy
options.rationale: Two of the three OGTT values are above the threshold; even a single value above the cut off establishes gestational diabetes under the Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society criteria (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy).

options.text: The result is suggestive of type 2 diabetes preceding pregnancy and a HbA1c should be requested to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by a fasting value at or above 7 mmol/L or a 2 hour value at or above 11.1 mmol/L; these values fall in the gestational diabetes range, not the overt diabetes range (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

options.text: The result meets criteria for gestational diabetes and she should be referred to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy service
options.rationale: The fasting value of 5.4 mmol/L and the 2 hour value of 8.6 mmol/L both exceed the ADIPS thresholds; any single elevated value establishes gestational diabetes and requires referral to a multidisciplinary team for dietary review, home glucose monitoring and consideration of pharmacotherapy (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy).

options.text: The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated in 4 weeks before starting any interventions
options.rationale: The ADIPS criteria do not require repeat testing when a value exceeds threshold; delaying management by 4 weeks worsens obstetric outcomes and is not standard care (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

options.text: The result is normal but she should commence metformin because of the family history of type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Metformin is not prescribed prophylactically in pregnancy based on family history alone; treatment is guided by glycaemic targets after diagnosis (Source: ADIPS gestational diabetes consensus 2022).

explanation.summary: Under the Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society criteria, gestational diabetes is diagnosed on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test when the fasting value is at or above 5.1 mmol/L, the 1 hour value is at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or the 2 hour value is at or above 8.5 mmol/L. Any single elevated value is sufficient for diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires a fasting value at or above 7.0 mmol/L or a 2 hour value at or above 11.1 mmol/L. Once gestational diabetes is diagnosed, referral to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy team is standard for dietary review, home monitoring and pharmacotherapy decisions.
key_points: ADIPS cut offs: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L.
Any single value at or above threshold diagnoses gestational diabetes.
Referral to a multidisciplinary diabetes in pregnancy service is standard.
explanation.pearls: In Australia the ADIPS 75 g OGTT cut offs are lower than the WHO 1999 values, so fasting 5.1 mmol/L is the diagnostic threshold rather than 5.5 mmol/L; even a single elevated point mandates management referral.

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic sequencing in primary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a birth suite. A 34 year old primigravida has had a normal vaginal delivery at 40 weeks of a live infant. She has an estimated blood loss of 900 mL 12 minutes after birth with an atonic uterus felt above the umbilicus. Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly was given at delivery of the anterior shoulder.

She is anxious but alert. Bimanual uterine massage has been started, an intravenous cannula placed, cross match is sent and 1 g of tranexamic acid intravenously has been given. Her bladder is empty via urinary catheter. Placenta appears complete on inspection.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C. She has no known allergies and no history of asthma or hypertension.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; atonic uterus above umbilicus; bimanual massage started; placenta complete on inspection; bladder empty
data_table.Interventions: Oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery; IV access; cross match sent; tranexamic acid 1 g IV given
data_table.History: Primigravida; 40 week NVD; no asthma or hypertension; no allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to administer?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intravenously as a slow push and repeat the dose after 5 minutes if uterine tone remains poor
options.rationale: Ergometrine is a reasonable second line uterotonic where blood pressure is controlled, however guidelines recommend a further oxytocin bolus or infusion before ergometrine because oxytocin remains the first line drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle and repeat every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Carboprost is used when oxytocin and ergometrine have failed to achieve tone; it is contraindicated in known asthma and is a later step in the sequence rather than the immediate next drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum as a single dose and reassess uterine tone after 30 minutes with continued bimanual massage
options.rationale: Misoprostol per rectum has a slower onset than intravenous oxytocin; it is used when intravenous access is delayed or as an adjunct after other uterotonics rather than as the immediate first line intravenous drug (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Oxytocin 5 units intravenously as a slow push, followed by an oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 1 litre of Hartmann's over 4 hours
options.rationale: After an atonic postpartum haemorrhage exceeding 500 mL despite prophylactic intramuscular oxytocin, the RANZCOG algorithm is a further slow intravenous oxytocin bolus followed by a maintenance infusion; ergometrine and carboprost are added if uterine tone does not respond (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

options.text: Repeat oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh and continue bimanual uterine massage while awaiting further intravenous access
options.rationale: Intramuscular oxytocin has slower onset than intravenous; when intravenous access is present the intravenous route with an infusion is preferred and repeat intramuscular dosing is a step backwards (Source: RANZCOG postpartum haemorrhage 2021).

explanation.summary: In primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony the RANZCOG algorithm is bimanual uterine massage plus tranexamic acid plus a stepwise sequence of uterotonics beginning with further oxytocin. A slow intravenous bolus of 5 units of oxytocin is followed by an intravenous oxytocin infusion at 40 units per litre over 4 hours. Ergometrine 250 micrograms is added second line when hypertension is not a concern. Carboprost is the third line uterotonic and is contraindicated in asthma; misoprostol is an option if intravenous access is delayed.
key_points: Oxytocin bolus plus infusion is the first drug after prophylactic dose has failed.
Ergometrine second line; avoid in hypertension.
Carboprost third line; contraindicated in asthma.
explanation.pearls: After a prophylactic 10 unit intramuscular oxytocin dose fails, give a further 5 unit slow intravenous bolus and immediately begin a 40 unit per litre infusion at 250 mL per hour before moving to ergometrine.

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive threshold in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old primigravida at 33 weeks. She was referred from clinic 3 hours ago with headache and epigastric pain. She has known pre-eclampsia diagnosed 4 days earlier and is on labetalol 200 mg orally twice daily.

On examination she is alert with mild epigastric tenderness. Reflexes are brisk with no clonus. Fetal heart rate is normal on cardiotocography.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 172/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat manual measurement, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Bloods show haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), ALT 68 U/L (less than 35), urinary protein creatinine ratio 45 mg/mmol (less than 30). Fetal heart rate 142/min. She has been given 4 g magnesium sulfate intravenous loading dose.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 172/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat; RR 18/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.7 C; FHR 142/min
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild epigastric tenderness; brisk reflexes; no clonus; CTG normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (115-165); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35); ALT 68 U/L (<35); UPCR 45 mg/mmol (<30)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg orally BD; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate blood pressure management?

options.text: Increase her oral labetalol to 400 mg three times daily and recheck the blood pressure in 60 minutes
options.rationale: An oral dose adjustment is too slow for a systolic blood pressure at or above 170 or diastolic at or above 110 mmHg; parenteral antihypertensive treatment is required within 30 to 60 minutes to reduce the risk of maternal stroke (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy).

options.text: Aim to reduce the blood pressure to less than 130/80 mmHg within the first hour using an intravenous nitroprusside infusion
options.rationale: An aggressive target below 130/80 mmHg risks compromising uteroplacental perfusion, and nitroprusside is not used in pregnancy due to fetal cyanide toxicity (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Give intravenous methyldopa 250 mg and repeat magnesium sulfate 4 g loading intravenous dose
options.rationale: Methyldopa is not available intravenously in Australian formularies and is a slow onset oral agent; repeat magnesium loading is not indicated because the maintenance infusion should follow the loading dose (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Perform emergency caesarean section as the definitive treatment before controlling the blood pressure
options.rationale: Blood pressure must be controlled before delivery to avoid a maternal stroke during anaesthesia and the peripartum period; delivery is the definitive treatment but is undertaken after acute stabilisation (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023).

options.text: Give intravenous labetalol 20 mg as a slow push and repeat every 10 minutes titrated to blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg
options.rationale: In severe hypertension of pregnancy at or above 170/110 mmHg the SOMANZ algorithm targets a blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg within 30 to 60 minutes using intravenous labetalol 20 mg with 10 minute repeats up to 300 mg total, or intravenous hydralazine or oral nifedipine (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension of pregnancy at or above 170 systolic or 110 diastolic mmHg is a hypertensive emergency requiring parenteral treatment within 30 to 60 minutes to reduce stroke risk. The SOMANZ options are intravenous labetalol 20 mg with 10 minute repeats up to 300 mg, intravenous hydralazine, or oral immediate release nifedipine. The target is a blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg while preserving uteroplacental perfusion, not normotension. Magnesium sulfate is given concurrently for eclampsia prophylaxis and delivery is planned once the mother is stabilised.
key_points: Severe range starts at 170/110 mmHg and needs parenteral treatment.
Target below 160/110 mmHg in 30 to 60 minutes.
Nitroprusside is contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs, atenolol and nitroprusside; the safe parenteral agents are labetalol and hydralazine, and immediate release oral nifedipine is a useful ward option when intravenous access is limited.

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum inpatient management
stem:
You are the obstetric resident reviewing a 26 year old primigravida at 9 weeks of pregnancy in the emergency department. She has had 3 weeks of daily vomiting with weight loss of 4.5 kg from a pre pregnancy weight of 68 kg. She has tried pyridoxine and doxylamine at home without benefit.

She looks unwell with a dry mouth and mild epigastric tenderness. Ketones are 3 on urinalysis, ultrasound at 8 weeks confirmed an intrauterine singleton pregnancy with fetal heart activity.

Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C. Bloods show sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 8.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), TSH 0.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits. She has been able to take small sips of water only in the last 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108/min; BP 104/62 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Dry mouth; mild epigastric tenderness; urinary ketones 3
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L (135-145); K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); urea 8.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90); TSH 0.4 mIU/L; free T4 within normal limits; ultrasound: singleton intrauterine pregnancy with FHR
data_table.History: Primigravida 9 weeks; 4.5 kg weight loss; failed pyridoxine and doxylamine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride plus potassium replacement, thiamine 100 mg intravenously and ondansetron 4 mg intravenously
options.rationale: The RANZCOG hyperemesis pathway admits for intravenous fluids using 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's with potassium replacement, thiamine 100 mg intravenously to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and an antiemetic such as ondansetron 4 mg intravenously as first line escalation (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019; TG Obstetric).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Discharge with an oral course of prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days and general practitioner review the next day with instructions to return if vomiting recurs or fluid intake fails
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after inpatient intravenous therapy has failed; oral prednisolone as a first line in a dehydrated hypokalaemic patient is not standard care (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular metoclopramide 10 mg and reassess before deciding on admission or discharge with an oral rehydration trial before deciding on disposition
options.rationale: A single antiemetic dose does not address the intravascular volume loss, ketonuria and hypokalaemia; intravenous rehydration with electrolyte correction is required (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Commence 5 percent dextrose infusion at maintenance rate and add pyridoxine 25 mg orally three times daily with regular antiemetic review over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Dextrose without prior thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in a malnourished pregnant patient; 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's are preferred as the initial fluid with thiamine given first (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

options.text: Arrange dilation and evacuation of the pregnancy given the severity of her symptoms and weight loss and refer to social work for support and information about future options
options.rationale: Termination is not standard care for hyperemesis; effective escalation of antiemetic therapy achieves symptom control in the majority of patients (Source: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum with intractable vomiting, weight loss over 5 percent of pre pregnancy weight, ketonuria and electrolyte disturbance requires admission for intravenous rehydration. First line fluids are 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's with potassium replacement guided by serum potassium, and thiamine 100 mg intravenously must be given before any dextrose to avoid Wernicke encephalopathy. First line antiemetics are pyridoxine and doxylamine; ondansetron and metoclopramide are used when the first line agents have failed. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases after inpatient escalation has failed.
key_points: 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's plus potassium as first line fluid.
Thiamine 100 mg intravenously precedes any dextrose in malnourished patients.
Corticosteroids only after conventional antiemetic escalation fails.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine 100 mg intravenously daily for at least 3 days before dextrose in any pregnant patient with sustained vomiting and weight loss, otherwise a glucose load risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

sources.label: RANZCOG nausea and vomiting in pregnancy 2019

subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery for asymptomatic placenta praevia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal fetal medicine clinic. A 33 year old para 1 at 34 weeks has known placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal os by 22 mm on transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks. She has had no bleeding episodes throughout pregnancy. Her first birth was a caesarean at term for fetal distress.

On examination she is well with no abdominal pain, no bleeding per vaginum and normal fetal movements. Speculum has not been performed. Fetal heart rate is 148 on cardiotocography.

Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Bloods show haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, blood group A positive, antibody screen negative. Estimated fetal weight is on the 60th centile with normal amniotic fluid index. She has been counselled to attend immediately if any bleeding occurs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 148/min
data_table.Examination: No abdominal pain; no bleeding; normal fetal movements; CTG normal
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: placenta covers os by 22 mm at 32 weeks; Hb 118 g/L; platelets 234 x10^9/L; group A+ antibody negative; EFW 60th centile; normal AFI
data_table.History: Para 1 previous LSCS at term for fetal distress; asymptomatic through pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and perform vaginal delivery given the absence of bleeding to date with continuous cardiotocography and immediate caesarean if bleeding occurs
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is not safe with a placenta covering the internal os by more than 10 mm; catastrophic haemorrhage occurs at labour onset and elective caesarean is required (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section at 39 plus 0 weeks with a magnetic resonance imaging scan to exclude placenta accreta first after multidisciplinary team discussion
options.rationale: Waiting until 39 weeks exposes the woman to a substantial risk of spontaneous labour with catastrophic haemorrhage; the earlier window at 36 to 37 plus 6 weeks is chosen for this reason (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Plan elective caesarean section between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity
options.rationale: The RANZCOG guidance for asymptomatic placenta praevia is to plan elective caesarean section between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, balancing prematurity risk against unplanned haemorrhage from spontaneous labour (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Admit now for continuous cardiotocographic monitoring until spontaneous delivery with cross match samples sent for transfusion readiness
options.rationale: Continuous inpatient monitoring in the absence of bleeding or contractions has no benefit and prolongs admission; outpatient monitoring with clear return advice is standard (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

options.text: Perform external cephalic version at 36 weeks and then await spontaneous vaginal delivery with continuous cardiotocography and inpatient monitoring after the attempt
options.rationale: External cephalic version is contraindicated in placenta praevia because manipulation of the uterus may precipitate placental bleeding (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018).
source_refs: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia with the placental edge covering the internal cervical os by more than 20 mm on transvaginal ultrasound after 32 weeks mandates elective caesarean section. The RANZCOG guidance is to plan the caesarean between 36 plus 0 and 37 plus 6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids because the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage with spontaneous labour is high while fetal maturity gains beyond 37 weeks are marginal. External cephalic version is contraindicated because it may precipitate haemorrhage. Ongoing outpatient monitoring with clear return advice is preferred over prolonged inpatient stay in the absence of bleeding or contractions.
key_points: Placenta covering os by more than 10 mm needs elective caesarean.
Delivery window 36 plus 0 to 37 plus 6 weeks with corticosteroids.
External cephalic version is contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: For asymptomatic placenta praevia the RANZCOG delivery window is deliberately early at 36 to 37 plus 6 weeks; a single course of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly 24 hours apart gives fetal lung maturity while pre empting spontaneous labour.

sources.label: RANZCOG placenta praevia and vasa praevia 2018

subtopic_detail: Surgical choice for tubal ectopic after contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old para 0 at 7 weeks of amenorrhoea with 3 days of right iliac fossa pain. She had a left salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for 8 months and would like future fertility preserved if possible.

On examination she has mild right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding but no peritonism. Speculum shows a closed cervix and no bleeding.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Serum beta hCG is 3200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a right adnexal complex mass measuring 32 by 28 mm with a yolk sac visible; no fetal cardiac activity is seen; there is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 118/70 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding; no peritonism; closed cervix; no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 3200 IU/L; Hb 128 g/L; TVUS empty uterus, right adnexal mass 32 x 28 mm with yolk sac, no fetal cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas free fluid
data_table.History: Para 0 at 7 weeks; left salpingectomy 3 years ago for ruptured ectopic; trying to conceive 8 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly and follow up with serial beta hCG measurements
options.rationale: Methotrexate would preserve the tube pharmacologically, however with an adnexal mass containing a yolk sac and pain there is a significant failure rate; more importantly this is the woman's only remaining tube and preserving its function is a priority, which favours a laparoscopic conservative approach given operative access and beta hCG below the RANZCOG surgical threshold (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform laparoscopic right salpingectomy given the higher risk of persistent trophoblast with tube conservation
options.rationale: Salpingectomy removes future spontaneous conception potential from that tube; in a woman with only one tube left the balance of persistent trophoblast risk against loss of tubal function favours salpingostomy (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Observe with expectant management and repeat beta hCG in 48 hours before deciding on intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic women with a small mass, no free fluid and a falling beta hCG below 1500 IU/L; this presentation with pain, free fluid and a mass with a yolk sac needs active management (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingostomy on the right tube with serial beta hCG follow up until zero
options.rationale: The woman has had a contralateral salpingectomy so the right tube is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy preserves tubal patency and future intrauterine fertility potential and is preferred over salpingectomy when tubal preservation matters, with serial beta hCG follow up to detect persistent trophoblast (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

options.text: Perform diagnostic laparoscopy with wedge cornual resection to preserve the fimbrial end of the tube
options.rationale: Cornual resection is used for interstitial or cornual ectopics, not for a mid tubal adnexal ectopic; it damages the myometrium and is not indicated for a typical ampullary ectopic (Source: RANZCOG tubal ectopic pregnancy 2018).

explanation.summary: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a tubal ectopic and a contralateral salpingectomy, salpingostomy on the remaining tube preserves future intrauterine fertility and is preferred over salpingectomy despite a modestly higher rate of persistent trophoblast, which is managed with serial beta hCG monitoring. The RANZCOG surgical threshold of a beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L pushes towards salpingectomy in a woman with a normal contralateral tube, but where the contralateral tube is absent the calculus flips towards conservation. Methotrexate is a reasonable alternative when the mass is small, there is no pain and beta hCG is below 5000 IU/L, but requires reliable follow up. Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic small ectopic pregnancies with a falling beta hCG below 1500 IU/L.
key_points: Only remaining tube: salpingostomy preferred over salpingectomy.
beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L is the RANZCOG surgical threshold when a normal contralateral tube exists.
Serial beta hCG follow up detects persistent trophoblast.
explanation.pearls: Whenever an ectopic occurs after a contralateral salpingectomy, the surgical default flips from salpingectomy to salpingostomy because loss of the last tube ends spontaneous intrauterine conception potential.

subtopic_detail: Augmentation of labour after previous caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birthing unit. A 32 year old para 1 at 40 plus 3 weeks was admitted 5 hours ago in spontaneous labour. Her previous birth was a lower segment caesarean section 2 years ago for breech presentation at term with a normal wound and no interval infection. She was counselled antenatally on trial of labour after caesarean and consented to it.

She is contracting 2 in 10 for 40 seconds with adequate strength. Her cervix is 5 cm dilated, fully effaced, station minus 1, with cephalic presentation. Amniotomy 2 hours ago was clear. She has an epidural in situ working well. Her partogram shows no cervical change over the last 2 hours.

Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C. Fetal heart rate on cardiotocography is 140 with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88/min; BP 122/78 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.9 C; FHR 140/min normal variability
data_table.Examination: Contracting 2 in 10 for 40 sec; cervix 5 cm, fully effaced, station -1, cephalic; membranes ruptured 2 h ago; clear liquor
data_table.Progress: No cervical change over 2 hours; epidural in situ
data_table.History: Previous LSCS 2 years ago for breech; consented VBAC; no interval infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a Foley catheter for mechanical cervical dilation without pharmacological augmentation to reduce uterine rupture risk and continue continuous cardiotocography with reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Mechanical cervical ripening with a Foley catheter is used for cervical ripening before labour, not to augment established labour that has stalled; oxytocin augmentation is the standard approach here (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Give a single dose of vaginal prostaglandin E2 3 mg to accelerate the labour and continue continuous cardiotocography with reassessment at 4 hours with continuous cardiotocography and reassessment at 4 hours
options.rationale: Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated for the augmentation of labour after previous caesarean due to a threefold increase in uterine rupture risk (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).
