options.text: Recommend immediate repeat caesarean section as the safest option given the failure to progress after discussing the risks and benefits with her and her partner in detail
options.rationale: Failure to progress for 2 hours in the active phase does not meet the definition of failure of labour after caesarean; a trial of oxytocin augmentation with careful monitoring is the standard first step (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Continue expectant management with intermittent auscultation and reassess cervix in 4 hours and offer analgesia adjustment as required by the epidural service
options.rationale: Intermittent auscultation is not appropriate in a woman with a previous caesarean because subtle changes in the fetal heart rate are an early sign of uterine rupture; continuous cardiotocography is required (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

options.text: Commence intravenous oxytocin infusion titrated to contractions of 4 in 10 with continuous cardiotocography and one to one midwifery care with escalation to the on call obstetric consultant if needed
options.rationale: A woman with a previous single low transverse caesarean, inadequate contractions in the active phase and no cervical progress over 2 hours may have oxytocin augmentation with careful titration and continuous cardiotocography; the RANZCOG guidance is oxytocin is not contraindicated after previous caesarean but rupture risk is increased and monitoring must be continuous with one to one midwifery care (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean 2019).

explanation.summary: In a woman attempting a trial of labour after caesarean with inadequate contractions and no cervical progress in the active phase, intravenous oxytocin augmentation is not contraindicated but requires careful titration with continuous cardiotocography and one to one midwifery care because the risk of uterine rupture is around 0.5 to 1 percent. Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated for augmentation after previous caesarean due to a threefold rupture risk. Intermittent auscultation is inadequate because subtle changes in the fetal heart trace are the earliest sign of scar rupture. Repeat caesarean is reserved for failure of the trial or for fetal or maternal compromise, not for a single 2 hour period of arrest.
key_points: Oxytocin can be used to augment labour after previous caesarean with continuous CTG.
Vaginal prostaglandins are contraindicated after previous caesarean.
Continuous cardiotocography detects early signs of uterine rupture.
explanation.pearls: After a previous single low transverse caesarean the baseline uterine rupture rate is around 0.5 percent and rises to around 1 percent with oxytocin augmentation, still allowing a monitored trial of labour to proceed.

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis and immediate management on the 26 week OGTT
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman at 26 plus 3 weeks in her second pregnancy who has just had her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her first pregnancy was 4 years ago at a different hospital and she delivered by uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with a birthweight of 3.6 kg with no antenatal or postnatal complications.

Her body mass index at booking was 27. There is no family history of type 2 diabetes. She has been walking 30 minutes most days and is following the routine antenatal diet.

Her 75 g OGTT today shows: fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour 8.7 mmol/L (less than 8.5). Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, urine dipstick negative for glucose and protein. Fetal fundal height is appropriate for gestational age today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg; fetal fundal height appropriate
data_table.Examination: Booking BMI 27; walking 30 min most days
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L; 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L; 2 hour 8.7 mmol/L (ADIPS thresholds 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5); urine dip negative
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1; previous NVD 39 weeks; birthweight 3.6 kg; no complications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Reassure that only one value exceeds the ADIPS threshold and repeat the 75 g OGTT in 2 weeks to confirm the diagnosis before starting any treatment
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes require only one abnormal value; repeating the OGTT would delay treatment without diagnostic utility (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence subcutaneous insulin isophane 10 units at night immediately after this consultation with home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily
options.rationale: Insulin is not a first line agent without a lifestyle trial; it is reserved for lifestyle failure or immediate use if there is severe hyperglycaemia or fetal overgrowth already (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence metformin 500 mg orally twice daily immediately after this consultation with monitoring capillary blood glucose 4 times daily as an outpatient
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is added after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle intervention if targets are not met; metformin first line without a trial of lifestyle is not the ADIPS pathway (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes, refer for dietitian and diabetes educator input, and commence home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily as an outpatient today
options.rationale: Any one abnormal value on the 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 or higher) diagnoses gestational diabetes; initial management is lifestyle plus home BGL monitoring 4 times daily (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Reassure that all three values are below the diagnostic thresholds and continue routine antenatal care with a repeat OGTT arranged only if she develops any symptoms of hyperglycaemia
options.rationale: The 2 hour value of 8.7 mmol/L is above the ADIPS threshold of 8.5, so she meets diagnostic criteria and continuing routine care would miss the diagnosis (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The ADIPS Consensus Guidelines diagnose gestational diabetes on the 75 g OGTT with any one abnormal value: fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L or more, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or more, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or more. Initial management is dietitian and diabetes educator referral, education, and home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily (fasting plus 2 hour post prandial). Pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) is added if lifestyle fails to meet targets over 1 to 2 weeks or if severe hyperglycaemia or fetal overgrowth is already present.
key_points: One value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM.
Start with lifestyle plus home BGL monitoring.
Escalate to metformin or insulin if targets missed at 1 to 2 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Targets on home monitoring are fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 2 hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L; use these for the metformin or insulin decision rather than repeating the OGTT.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite at a tertiary centre reviewing a 28 year old primigravida at 34 plus 2 weeks referred from her general practitioner with new headache and epigastric pain. She had a blood pressure of 158/108 mmHg in the community and 162/110 mmHg on repeat 15 minutes later on arrival to the birth suite.

She describes a right upper quadrant ache and one episode of vomiting overnight. She has no visual disturbance and no chest pain. There has been no vaginal bleeding.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 162/110 mmHg confirmed on manual repeat, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140 bpm on CTG which is reactive. Urine protein to creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol (less than 30). Platelet count 88 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 128 U/L (5-35), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90). Reflexes are 3 plus with 2 beats of ankle clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 162/110 mmHg repeat; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 140 bpm reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant ache; 3 plus reflexes; 2 beats of ankle clonus; no focal deficit; no visual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 78 mg/mmol; platelets 88 x10^9/L; ALT 128 U/L; creatinine 96 micromol/L
data_table.Obstetric: G1P0 at 34 plus 2 weeks; new headache and epigastric pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous methyldopa 500 mg as a stat dose and observe for 4 hours while awaiting placental function investigations to guide the timing of delivery decisions
options.rationale: Methyldopa is not an acute intravenous antihypertensive; onset of action is too slow for severe pre-eclampsia and the treatment does not cover seizure risk (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give oral labetalol 200 mg only and repeat blood pressure every 15 minutes with senior review if it does not drop below 160/110 mmHg within one hour of the dose
options.rationale: Antihypertensive therapy alone does not address seizure risk; magnesium is added when there are severe features or neurological symptoms, and IV rather than oral antihypertensive is preferred acutely (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give diazepam 10 mg intravenously as seizure prophylaxis and commence oral labetalol 100 mg while awaiting the consultant to make a decision about delivery
options.rationale: Diazepam is not the seizure prophylaxis of choice in pre-eclampsia; the MAGPIE trial established magnesium as superior with lower recurrent seizure rates (Source: MAGPIE trial; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and observe without other intervention because delivery is likely to be required within the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are appropriate before 34 plus 6 weeks but do not address the immediate seizure and hypertensive risk; magnesium and antihypertensive are needed alongside (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose 4 g over 20 minutes then infusion 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis and treat the hypertension
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus) mandates seizure prophylaxis with intravenous magnesium; SOMANZ protocol is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus), thrombocytopaenia, or hepatic dysfunction requires seizure prophylaxis with intravenous magnesium sulfate. The SOMANZ regimen is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then a 1 g/hour infusion, targeting a therapeutic level of 2 to 3 mmol/L. Acute severe hypertension is controlled with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine. Delivery is the definitive treatment after stabilisation and corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity before 34 plus 6 weeks.
key_points: Severe features plus neurological symptoms equals give magnesium.
SOMANZ regimen: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/hour infusion.
Diazepam is inferior to magnesium (MAGPIE trial).
explanation.pearls: Monitor magnesium clinically with 4 hourly reflexes, respiratory rate over 12, urine output over 25 mL/hour; if signs of toxicity stop infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes.

subtopic_detail: Suitability for planned VBAC per RANZCOG
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman at 36 plus 4 weeks in her third pregnancy at the antenatal clinic. Her first birth was an emergency caesarean at 38 weeks for fetal distress with a lower segment transverse incision. Her second birth was an uncomplicated VBAC at 40 weeks with a birthweight of 3.4 kg and no perineal trauma.

She has been counselled at earlier visits about mode of delivery options. She has a body mass index of 26. There is no previous uterine rupture, no previous classical caesarean, and no previous uterine perforation. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated with an anterior placenta.

Blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, no proteinuria, fetal fundal height corresponds to gestation, and cephalic presentation is confirmed by ultrasound today with an estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg; no proteinuria; fetal fundal height appropriate
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation confirmed on ultrasound; EFW 50th centile; anterior placenta
data_table.History: First birth emergency caesarean at 38 weeks for fetal distress (LSCS transverse); second birth uncomplicated VBAC at 40 weeks BW 3.4 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Recommend a planned VBAC because prior successful VBAC substantially raises the chance of a successful subsequent VBAC and reduces the rupture risk in this labour
options.rationale: Prior successful VBAC increases the probability of subsequent VBAC to 85 to 90 percent and reduces uterine rupture rates to about 0.5 percent; RANZCOG supports planned VBAC in this scenario (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks because any previous caesarean scar carries an unacceptable rupture risk with a subsequent labour and vaginal delivery attempt
options.rationale: A single previous lower segment transverse caesarean is not a contraindication to VBAC; a prior successful VBAC substantially reduces subsequent rupture risk to about 0.5 percent (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 vaginal pessary at 39 weeks because this shortens labour duration and reduces the risk of a subsequent emergency caesarean
options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction of labour after previous caesarean approximately triples uterine rupture risk and is generally avoided in favour of mechanical methods (balloon catheter) or spontaneous labour (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend elective repeat caesarean because the interpregnancy interval is under 24 months and this substantially increases the risk of uterine rupture with a trial of labour in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Interpregnancy interval under 18 months is the accepted risk threshold; her previous VBAC was more than 2 years ago and interval is not the concern here (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

options.text: Recommend home birth because her previous VBAC was uncomplicated and she is at very low risk of any labour complication warranting hospital based intrapartum monitoring and support
options.rationale: Planned VBAC should occur in a facility with continuous electronic fetal monitoring and immediate access to caesarean; home birth after previous caesarean is not supported by RANZCOG (Source: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section).
source_refs: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

explanation.summary: RANZCOG supports planned vaginal birth after caesarean for women with a single previous lower segment transverse caesarean and no other contraindications. A prior successful VBAC increases the likelihood of a subsequent successful VBAC to 85 to 90 percent and reduces uterine rupture risk to about 0.5 percent. Contraindications include previous classical caesarean, previous uterine rupture, more than two previous caesareans, and placenta praevia. Induction with prostaglandins is generally avoided because it approximately triples rupture risk; mechanical induction or spontaneous labour is preferred.
key_points: Prior successful VBAC gives 85 to 90 percent success next time.
Rupture risk about 0.5 percent after prior successful VBAC.
Avoid prostaglandin induction because rupture risk is tripled.
explanation.pearls: Counsel women that planned VBAC requires continuous electronic fetal monitoring in labour and immediate access to emergency caesarean, so it is not appropriate for planned home birth or standalone birth centres.

sources.label: RANZCOG Planned vaginal birth after caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Cervical priming decision using the Bishop score
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old primigravida on the antenatal ward at 41 plus 3 weeks admitted for post dates induction of labour. Her antenatal course has been uncomplicated. She has no medical comorbidities and body mass index at booking was 24. There is no known contraindication to vaginal delivery. The fetus is cephalic on ultrasound with an estimated weight of 3.6 kg.

On vaginal examination the cervix is posterior, 1 cm long, of firm consistency, and closed. The fetal head is 3 cm above the ischial spines. Membranes are intact.

Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, fetal heart rate 138 bpm reactive on CTG. Bloods are within normal limits. Group B streptococcus screening at 36 weeks was negative. The team has discussed induction options with her and she has consented to the process being started today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg; fetal heart rate 138 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix posterior; 1 cm long; firm; closed; head 3 cm above spines; membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits; GBS screen negative
data_table.Obstetric: G1P0 at 41 plus 3 weeks; cephalic; EFW 3.6 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in induction of labour?

options.text: Perform artificial rupture of membranes now and commence a titrated intravenous oxytocin infusion 1 hour after the amniotomy is performed on the labour ward
options.rationale: An unripe cervix (Bishop score 1) is not suitable for amniotomy; cervical ripening is required first because forcing amniotomy risks failed induction and prolonged rupture of membranes (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Insert a Foley or double balloon transcervical catheter overnight for mechanical cervical priming and reassess the Bishop score in the morning after balloon removal
options.rationale: With a Bishop score of 1, mechanical cervical priming with a transcervical balloon (Foley or Cook double balloon) is a preferred first step and is safe for parous or nulliparous women (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Insert vaginal misoprostol 25 microg every 4 hours to a maximum of 4 doses over 24 hours and reassess the Bishop score after each dose before proceeding to amniotomy
options.rationale: Misoprostol is an acceptable ripening agent but at RANZCOG the standard prostaglandin option is dinoprostone; misoprostol dosing above 25 microg increases tachysystole and misoprostol is not the default first line agent (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Commence a titrated intravenous oxytocin infusion starting at 2 milliunits per minute now and increase every 30 minutes according to uterine contraction frequency and CTG trace
options.rationale: Oxytocin alone is not appropriate for cervical ripening with an unfavourable cervix; the risk of hyperstimulation and failed induction rises without priming (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

options.text: Perform an urgent caesarean section today given that induction of labour with an unripe cervix is likely to fail and would expose her to prolonged labour and morbidity risk
options.rationale: Post dates induction with an unripe cervix is not itself a caesarean indication; success rates after mechanical priming and appropriate agents are high (Source: RANZCOG Induction of labour statement).

explanation.summary: The Bishop score summarises cervical readiness for induction across five features (position, length, consistency, dilatation, station). A score of 6 or less indicates an unripe cervix requiring priming before amniotomy or oxytocin. Options for priming are mechanical (Foley or Cook double balloon transcervical catheter) or prostaglandin (dinoprostone in Australia; misoprostol at low doses in selected settings). Amniotomy and oxytocin are appropriate first steps only when the cervix is favourable (Bishop score more than 6).
key_points: Bishop score 6 or less equals unripe cervix, needs priming.
Mechanical priming (Foley or Cook double balloon) is preferred first line.
Amniotomy and oxytocin follow when the cervix is favourable.
explanation.pearls: Mechanical balloon priming avoids uterine hyperstimulation risk associated with prostaglandins and is particularly useful in women with previous caesarean or in outpatient priming pathways.

subtopic_detail: First line uterotonic choice in atonic PPH with hypertension excluded
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 29 year old primigravida who delivered a 4.2 kg baby by normal vaginal delivery 20 minutes ago after a 90 minute second stage. The placenta was delivered by active management with intramuscular oxytocin at the delivery of the anterior shoulder and appeared complete. She has developed a heavy PV loss estimated at 1200 mL and ongoing.

On examination the uterus is boggy and above the umbilicus. There is no visible cervical tear on speculum inspection and the perineum has an intact second degree tear that has not been sutured. She has no history of hypertension, no known bleeding disorder, no drug allergies, and she did not have pre-eclampsia in this pregnancy.

Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Two large bore intravenous cannulae are in place. Group and hold is available and cross match has been sent. Baseline blood pressures throughout pregnancy were 105 to 115 systolic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min; BP 88/52 mmHg; RR 24/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy above umbilicus; no cervical tear; second degree perineal tear unsutured; ongoing PV loss
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold available; cross match sent
data_table.Obstetric: Primigravida; NVD 20 min ago; baby 4.2 kg; second stage 90 min; active third stage with IM oxytocin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Misoprostol has slow onset compared to intramuscular ergometrine and is reserved for settings without access to injectable uterotonics; not first line in a hospital setting with ongoing loss (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Carboprost is a third line uterotonic reserved for continued PPH despite oxytocin and ergometrine; jumping to it before ergometrine skips the standard sequence (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Second line uterotonic after failed oxytocin in atonic PPH is intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg; her blood pressure is low so no contraindication exists, and bimanual compression is added mechanically (Source: RANZCOG PPH; AMH).

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is given within 3 hours of onset as adjunct therapy but does not replace uterotonics; her uterus is atonic so uterotonic escalation is the priority (Source: WOMAN trial; RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 100 microg with continuous blood pressure monitoring and bimanual uterine compression while further intravenous access and blood products are being organised urgently
options.rationale: Adrenaline is not a uterotonic and has no role in atonic PPH; resuscitation should focus on blood products and directed uterotonics (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH is managed by simultaneous resuscitation and stepwise uterotonics. After failed initial oxytocin (IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder), the second line uterotonic is intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg unless the woman has hypertension or coronary disease. Third line is intramuscular carboprost 250 microg (avoid in asthma). Tranexamic acid is added within 3 hours as an adjunct per the WOMAN trial. Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, uterine balloon) run in parallel with uterotonic escalation.
key_points: Second line uterotonic is IM ergometrine 250 microg when no contraindication.
Third line is IM carboprost 250 microg; avoid in asthma.
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours as adjunct per WOMAN trial.
explanation.pearls: Always call for help early, quantify blood loss with weighed swabs, and activate massive transfusion protocol before hypotension becomes refractory; PPH deaths are usually delays in escalation rather than absence of an available treatment.

subtopic_detail: Surgical management preference after prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman in the early pregnancy unit who has had a positive urine pregnancy test at home and now presents with right sided pelvic pain and light PV bleeding at an estimated 6 weeks by last menstrual period. She had a right sided salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured right tubal ectopic pregnancy at a different hospital and has since had 12 months of unsuccessful natural conception attempts.

She has no dizziness, no shoulder tip pain, and no syncope. Her past history includes chlamydia treated 5 years ago and one previous laparoscopy for pelvic pain. She is haemodynamically stable and reports her left tube was described intraoperatively at the previous salpingectomy as macroscopically normal.

Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Serum beta HCG is 4600 IU/L today with a previous value of 4400 IU/L 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 8 mm, an adnexal mass measuring 22 x 18 mm in the left tube containing a yolk sac and no visible cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88/min; BP 118/74 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Mild right sided pelvic tenderness; no rebound; light PV bleeding on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Beta HCG 4600 IU/L today (from 4400 IU/L 48 h prior); TV US empty uterus; left tubal mass 22 x 18 mm with yolk sac no cardiac activity; no free fluid; Hb 128 g/L
data_table.History: G2P0 with prior right salpingectomy for ruptured ectopic; 12 months trying to conceive; chlamydia 5 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre as a single dose today with weekly beta HCG monitoring until it falls below 15 IU/L on the standard early pregnancy unit pathway
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a reasonable option for haemodynamically stable ectopic with beta HCG under 5000 IU/L, no cardiac activity and no rupture, but her only remaining tube would be preserved by tubal surgery which is preferred here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy; AMH).

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy today because ectopic recurrence in the same tube is high and salpingectomy avoids the risk of persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic in the future
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingectomy would leave her with no tubes and mandate IVF, so salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta HCG measurements every 48 hours and repeat ultrasound weekly to allow the ectopic to resorb spontaneously without needing surgical or medical treatment
options.rationale: Expectant management requires beta HCG under 1000 IU/L and falling; her level is 4600 IU/L and rising, so expectant management is not appropriate here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingostomy today with linear salpingostomy over the ectopic and weekly beta HCG monitoring to detect any persistent trophoblast that may need methotrexate rescue
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy preserves the tube and future fertility, with the trade off of monitoring for persistent trophoblast that may need methotrexate rescue (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

options.text: Laparotomy with left salpingectomy urgently today because there is a substantial risk of rupture in the next 24 hours given the size of the mass and the rising beta HCG level on serial testing
options.rationale: She is haemodynamically stable with no free fluid; laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy, and salpingectomy in her only remaining tube commits her to IVF unnecessarily (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Choice between salpingectomy and salpingostomy for tubal ectopic pregnancy depends on the state of the contralateral tube. When the contralateral tube is healthy, salpingectomy is preferred because rates of persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic are lower and fertility outcomes are similar. When there is a prior contralateral salpingectomy or the contralateral tube is diseased, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility, with the trade off of monitoring beta HCG weekly for persistent trophoblast that may require methotrexate rescue.
key_points: Healthy contralateral tube equals salpingectomy preferred.
Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts to salpingostomy preferred.
Weekly beta HCG monitoring after salpingostomy to detect persistent trophoblast.
explanation.pearls: When the answer seems to obviously be the more definitive procedure (salpingectomy) in a stable patient, look for a prior contralateral surgical history that flips the standard answer; this is the T14 historical bilaterality inversion pattern.

subtopic_detail: Immediate first line manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite for a suspected shoulder dystocia. A 30 year old multiparous woman at 39 plus 6 weeks has just delivered the fetal head after a normal vaginal delivery. The head has emerged but retracted against the perineum in a turtle sign after failure of restitution and no descent of the shoulders with routine axial traction on the next contraction.

Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a birthweight of 4.1 kg. This pregnancy has been complicated by well controlled gestational diabetes on diet alone. The estimated fetal weight at her 36 week ultrasound was on the 95th centile. Her BMI at booking was 32.

Fetal heart rate immediately before delivery of the head was 138 bpm. The midwife is at the woman's head; the birth suite senior midwife has entered the room. A time keeper has been designated and the paediatric team has been paged. There is no clinical evidence of maternal haemorrhage at this stage in the delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal stable; FHR 138 bpm immediately prior to delivery
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign after delivery of head; no descent with routine axial traction
data_table.Team: Time keeper set; senior midwife present; paediatric team paged
data_table.History: Multiparous; previous BW 4.1 kg; well controlled GDM diet only; EFW 95th centile at 36 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Deliberate posterior arm delivery by the accoucheur immediately after diagnosis; do not attempt McRoberts as it delays disimpaction of the anterior shoulder for the mother
options.rationale: Posterior arm delivery is an effective internal manoeuvre but is second line after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure; brachial plexus injury risk rises without prior external manoeuvres (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Rubin II internal rotation manoeuvre by the accoucheur immediately after diagnosis; do not attempt McRoberts as it delays internal disimpaction of the anterior shoulder
options.rationale: Internal rotation manoeuvres are second line after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail; jumping to them first misses the highest yield low morbidity first line intervention (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Immediate deliberate cephalic replacement (Zavanelli manoeuvre) and preparation for a category 1 caesarean section by the obstetric consultant on call for the birth suite
options.rationale: Zavanelli manoeuvre is a last resort after HELPERR has failed; using it before McRoberts is not indicated and adds unnecessary morbidity (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Fundal pressure applied by a second midwife on top of routine axial traction of the fetal head to encourage the anterior shoulder to slip beneath the pubic symphysis
options.rationale: Fundal pressure worsens shoulder impaction and increases risk of uterine rupture; it is explicitly contraindicated in shoulder dystocia (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure applied by an assistant immediately after positioning; continue axial traction on the fetal head with the next contraction
options.rationale: HELPERR sequence starts with McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips onto abdomen) plus suprapubic pressure; this resolves about 50 percent of shoulder dystocias and is the mandated first manoeuvre before internal manoeuvres (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia; ALSO).

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency requiring a fixed drill (HELPERR) after calling for help. The first manoeuvre is McRoberts (hyperflexion of the hips onto the abdomen) plus suprapubic pressure by an assistant; this resolves about 50 percent of cases. If unsuccessful, proceed to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, posterior arm delivery). Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement) is a last resort. Documentation with time keeping is essential and helps subsequent clinical governance and litigation defence.
key_points: First manoeuvre is McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure.
Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
Sequence: HELPERR - Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure suprapubic, Enter for internal, Remove posterior arm, Roll to all fours.
explanation.pearls: Time keeping starts at diagnosis of dystocia; the risk of hypoxic injury and brachial plexus injury rises after 5 minutes but many drills are completed in under 90 seconds if McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the impaction quickly.

subtopic_detail: Delivery of the second twin after the first with a transverse lie and cord accessible
stem:
You are the senior obstetric registrar on the birth suite at a tertiary centre. A 34 year old primigravida with dichorionic diamniotic twins at 37 plus 3 weeks has just delivered twin 1 vaginally in a cephalic presentation with a birthweight of 2.7 kg after a straightforward labour and second stage.

Ultrasound in the birth suite immediately after delivery of twin 1 shows twin 2 in a transverse lie with the back downwards, an estimated fetal weight of 2.9 kg, and intact membranes. Cardiotocography of twin 2 is currently reactive at 140 bpm.

Maternal vital signs are stable; the woman is well analgesed with an epidural in situ. Consultants in obstetrics, anaesthetics and neonatology have been briefed antenatally regarding the intrapartum options and the woman has had a thorough discussion of them. The bladder is empty and the room is set up for both vaginal and operative delivery. No maternal or fetal contraindication to internal manoeuvres has been identified through her admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal stable; twin 2 FHR 140 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Twin 2 transverse lie with back down on ultrasound; membranes intact; EFW 2.9 kg; epidural in situ; bladder empty
data_table.Team: Obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatology briefed; consented intrapartum
data_table.Obstetric: G1P1 after delivery twin 1 cephalic 2.7 kg; DCDA twins 37 plus 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the delivery of twin 2?

options.text: Perform internal podalic version of twin 2 to a footling breech followed by breech extraction under epidural anaesthesia with continuous cardiotocography and the neonatal team ready
options.rationale: For twin 2 in a transverse lie with a back down orientation, internal podalic version to a footling breech followed by breech extraction is the standard tertiary approach and is safer than caesarean of a second twin (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform external cephalic version of twin 2 to a cephalic presentation under continuous cardiotocography then amniotomy and titrated oxytocin augmentation to achieve vaginal delivery today
options.rationale: External cephalic version with a transverse back down lie and intact membranes has a low success rate and delays; internal podalic version and breech extraction has the highest success in this setting with an experienced accoucheur (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform an emergency category 1 caesarean section for twin 2 under general anaesthesia in view of the transverse lie and back down orientation and the risk of cord prolapse if membranes rupture
options.rationale: Caesarean of second twin after vaginal delivery of first twin carries significant maternal morbidity; internal podalic version and breech extraction avoids caesarean and has good fetal outcomes in experienced hands (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform artificial rupture of twin 2 membranes now and observe with continuous cardiotocography for spontaneous conversion to a longitudinal lie over the next 30 minutes with the woman on the bed
options.rationale: Rupturing membranes with a transverse lie risks cord prolapse and does not reliably convert to a longitudinal lie; membranes should be kept intact until the presenting part is engaged (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

options.text: Perform amniotomy of twin 2 and immediate ventouse assisted vaginal delivery under continuous cardiotocography with the neonatal resuscitation team ready in the birth suite for the delivery
options.rationale: Ventouse assisted vaginal delivery is not possible for a transverse lie; the presenting part is not cephalic and instrumental delivery is not applicable to a non cephalic non longitudinal lie (Source: RANZCOG Management of twin pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Delivery of the second twin in transverse lie is best managed by internal podalic version followed by breech extraction when the accoucheur is experienced and the woman has been consented antenatally. External cephalic version has a low success rate in the intrapartum period and rupturing membranes with a transverse lie risks cord prolapse. Caesarean of the second twin after successful vaginal delivery of the first twin carries significant maternal morbidity and is reserved for cases where internal manoeuvres fail or are contraindicated.
key_points: Internal podalic version and breech extraction is preferred for transverse twin 2.
Keep membranes intact until presenting part is engaged.
Caesarean of twin 2 after vaginal delivery of twin 1 carries the highest maternal morbidity.
explanation.pearls: Success of internal podalic version and breech extraction depends on operator experience; twin delivery drills at tertiary centres include simulation training for this specific manoeuvre and both consultant obstetrician and anaesthetist should be at the bedside from delivery of twin 1.

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis after an earlier sensitising event
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 28 weeks. She is blood group O RhD negative and her partner's group is unknown.

At 20 weeks she had a small painless vaginal bleed, was assessed in the day unit and received a dose of anti-D immunoglobulin at that time with a Kleihauer showing no excess fetal cells. She has had no bleeding since and reports normal fetal movements. Her antibody screen taken today is negative and her fetal morphology scan at 20 weeks was reported as normal with a posterior placenta clear of the os. She asks whether she needs anything further before delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 112/68, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative; antibody screen negative today; symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No further anti-D immunoglobulin, since a dose was already given for the bleed at 20 weeks
options.rationale: Anti-D given for a sensitising event does not substitute for routine antenatal prophylaxis, because the protection from that dose has waned well before the third trimester (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: The 250 international unit dose is the near pair used for first trimester sensitising events, whereas routine third trimester prophylaxis requires the larger dose (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Australian practice for a non sensitised RhD negative woman is routine antenatal prophylaxis with 625 international units at both 28 and 34 weeks, independent of any earlier event based dose (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin; National Blood Authority).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin deferred until after delivery once the cord blood group has been determined
options.rationale: Postnatal prophylaxis is given in addition to antenatal doses, and deferring the antenatal doses leaves the third trimester unprotected against silent transplacental haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

options.text: Kleihauer testing today with anti-D immunoglobulin given only if fetal cells are demonstrated
options.rationale: Kleihauer testing quantifies bleeding after a sensitising event to determine whether extra doses are needed, and it is not a gate for routine antenatal prophylaxis (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin).
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis reduced the rate of RhD alloimmunisation from around 1 per cent to well under 0.5 per cent by covering silent transplacental haemorrhage that produces no symptoms. Australian practice gives 625 international units at 28 and 34 weeks to every non sensitised RhD negative woman, then a further 625 international units within 72 hours of birth if the baby is RhD positive. Event based doses for bleeding, amniocentesis, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma or termination are given in addition to and never instead of the routine schedule. Once anti-D antibodies are genuinely present from prior sensitisation, prophylaxis no longer has a role and management shifts to titre surveillance and middle cerebral artery Doppler.
key_points: Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 international units at 28 and 34 weeks in Australia
Event based doses are additional to, not a substitute for, the routine schedule
The first trimester sensitising event dose is 250 international units
A positive antibody screen from established sensitisation means prophylaxis no longer applies
explanation.pearls: A passively acquired anti-D from prophylaxis can appear on an antibody screen at a low titre for up to eight weeks; check the timing of the last dose before treating a weak positive screen as true sensitisation.

sources.label: RANZCOG Guidelines for the Use of Rh D Immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Bundle of care in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a level 4 regional hospital assessing a 31 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 29 weeks and 3 days. She has had regular painful contractions every four minutes for two hours.

Speculum examination shows a closed cervix visually but digital examination finds the cervix 3 cm dilated and 80 per cent effaced. Her membranes are intact. She has had no corticosteroids in this pregnancy. She is afebrile with no uterine tenderness and her urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 145 and normal variability. The neonatal unit here manages babies from 32 weeks and the tertiary centre is 90 minutes away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate baseline 145
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph reassuring with normal variability; urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular betamethasone, intravenous magnesium sulfate and transfer to the tertiary centre
options.rationale: Below 30 weeks with birth anticipated within 24 hours the bundle is antenatal corticosteroid for lung maturity, magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, and in utero transfer to a unit that can care for the gestation (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intramuscular betamethasone alone with observation in the birth suite and reassessment in six hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is essential but omitting magnesium sulfate forgoes a proven reduction in cerebral palsy at this gestation, and staying in a unit that cannot care for a 29 week neonate risks ex utero transfer (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate alone with transfer arranged once contractions have been suppressed
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate provides neuroprotection but does not mature the lungs, and antenatal corticosteroid is the single intervention with the largest mortality benefit at this gestation (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Oral nifedipine tocolysis alone with reassessment of the cervix after four hours of treatment
options.rationale: Tocolysis has a supporting role to buy time for corticosteroids and transfer but does not improve neonatal outcomes on its own, so it is never the whole plan (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus prophylaxis with observation in the birth suite
options.rationale: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated once preterm labour is established, but giving it in isolation omits the two interventions that change neonatal mortality and neurological outcome (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm birth is managed as a bundle rather than a single decision, and the components are corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate where the gestation qualifies, consideration of tocolysis, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and in utero transfer. Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34 weeks and reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death. Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given below 30 weeks when birth is expected within 24 hours, with a number needed to treat of about 60 to prevent one case of cerebral palsy. Tocolysis is used to create the window for the other interventions rather than to prolong pregnancy for its own sake, and in utero transfer consistently outperforms transferring a sick neonate afterwards.
key_points: Antenatal corticosteroids apply from 24 to 34 weeks and carry the largest mortality benefit
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection applies below 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours
Tocolysis buys time for steroids and transfer rather than improving neonatal outcome itself
In utero transfer produces better outcomes than transferring a preterm neonate after birth
explanation.pearls: Betamethasone gives its full benefit from 24 hours after the first dose and persists for about seven days; a birth occurring even a few hours after the first dose still confers measurable benefit, so never withhold it because delivery looks imminent.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Guideline
Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth National Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 32 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago followed by continued dampness.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with no bleeding and a closed cervix. She has no contractions and no uterine tenderness. Her temperature is normal, her white cell count and C reactive protein are within normal limits, and the cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 138. Her group B streptococcus status is unknown and her low vaginal swab has just been sent. She had betamethasone commenced one hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/70, RR 15, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate baseline 138
data_table.Examination: Speculum: pool of clear liquor, cervix closed, no bleeding, no uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits; cardiotocograph reassuring; low vaginal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is the near pair that must be avoided in this setting because it is associated with a significant increase in neonatal necrotising enterocolitis (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Oral erythromycin for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management with surveillance
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs the latency period, reduces chorioamnionitis and reduces neonatal morbidity in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without the necrotising enterocolitis signal seen with other agents (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin now and continuing until delivery for group B streptococcus cover
options.rationale: Intrapartum prophylaxis is given once labour starts or delivery is planned rather than continuously during expectant management, which would select resistant organisms over weeks (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: No antibiotics with daily observations, and treatment commenced only if maternal fever develops
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics loses the demonstrated reduction in chorioamnionitis and the prolongation of latency that allows corticosteroids to take effect (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

options.text: Oral metronidazole for seven days with repeat vaginal swabs performed at weekly intervals
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobic vaginosis and has not been shown to improve outcomes after membrane rupture, and it does not cover the organisms driving ascending infection here (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes before 37 weeks is managed expectantly to about 37 weeks provided there is no chorioamnionitis, no fetal compromise, no significant bleeding and no established labour. Ten days of erythromycin is standard because it prolongs latency and reduces neonatal morbidity, while amoxicillin with clavulanate is specifically avoided after trial data showed increased necrotising enterocolitis. Antenatal corticosteroids are given as they would be for any threatened preterm birth in the eligible gestational window. Surveillance for chorioamnionitis relies on maternal temperature, pulse, uterine tenderness, liquor character and cardiotocograph rather than on serial inflammatory markers, which perform poorly in this setting.
key_points: Erythromycin for ten days is the recommended antibiotic after preterm membrane rupture
Amoxicillin with clavulanate is avoided because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Expectant management continues to about 37 weeks if surveillance stays reassuring
Group B streptococcus prophylaxis is given intrapartum rather than throughout expectant care
explanation.pearls: Serial C reactive protein has poor sensitivity and specificity for chorioamnionitis after membrane rupture; a rising maternal pulse with fetal tachycardia is the earlier and more reliable warning pair.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Guideline
RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite with a 30 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 39 weeks and 2 days, now in established labour at 5 cm dilated with intact membranes.

Her routine 36 week low vaginal swab grew group B streptococcus. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was not requested on that isolate and the laboratory advises that the specimen is no longer available. Her allergy history records anaphylaxis to amoxicillin at age 22 requiring adrenaline and an overnight admission. She has no other allergies. Her observations and the cardiotocograph are reassuring and delivery is anticipated within the next four to six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9, fetal heart rate baseline 140
data_table.Investigations: 36 week low vaginal swab positive for group B streptococcus; susceptibility testing not performed and isolate unavailable; cardiotocograph reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with adrenaline and resuscitation equipment available at the bedside
options.rationale: Rechallenge with a beta lactam after documented anaphylaxis is not acceptable practice when effective alternatives exist, regardless of what monitoring is available (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin, since cross reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is uncommon
options.rationale: Cefazolin is appropriate for a low severity penicillin allergy such as a delayed rash, but documented anaphylaxis places her in the high severity group where cephalosporins are avoided (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin, which is the standard alternative agent in severe penicillin allergy
options.rationale: Clindamycin is used only when the isolate has been confirmed susceptible, and Australian group B streptococcus resistance to clindamycin is high enough that empirical use is unreliable (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval
options.rationale: With documented anaphylaxis to a penicillin and no clindamycin susceptibility result available, vancomycin is the recommended intrapartum agent because group B streptococcus remains uniformly susceptible to it (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

options.text: Intravenous erythromycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in group B streptococcus is common and erythromycin achieves poor fetal levels, so it is not recommended for intrapartum prophylaxis (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for group B streptococcus aims to have at least four hours of maternal therapy before delivery, which is when neonatal colonisation falls most. Benzylpenicillin is first line, with cefazolin substituted for low severity penicillin allergy such as an isolated delayed rash. High severity allergy, meaning anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory distress or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, requires clindamycin only where susceptibility is proven and otherwise vancomycin. This is why laboratories should be asked for clindamycin susceptibility whenever a screening swab from a penicillin allergic woman grows the organism, since that single request determines whether vancomycin can be avoided later.
key_points: Aim for at least four hours of intrapartum therapy before delivery
Benzylpenicillin first line, cefazolin for low severity allergy
Clindamycin only when the isolate is confirmed susceptible
Vancomycin where allergy is severe and susceptibility is unknown
explanation.pearls: Request clindamycin susceptibility at the time the 36 week swab is collected for any penicillin allergic woman; without it the default in labour becomes vancomycin, which needs an infusion time that a rapid labour will not allow.

sources.label: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus Guideline

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding with iron deficiency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41 year old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon hourly on her heaviest two days and passing clots the size of a fifty cent coin. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and this pattern has been present for two years.

She has completed her family and does not want further children, and would prefer to avoid an operation. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for human papillomavirus. Her transvaginal ultrasound reports a normal uterus with no fibroid, no polyp and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Her thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal uterus, no fibroid or polyp, endometrial thickness 6 mm; cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Oral tranexamic acid taken on the heaviest days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by around a third and is a reasonable second choice, but it provides no contraception and is less effective than the recommended first line option (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: Oral mefenamic acid taken through the bleeding days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory agents reduce loss by only about 20 to 30 per cent and are the least effective of the medical options offered here (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: Referral for endometrial ablation at the next available gynaecology outpatient appointment
options.rationale: Ablation is effective but is a surgical procedure she has asked to avoid, and it is offered after medical therapy has failed rather than before it is tried (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a hormone free interval and oral iron
options.rationale: The combined pill is effective and does provide contraception, but it reduces menstrual loss less than the intrauterine option and carries thrombotic risk that rises after age 40 (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted in the practice with oral iron replacement
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 90 per cent, outperforms all oral medical options, provides contraception and avoids surgery, which matches every stated preference here (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Guideline).

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its effect on the woman rather than by a measured volume, and structural assessment is directed by symptoms and risk rather than performed reflexively in every case. Where the uterus is structurally normal, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line because it reduces blood loss more than any oral agent and preserves fertility and the uterus. Tranexamic acid and non steroidal anti inflammatories are useful for women who want cycle specific treatment without hormones, and the combined pill suits those wanting cycle control plus contraception. Iron deficiency is treated in parallel rather than after the bleeding is controlled, because ferritin recovery takes months and symptoms of deficiency respond before the haemoglobin does.
key_points: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line for heavy bleeding with a structurally normal uterus
It reduces blood loss by 70 to 90 per cent, more than any oral agent
Tranexamic acid reduces loss by about a third and gives no contraception
Treat iron deficiency concurrently rather than waiting for bleeding control
explanation.pearls: Warn about irregular spotting for the first three to six months after insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system; unwarned bleeding is the commonest reason for early removal, and most women become oligomenorrhoeic or amenorrhoeic by twelve months.

subtopic_detail: Ovulation induction agent selection in polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner with a special interest in women's health seeing a 27 year old woman who has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her cycles come every 45 to 70 days and she has hirsutism affecting her chin and upper lip.

Her body mass index is 31 kg/m2 and she has lost 4 kg over the last four months with dietitian support. Her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. A hysterosalpingogram shows both tubes patent with normal uterine cavity contour. Her prolactin, thyroid function and 17 hydroxyprogesterone are within normal limits, and her pelvic ultrasound shows an antral follicle count of 28 in the right ovary. She has taken folic acid for six months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Antral follicle count 28 in the right ovary; hysterosalpingogram both tubes patent; partner semen analysis normal on two occasions
data_table.Blood tests: Prolactin, thyroid function and 17 hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to induce ovulation?

options.text: Letrozole taken for five days early in the cycle with ultrasound follicle tracking
options.rationale: Letrozole is the recommended first line ovulation induction agent in polycystic ovary syndrome, producing higher live birth rates than clomifene, particularly at higher body mass index (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Clomifene citrate taken for five days early in the cycle with ultrasound follicle tracking
options.rationale: Clomifene is the near pair and remains effective, but its antioestrogenic effect on endometrium and cervical mucus gives lower live birth rates than the aromatase inhibitor (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Metformin taken twice daily as sole therapy with monitoring of cycle length over six months
options.rationale: Metformin improves ovulation rates modestly and is used as an adjunct or where letrozole is unavailable, but it is inferior to letrozole for live birth as monotherapy (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Gonadotrophin injections given in a low dose step up protocol with ultrasound follicle tracking
options.rationale: Injectable gonadotrophins are second line after oral agents fail, and they carry substantially higher risks of multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Referral for in vitro fertilisation with a planned single embryo transfer in the first cycle
options.rationale: Assisted reproduction sits on a different treatment axis and is reserved for failure of ovulation induction or for coexisting tubal or male factors, neither of which is present (Source: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed on the Rotterdam criteria, requiring two of oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology, after exclusion of thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Anovulation is the fertility problem, so treatment is directed at restoring ovulation rather than at the ovarian appearance. Lifestyle intervention comes first and even 5 to 10 per cent weight loss can restore ovulation, but it is pursued alongside rather than instead of pharmacological induction when time matters. Letrozole displaced clomifene as first line on the strength of trials showing higher ovulation and live birth rates, and any induction cycle needs follicle tracking to limit multiple pregnancy.
key_points: Rotterdam criteria need two of three features after exclusion of mimics
Letrozole is first line for ovulation induction ahead of clomifene
Metformin is adjunctive rather than a primary fertility agent
Gonadotrophins and assisted reproduction follow failure of oral induction
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound follicle tracking in the first induction cycle is what keeps the multiple pregnancy rate near 5 per cent; untracked cycles with either oral agent run several times that risk in women with a high antral follicle count.

sources.label: International Evidence Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Antenatal planning for suspected placenta accreta spectrum
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a district hospital reviewing a 36 year old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks. She has had two previous lower segment caesarean sections and one vaginal birth.

She has had no bleeding in this pregnancy and feels well. Today's transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound reports an anterior placenta covering the internal os, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, multiple placental lacunae, and bridging vessels crossing the uterine serosa toward the bladder. The myometrial thickness overlying the placenta measures 1 mm. Her haemoglobin is 118 g/L and her blood group is A positive with a negative antibody screen. The nearest tertiary centre with an interventional radiology service is 40 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 114/70, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, fetal heart rate baseline 144
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: anterior placenta covering the internal os, loss of retroplacental clear zone, multiple lacunae, bridging vessels, myometrium 1 mm
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); blood group A positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound at 36 weeks and plan a caesarean section here at 39 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks in a non specialist unit exposes her to emergency haemorrhage before the planned date, since a third of these women bleed and require unplanned delivery (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the diagnosis before making any referral decision
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging adds little when ultrasound findings are this characteristic and is used to define topography at the referral centre rather than as a gate to referral (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline).

options.text: Refer now to a specialist centre for planned delivery between 34 and 36 weeks with a multidisciplinary team
options.rationale: Two prior caesareans with an anterior praevia and these sonographic markers indicate placenta accreta spectrum, where planned preterm delivery in a centre with blood bank, interventional radiology and gynaecological oncology support halves maternal morbidity (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline).

options.text: Plan a trial of vaginal birth given her previous successful vaginal delivery and absent bleeding
options.rationale: A placenta covering the internal os is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth irrespective of obstetric history or the absence of bleeding (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Guideline).

options.text: Plan a caesarean section here at 37 weeks with two units of cross matched blood available
options.rationale: This is the near pair to correct management but underestimates the requirement, since these cases can lose several litres and need a team, cell salvage and massive transfusion capability rather than two units (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline).

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum arises where a placenta implants over a uterine scar, so the risk climbs steeply with the number of previous caesareans in the presence of an anterior praevia. Sonographic markers include loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, bridging vessels, bladder wall interruption and thinning of the overlying myometrium, and several markers together make the diagnosis highly likely. Outcomes depend more on where and when delivery happens than on any intraoperative decision, which is why antenatal recognition and referral are the critical steps. Planned delivery is usually scheduled between 34 and 36 weeks to balance prematurity against the risk of unscheduled bleeding, with antenatal corticosteroids given beforehand.
key_points: Risk rises with the number of previous caesareans when the placenta is anterior and praevia
Loss of the clear zone, lacunae, bridging vessels and thin myometrium are the key sonographic markers
Planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks in a specialist centre with a multidisciplinary team
Placenta covering the internal os is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth
explanation.pearls: Ask about the number of previous caesareans at the morphology scan of every woman with an anterior low placenta; with three or more prior caesareans and a praevia, the risk of accreta spectrum exceeds 40 per cent and the scan should be re-reported with that question in mind.

subtopic_detail: Discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks and 4 days. Chorionicity was established at the 11 week scan by the T sign and a single placental mass.

She reports increasing abdominal tightness and breathlessness over ten days. Today's scan shows twin one with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm and a bladder that is not visualised over 40 minutes of observation, and twin two with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm and a full bladder. Both twins have normal umbilical artery Doppler waveforms with positive end diastolic flow and normal ductus venosus waveforms. Neither twin is hydropic and the estimated fetal weights differ by 14 per cent. Her cervical length is 34 mm and she is not contracting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with bladder not visualised; twin two deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with full bladder; umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers normal in both; cervical length 34 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks as part of the standard monochorionic surveillance schedule
options.rationale: Two weekly surveillance is for a normal monochorionic pregnancy, and a fortnight of observation once the sequence is established carries a very high risk of double fetal loss (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Urgent referral to a fetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
options.rationale: Deepest vertical pockets below 2 cm and above 8 cm in a monochorionic diamniotic pair with an absent bladder in the donor establish the diagnosis at stage two, where laser ablation of the placental anastomoses is the treatment that improves survival before 26 weeks (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac with repeat drainage as maternal symptoms recur
options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves maternal symptoms and reduces preterm labour risk but does not treat the underlying vascular anastomoses, and it gives worse survival and neurological outcomes than laser (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Delivery by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids has been completed
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is below the threshold of viability and would result in the loss of both twins, whereas intrauterine treatment offers a realistic chance of survival (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the co twin from injury
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for advanced disease with an unsalvageable twin or where laser is not feasible, and Dopplers here remain normal in both twins (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates about 10 to 15 per cent of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies through unbalanced flow across placental vascular anastomoses. Diagnosis requires monochorionicity plus discordant amniotic fluid, defined in Australian practice as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other, and growth discordance is neither necessary nor sufficient. The Quintero staging system runs from stage one, with discordant fluid alone, through absent donor bladder at stage two, abnormal Dopplers at stage three, hydrops at stage four and demise at stage five. Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation is the treatment of choice before 26 weeks because it addresses the anastomoses rather than the fluid, and it is why chorionicity must be established in the first trimester and surveillance run fortnightly from 16 weeks.
key_points: Diagnosis needs monochorionicity plus a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm and above 8 cm
An absent donor bladder defines Quintero stage two
Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation is first line before 26 weeks
Amnioreduction treats symptoms but not the underlying anastomoses
explanation.pearls: Growth discordance alone does not diagnose twin to twin transfusion syndrome; selective fetal growth restriction in a monochorionic pair has normal amniotic fluid in both sacs and is managed with Doppler surveillance rather than laser.

sources.label: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline
Australasian Society for Ultrasound in Medicine twin guidance
