Impaired detrusor contractility with a raised residual makes both antimuscarinic therapy and any obstructive procedure hazardous, so conservative management comes first and the residual is rechecked. Beta 3 agonists such as mirabegron are often preferred over antimuscarinics in this situation because they relax the detrusor during filling without impairing the voiding contraction to the same degree.
key_points: Treat the component of mixed incontinence that troubles the woman most
Voiding dysfunction is a firm indication for urodynamic testing
A raised post void residual makes antimuscarinics and slings hazardous
Conservative therapy with timed and double voiding precedes any procedure
Botulinum toxin requires willingness to perform intermittent self catheterisation
explanation.pearls: Mirabegron is the preferred pharmacological choice when detrusor contractility is impaired, but it must be avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and blood pressure should be checked before starting and after a month.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic threshold and feeding advice in a lactating woman with a red painful breast
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A woman who gave birth three weeks ago presents with a hot painful area in the upper outer part of her right breast that she first noticed 18 hours ago after a long stretch between feeds. She has been shivery and aching since last night.

She has been feeding from that side but says it hurts so much she has started to skip it. There is a firm wedge shaped area of redness and tenderness in the upper outer quadrant with no fluctuance and no discrete lump. The nipple has a shallow fissure. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy and the overlying skin is not peeling or blistered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema and induration in the right upper outer quadrant, no fluctuant collection, shallow nipple fissure, no axillary nodes
data_table.Investigations: Breast milk culture not routinely performed; ultrasound not yet arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease feeding from the affected breast and express and discard the milk for 48 hours
options.rationale: Stopping drainage is what allows a simple inflammation to progress to abscess, and the milk remains safe for the infant even when the mother is receiving antibiotics (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Prescribe oral di or flucloxacillin, continue feeding from that breast and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Symptoms beyond 12 to 24 hours with fever and a nipple fissure indicate bacterial infection rather than simple milk stasis, Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism, and continued drainage is part of the treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Advise frequent feeding and cold packs alone and review her again in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Conservative management alone is appropriate for the first 12 to 24 hours of symptoms without fever, and it is now beyond that window with rigors and a portal of entry (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Arrange a breast ultrasound today and withhold antibiotics until the result is available
options.rationale: Ultrasound is for suspected abscess, signalled by a fluctuant or discrete mass or by failure to improve after 48 hours of antibiotics, and deferring treatment for imaging now is unnecessary (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cabergoline to suppress lactation and change the infant to formula feeding
options.rationale: Lactation suppression is used when a woman has decided to wean or after infant loss, and using it here removes both the drainage and the feeding relationship unnecessarily (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis begins as inflammation from milk stasis, and only some cases progress to bacterial infection, which is why the first 12 to 24 hours of a red tender wedge without systemic upset are managed with effective drainage, cold packs and anti inflammatory analgesia. The features that shift the balance towards infection are persistence beyond that window, fever with rigors, and a cracked nipple providing a portal of entry for skin flora. Because Staphylococcus aureus predominates, an antistaphylococcal penicillin is first line and cefalexin or clindamycin is used in penicillin allergy. Continuing to feed or express from the affected side is not merely permitted but therapeutic, and the milk poses no risk to a healthy term infant.
key_points: Conservative management is appropriate only in the first 12 to 24 hours without systemic features
Fever with rigors and a nipple fissure indicate bacterial infection needing antibiotics
Di or flucloxacillin is first line, with cefalexin or clindamycin in penicillin allergy
Continue feeding or expressing from the affected breast throughout treatment
Failure to improve within 48 hours prompts ultrasound to look for an abscess
explanation.pearls: A woman whose mastitis has not improved after 48 hours of an appropriate antistaphylococcal penicillin needs a breast ultrasound the same day, since abscess is the reason for failure far more often than resistance.

subtopic_detail: Formulation and route of menopausal hormone therapy in a woman with migraine with aura and obesity
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 52 year old woman has not had a period for 16 months and has 12 or more hot flushes a day with drenching night sweats that wake her repeatedly. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol without benefit and says her work is suffering.

She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month, unchanged for years. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 128/78. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thromboembolism, and has no personal or family history of breast cancer. Her cervical screening and mammogram are both up to date and normal. She asks specifically for something that will stop the flushes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, no breast masses, normal abdominal and pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus 8 months ago; mammogram normal 5 months ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen with continuous oral medroxyprogesterone acetate
options.rationale: An oral oestrogen passes through the liver and raises venous thromboembolism risk, which is the specific hazard being avoided in a woman with obesity and aura (Source: Australasian Menopause Society; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated by migraine with aura at any age because of the ischaemic stroke risk, and it delivers far more oestrogen than symptom control requires (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Oral venlafaxine titrated for vasomotor symptoms with review of the response in eight weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the option when hormone therapy is contraindicated or declined, and it is less effective than oestrogen for flushes of this severity (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch with continuous oral micronised progesterone at night
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass hepatic metabolism so it does not raise thromboembolic risk, migraine with aura does not contraindicate it, and an intact uterus requires progestogen for endometrial protection (Source: Australasian Menopause Society; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch alone with an endometrial ultrasound every twelve months
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, and surveillance scanning does not substitute for the progestogen that prevents it (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, and the modern discussion is about route and formulation rather than whether to offer it at all. Transdermal oestradiol bypasses hepatic first pass metabolism, so unlike oral oestrogen it does not increase venous thromboembolism or stroke risk, which makes it the preferred route in women with obesity, migraine with aura, or other thrombotic risk factors. Any woman with an intact uterus needs a progestogen, and micronised progesterone is favoured over older synthetic progestogens because of a more favourable breast and cardiovascular profile. Migraine with aura contraindicates combined hormonal contraception because of the ethinylestradiol dose, but it does not contraindicate physiological transdermal oestradiol replacement.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol does not raise venous thromboembolism risk whereas oral oestrogen does
Migraine with aura contraindicates combined contraception but not transdermal replacement
An intact uterus always requires progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen for its breast and metabolic profile
Non hormonal options such as venlafaxine are second line when hormone therapy is unsuitable
explanation.pearls: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device provides endometrial protection alongside transdermal oestradiol and is the practical choice when a woman also wants contraception in the perimenopause.

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception method choice at the outer limit of the window with a high body mass index
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman who had unprotected intercourse 96 hours ago. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and today is day 13. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2.

She says she does not want to be pregnant and would also like ongoing contraception she does not have to think about. She has no allergies, takes no regular medications and has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, soft non tender abdomen, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus anteverted and normal size
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate option to recommend?

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device today and treat presumptively if the swabs return positive
options.rationale: The copper device is effective up to five days after intercourse and is unaffected by body weight, and it simultaneously provides the long acting method she wants (Source: Family Planning Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now and start a combined oral contraceptive tomorrow
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only to 72 hours and its efficacy falls further with a body mass index above 26, so it is the weakest option in this specific situation (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Give oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and arrange an etonogestrel implant next week
options.rationale: Ulipristal does work to 120 hours but is less reliable at higher body weight than a copper device, and a progestogen started soon afterwards reduces its effect (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today and repeat a pregnancy test in three weeks
options.rationale: The hormonal device is excellent ongoing contraception but does not reliably prevent implantation after intercourse has already occurred, which is what the copper device does (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Advise that the window has closed and arrange a pregnancy test in two weeks instead
options.rationale: The window for both ulipristal and the copper device extends to five days after intercourse, so emergency contraception is still available at 96 hours (Source: Family Planning Australia).

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception has three options in Australia and they differ in both time window and the effect of body weight. Levonorgestrel is licensed to 72 hours and loses efficacy above a body mass index of about 26, ulipristal acetate extends to 120 hours and performs better but is also weight sensitive, and the copper intrauterine device works to 120 hours with a failure rate under 1 per cent that is independent of weight. Where a woman also wants long acting contraception the copper device answers both questions in one visit, which is why it is the preferred recommendation when insertion is available. Pending sexually transmitted infection results do not delay insertion in an asymptomatic woman, since treatment can be given if the swabs return positive.
key_points: Copper intrauterine device is the most effective emergency method and works to 120 hours
Levonorgestrel is limited to 72 hours and loses efficacy with rising body mass index
Ulipristal extends to 120 hours but progestogen started soon afterwards reduces its effect
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device is not an emergency contraceptive
Asymptomatic pending swabs do not contraindicate same day insertion
explanation.pearls: If ulipristal acetate is used, wait five days before starting or restarting a progestogen containing method, because the progestogen competes at the receptor and undermines the ulipristal effect.

subtopic_detail: Perineal assessment after an apparently second degree tear and the consequence of understaging
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite after a spontaneous vaginal birth. A woman in her first pregnancy has just given birth to a 4100 g baby after a 40 minute second stage with a rotational forceps delivery. The midwife reports a tear she has graded as second degree and asks you to repair it in the room.

The perineal skin and the bulbospongiosus and transverse perineal muscles are torn. On systematic rectal examination with a finger in the anal canal and a thumb on the perineum, you can feel a gap in the fibres of the external sphincter over about a third of its circumference, and the internal sphincter is intact. There is no buttonhole into the rectal mucosa. Estimated blood loss is 350 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Perineal body torn, partial defect of the external anal sphincter over less than half its thickness, internal anal sphincter and anorectal mucosa intact
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); estimated blood loss 350 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repair the perineal muscles and skin in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration
options.rationale: Repairing this as a second degree tear leaves the sphincter defect unopposed, and unrecognised sphincter injury is a leading cause of later faecal incontinence (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Pack the perineum, start intravenous antibiotics and plan a delayed repair in six weeks
options.rationale: Delayed repair is reserved for injuries recognised late or with gross contamination, and primary repair at the time of birth gives substantially better continence outcomes (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Transfer to theatre for repair by an experienced operator under regional or general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A partial external sphincter defect is a third degree tear, and outcomes depend on repair in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, lighting and assistance by an operator trained in sphincter repair (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Arrange an endoanal ultrasound scan in the ward before deciding on the mode of repair
options.rationale: Endoanal ultrasound has a role in later assessment of persisting symptoms, but the defect is already palpable and imaging only delays the primary repair (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Repair the tear in the birth suite and arrange colorectal review before she is discharged
options.rationale: Deferring the sphincter to a later specialist opinion accepts a suboptimal primary repair, which is the step that most determines long term continence (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is understaged when the perineum is inspected without a systematic rectal examination, and understaging is the single commonest reason a woman ends up with faecal incontinence after childbirth. The classification runs from 3a, less than half the external sphincter thickness, through 3b, more than half, to 3c, which involves the internal sphincter, and fourth degree, which breaches the anorectal mucosa. Risk factors are first vaginal birth, instrumental birth particularly with forceps, birthweight above 4 kg, prolonged second stage and occipitoposterior position. Repair belongs in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia so the sphincter ends can be identified and apposed, followed by broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining on the repair, and physiotherapy with structured follow up.
key_points: Perform a rectal examination on every woman after vaginal birth before grading a tear
A partial external sphincter defect is 3a and a defect beyond half its thickness is 3b
Primary repair in theatre by a trained operator gives the best continence outcome
Instrumental birth, birthweight over 4 kg and first vaginal birth are the main risks
Postoperative care includes antibiotics, laxatives and pelvic floor physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Prescribe a stool softener such as lactulose rather than a bulking agent after sphincter repair, since a bulky stool passing over a fresh repair is a recognised cause of early breakdown.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic confirmation before labelling ovarian insufficiency in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in clinic. A 34 year old woman has had no periods for seven months after a lifetime of regular cycles. She has hot flushes at night and says intercourse has become uncomfortable. She and her partner had been planning a pregnancy this year.

She has never been pregnant, uses no hormonal contraception and stopped none recently. She has had no chemotherapy, radiotherapy or pelvic surgery. Her weight is stable, she exercises moderately and there is no excessive exercise or dietary restriction. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Blood taken three weeks ago showed follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2 to 10 in the follicular phase), oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110 to 400) and normal thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin. She asks whether this means she is in menopause.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism or acanthosis, atrophic vaginal appearance, normal sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2-10 follicular); oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110-400); thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin within normal limits; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her symptoms again in three months
options.rationale: Hormone replacement is needed eventually to protect bone and cardiovascular health, but starting it before the diagnostic samples are complete removes the ability to confirm the diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and measure anti Mullerian hormone
options.rationale: Antral follicle count and anti Mullerian hormone estimate ovarian reserve for fertility planning but neither is a diagnostic criterion for this condition (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Refer directly to a fertility service for donor oocyte counselling and treatment planning
options.rationale: Donor oocyte counselling becomes relevant once the diagnosis is confirmed, and spontaneous ovulation still occurs intermittently in this condition so the diagnosis must be secure first (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Perform a progestogen withdrawal challenge and assess whether she has a withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: A withdrawal bleed distinguishes outflow tract obstruction from anovulation, a question already answered by a high follicle stimulating hormone with a low oestradiol (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Repeat the follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol at least four weeks apart to confirm
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires amenorrhoea for at least four months plus two raised follicle stimulating hormone results taken at least four weeks apart, because a single elevated value can reflect a transient rise (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is loss of ovarian function before the age of 40 and is diagnosed on amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for at least four months together with two follicle stimulating hormone measurements in the menopausal range taken at least four weeks apart. The requirement for two samples exists because fluctuating gonadotrophins are common and a single high value can be transient, and the label carries lifelong consequences for bone density, cardiovascular risk and fertility. Once confirmed, the aetiological workup includes a karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and adrenal and thyroid autoantibodies, since Turner mosaicism, the FMR1 premutation and autoimmune polyglandular disease are all recognised causes. Hormone replacement is then continued until the average age of natural menopause rather than being viewed as optional symptom relief, and spontaneous conception remains possible in a small proportion so contraception must be discussed if pregnancy is not wanted.
key_points: Diagnosis needs two raised follicle stimulating hormone results at least four weeks apart
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for at least four months is the other criterion
Confirmed cases need karyotype, fragile X premutation and autoantibody testing
Hormone replacement continues to about age 51 for bone and cardiovascular protection
Intermittent ovulation persists so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is unwanted
explanation.pearls: Around 5 to 10 per cent of women with confirmed premature ovarian insufficiency conceive spontaneously, so the diagnosis is never given as a statement that pregnancy is impossible.

subtopic_detail: White atrophic vulval plaques with architectural change and the role of biopsy alongside treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman referred with two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has been given three courses of topical antifungal cream and a low potency hydrocortisone ointment by different doctors with no lasting benefit, and says intercourse has become painful at the entrance.

The labia minora are partly resorbed into the labia majora and the clitoral hood is fused over the clitoris. There are ivory white thickened plaques extending around the vulva and perianal skin in a figure of eight, with two small areas of purpura but no ulcer, nodule or fixed thickening. The vaginal mucosa itself is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: White sclerotic plaques over labia and perianal skin, loss of labia minora, clitoral hood fusion, purpura, no ulcer or nodule, normal vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab for candida negative; no biopsy performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a potent topical corticosteroid ointment with long term maintenance and review
options.rationale: An ultrapotent or potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for this sclerosing dermatosis, and continued maintenance rather than a short burst is what controls symptoms and reduces later scarring and malignancy (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Prescribe a further course of topical antifungal cream and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Repeating an antifungal after a negative swab and three failed courses treats the wrong diagnosis, and architectural loss is not a feature of candidal vulvitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly and review the vulval appearance in three months
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary atrophy of menopause, whose distinguishing feature is a pale thin vaginal mucosa rather than white plaques on keratinised vulval and perianal skin (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

options.text: Arrange a vulval punch biopsy first and withhold all treatment until the histology returns
options.rationale: Biopsy is mandatory for an ulcer, nodule, fixed thickening or failure to respond, but the appearance here is characteristic and withholding treatment leaves her symptomatic for weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and resurfacing of the vulval skin
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for the functional consequences of scarring or for proven malignancy, and operating on active inflamed skin risks recurrence at the incision (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Dermatoses).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis of the anogenital skin that classically produces intense nocturnal itch, ivory white sclerotic plaques in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus, purpura from fragile skin, and progressive architectural loss with resorption of the labia minora and burial of the clitoris. It is frequently mistaken for candidiasis or atrophy and treated with antifungals or oestrogen for years before the diagnosis is made. Treatment is a potent or ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, initially daily and then reduced to a maintenance frequency that is continued indefinitely, because ongoing control reduces both scarring and the risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Around 4 to 5 per cent of affected women develop that malignancy, so any ulcer, nodule, fixed area or lesion that fails to respond to adequate steroid must be biopsied.
key_points: Nocturnal itch with white plaques and loss of labia minora is the defining picture
The distribution is a figure of eight around vulva and anus with sparing of the vagina
Potent topical corticosteroid with long term maintenance is the standard treatment
Biopsy any ulcer, nodule, fixed thickening or steroid unresponsive area
Lifelong surveillance is needed because of the squamous cell carcinoma risk
explanation.pearls: Sparing of the vaginal mucosa separates lichen sclerosus from erosive lichen planus, which involves the vagina and can cause vaginal stenosis, and that single examination finding changes both treatment intensity and prognosis.

subtopic_detail: Imaging and first line treatment choice in heavy menstrual bleeding with a diffusely enlarged uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 42 year old woman describes eight years of increasingly heavy periods that now flood through a pad hourly on the worst two days, with deep cramping pain that starts three days before bleeding and continues throughout. Her family is complete and she does not want surgery if it can be avoided.

On examination the uterus is smoothly enlarged to about 12 weeks size, is tender on bimanual palpation and is mobile with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally bulky uterus with asymmetric myometrial thickening, indistinct border between endometrium and myometrium and small myometrial cysts, and no discrete mass. The endometrium is 6 mm and regular. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-165) and her ferritin is 8 mcg/L (15-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Smoothly enlarged tender mobile uterus of about 12 weeks size, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound as described; endometrial thickness 6 mm; haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 mcg/L (15-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and start oral iron replacement at the same time
options.rationale: Embolisation is an established option for fibroids and is used selectively for diffuse myometrial disease, but it is not the first line treatment when a reversible medical option has not been tried (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Perform hysteroscopy with endometrial resection and start oral iron replacement afterwards
options.rationale: Endometrial ablation targets the endometrium, whereas the pathology here lies within the myometrium, so failure rates and later hysterectomy are high in this group (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device and treat the iron deficiency with oral iron
options.rationale: The ultrasound pattern of a bulky uterus with indistinct junctional zone and myometrial cysts indicates adenomyosis, for which a levonorgestrel intrauterine device is the first line uterus conserving treatment and also addresses the dysmenorrhoea (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange endometrial pipelle sampling and defer any treatment until the histology is available
options.rationale: Sampling is indicated for a thickened or irregular endometrium or for persistent bleeding after treatment failure, and a regular 6 mm endometrium in a premenopausal woman does not require it before starting therapy (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid on bleeding days only and review her haemoglobin in six months
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by around a third but does not treat the associated pain or the underlying myometrial disease, so it is a partial answer for a woman with this symptom burden (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding with a bulky uterus is commonly assumed to be fibroids, but adenomyosis produces a different ultrasound signature and responds to different treatment. The features that separate them are a globally enlarged tender uterus with asymmetric myometrial thickening, loss of a crisp junctional zone and small myometrial cysts, as against a discrete well demarcated mass with a peripheral vascular rim in a fibroid. The distinction matters because endometrial ablation performs poorly in adenomyosis, since the disease sits deep in the myometrium rather than at the surface. A levonorgestrel intrauterine device is the first line uterus conserving treatment because it addresses both the bleeding and the dysmenorrhoea, and correcting the iron deficiency is a necessary parallel step rather than an alternative.
key_points: A tender globally bulky uterus with an indistinct junctional zone suggests adenomyosis
A discrete demarcated myometrial mass with a peripheral rim suggests a fibroid
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device is first line for uterus conserving treatment
Endometrial ablation has high failure rates when the disease is myometrial
Always treat the coexisting iron deficiency, not just the bleeding
explanation.pearls: Magnetic resonance imaging showing a junctional zone thickness above 12 mm supports adenomyosis when the ultrasound is equivocal, and it is the investigation to request before committing a woman to hysterectomy.

subtopic_detail: Acute painful vulval swelling and the drainage technique that reduces recurrence
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department. A 27 year old woman presents with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down or walk comfortably and has not been able to sleep.

She is not pregnant, has no urinary symptoms and has had no previous similar episode. On examination there is a tense fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across in the posterior part of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus. The overlying skin is thin and shiny but the surrounding vulval and perineal skin is not indurated or discoloured, and there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling in the posterior right labium majus distorting the introitus, thin shiny overlying skin, no surrounding induration or crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incise and drain under local anaesthetic and insert a Word catheter
options.rationale: Drainage relieves the pain immediately, and leaving a balloon catheter in place for several weeks allows a lined tract to epithelialise, which is what lowers the recurrence rate compared with simple incision (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin and metronidazole with twice daily warm baths
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not decompress a walled off collection, and they are added to drainage only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic upset or immunosuppression (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Aspirate the swelling with a wide bore needle and send fluid for culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration empties the cavity but leaves no drainage tract, and the collection reaccumulates in a high proportion of women within weeks (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next elective gynaecology list
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for repeatedly recurrent disease because it carries bleeding, scarring and dyspareunia risks, and it does not address tonight's pain (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Refer for biopsy of the swelling to exclude an underlying malignancy
options.rationale: Biopsy at the time of drainage belongs to women over 40 or with a solid irregular mass, and an acutely fluctuant tender swelling in a woman of 27 does not meet that threshold (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the duct of the greater vestibular gland produces a cyst that becomes an abscess when it is infected, and the organisms are usually mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than a sexually transmitted pathogen. The therapeutic goal is not just to empty the cavity but to create a durable drainage tract, which is why a balloon tipped catheter or marsupialisation outperforms simple incision or aspiration. Antibiotics are an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression. Age is the other decision point, because a vulval mass in a woman over 40 should prompt biopsy to exclude carcinoma of the gland.
key_points: Drainage plus a maintained tract is what prevents recurrence
A Word catheter is left in place for two to four weeks
Antibiotics are adjunctive, not a substitute for drainage
Simple incision or needle aspiration alone recurs frequently
Biopsy a vulval mass in a woman over 40 at the time of drainage
explanation.pearls: A Word catheter is left in for two to four weeks to epithelialise the tract, and removing it at the first review a week later is the common error that returns the woman to the emergency department.

subtopic_detail: Household varicella exposure in a seronegative woman in the second trimester
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic doctor. A 29 year old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy telephones because her 4 year old daughter developed a widespread blistering rash two days ago and the general practitioner has diagnosed chickenpox. They share a bedroom while her partner works away.

She has never had chickenpox herself and has not been vaccinated. Her booking bloods, taken at 9 weeks, recorded varicella zoster immunoglobulin G as not detected. She feels completely well today, has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms, and her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with a normal first trimester ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No rash on skin survey, chest clear, uterus palpable just below the umbilicus
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected; rubella immunoglobulin G immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the live attenuated varicella vaccine and repeat serology in six weeks
options.rationale: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, and vaccination is instead offered in the postpartum period before discharge (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir now and continue it until 21 days after exposure
options.rationale: Antiviral treatment is given if she develops the rash, and post exposure antiviral prophylaxis is a second line option only when immunoglobulin is unavailable or the window has closed (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin today and advise on warning symptoms
options.rationale: A seronegative pregnant woman with significant household contact should receive zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and within 96 hours where practicable, which both attenuates maternal disease and reduces the risk to the fetus (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Repeat varicella immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result next week
options.rationale: Serology has already been documented as negative in this pregnancy, and waiting for a repeat result consumes the narrow window in which immunoglobulin still works (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Reassure that the risk period has passed and review only if a rash appears
options.rationale: Congenital varicella syndrome risk extends across the first and second trimesters rather than ending at 12 weeks, so 16 weeks is still within the period of concern (Source: RANZCOG Infection in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy carries two separate risks: severe maternal disease with pneumonitis, which is markedly more common in adults than children, and fetal infection. Congenital varicella syndrome complicates a small percentage of maternal infections occurring up to about 28 weeks, with the highest risk between 13 and 20 weeks. Zoster immunoglobulin given promptly after exposure to a seronegative woman attenuates maternal illness and is the intervention of choice, while aciclovir is used for treatment once a rash appears. Infection in the week before to the week after delivery is the separate neonatal emergency requiring immunoglobulin for the baby.
key_points: Check varicella serology at booking in women with no history of infection or vaccination
Zoster immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible after significant exposure
Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and given postpartum
Fetal risk continues into the second trimester rather than ending at 12 weeks
Maternal pneumonitis is the leading cause of severe maternal illness
explanation.pearls: Zoster immunoglobulin works best within 96 hours of exposure and can still be given up to 10 days, so the woman who telephones on day four is offered it that day rather than told she has missed the window.

subtopic_detail: Viral load threshold for antiviral prophylaxis to prevent perinatal hepatitis B transmission
stem:
You are the doctor in a hospital antenatal clinic reviewing a 31 year old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her booking bloods showed hepatitis B surface antigen positive, and she has known about her infection since a screening test in her teens but has never needed treatment.

She feels well, has no jaundice or abdominal pain, and takes no medication. Her liver is not enlarged and there are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Her partner and her mother are both hepatitis B surface antigen positive. Fetal growth and liquor volume were normal on the morphology scan.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive; hepatitis B e antigen positive; hepatitis B virus DNA 3.2 x10^7 IU/mL; alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 35); bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20); platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no ascites or spider naevi

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to reduce transmission to her baby?

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce transmission
options.rationale: Mode of delivery does not reliably alter perinatal hepatitis B transmission, unlike the situation with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Rely on neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine at birth without an antiviral
options.rationale: Immunoprophylaxis is given to every exposed newborn but still fails in up to one in ten babies of women with very high viral loads, which is the gap maternal antiviral therapy closes (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start entecavir now and stop it at the onset of established labour
options.rationale: Entecavir lacks the pregnancy safety data of tenofovir and is not the agent chosen in this setting, and stopping at delivery risks a postpartum hepatitis flare (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Advise formula feeding from birth to reduce the risk of transmission
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is not a route of concern once the infant has received immunoglobulin and vaccine, and advising against it removes a benefit for no gain (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start tenofovir disoproxil at 28 weeks and continue it after delivery
options.rationale: A maternal viral load above 200,000 IU/mL is the threshold for antiviral prophylaxis from about 28 to 32 weeks, and tenofovir is the agent with the best pregnancy safety data with monitoring for a flare after cessation (Source: ASHM Hepatitis B in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Perinatal transmission is the dominant route of chronic hepatitis B acquisition worldwide, and the risk tracks with maternal viral load rather than with symptoms or liver enzymes. Every infant born to a surface antigen positive woman receives hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth dose of vaccine within 12 hours, followed by the routine schedule and serological testing at nine months. Immunoprophylaxis alone fails in a meaningful proportion of babies when the maternal load is very high, so maternal antiviral therapy in the third trimester is added above the accepted threshold. The mother also needs ongoing hepatology follow up, since postpartum flares are common in the months after delivery.
key_points: Transmission risk is driven by maternal viral load, not by liver enzymes
Antiviral prophylaxis is indicated above 200,000 IU/mL
Tenofovir disoproxil is the preferred agent in pregnancy
Every exposed newborn gets immunoglobulin plus vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Test the infant serologically at nine months to confirm protection
explanation.pearls: Alanine aminotransferase can be entirely normal in a woman with a viral load above 10 million IU/mL, so the decision to start tenofovir at 28 weeks rests on the hepatitis B virus DNA result and not on liver function tests.

subtopic_detail: Counselling and timing at 41 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 30 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 41 weeks and 0 days. Her dates were confirmed by a crown rump length measurement at 9 weeks.

The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, with normal growth on clinical assessment and normal fetal movements reported today. The fetus is cephalic with the head engaged, the cardiotocograph is normal, and vaginal examination gives a Bishop score of 4. She tells you she has been reading about induction and would prefer to wait for labour to start by itself, and she asks what you would do in her position.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 39 cm, cephalic presentation with the head engaged, cervix 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, mid position, soft, station minus 2
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 140 and moderate variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Arrange twice weekly cardiotocography and fluid assessment until 42+6
options.rationale: Surveillance beyond 42 weeks does not prevent the rise in stillbirth and neonatal morbidity that accrues in that fortnight, and Australian practice offers birth before then (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Offer a membrane sweep today and book induction before 42+0 weeks
options.rationale: Sweeping the membranes increases the chance of spontaneous labour and reduces the need for formal induction, and booking birth before 42 weeks respects both her preference and the rising perinatal risk (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Admit her today for prostaglandin induction whatever her preference is
options.rationale: Induction at 41 weeks and 0 days is offered rather than imposed, and overriding an informed preference when there are several days of safe window is not justified (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean section given the unfavourable cervix
options.rationale: A Bishop score of 4 predicts a longer induction rather than a failed one, and caesarean without an obstetric indication exposes her to surgical risk in this and later pregnancies (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

options.text: Review her in one week and reassess only if she has not laboured then
options.rationale: Deferring the conversation to 42 weeks removes the option of a planned induction within the recommended window and leaves her without fetal surveillance in the interval (Source: RANZCOG Prolonged Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Perinatal mortality begins to climb from about 41 weeks and rises more steeply beyond 42 weeks, which is why Australian guidance offers induction between 41 and 42 weeks rather than waiting indefinitely. The counselling should present the absolute rather than the relative risk, since the numbers are small and the woman is entitled to weigh them. Membrane sweeping is a low cost intervention that brings forward spontaneous labour and reduces the proportion of women who need formal induction. If a woman declines induction after full discussion, the fallback is increased surveillance with a documented plan and a date for review rather than discharge from the pathway.
key_points: Induction is offered between 41 and 42 weeks in uncomplicated pregnancy
Membrane sweeping reduces the need for formal induction
A Bishop score below 6 predicts a longer induction, not a failed one
Present absolute risk figures when counselling about prolonged pregnancy
Document a surveillance plan if induction is declined
explanation.pearls: Stillbirth risk approximately doubles between 41 and 42 completed weeks even though it remains low in absolute terms, and quoting that as events per thousand rather than as a doubling is what allows a genuine choice.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Induction of Labour

subtopic_detail: Storage symptoms in a midlife woman and the sequence of conservative and drug treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54 year old woman who has been rushing to the toilet for the past eight months and has twice not made it in time. She passes urine about ten times a day and wakes twice at night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She drinks four cups of coffee and two cups of tea daily and has cut her water intake right down to try to control the problem. Her last period was three years ago and she takes no medication. Pelvic examination shows well oestrogenised vaginal skin with no prolapse beyond the hymen and a good pelvic floor contraction, and her post void residual measured on bladder scan is 30 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No prolapse beyond the hymen, no leakage on cough with a full bladder, good voluntary pelvic floor contraction, post void residual 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy and culture no growth; fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); bladder diary shows 10 daytime voids and 2 nocturnal voids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy follows a trial of conservative measures, and oxybutynin in particular carries the highest anticholinergic burden of the class with dry mouth, constipation and cognitive effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology; RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Refer for a mid urethral sling procedure on the gynaecology waiting list
options.rationale: A sling supports the urethra during rises in abdominal pressure and treats stress leakage, and she does not leak on coughing or lifting (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before deciding on any further treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for mixed or unclear pictures, previous surgery or planned surgery, and it does not change management in a woman with clear storage symptoms and a normal residual (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week for three months
options.rationale: Local oestrogen helps when there is genitourinary atrophy contributing to urgency, and her vaginal skin is well oestrogenised on examination (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence).

options.text: Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and normalised fluid intake
options.rationale: Bladder retraining with timed voiding, urge suppression, reduction of caffeine and correction of fluid restriction is the recommended first step for storage symptoms and cures or improves a large proportion of women before any drug is needed (Source: RANZCOG Urinary Incontinence; Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology).

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder is a symptom diagnosis of urgency with or without urgency incontinence, usually with frequency and nocturia, once infection, glycosuria and incomplete emptying have been excluded. The bladder diary does most of the diagnostic work and also reveals the two self imposed aggravators seen here: heavy caffeine intake and paradoxical fluid restriction, which concentrates urine and worsens urgency. Conservative treatment over six to twelve weeks is effective and free of adverse effects, so it precedes drug therapy. When medication is needed, a beta 3 agonist or a more selective antimuscarinic is preferred over oxybutynin, particularly in older women where anticholinergic load matters.
key_points: Exclude infection, diabetes and incomplete emptying before labelling storage symptoms
A three day bladder diary guides both diagnosis and behavioural treatment
Fluid restriction concentrates urine and worsens urgency
Bladder training precedes drug therapy and works in a large proportion of women
Oxybutynin carries the highest anticholinergic burden of the class
explanation.pearls: Caffeine above about 200 mg daily measurably worsens urgency, so cutting six caffeinated drinks to two while restoring normal water intake is a specific instruction that outperforms a vague advice to drink less.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding with a focal endometrial abnormality on transvaginal ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic. A 58 year old woman was referred after two episodes of light vaginal bleeding, six years after her last period. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and has a body mass index of 34 kg per square metre.

Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and no blood in the vault today. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a discrete echogenic lesion 14 mm across within the cavity, which has a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, and normal ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, mobile non tender uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness 11 mm with a 14 mm intracavity echogenic lesion and a single feeding vessel, normal ovaries, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and removal of the lesion
options.rationale: A focal lesion needs to be seen and removed under direct vision, because a blind sampling device can pass alongside a polyp and return a reassuring result while the abnormal tissue remains in the cavity (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Perform an office endometrial pipelle biopsy and act on the histology
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling performs well for diffuse endometrial disease but samples only a fraction of the cavity, so it is the wrong instrument once a focal lesion has been demonstrated (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Reassure her and repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months
options.rationale: Repeat imaging without tissue would be defensible only with a thin regular endometrium under 4 mm and no focal lesion, which is not what this scan shows (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and arrange computed tomography of the abdomen
options.rationale: Tumour markers and cross sectional imaging belong to the staging of a proven cancer or the assessment of an adnexal mass, and her ovaries are normal (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Start cyclical oral progestogen and review her bleeding in three months
options.rationale: Progestogen treats confirmed hyperplasia without atypia after tissue diagnosis, and giving it first masks bleeding while leaving a possible carcinoma undiagnosed (Source: RANZCOG Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma, and the assessment is structured around the ultrasound. A uniformly thin endometrium at or below 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and can justify observation for a single episode, while a thickened or focally abnormal endometrium requires tissue. The instrument is chosen by the pattern: blind sampling for diffuse thickening, hysteroscopy for a focal lesion. Obesity is the dominant modifiable risk factor through peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen, and recurrent bleeding after a negative sample always warrants re-evaluation rather than reassurance.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries about a 10 per cent risk of endometrial cancer
An endometrial thickness at or below 4 mm has high negative predictive value
Focal lesions require hysteroscopic assessment rather than blind sampling
Obesity raises endometrial cancer risk through peripheral oestrogen production
Recurrent bleeding after a benign sample needs repeat assessment
explanation.pearls: A blind pipelle misses a meaningful proportion of focal lesions such as polyps and localised carcinoma, so a benign pipelle result in a woman whose scan showed a discrete intracavity lesion does not close the episode.

subtopic_detail: Severe oligozoospermia on a first semen analysis and the workup it triggers
stem:
You are the doctor in a fertility clinic seeing a couple who have been trying to conceive for 14 months with intercourse every two to three days. The woman is 29 with regular 29 day cycles, a normal pelvic ultrasound, an anti-Mullerian hormone in the expected range for her age, and patent tubes on hysterosalpingogram.

Her 32 year old partner has fathered no previous pregnancies. He is well, takes no medication and does not use anabolic steroids. His testes are of normal volume with no varicocele and both vasa are palpable. His first semen analysis, produced after three days of abstinence, is shown below and he has not previously had one.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal secondary sexual characteristics, testicular volume 18 mL bilaterally, both vasa palpable, no varicocele
data_table.Investigations: Semen volume 2.8 mL; sperm concentration 4 x10^6 per mL; progressive motility 20 per cent; normal morphology 2 per cent; no antisperm antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to intrauterine insemination in her next ovulatory cycle now
options.rationale: Insemination depends on an adequate total motile count after preparation, and success rates fall away at the concentration seen here (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Repeat the analysis in three months with testosterone, FSH and LH levels
options.rationale: A single abnormal result is confirmed on a repeat sample after a full spermatogenic cycle of about 72 days, and a concentration this low triggers endocrine assessment to separate primary testicular failure from a hypothalamic pituitary cause (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand; RACGP Male Infertility).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Refer directly for intracytoplasmic sperm injection using this sample
options.rationale: Injection is likely to be needed eventually, but committing before confirmation skips the karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing that changes counselling about a son inheriting the defect (Source: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Prescribe clomifene for him and reassess his semen in three months time
options.rationale: Off label clomifene is used in selected men with proven hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, so it cannot be chosen before the gonadotropins have been measured (Source: RACGP Male Infertility).

options.text: Advise another 12 months of timed intercourse before further assessment
options.rationale: Investigation is indicated after 12 months of unprotected intercourse, and this couple has already crossed that threshold with a demonstrated abnormality (Source: RACGP Male Infertility).

explanation.summary: A male factor contributes to about half of couples presenting with infertility, and semen analysis is the single most informative test, but it is also biologically variable between samples. Because spermatogenesis takes approximately 72 days, a repeat sample is taken after an interval that reflects a full cycle rather than a fortnight later. A concentration below 5 million per mL is the accepted threshold for karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing, since chromosomal causes are found in a meaningful minority and are transmissible to male offspring through injection techniques. Gonadotropins and testosterone separate primary testicular failure, which shows a high follicle stimulating hormone, from the rarer treatable central causes.
key_points: Confirm an abnormal semen analysis on a repeat sample after about three months
A raised follicle stimulating hormone points to primary testicular failure
Concentration below 5 million per mL prompts karyotype and Y microdeletion testing
Intrauterine insemination depends on the total motile count after preparation
Genetic results change counselling before intracytoplasmic sperm injection
explanation.pearls: Spermatogenesis takes about 72 days, so a repeat semen analysis is scheduled at three months rather than at three weeks, and a febrile illness in the preceding two months is enough to explain a transiently poor result.

sources.label: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea and a uterus present on imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period, and for the last eight months has had lower abdominal pain that lasts three or four days and comes at roughly monthly intervals.

Her breast development and pubic hair are fully developed and her growth has followed the 50th centile. She has no cyclical nasal or urinary symptoms. On examination her abdomen is soft with a tender suprapubic mass palpable two finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. Inspection of the introitus shows a normal hymenal opening with no bulging blue membrane, and a gentle cotton bud examination meets a smooth blind end after about 3 cm. Ultrasound reports a uterus containing echogenic fluid, both ovaries normal, and both kidneys present.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, tender suprapubic mass, normal hymenal opening, vagina ending blindly at about 3 cm
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus distended with echogenic fluid, normal ovaries and two normal kidneys

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Incise the membrane at the introitus under local anaesthetic in clinic
options.rationale: A simple incision drains an imperforate hymen, which presents with a bulging blue membrane at a normal introitus, and blind incision of a higher obstruction risks injury to bladder and rectum (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea; RCH CPG: Gynaecology).

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any further imaging
options.rationale: Androgen insensitivity is characterised by absent or sparse pubic hair with no uterus, and a uterus filled with menstrual blood excludes it (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

options.text: Start a continuous combined oral contraceptive to suppress her cycles
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression relieves the pain temporarily but leaves obstructed blood in the uterus and tubes, with retrograde spill and endometriosis as the consequence (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

options.text: Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and refer to a specialist unit
options.rationale: With a uterus present and a blind ending vagina the obstruction lies above the hymen, and imaging is needed to define the level, thickness and any associated anomaly before a single definitive operation is planned (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea; RCH CPG: Gynaecology).

options.text: Book diagnostic laparoscopy to inspect the pelvis and drain the uterus
options.rationale: Laparoscopy assesses the peritoneal cavity but does not define the vaginal anatomy that determines the surgical approach, and it is not the first investigation (Source: RANZCOG Amenorrhoea).

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and cyclical pain points to an outflow obstruction rather than to an endocrine cause, because the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis is clearly working. The examination separates the two levels: a bulging blue membrane at a normal introitus is an imperforate hymen, while a normal hymen with a short blind ending vagina indicates a transverse septum or vaginal agenesis higher up. Magnetic resonance imaging defines the thickness of the obstructing segment and the length of the upper vagina, both of which dictate the operation and the likelihood of needing graft reconstruction. These procedures belong in a unit with paediatric and adolescent gynaecology experience, because a poorly planned first operation creates stenosis that is difficult to salvage.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain suggests obstruction, not endocrine failure
A bulging blue membrane means imperforate hymen and simple incision
A normal hymen with a blind vagina means a higher obstruction needing imaging
A uterus present on imaging excludes androgen insensitivity
Renal tract anomalies commonly accompany Mullerian anomalies
explanation.pearls: A transverse vaginal septum thicker than about 1 cm on magnetic resonance imaging predicts the need for graft or flap reconstruction rather than simple excision, which is why the scan precedes the knife.

subtopic_detail: Median nerve symptoms in the third trimester with motor signs
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 33 year old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy who has had pins and needles in both hands for six weeks. It began at night and woke her, and she used to relieve it by hanging her hand out of the bed.

For the past fortnight the numbness in the right thumb, index and middle fingers has been constant rather than intermittent, and she has dropped her cup twice and cannot fasten her bra. Her blood pressure is 110/70 with no proteinuria and her ankles are only mildly swollen. On the right, thumb abduction is weak against resistance and there is early flattening of the thenar eminence. Sensation over the thenar skin itself is preserved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over the right thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar skin, weak thumb abduction, early thenar wasting, symmetrical reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick no protein; thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit night wrist splints and reassure her that it settles after delivery
options.rationale: Splinting with reassurance is right while symptoms are sensory and intermittent, but established weakness with wasting will not reliably recover if treatment waits for delivery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; RANZCOG Common Problems in Pregnancy).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for two weeks and review her hands in the clinic
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid gives short lived symptomatic benefit only and does not decompress a nerve that is already showing motor loss (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and urgent hand surgical assessment
options.rationale: Motor weakness with thenar wasting is the red flag that converts expectant management into assessment for decompression, and studies quantify the block and confirm the lesion is at the wrist (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; RANZCOG Common Problems in Pregnancy).

options.text: Take preeclampsia bloods and arrange review in the day assessment unit
options.rationale: Generalised oedema from preeclampsia can precipitate median nerve compression, but a normal blood pressure with no proteinuria makes that diagnosis untenable here (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

options.text: Arrange cervical spine imaging after delivery for a possible radiculopathy
options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy produces neck and radiating arm pain with an altered reflex and sensory loss over the thenar skin, and thenar sensation is spared here because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist affects a substantial minority of pregnant women, driven by fluid retention in the third trimester, and the great majority resolve within weeks to months of delivery. That benign natural history creates the anti-pattern: symptoms are attributed to pregnancy and the examination that would detect motor involvement is not performed. Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence is the anatomical clue that the lesion sits at the wrist rather than in the neck, since the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Persistent numbness with weakness and wasting predicts incomplete recovery and warrants surgical assessment rather than waiting.
key_points: Most pregnancy related carpal tunnel syndrome resolves within months of delivery
Test thumb abduction strength and look for thenar wasting at every review
Preserved thenar skin sensation localises the lesion to the wrist
Night splints are first line while symptoms remain sensory and intermittent
Weakness or wasting warrants nerve conduction studies and surgical review
explanation.pearls: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves proximal to the flexor retinaculum, so numbness that includes the thenar skin points away from the carpal tunnel and towards a C6 root lesion.

subtopic_detail: Breast lump in a lactating woman that has not resolved with appropriate treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who is nine weeks postpartum and breastfeeding. Three weeks ago you treated her for a hot tender left breast with a full course of flucloxacillin, and the fever and redness settled within four days.

The lump itself has not gone. She says it feels the same size or slightly larger, and the skin over it has become dimpled and thickened in the last week. She is afebrile and systemically well and milk supply is good. On examination there is a firm irregular 4 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, tethered to overlying skin with peau d'orange, and a 1.5 cm firm mobile node in the left axilla. The breast is not warm and there is no fluctuance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular 4 cm mass in the left upper outer quadrant tethered to skin with peau d'orange, no fluctuance or warmth, 1.5 cm firm mobile left axillary node
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a second longer course of flucloxacillin and review in two weeks
options.rationale: A further antibiotic course is justified when infection is still active with fever, warmth and raised inflammatory markers, and none of those persist here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise her to wean from the left breast and review the lump afterwards
options.rationale: Stopping feeding causes engorgement and stasis, and it neither treats infection nor advances the assessment of a persistent mass (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association; Cancer Australia Breast Changes).

options.text: Refer for incision and drainage of the collection under local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Drainage treats an abscess, which is fluctuant and tender with a collection on imaging, and current practice favours ultrasound guided aspiration over open incision in any case (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Reassure that this is a blocked duct and teach positioning and massage
options.rationale: A blocked duct is a soft tender segmental swelling that changes with a feed, not a hard mass tethering the skin with an axillary node (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Arrange urgent breast imaging with biopsy and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: A lump that persists after adequate treatment of infection, with skin tethering and a node, requires triple assessment on an urgent pathway, and lactation is not a reason to delay imaging or core biopsy (Source: Cancer Australia Breast Changes).

explanation.summary: Breast cancer occurring in pregnancy or lactation is uncommon but is diagnosed late with depressing regularity, because the symptoms are attributed to mastitis and treated with successive antibiotic courses. The safeguard is a fixed rule rather than clinical impression: any mass that does not fully resolve after appropriate treatment of infection gets imaged. Ultrasound is the first modality in a lactating breast, with mammography added as needed, and core biopsy is safe during lactation with a small risk of a milk fistula. Peau d'orange with a rapidly enlarging breast raises inflammatory carcinoma, which is frequently mistaken for infection and carries a worse prognosis when the diagnosis is delayed.
key_points: Any breast lump persisting after treated mastitis requires imaging
Ultrasound is the first line modality in a lactating breast
Core biopsy is safe during lactation and should not be deferred
Skin tethering, peau d'orange and a firm node are not features of infection
Weaning does not need to precede assessment
explanation.pearls: Mastitis that fails to resolve within two weeks of appropriate antibiotics is imaged rather than re-treated, because inflammatory carcinoma is the diagnosis most often lost to a second antibiotic course.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics and evacuation in secondary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar called to the emergency department. A 29 year old woman is 12 days after a normal vaginal birth at term with an estimated blood loss of 350 mL at delivery. Her lochia had almost stopped, but for two days she has been soaking a pad every hour and passing clots.

She has lower abdominal pain and offensive vaginal discharge. She is not dizzy and has passed urine normally. On examination the uterus is bulky and tender at the level of the umbilicus, the os admits a fingertip, and there is no cervical or vaginal laceration. Bedside ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material of 22 mm within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler. Bleeding continues while you examine her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 104/62, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.3
data_table.Examination: Bulky tender uterus at the umbilicus, offensive lochia, os admits a fingertip, no genital tract laceration
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165); white cell count 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); ultrasound shows 22 mm of vascular echogenic intracavity material

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics and evacuate the uterus once cover is running
options.rationale: Bleeding this heavy with retained vascular tissue will not settle on antibiotics alone, and instrumenting an infected uterus before antibiotics are circulating provokes bacteraemia, so cover is started first and the evacuation follows promptly by an experienced operator (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Take her directly to theatre for curettage before antibiotics are started
options.rationale: Curettage of an infected soft puerperal uterus without antibiotic cover risks bacteraemia and perforation, and the few minutes taken to start the infusion do not delay haemostasis meaningfully (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review her in the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Oral therapy with outpatient review suits a woman who is haemodynamically stable with light bleeding, and a pulse of 112 with a haemoglobin of 92 g/L is not that patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intramuscular ergometrine and observe her on the ward overnight
options.rationale: Uterotonics reduce bleeding from an atonic uterus but cannot expel adherent vascular tissue, and observation alone leaves both the haemorrhage and the sepsis untreated (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Arrange uterine artery embolisation as the initial definitive intervention
options.rationale: Embolisation is the option for bleeding that continues after evacuation or for a suspected arteriovenous malformation, not the first line for retained products with endometritis (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after birth and is usually caused by retained products, endometritis, or both together, since retained tissue is the substrate that infection grows in. The clinical judgement is about sequence rather than about which single treatment to pick. Antibiotics are started first so that the operator is not disseminating organisms during instrumentation, and evacuation follows without a prolonged delay when bleeding is heavy. Curettage of the soft postpartum uterus carries a real risk of perforation and of later intrauterine adhesions, so it is done gently, ideally under ultrasound guidance and by a senior operator. Persistent bleeding after evacuation should prompt thought about an arteriovenous malformation or gestational trophoblastic disease.
key_points: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage spans 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth
Retained products and endometritis usually coexist
Start antibiotics before instrumenting an infected uterus
Gentle evacuation by a senior operator limits perforation and adhesion risk
Consider arteriovenous malformation or trophoblastic disease if bleeding persists
explanation.pearls: Send the evacuated tissue for histology in every secondary postpartum haemorrhage, because gestational trophoblastic disease presents this way and a normal beta human chorionic gonadotropin at the time does not exclude it.

subtopic_detail: Entry dyspareunia with normal vulval skin and repeatedly negative swabs
stem:
